I bought this game at launch because my friend urged me to get it. She told me there were going to be multiplayer heists, and that was the selling point for me. Since I loved the Payday games, I figured Grand Theft Auto would knock this out of the park since it already has the driving mechanics in the game to allow for getaway driving and shooting while moving, none of which existed in a Payday game at the time.
Instead, what I got were heists that paled in comparison to what is in the Payday franchise, in my opinion at least, and poorly designed segments of the heist, such as having
player fly a plane from A to B for several minutes while the rest of the crew has little to nothing to do, and if the person flying the plane screws up, everyone has to wait for it to happen all over again. The heists take a lot longer to do than in Payday, which is a terrible idea, given that one big slip-up means having to redo an entire heist segment.
Then, at payout, the person hosting the heist gets to decide the payout. My friend who told me to get the game claims that because she had to pay to buy into the heist itself and doesn't know how much it costs, nor is she going to look it up and adjust pricing, she's going to give our mutual friend and I about 10% or so of the cut, each. Despite me urging her to let us price the buy-in and adjust payouts to something fair, she gives us what she deems fit, and we never played the game again. The game should automatically compensate the person who bought the heist accordingly and give fair payouts to the whole team.
The game allowing a player to be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and screw everyone over by distributing them terrible payouts after their hours of playing
heist, though realistic, sucks. If I wanted realism in my robberies, I'd be doing time in prison right now, or dead and buried from succumbing to gunshot wounds. =/
Payday games aren't designed so you can screw people over like that. Technically, someone could kick you from the game, but the devs of that game, pay everyone more money if everyone completes the level, so that's even handled well in that game, too. Grand Theft Auto V tried to compete with Payday in regard to heists, and it's a sorry competitor in that area. If the heists are your main interest, turn back now, because GTAV's heists are, in my opinion, far less fun and rewarding than Payday 2's.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I thought Dark Crusade was hard, but when I started to play Soulstorm, I wasn't even ready for the improvements from the last expansions. In Dark Crusade you try to conquer a single planet (named Kronus), which is represented by a single meta-map. However, on Soulstorm you are shown a solar system featuring 6-7 distinct planets, each being fought by 8 different races (including your own race and two new races: Dark Eldar + Sisters of Battle).
I was dazzled by this freedom to conquer different planets, grow my army with planetary points and expand my races empire galactically. I was also raging at times, as the AI is a lot more unpredictible, yet very tactical about how they; not only move around each planet to prevent you from taking over, but how they swiftly send troops to demolish your base if you aren't playing the game fast enough. If there is two tips to give anyone who wants to play, then the first would be: To do everything you can as quickly as you can, you should never be idle in the game (technically, unless you're winning/waiting on resources).
Second tip would be for you to keep saving Planetary points for your character/army at all times. It's really useful when you want to invade a stronghold and you need Honor Guard Units to help you sweep the enemy in an early match. 100/100!

Rather than me going into detail, I'll just sum up my conclusion to Lord of the Rings Online.
It is one of those games where it has a beautifully constructed world in which you can admire the beauty of Middle Earth for ages, and one of those games that inherently has a plot with deep, rich storyline and lore. It is also a game that gives you great ways of specialising your class for different roles and changing between your configurations on the fly while out of battle, which I find to be incredibly useful. It is also really one of those games with a great, polite community who are more than happy to help with nearly everything that crops up if they can.
But hey, I've got to get to the bad points as well...
Inherently because of it's traditional MMORPG mechanics, it is often a stand-and-fight-with-ridiculous-piles-of-abilities affair, and role-filling is still essential for a successful raid or fellowship quest. And of course... the grinding. Now I know I'm not the first to say MMOs can be grindy and you have to force yourself to get up there, but there is a LOT of grinding in this game. I make no small remark there. If you intend to solo through quests to level up, and without exp boosts, it will take you a while just to get to level 30. Get to level 20 and then the levelling starts to really slow down. When you're level 30, you'll want to be grouping up with other players to get quests done and level up more efficiently by doing fellowship quests. Choose your server wisely because if you end up on a low population server like I did, you'll burn out long before you even reach half way to level cap. And of course, microtransactions.
Lets be honest though. You're getting a lot of content for free, and microtransactions are done in a way in that quest packs and areas can be earned by grinding through deeds, earning the turbine coins and spending them on quest packs. You can play entirely free to play, but there is still the issue of grinding. HEAVY grinding. That, and the gold cap on free players.
Combat may get boring and repetetive after a while, and you won't really get the experience you want without a server with lots of people to adventure with, so take all this into consideration.
It is a good game, but with some inherent flaws. Make of it what you will, but it is what it is.
I rate it a 3/5.

The Lord of the Rings Online is an overall good game with some flaws that could turn people away. I've played this game for many thousands of hours on the non-Steam client. I've ran every raid in the game and have completed every instance. I've even completed almost every deed and quest on my main character.
My Positive Thoughts:
Levels 1-65 are a blast for me. I found that all the zones up to Mirkwood are amazingly designed and are brimming with detail. I have spent vast portions of time just wandering around to see if I could find something cool. Shard droppers spice up the exploration and make it feel like you've discovered a secret when you happen to find these mini-bosses scattered in the far reaches of the land where few people venture. Most of the raids and instances are very well designed and have unique mechanics. The crowning achievement of the instances in the game for me was the six instances in The Mines of Moria. Each has an interesting mechanic which keeps them from getting boring. To achieve the challenge mode in the instances, you have to do something that makes the instance harder or pushes your fellowship to rush. In The Forges, after killing the first boss, you have to make it to the final boss in less than twenty minutes or you don't get the good loot. In Fil Gashan, you have to dress up in orc costumes and sneak around to avoid pulling vast hordes of enemies (alternatively you can have AOE classes and create a blender of murder that is really fun). The last boss makes you step carefully and avoid traps on the floor while getting the boss to walk into them. The Grand Stairs is a race against the clock. You only have ten minutes to get to the second boss and kill him before failing challenge mode. The Dark Delvings makes you stay in the light or suffer a debuff. The last boss is made more difficult by having to fight him in the darkness while has the ability to essentially one shot you by knocking you off a cliff. The 16th Hall makes you mind your AOEs by giving a ton of 1hp mobs that you can't kill for challenge mode while you DPS the boss down. Skumfil makes you do the instance three times to get challenge mode. You have to clear both the right and left sides on alternate runs to get the key to unlock the boss room. With the key, you have to quickly work your way through the room by killing the spiders that respawn quickly and kill the boss before you are overwhelmed. These are just six of the instances. The raids are excellent. The classes are diverse in the game. I feel as if it takes talent to actually learn how to play each class effectively. Wardens are unique in that they require you to memorize series of skills to unleash an actual attack. Rune-Keepers require you to use less damaging skills to raise attunement so you can unleash really powerful ones. Burgs use stealth to start at the fight with a massive spike of damage or a vicious bleed that drains the foes health over the course of the fight. There is a class for pretty much every play style in the game.
My Negative Thoughts:
This game is a grind. Quests, much like many of WoW's, require you to kill x number of mobs or collect x number of these items. There are a couple standout quests (the epic quests are fun for the most part) but most of them are horrible. It is my opinion that the game got significantly worse after it went free to play. I have a lifetime account so it didn't affect me in a monatary way. Content seems to be more lackluster and monotonous now. New zones look exactly the same as old zones: large fields with a couple buildings. Raids and instances seem to have lost their luster and are just boring. Crafting is horrible. It takes a ridiculous amount of time to gather the materials to master each tier of crafting. Some vocations take significantly longer than others. You can achieve the top tier level of crafting in farming and cooking in a day whereas you will be running around ruins looking for scholar boxes for days if you are a historian. Deeds in the game require you to slay up to 450 enemies to increase a virtue by 1. Each virtue levels up to 16 and you can equip 5 virtues. That's 36,000 enemies for just your virtues (this is if you don't do some of the deeds which are just exploration, I did that for a point). The free to play is constantly shoved down your throat - even if you pay for the game. PvP is pathetic. This game has been running for a long time now and there is only one zone in which to PvP. After six years of playing the game, you will know this zone like the back of your hand. Unfortunately, the area itself is obnoxious. The free people and the monster players both will turtle inside keeps and refuse to come out and actually fight. Only a couple of the servers even have enough people to have epic fights. On the monster player side, if you aren't willing to grind a bunch of repeatable quests over and over again, it can take up to six or seven minutes to return to the fight after death. Everything in this game is grindy.
Conclusion: If you are willing to pay for the game, I would say it is worth it. The exploration of Tolkien's world was enough for me (a great deal of Middle-earth is in the game and they are still releasing almost yearly expansions). It does a good job with lore. If you don't want to spend money, you will be doing nothing but farming enemies over and over again to get Turbine points to get quests packs for the zones.

GTA V is an open world sandbox game with a decent story mode, but a multiplayer experience that is a bit iffy.
Story Mode/Singleplayer has a great story with the 3 protagonists you can play as and is moddable with third-party programs such as OpenIV, a modding tool which allows people to create player models, vehicles, and several other additions. Singleplayer alone is a good reason to get this game.
Online is just a mess that makes you unsure if you either love it or hate it. Reasons to love it would be that it's one of the best ways to play a sandbox game with friends, plus it has quite a few good gamemodes like deathmatches, races or jobs which are all enjoyable. Reasons to hate it is that it's VERY grindy to get everything you want like supercars, weapons, owned property, literal fighter jets which are all above GTA$1,000,000. Because it's so grindy, players are encouraged to buy Shark Cards with actual money for in-game money. Around $55 in real money is $8,000,000 in GTA money, which is just SO f**king greedy for Rockstar to do. Sure, you can get some sort of business to gain money, but even that is slow, boring and still grindy. Though, if you do want lots of money fast, doing heists when you're lv12 and have a high-class apartment is the way to go (Alternatively, a challenge called 'Criminal Mastermind' rewards you with $10 million IF you play all the heists with the same people and DON'T DIE AT ALL).
Overall, Singleplayer is great, Online is a mess, you decide if you want this. I'm outt of here.

Well, this is curious. I had put myself – or rather the chance to review a restaurant with me – forward as an auction prize some time ago. The winner was Ronni Astroff, a financial whizz by day, food connoisseur by night. It was a delight to meet someone with such enthusiasm and energy for the job. For once, all I needed to do was be the guest. Over to Ronni…
'I am excited, admittedly overly so. I'm about to embark on a covert operation rather different from my ordinary job of analysing numbers at my desk. My mission: to evaluate the London outpost of an established French restaurant without being detected. This is made more precarious by the 110 different wines on offer. (Perhaps I've gotten a bit carried away, but the experience did involve secret booking names and I have been watching a box set of The Americans, so let me have this one.)
"The mission does not begin well. I arrive a few minutes after my dining companion and the maître d' has seated her at the table directly opposite the door – arguably, the worst in the restaurant. She decorously complains. The manager explains that he is unable to move us, as the restaurant is fully booked. The restaurant seats about 70 across two rooms, and at this point is largely empty. As we dine, the tables fill with suits; we make out Russian conversations left and right.
"Before we can get properly cranky, our waitress comes to reseat us and brings us two conciliatory glasses of Delamotte Brut NV champagne. She hands us a triple-width menu that looks like an accountant's spreadsheet – a column of food, each dish aligned with four columns of wines by the glass, arranged in ascending price. The most affordable group is £8 or less, the dearest more than £20, with certain glasses far above this, to cater to both the wine snob and the everyday drinker.
"There are many uncommon wines on the list, but the sommelier is on hand to help. The selection is truly extraordinary, with established areas and producers side by side with unusual and emerging areas.
"I start with the poached duck egg and its suggested Moroccan Syrah pairing. The egg is poached in red wine and comes with mushrooms, lardons and two mini deep-fried breadsticks (in a refined way). The dish isn't cohesive; the component parts are good, but not remarkable. The wine is the star, fruity and surprisingly excellent. According to the sommelier, it was produced by a winemaker from the Northern Rhône who had taken his vines to a new terrior.

PROs:
> Action can start virtually immediately after the game starts. Most RTS games require a period of base building that can become repetitious and makes the early game boring. Soul Storm doesn't really have a lot in the way of base buildings, although it certainly is a component of the game. Unlike games such as Age of Empires, you can choose to start the combat as early as you like.
> Resources are linked to map control. You actually have to play the game and compete with the other players for strategic locations. Capturing these and controlling them gives you your base resources, with the exception of necrons
> EPIC MODS: Such as titanium wars and Ultimate Apocalypse mod completely overhaul the size of the game in case you ever feel like something more
> No stalemates. Unlike many RTS games, where defenses can indefinitely stall the game, Armies in SS are the dominant force. The winner is the player with the biggest gun, not shield.
> Logical and straigtforward mechanics: There are two types of resources and both have very different acquisition methods, exceptions for Orks and Necrons. There are many races, and all of them are as different as can reasonably be expected. The more similar a race is, the more similar their game play. Units work by building squads, not individual units, which reduces the requirements for micromanagement in fights, which speeds up the game instead of simplifying it.
> Unique game play, styles and abilities for different races.
> Active Online community, with plenty of competent players
> Sound track is well suited, easy to listen to for hours on end.
> Play with your friends for added fun
> Still highly enjoyable after 100 hours (especially with mods)
CONs:
> Not every race is equally powerful. Dark Eldar are objectively the weakest, absolute trash.
> Multitude of balance tweaks required.
> Campaign is utterly lackluster, repetitious and grinding.
> Camera zoom is very close, and off-putting for your first few games
Overall: 8/10. Very satisfactory for an RTS. All RTS players ought to try this game.

I've  been a fan of Lord of the Rings and the Hobbit since I read the books way back when. The movies where amazing. So when my brother introduced me and got me into the game ( A change of pace from my usual Chaos Space Marines)  but the opportunity to play a fantasy realm in witch we both were avid fans about, I took the chance.  Both of us being our favorite hero as Gimli, son of Gloin, we took to the character creation with an idea of mind. ( I'm also a dwarf slayer fan from the Gotrek and Felix novels.) To be long bearded, axe toting dwarves. And as it was , we could! Other than dwarves you can play as other races of the Free Peoples of Middle Earth...men, hobbits and elfs. Also like other rpg's you can choose from various classes. Champion, Guardian, Hunter, Burgler and Loremaster. Each class and race brings to the game a specific play style along with culture and language and skills and story line. Dwarves for example, get and axe damage bonus and a stamina regenerative bonus for being a harty people.  So choosing and making you're character does change you're online game experience.
The game itself is so fully in depth and full of fantasy lore that its hard not to be overwhelmed and lost in it. Even if your just a fan of the books, or just the movies or just like rpg's. You'll find yourself reading the quests and missions, enjoying the simple basic rpg mechanics( Legendary weapons is A LOT of fun) and instances its hard not to be captured by Tolkiens world. Its all there, down to the movies soundtrack to add to you actually want the music up and loud when you’re slaying goblins in the Misty Mountains. In game you play as a hero of the Free Peoples defeating every orc and goblins in league with evil, from Erin Luin to Moria (my favorite) to Gondor.
Community wise it has to be the most friendly based I have ever played with. There is always a fellowship, kinship out there to help with a quest or instance or get items or even craft them for you free of charge. Honestly it has a great atmosphere with a '' Were in this together'' and ''All for one and one for all '' attitude. A great game if you like joining with others and having fun rpg dungeon crawl wise.
As a free to play game technically, there is a pay to play feature. With real money you can buy traits, skills, steeds, quests and maps that can easily create a large hole in your pocket. But if you choose to pay you definitely wont be found wanting. Even as a free to play game there is plenty of content and game play that you won’t be crying exactly that you didn't get the full experience. but there is so much more, if  you are willing to pay for it. It doesn’t make your character so much better than others or game changing where you become a God amongst men, but it definitely can change your experience. To make your steed go 250% faster or to play that one instance where you defeat the orc armies of the Iron crown. It’s up to you. As a free to play player myself sometimes you do wish you could do a certain quest or skirmish and there is a way. In game, for completing quests and deeds you can earn Turbine points which can pay for real money perks! It's a nice way to get some of those pay to play perks for us that have empty wallets.

I'll admit, I haven't played many MMOs, but LoTRO is one of the best that I've played. You'll enjoy this game somewhat if you're more of a fan of the Peter Jackson movies, but if you're a fan of J.R.R. Tolkien's classic books, like me, you'll go crazy over this game.
Another clever thing that Turbine has done is the in-game store. In order to buy things like quest packs, war-horses, and dyes, you use "Turbine Points". How do you get Turbine Points? You could buy them...or you could complete deeds like doing so many quests, killing so many orcs/giant fly things/wolves/brigands, or finding different locations in the game world.
There is just one big problem this game has: The riding. Not the riding itself, but the riding skill. You need to buy it from the store. And it's not cheap. It's 95 Turbine Points. Considering the most Turbine Points you can get from a deed is 15, and that's for doing over 30 quests, that's quite a lot.
In short, if you want a good open-world MMO with a great story, pick this up.
PRO TIP: Find and buy a boxed copy of the Mines of Moria expansion pack. You get a extra character per server, VIP for a month, and of course, access to Moria.

Yes, the game is a low-content retread of Far Cry 3. However, it stands on its own for one simple reason: No one intended Blood Dragon to be taken seriously.
While the game plays on the very real Cold War fears of the early 80s, it throws in the most memorable movie and game lines of the 80s together in all of their cheesy glory, and adds in a ton of corny one-liners in combat. All of this takes place in the context of a modern open world shooter.
If Blood Dragon took itself seriously, it would be absolutely awful. However, it embraces the cheese, and if you remember the 80s, you shouldn't be able to help but enjoy the humor that results.
All in all, it's not like it's the greatest game ever made. It's simply unbridled cheesy 80s fun.

I made the mistake of purchasing this game for PC. I waited, and was excited. I took the numerous delays that this port experienced with stride. Upon playing this game for an amount of time that has left me disgusted and embarrased, I can really only say one thing to summarize: the hacking is terrible, and the game grinding is worse.
Every so often, I return to this game asking myself "Why did I stop playing again?" The answer comes in less than 10 minutes of playing in a public lobby, when a hacker will do any of the following: teleport me over the ocean, blow me up, blow my vehicle up but make it seem as though I blew it up (so you have to pay a premium to get it back), kill me from across the map, teleport me the the ceiling for a free fall with no parachute, take money from my in game account, spam blow me up in a constant cycle of death, sticking a firepit onto my character so that he will burn to death constantly (the firepit never goes away unless you restart the game itself), or simply crash my game entirely.
Oh wait, my GOSH, they did address the hacking. No more OpenIV Liberty City for GTA V. Those dastardly spawns of Satan within OpenIV are surely more of a threat than actual in-game hackers that have ruined countless gaming experiences, right? Wait a minute here....something seems a little fishy...
Perhaps Rockstar, or TakeTwo for that matter, likes in-game hackers more than OpenIV for one simple reason: OpenIV stands to cut into possible revenue for TakeTwo (why play Online where there is money to be made by Rockstar when I can play in a Liberty City mod for freeeee); while hackers take players' money, which opens up the potential for more time spent in-game to earn the money back, or the possible purchase of a Shark Card. Seems simple enough for me.
On to the other bone I have to pick (oh Rockstar, why have you left so many for me to chew on?): in-game prices. "Free DLC" is a blantant lie. It's free if you have no life in order to play the game constantly for the medicore payouts that you get for completing "high paying, high risk work" that is required to pay for all of this "free content". However, if you have other priorities in life that exceed making bank as a major criminal in this world of photons and hacking, then your best bet of experiencing any kind of new content is to look up the myriad of videos that are posted by the deplorable YouTubers of the GTA community (you know the ones), and you will surely have your fill of this content. Or you can ask one of the numerous hackers in this game to simply spawn you some of the new content. Have I mentioned that there are hackers galore in this game, by the way?
Honestly though, just look at the prices for Shark Cards, and then look at the prices for in game content. Your question as to why a flying bike that shoots homing missile was added, has been dutifully answered.
This game has left me beyond disappointed in the end, and quite the sour taste in my mouth. My disgusting amount of hours in-game speak for themselves: I enjoyed it at one point, but the constant grinding for a game with little reward, hardly any payout for in-game work, the exorbitant prices for any new content, and the experience ruining hacking has left me with little desire to ever play the game again. And, I surely don't plan on it. You, oh reader of my woe, might be able to still save yourself.

Brawlhalla is basically a free, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ version of Super Smash Bros. That's not to say this game is bad, but just worse than Smash Bros. Many of the characters play exactly the same, and all characters are spammy. There's not much variety in characters, weapons or moves. That being said, this game is free, and pretty bug free. I'd definitely recommend it to those who want to scratch their Super Smash Bros itch. The game has a nice art style, and few different game modes to keep you entertained. Theres a few game modes, such as 1v1 knockout, where you choose 3 different legends, and when one gets knocked out, it goes to the next. Each player has three lives, no matter the game mode, unless it's a private match with custom settings. Each match lasts for 8 minutes max (then it goes to sudden death if both players have the same amount of lives). There is also a 1 vs all (4 players total). Brawlhalla also has 2 ranked modes, of which consists of 1v1 ranked, or, if you have a friend, a 2v2 mode. You have 2 ranks. One is your overall rank, and the other is your rank with each individual legend. Overall, Brawlhalla definitely has a ways to go, but it's definitely getting there. I highly recommend this game to people who want something like Smash Bros, want to play with friends, want something they can sit down, relax and play.

Trine 2 is probably the best game I've bought which was full price <$25, and anyone who wants a co-op game or something other than an FPS should play it.
First of all, I want to say how my decision was influenced. I decided to buy this game having known nothing about it whatsoever, and looking for a coop game for my girlfriend and I to play. See where it says "Download Demo"? If it hadn't been for that, I probably wouldn't be so enthusiastically happy about even writing this review. The fact that I got to TRY the game before I bought it alone made me want to purchase it, but then I played it and it was heaven. Everything  from the art style, to the dialogue, to the music, to the game mechanics.. THIS is what PC gaming should be about! This is what STEAM should be about! Releasing high-quality, outside-the-box games that, if you have a computer so much stronger than a console, should let you take advantage of that power and give you the option to play with another human being who's in the same room!
I won't lie, I know there are a dozen thousand side-scrollers on STEAM but the majority of these look like they were made by people who don't quite want to leave the 80s behind, graphically. I can understand the appeal, to a degree, but at a certain point games are designed to make use of the hardware and look like they've advanced a little in the last 20 years. THIS game does that. Having played Skyrim, Far Cry, Dragon Age, etc. I can truly say that this games appearance blew me away. While it may not be the pinnacle of technological development, it's a DAMN good looking game!
The puzzle mechanics of the game are, in my mind, what set it apart from so many others. The dynamic of having 3 controllable characters while playing with one other person seals the deal. Being able to play with someone who's on the same brainwave and switching up characters while solving puzzles is quite the feeling. Makes you realize what's been missing from all these games that lack coop over the years. I will admit, at some points it can be frustrating to figure out what to do next but it really does force you to get as creative as you can with the characters abilities.
To end my meandering review, I'll say this: for $25, you can go to the movies and watch something decent for 2 hours and be satisfied; or you can buy half of a Triple-A title (which based on games this past year will most likely be half-baked anyways); OR, you can buy this game and actually feel like your money has been put to amazing use. I really hope they make a Trine 3, I will be there Day 1!

A nice short little adventure with easy achievements. Really enjoyed it, although there are some minor things that bothered me, which makes the universal praise a bit confusing to me.
First off the positive aspects though. The mechanic of controlling each brother individually was definitely unique and entertaining. Sometimes I had to figure out who's who, so I always preferred having the older brother on the left and the younger one on the right, so that they align with the analog sticks they're controlled with, but once you get used to the controls it's somewhat fascinating to play two characters at once. It's surreal to look at the screen and see them move so naturally and despite being in control it disconnects you from what's happening. I felt like I'm watching a movie or something. That's not a bad thing, it only underlines how idiosyncratic the feature is.
What I didn't like was the gibberish language they were talking. Growing up in a multicultural area, and being a son of migrants myself, most words sounded familiar, but didn't make sense at all. So it really took a lot of immersion away from the game when they just sounded completely ridiculous in, what supposed to be, moving scenes.
It also felt a bit incoherent, because this game got really, really ♥♥♥♥ing dark all of a sudden. At first it was a beautiful hike through the woods, but then it was all about death, halucinations and what not. You could argue the sudden change is an artistic tool to add more weight to the events, but it just felt out of place.
Still an enjoyable experience and alone the gameplay mechanics make it worth being played.

The Mean Greens Plastic Warfare is an interesting game. It's a hidden gem on Steam, and for a multiplayer only title, that isn't good. The playerbase is so miniscule, you'll often times end up in matches with the same people. However it isn't hard to get into a game, and once you are in a game, the game is a blast. Right off the bat, you'll notice the visuals are amazing. Some of the textures could use some work but it's overall one of the better looking games I've tried, especially in terms of art direction and the creativity of this game's settings. The different maps are all distinct, vibrant and fun. The levels are based on different areas in a house each with creative objectives. There's one level that takes place in a freezer where you have to thaw out your team's dinosaur with your flamethrower before the other team, another map where you have to light candles on a cake and a level where you play on a foosball table to name a few.The soundtrack is also pretty memorable, if not a bit repetitive. This game is a 3rd person shooter, something we don't see often. The mechanics of the game are really solid, and the way the weapons are implemented. They basically run a cooldown system where you hold all 6 weapons. The catch is, if you use one too much the weapon will have to recharge before you can use it again, which also carries over after you die. This forces you to use a variety of weapons instead of running around with a shotgun or camping with a sniper for the entirety of the round. The gunplay is definately something I have yet to get used to but it's still a great concept and I can't wait to play more. A few gripes I have with this game, there are some maps where you are forced to platform which in a multiplayer only title can be annoying, especially when your internet hiccups which can make your platforming become imprecise. Another much larger issue is the lack of any depth. I'm not expecting much out of a $10 Indie game, but I really don't feel compelled to replay this game. The only replay value this game has is in the form of achievements, and nothing else. You start out with all the weapons, you can't change the look of your soldier, there's no singeplayer, there is only 10 maps all with unique modes, etc. Again, variety isn't a bad thing and when all the maps are catered to a specific mode they are overall higher quality. However this results in the game getting repetitive. Here's why I think the population is so low, there's nothing to come back to. Nothing to unlock and no secrets. Once you've seen all the maps, that's it. As much as I criticize the game, it's still being actively updated and the developers are pretty open to feedback, especially on social media. All of my issues can be altered in future versions of the game. Right now, for $10, I still think this game deserves a purchase. It's creative, bright, and fun with some really nice gunplay. For the price, it's one of the best on the market. If you're on the edge or want an shooter that you can really spend hundreds of hours on, I'd still wait for a sale to purchase this game. However, one way or another, you need to play this game.

From the title screen, it looked like one of those flash games you might find on sites that someone made during their spare time and put some care and refining into that. This... is
to however, be a game developed by WayForward, people who have in the past impressed me greatly. If you're a fan of sidejumping in Mario games, the BloodRayne sidejump will probably mess you up a dozen or so times. If you've walljumped in Megaman X, don't worry, they expect you to do that here.
Right from the get go, there is no real story given to you at all about anything, other than you're working with people who don't trust you on account of being a dhampir, and that you kill things with great prejudice. I've gotten about three levels in and there has been almost no exposition besides finding an underground castle. I had to stop when I came to a jump I don't know how the devs expected you to make. Apparently via sidejump, except I crash into spikes, and walljumping seems out the window.
The controls are just frustrating, much less so on a controller. The gameplay is very repetitive. The one boss I encountered was a mechanical crab steampunk-esque monster that just... appeared. No rhyme or reason. You're often shot while in the middle of a combo, can't shoot back fast enough to interrupt the guy pulling a gun, and while you're crouched down charging an attack or in the middle of a combo, you can still be hit. To be good at the game requires some level of devotion while not providing much of an incentive to get better or even continue playing. You get either slashy blades or a magnum. No combos to buy, no weapon upgrades several levels in, or rewards for doing well. All I had to do for the most part was just hit the attack button, only slightly deviating now and again to try and keep it interesting for myself. And if you have to change your own style of gameplay for the sole purpose of making it entertaining to yourself, you know something is wrong.

This is a wonderful game. Where did this come from? This is one man's labour of love. There are so many great ideas in this game. Woefully underrated. Pick sides in a robot civil war. There is an interesting story with multiple endings but the fun of the game is in exploring the world. A world is generated at random at the start of the game, full of buildings, bases, shops, and populated with two sides in a huge conflict between robots. Red vs Blue. The further out from the center you go, the more difficult it gets, and the better loot you get.
It plays kind of like Borderlands mixed with Minecraft mixed with a roguelike. There are lots of ways to get around, you can fly around in aircraft, you can surf on a hoverboard, there is a teleporter system as well, and a teleportation gun. The missions are all randomly generated, a lot of the time they don't make a lot of sense, like planting a bug on an enemy only to immediately murder him, but I found it fun. Maybe you're killing an enemy to get an item, fighting a leader, spying, planting bugs, talking to people. dropping stuff off, doing escort missions, and it's all randomly shuffled around, with the high level missions requring you to do 5 or 6 of these.
You are rewarded with points to spend upgrading your character, there are a lot of different options depending on how you want to build your character. You can go melee, or put it into guns, or prestige to allow you to recruit a little army, or piloting for aircraft, hp, carrying capacity, etc. You can also build your own buildings, add storage boxes, make teleporters, build airships. And everything just comes together in this beautiful way. It's extremely addicting. The reviews turned me off this game, but they were very wrong. This game is charming and wonderful. One of the best open world games I've played in quite a while. There's also a lot of good support from the developer, almost too much support, he responds to almost everybody, and he even commented on one of the bad reviews, explaining the reasons behind his decisions. A lot of love went into this game and it shows. Stunning, truly amazing. I can't wait for 5089.
Incidentally, I played a bit of 4089 but I didn't like it much, it was punishingly difficult, I just died and died over and over and each time I died my character got weaker. It looks interesting too, but it's a dungeon crawler rather than an open world game. Maybe I'll get into it later, but for now, I say go with 3089, it's great. You'll thank me later.

A mediocre platformer overall, I think. BloodRayne: Betrayal is a platformer from Abstraction Games. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
The artwork in this game was great. It had a very retro/comic book feel to it (something that really works for platformer games, in my opinion). The animations were, likewise, well done. Combat looked good and everything played out smoothly. Movement looked smooth, but there were some problems there that’ll I’ll get to in a bit.
There was a sufficient amount of gore; definitely as much as you’d want from a vampire game. Occasionally there is a Mortal Kombat-esque blood explosion, but it really adds to the whole atmosphere in it’s own charming way.
The Bad
Movement is pretty clunky in BR:B. Some areas require you to perform a ridiculous backflip to access. If you knew how tedious it is to perform a backflip in this game, you’d know why that is a bad thing. Or, you can just take my word for it.
Spike traps are a lot more like “let’s plaster razors on everything traps”. Barely grazing the side of a spike trap will result in a hefty amount of damage to you.
As far as I can tell, this game didn’t have much of a story line if it had one at all.
The Meh
The game itself is repetitive in several aspects. Enemy variety is limited and you’ll be fighting a lot of the same monsters over and over again in varying quantities. The music is okay at first, but it too gets old after a while. While the combat animations are pretty nice, combat will seem repetitive in a hurry as well.
The controls really aren’t all that streamlined as far as platformers go and gameplay starts to become a bore.
Verdict: Nay
It’s been a few reviews since I had to give a game the thumbs down. BR:B is mediocre, at best, but, if you’re a fan of the Blood Rayne franchise, you may enjoy it. As always, thanks for reading.

Alright, it's about time I give this absolutely amazing game the review it deserves. This game is honestly one of the best, my personal favourite, RPG games ever made. This game has everything that makes it entertaining and enjoyable to play. Just to put this out there, I've put in only over 30+ hours and I still haven't beat the story; so I won't be commenting on that just yet, I will hopefully edit it once I've completed it and give my final thoughts + opinions on it. So, to start off, I'll talk about the art of the game.
This game is simply beautiful. Like, really. The locations that you visit are honestly some of the most astounding places I've been able to visit in a video game; and that's just the best feeling I've experienced within a game. The places fit their names perfectly, if the name is something drab and gloomy, the level makes sure to match the atmosphere it's trying to portray. If the name however is something cheery and pleasent, you can certainly expect an amazing looking level with many, many bright colours and just making it a downright beautiful level.
The art for enemies is honestly so well done and it makes the game feel that bit more creepy and dark. The enemies all seem like they could fit into any serious and dark horror film. Enemies in this game are made perfectly from an art standpoint, like seriously. I know it sounds like I'm repeating myself but this game would give me nightmares if the enemies used were in a horror movie. They're just like nightmares except personified. The dark enemies can lead to some of the game feeling like an absolute hell, and the bosses are just.. Well, just as great as the normal enemies to be frank.
Speaking of bosses, the art on them is absolutely top-notch and cannot be topped. I wish I could talk about the bosses without spoiling anything, but that just won't be possible, so I'm afraid I'll cut that there. Just know that the boss art is actually amazing and once again, using this horror movie bit, could make anything horrifying and downright terrifying. I think that to truly see what the bosses are like in this game, you should 100% get the game just to see the art of the bosses and enemies alone.
Now, to talk about something that I adore in this game and something that makes this game seem like it's had years upon years of work put into it; the sheer amount of items in this game. Like, seriously. This game has weapons for everyone. Want a giant hammer to smash your foes? This game's got it! Prefer to use guns to shoot your enemies and inflict massive damage? Check! Want a massive amount of weapons which aren't limited to a certain class and can be used by any class? Well, this game has it! Yes, that's right, there are no class limitations on weapons (mostly!).
The weapons in this game are so unique and there's almost no weapon like another. What I mean is, all weapons are somewhat unique compared to any other weapon in this game. The different types of which loot you can get (I mean like common, elemental, rare, etc!) are all a unique way of making sure that every weapon is so different and has it's own stats. Like, maybe it adds some extra fire damage or even some ice damage. Hell, throw some poison onto that bad boy and make it a real powerhouse of damage!
Speaking of damage, don't expect all weapons that you get to be super-mega-hyper-ultra OP. Most weapons are actually pretty darn bad from a damage perspective;  but make up for it with an amazing damage OUTPUT. What I mean by that is, the damage may be bad but with the amount of leveling up you can do and the amount of skill points which can be contributed to each skill, you do end up doing more damage than the weapon claims. Say the weapon says that it does 60 damage, you may end up doing somewhere between 200-300 dependant on your skill points and enchantments.
Something else this game does is enchantments. Each piece of equipment that you get can be enchanted by a special person in each town. This Racoon-type person will enchant all weapons or armour for a price. The enchantments can be great - or not so great - just because, well, it's an RPG so you can't expect a walk in the park! The enchantments are fairly basic but at the same time can really help you in a major way. From adding fire or electric armour to adding health stolen on hit!
So, enough about the art and more about the actual enemies and bosses themselves. Each enemy in this game is unique and unlike the other, mostly. Some of the bosses are downright so enjoyable that I can't wait to fight them again when I start a Newgame+. The game does an excellent job of making you feel like the bosses are tough but beatable, and getting late-game you really start to experience that feeling. Some of the bosses may seem like they're easy at first glance, but damn do they get hard. Don't go to any boss expecting it to be an easy ride.
The game allows you to experience it at your own pace, be you a slow player who wants to take it all in and explore all the areas that the game has to offer to you or maybe you want to ignore all the enemies and speedrun the game as fast as you want. The game allows you to play at YOUR pace. Once again, this is good for letting everyone have their own option in how they want to play. You want a game which doesn't hold your hand but somewhat lets you play fast? This game is PERFECT.
In conclusion, because I can feel myself droning on and on, this game is honestly turning into one of my favourite games of all time - yes, all time! - This game has so much to offer me as a player and lets me want to play over and over and over. This game is down-right amazing and I cannot wait to keep playing and playing. Thanks for reading, and for sure get this game if you see it on sale - even if it DOESN'T look like your type of game.

Runic Games provides us with an invigorating spin to your standard RPG game with dynamic evolving dungeons. Unlike most AI managers Torchlight II doesn’t just update enemy spawns, but also creates new terrain with each experience.
Torchlight II takes place in a time far beyond the reign of Ordrak the daemon who caused dismay to the little town of Torchlight; yet, despite his fall the corruption he spread was not lost. An evil alchemist takes up his power and destroys the town of Torchlight as your quest begins to bring civility back to reality. You progress through the various worlds of the Torchlight universe from various towns in unique environments from mountains, desserts, tundra’s, and swamps. There is no end to the evil that Ordrak spirit has spread.
Torchlight II is separated into four Acts: Estherian Steppes, Mana Wastes, Grunnheim, and Broken Mines. Unlike in the first Torchlight the second offers multiple towns which provide unique experiences that help evolve the game. Each town offers unique merchants that evolve with the difficulty of the game providing better items and new elements to the mix. The campaign, depending on your play style, can easily last up to 30-hours. The game has a good difficulty curve which allows the game to readily scale to the player’s level. Plus by utilizing the randomly generated experience the game offers players can also out-level their environments if they feel like they the game is too difficult.
Torchlight II expands on the original by providing four rather than three unique experiences: The Engineer, Outlander, Berserker, and Embermage.
The Engineer is a melee class which utilizes heavy armor and has abilities to summon various support style minions. My main complication with the Engineer is that this task is clearly designed around being a support/tank role, but has not taunting abilities. This essentially makes team work relatively difficult as you cannot get your enemies to readily focus on you.
The Outlander similar to the Vanquisher is a rained base class that utilizes mainly dexterity based building. This class offers trapping, dual wielding, and high speed attacks. The design of the outlander makes it great for kiting and boss fights, but relatively poor against swarms of enemies.
The Beserker follows your typical fighting class by utilizing melee weapons with high speed combat and not being reliant on armor. The unique playstyle of the Beserker allows you to summon wolves to your aid, throw down with massive melee damage, and utilize frost and lightning buffers to enhance your combat. The beserker does great with live recovery items and high health units, but can easily get swarmed by low hit point units.
Finally the Embermage, which as you can tell is a magic class champion. Focusing on mostly magic attributes the Embermage utilizes spellcasting to defeat their enemies. This is the only class I didn’t beat the game with, but from my understanding they are incredibly useful for supporting roles and are as strong as they are in mana. Mostly focusing on mana stealing items and mana pots this class fights at range and doesn’t do well in swarms.
Sadly Torchlight II did not adjust the control mechanics that are utilized through Torchlight I. The champion is still controlled entirely by the users mouse. Moving the character and attaching are both controlled by holding the left click of the mouse, rather than moving with the keyboard and fighting with the mouse. On Melee classes this is fine, but on ranged classes more than not you run into battle because you click next to an enemy; because your champion ran into battle they are then killed and your kiting has failed.
I personally played Torchlight II before completing Torchlight I. This game provides a unique experience somewhere in between Diablo III and Spelunky. Through randomly generated dungeons and it’s combat experience Torchlight II is guaranteed to provide your typical RPG style player with an enjoyable dynamic experience; although the generated dungeons don’t provide much replay value with the same class they are just a touch unique enough to make playing each other class fun and original. Even though I purchased this game on sale I would still recommend it at full price.
Pros:
+Four unique classes that provide diversifying experiences through their unique playstyles and skill trees.
+Multiplayer cooperative experience
+Pets which provide benefit to the player as either a way to sell items, a some-what tank, or even a healer.
+Two types of leveling for a character: Experience and Fame. Fame allows you to level only your abilities, while experience gives you five points to level your characters base stats and a point to level abilities.
+Dynamic environment that evolves and changes each play through.
+Fun bosses that offer interesting battles that vary based on swarming, spell dodging, terrain shifting, and time management.
Cons:
-Character controls that sadly cannot be adjusted. You must control your character with the mouse for both movement and combat, which causes a lot of times where you die due to poor controls rather than skill.
-Random generated dungeons occur on time base rather than if the player quits. This means if you are in an areas sub-dungeon it is possible the first floor regenerates. Ultimately this means if you die you must start over again.
-Fishing provides your pet with cool skin/ability changes, but typically is more cumbersome than it’s worth. Similar to the first Torchlight you just simply wait as a circle expands and retracts until it hits the middle for a fraction of a second where you must click the reel in button.

I made the mistake of purchasing this game for PC. I waited, and was excited. I took the numerous delays that this port experienced with stride. Upon playing this game for an amount of time that has left me disgusted and embarrased, I can really only say one thing to summarize: the hacking is terrible, and the game grinding is worse.
Every so often, I return to this game asking myself "Why did I stop playing again?" The answer comes in less than 10 minutes of playing in a public lobby, when a hacker will do any of the following: teleport me over the ocean, blow me up, blow my vehicle up but make it seem as though I blew it up (so you have to pay a premium to get it back), kill me from across the map, teleport me the the ceiling for a free fall with no parachute, take money from my in game account, spam blow me up in a constant cycle of death, sticking a firepit onto my character so that he will burn to death constantly (the firepit never goes away unless you restart the game itself), or simply crash my game entirely.
Oh wait, my GOSH, they did address the hacking. No more OpenIV Liberty City for GTA V. Those dastardly spawns of Satan within OpenIV are surely more of a threat than actual in-game hackers that have ruined countless gaming experiences, right? Wait a minute here....something seems a little fishy...
Perhaps Rockstar, or TakeTwo for that matter, likes in-game hackers more than OpenIV for one simple reason: OpenIV stands to cut into possible revenue for TakeTwo (why play Online where there is money to be made by Rockstar when I can play in a Liberty City mod for freeeee); while hackers take players' money, which opens up the potential for more time spent in-game to earn the money back, or the possible purchase of a Shark Card. Seems simple enough for me.
On to the other bone I have to pick (oh Rockstar, why have you left so many for me to chew on?): in-game prices. "Free DLC" is a blantant lie. It's free if you have no life in order to play the game constantly for the medicore payouts that you get for completing "high paying, high risk work" that is required to pay for all of this "free content". However, if you have other priorities in life that exceed making bank as a major criminal in this world of photons and hacking, then your best bet of experiencing any kind of new content is to look up the myriad of videos that are posted by the deplorable YouTubers of the GTA community (you know the ones), and you will surely have your fill of this content. Or you can ask one of the numerous hackers in this game to simply spawn you some of the new content. Have I mentioned that there are hackers galore in this game, by the way?
Honestly though, just look at the prices for Shark Cards, and then look at the prices for in game content. Your question as to why a flying bike that shoots homing missile was added, has been dutifully answered.
This game has left me beyond disappointed in the end, and quite the sour taste in my mouth. My disgusting amount of hours in-game speak for themselves: I enjoyed it at one point, but the constant grinding for a game with little reward, hardly any payout for in-game work, the exorbitant prices for any new content, and the experience ruining hacking has left me with little desire to ever play the game again. And, I surely don't plan on it. You, oh reader of my woe, might be able to still save yourself.

Idea Factory and Compile Heart games have a notrious reputation for being low-effort, and what do you get if you take their most popular Neptunia franchise and make a spin-off? The most medicore low-effort forgetable game.
Neptunia games live and die off their writing and even though the actual quality is rather debatable Megatagmention hits a very low point. The plot tries to sell its self on its cast trying to save its high school by making a zombie movie using the current sudden zombie outbreak to attract more students. It really, really tries to get into that its so bad its good category and ocassionaly there is a gem, but at all other times its meh.
Graphicaly the game looks exactly like a PSVITA game because that's what it is, and it rather bland forgetable environmen.ts. Enemies in the main campaign are a first for the series but repeat very often, while the multiplayer mode takes enemies from Action Unleashed.
Musically the game is average; some tracks such as the menu theme are above average, and transformation music for Neptune and co. are quite nice, but nothing sticks out compared to the previous mainline game Megadimension, so you won't be hearing anything on the level of 'Will be Venus' or 'Dimension Zero'.
Gamplay wise, this is where this game really shows its lackluster design. Basic hack and slash mechanics are there for all the characters, which can all perform one or two combos each, and can transorm to change up their small moveset slightly. MegaTagmention controls relatively well, combos have weight and moves are satisfying to pull off, however jumping feels very heavy and unnatural, and the double jump timing is very strick. Characters have a dodge technique whcih blasts them across the field at the speed of sound, but feels highly difficult to aim. Besides basic combos, guards and counterattacks also exist, however they can be slightly difficult to activate due to the unoptimised controller layout straight from PSVITA. Characters have 4 special attacks that they can use when their SP Gauge fills up and these can be very useful for crowd control. Characters can bring two allies into battle which can be used via a button combination that can boost attack, defense, restore HP, restore transform gauge or other effects. You'll quickly discover all you need is transofrm gauge recovery and HP recovery.
Your transformation gauge is charged by hitting enemies, and when it is filled to half or more you can transform into the CPU or a more souped up form of your current character that has different combos, different SP moves and is more powerful. It can also be used to perform powerful EXE and Lily attacks (attacks based on your bond with a different character, raises the more you fight with them). EXE attacks however have a severe oversight where they will knock enemies out of their combos, meaning it will do a fraction of the possible damage.
The two characters you chose into battle when they win (or lose) will gain experience and a boost in their Lily Rank plus money and drops, which presents a problem for the short 6-7 hour campaign. Characters that you don't use won't level up meaning that if you want to use them you will have to grind them up, meaning you will keep sticking with your tried and true character combination. This would be more of a problem if the game wasn't so easy. Enemies largely sit around and look pretty, there isn't much variation in big enemies besides hit and dash, and the game doesn't even feature a proper boss until the end of the campaign! Map design is very small and linear, and largely doesn't effect the way you fight foes. Due to the game featuring more then 10 characters in its short-campgin you won't get bored until the end.
Money can be used to buy weapons, patches, and visual accessories at the store to applly to those weapons to give to your characters to buff them making fights easier. Patches and drops can be fused together to make even better patches, and drops you obtain from mission can be used to unlock costumes for your characters. This system is rather basic, but can be fun to play around with. However, buying weapons reinforces using a minimal amount of characters for your playthrough.
From my brief 1 hour experience with multplayer, enemies from Action Unleashed are back providing much needed variety and 6 big proper bosses that should of been in the main story, alongside a use for your much stronger weapons. Multiplayer gets rid of allies, Lily attacks, and bring two characters in exchange to work together with 3 other players, being able to freely revieve them, and to use a character pre-transormed or that one in the base form unable to tranasofmr. Due to the higher difficultly, better play is required but not too much. I had no connection issues, and the communicatioon menu provided gives a wide range of options to say phrases that translate to other languages well.
In closing, MegaTagmention Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies is a medicore hack and slash game that doesn't feature anything noticable of interesting. It plays perfectly fine with some minor quips with controls and physics, but the story is very, very weak, with few funny moments typical of Neptunia games. Idea Factory and Compile Heart have showed they can make quality games with the release of Megadimension Neptunia VII, but they haven't followed through with their efforts with spin-off games. Skip this unless you are a big Neptunia wee-I mean fan AND only if it is on sale.

MegaTagmension Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies is a Hack and Slay game like Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed was. But there are some differences between those two games. MegaTagmension has a bigger selection of characters than Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed. The combat also feels faster which made this as a Hack and Slay a lot more enjoyable. The quests you do don't just take place on a big stage anymore where you have to defeat a bunch of enemies but rather on a bigger area where the enemies are sometimes scattered throughout said area. But this only applies sometimes to even rarely. Most of the enemies spawn at the same spot as you do and most of the quests can be done on this said spot. Most of the quests take place on bigger areas but most of them don't use them effectively as you only have to fight your way through the enemies at one spot. Because of this most of the quests can be done in under one minute, which also feels kinda odd when they are giving you a time limit of 30-60 minutes. Also there isn't much variety of the enemy types you are going to face. The enemies you fight at the beginning are also the ones you are going to face throughout the entire game. This also applies to all of the bosses except for the final one of course. If you get the hang of these bosses you will most likely get bored to face the same bosses over and over again. On a positive note. All of the characters you are able to play feel different and you will most likely find one that suits your playstyle best. But there is also one problem with leveling those characters. You unlock more characters as you make your way through the story of this game. The problem with that is that all the characters that join your party at a later point are at a very low level and you either have to grind with them first to use them on the current quest you have to do effectively or just ditch them and stick with the characters you used up to this point. Also the amount of EXP you get for each quest isn't as high as it used to be in Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed. It feels like you don't get enough EXP for each quest. To level up even once you have to do the same quest multiple times. So if you want to beat the story as fast as you can it may be best to stick with the characters you get at the beginning. The last point I'm going to talk about is the story. The story is enjoyable but it's not very good. To keep it short. Blanc and her friend are trying to make a movie to save their school. While they're filming a zombie virus is spreading all over their school and they have to take care of that. That's all you need to know for now. All the characters behave the way you expect them to behave and the setting is pretty refreshing for a Neptunia game. After you beat the story there isn't much to do anymore. You don't unlock additional quests or challenges. You can only play through the story missions again.
In conlusion the game is best suited for you if you are fan of the Neptunia franchise and enjoyed Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed. The dialogue is pretty funny and the game uses original music aswell as music from previous installments. The game has it's flaws but it is also very enjoyable. But due to it's short playtime I would recommend to buy this game on sale.

The Mean Greens Plastic Warfare is an interesting game. It's a hidden gem on Steam, and for a multiplayer only title, that isn't good. The playerbase is so miniscule, you'll often times end up in matches with the same people. However it isn't hard to get into a game, and once you are in a game, the game is a blast. Right off the bat, you'll notice the visuals are amazing. Some of the textures could use some work but it's overall one of the better looking games I've tried, especially in terms of art direction and the creativity of this game's settings. The different maps are all distinct, vibrant and fun. The levels are based on different areas in a house each with creative objectives. There's one level that takes place in a freezer where you have to thaw out your team's dinosaur with your flamethrower before the other team, another map where you have to light candles on a cake and a level where you play on a foosball table to name a few.The soundtrack is also pretty memorable, if not a bit repetitive. This game is a 3rd person shooter, something we don't see often. The mechanics of the game are really solid, and the way the weapons are implemented. They basically run a cooldown system where you hold all 6 weapons. The catch is, if you use one too much the weapon will have to recharge before you can use it again, which also carries over after you die. This forces you to use a variety of weapons instead of running around with a shotgun or camping with a sniper for the entirety of the round. The gunplay is definately something I have yet to get used to but it's still a great concept and I can't wait to play more. A few gripes I have with this game, there are some maps where you are forced to platform which in a multiplayer only title can be annoying, especially when your internet hiccups which can make your platforming become imprecise. Another much larger issue is the lack of any depth. I'm not expecting much out of a $10 Indie game, but I really don't feel compelled to replay this game. The only replay value this game has is in the form of achievements, and nothing else. You start out with all the weapons, you can't change the look of your soldier, there's no singeplayer, there is only 10 maps all with unique modes, etc. Again, variety isn't a bad thing and when all the maps are catered to a specific mode they are overall higher quality. However this results in the game getting repetitive. Here's why I think the population is so low, there's nothing to come back to. Nothing to unlock and no secrets. Once you've seen all the maps, that's it. As much as I criticize the game, it's still being actively updated and the developers are pretty open to feedback, especially on social media. All of my issues can be altered in future versions of the game. Right now, for $10, I still think this game deserves a purchase. It's creative, bright, and fun with some really nice gunplay. For the price, it's one of the best on the market. If you're on the edge or want an shooter that you can really spend hundreds of hours on, I'd still wait for a sale to purchase this game. However, one way or another, you need to play this game.

Let me be clear, I love Plastic Army Men, and I like this game, but while it is far better than the abysmal shooters from two console generations ago, that isn't saying much. I also accept the dev team isn't asking for much in payment, and they really care about making this game better for what it's worth, but for a less forgiving individual that doesn't look back on Army Men through rose-tinted nostalgia glasses, can I recommend this game?
Not really.
First the good things... The art style is dead on. The graphics aren't amazing or anything, but Army Men is the one series I think gets a pass on this front. The game is colorful and level design is as imaginative as when we played with Plastic Army Men ourselves. The OST is also quite good; a bit overly brassy perhaps, but it sets the tone quite well. This is clearly intended to be a game you simply play to unwind. Deep strategy is not necessary, just point and click, simple!
There is a great variety of game modes as well. Each map has its own objectives, but they beg to be played on other maps as well. Chances are, you will find some game modes/maps you like, and others you don't. Unfortunately, there is no way to play a mode divorced from its corresponding map, so you will quickly become bored of seeing the same scenarios play out every time.
The Weapons don't help matters. You get 6, if you include Grenades, less variety than the offerings in a pack of Army men you can literally pick up at the dollar store; seriously, what happened? Army Men are supposed to be easy to pick up and know what every character's purpose is, like so...
"Rifle guy? He must be pretty good at range huh?"
"Flamer guy? He must be good up close and vs buildings huh?"
"Bazooka guy? He must be good vs vehicles huh?"
Little of this fundamental logic carries over to The Mean Greens, however. Why we even have a bazooka when there are no vehicles at the time of this review is beyond me. The guns only come in a few flavors; a peashooter automatic rifle, a sniper with no scope sway and 1-shot head shot kills, and a shotgun which has earned my hatred for being pretty much the best gun, and that's it really. There is a Flamethrower, but the range is less than the diameter of a dime, so it's basically worthless. No Pistol, Mortar, Machinegun, Radio, or Minesweeper (ok, we could all do without this guy TBH,) whatsoever, even though these things were already in Army Men games from a decade ago.
Finally, there's the elephant in the room. There's next to no player base, and no AI bots to occupy a player in their absence. I get that bots are quite hard to program, especially if you want something more sophisticated than simply running towards the player, and to give the devs credit, they say bots are on their to-do list, but when you have a game like this out for almost a year, and these components I consider integral to a good Plastic Army Men game are missing, it's impossible to ignore.
Worse, there is no incentive to continue playing the game. There's no unlocks, no ranking up, no build your own class (everyone gets every weapon at all times,) there's not even alternate team colors like Red, Blue, Gray Orange, etc. to make maps seem even a little different between sessions. It' Green vs Tan every map except 1, and the same scenario on the same map every time. Is it any wonder player numbers are so low?
To sum it all up,
The Mean Greens is a noble attempt to reinvigorate a dead franchise we loved as kids, and compared alongside the likes of Army Men 3D, the best of the PS1 generation, it blows that game out of the water easily, but it's more than a decade later, and this game just doesn't have much to offer anyone but the most die hard Army Men fans like myself. If you're dying for a new Army Men game, by all means, pick this up, but if you're looking for a gratifying shooter experience, I'd look elsewhere.
In the meantime, I'd keep my eye on this project, because unlike some developers today, there is hope for Virtual Basement to learn from their mistakes.

I composed most of the songs for this game and got the game for free, but i kinda wanna give this game a review from a consumer perspective.
The Quarter game is a very short and cheap game, i think for the amount of fun you'll have with this game, the price is worth it.
Gameplay wise, think a Beat 'em Up combined with Touhou (danmaku in general) with some minor puzzle elements thrown in the mix.
Realistically, you will probably finish your first playthrough in less than 30 minutes, however, the game is designed with speedrunning in mind, and there are achievements for that further prove that.
You have a dash attack that is quite nice, the effect trial that you leave behind causes enemies to take damage and get dragged along with you, if you master this tech, you can really have a lot of fun manipulating the movement of enemies.
There's also a reflection attack that allows you to reflect most projectiles, the game has a pretty neat design choice, because enemies will telegraph reflectable attacks, it makes it feel a lot fairer when you die, because you will understand how you got killed better.
The story is nothing to write home about, but there's a few funny lines here and there.
The graphics are okay, you have to keep in mind it's an indie game.
One thing that is a bit bothering is the artstyle incosistency, the sprites are very rough, but the portrait artwork is a lot different in style compared to it, it's not a case of bad quality, but it just doesn't mix super well.
I can't really say much about the soundtrack since i took a pretty big part in it, but i have a complaint about the sound design, some of the sound effects are very loud compared to the music, and when a lot of sound effects overlap, they can sound louder than usual, so be aware of that.
There's a few minor glitches, like when sometimes when you enter a room, you can't move unless you go in a different direction for a second, also, if you try very hard, you can get stuck in some walls.
Overall, i think this game is a nice and short experience.
I reccomend this game if you want to play something quick while you are bored or if you enjoy practising your speedrunning skills, since this game is short, the amount of mistakes you can make is also shorter, so i think this game might be a good choice if you are an entry level speedrunner, but i'm pretty sure everyone can enjoy it

A short but fun game that is surprisingly enjoyable to replay several times.
The combat is unique and fastpaced with lots of options for every situation. It's an easy game to learn, but hard to master. Recovery items are (for the most part) well spread out, helping the player immensely. Despite this the game remains to be a game that can really border between being easy or tough but doable, depending on the player.
The limited color palette is a nice touch and pretty to look at (although it is a bit of a shame that some character portraits break the limited colors).
The minigame in the second level is a great and fun reminder to actually use the shine.
And of course, how can one not mention the music? Each and every song is amazing and encourages the fast pacing even more.
Of course no game is perfect, but the flaws are definitely not the end of this world. The creator is reliable when it comes to fixing things though, which is a big plus.
Turning directions (on keyboard at least) does seem to be a bit unresponsive at times.
The sprite quality occasionally differs noticeably, but I personally didn't find it bothersome.
The achievements feel like fun incentives to replay the game as well. This game is built for speedrunning and that makes it all the more enjoyable to try going for fast times. It'll be interesting to see people aiming for the fastest time.

Haven't had this much fun with an action-platformer since Blood of the Werewolf. I've heard a lot of complaints concerning the way the game controls, but I managed to make my way from beginning to end without ever feeling like it was the fault of the game. The difficulty is high, but for anyone who grew up on Sega Genesis or Super NES games it'll be a walk in the park.
The enemy types can get repetitive, but the levels were varied enough in design and challenges that it didn't bother me much. Combat is a lot of fun, the blood drinking mechanic being my personal favorite touch. I will advise that the game doesn't sprinkle checkpoints every ten steps you take like some modern platformers, so if you're easily frusturated by unorthodox jumps that lead to instant death, you might want to try something more along the lines of Super Meat Boy (high challenge but smaller areas).
Got the game on sale for two bucks, and it is now one of my favorites. Highly recommended to anyone who likes a good semi-hardcore action romp.
