Mankind Divided is a thrilling journey into a stunningly rendered dystopian future in a surprisingly original European cyberpunk setting. In terms of gameplay, it improves on most, if not all, of what its predecessor did—the most notable additions being Remote Hacking and the new cover system, in my opinion, which suited my stealthy inclinations perfectly. I thoroughly enjoyed the story of this instalment, both for its complex and nuanced developments, and for the fact that it isn't just another "race to prevent the end of the world" type of deal—I found the fact that it was a bit more down-to-earth refreshing.
An obvious cliffhanger points to the fact they're going to milk this Deus Ex universe as much as they can, but at this stage that doesn't feel like a bad thing to me provided they maintain the same quality—personally I can't get enough Deus Ex. Both the action and narratives form an incredibly well-paced whole that allows for the usual freedom in approaching any given situation according to your play-style.
In terms of the world itself, Prague is a very well designed "main location" with plenty of things to do. However, since you spend most of your time there, the initial wow factor eventually wears off, and part of me ended up wishing it was a bit more sci-fi in its design, like the brilliant Útulek Complex section which is over way too soon.
My main grievance is with the Desperate Measures DLC, and arguably it's nothing major: it just feels out of place being accessed completely outside of the main game considering it's set right in the middle of its narrative. It just ends up feeling disappointingly uninvolving.
Breach is a nice little extra after finishing the main game a few times. It takes a far stricter approach to augmentations and upgrades, as well as applying tough constraints to the situations it has you deal with. In terms of content it's nothing like the main game, but worth it for a bit of fun, especially once you reach the later levels of Tier 2. The
is a shame and feels like a cheap move (especially single use pre-order DLCs), but I wouldn't go so far as to call it PTW: I had no problem finishing Breach without any of that crap and as a matter of fact, the less help you get in Breach, the more interesting it becomes.

I have played DX:HR multiple times, and I have seen enough let's plays to know that I will love this one.

Edit: I did love this one, although I have to agree with the reviewers who say the ending is a little weak. The mission itself is fine but the way it wraps up, via tv news exposition is a little weak. Feels like they want this game to lead into an expansion or sequel.
I also think this game is easier compared to Human Revolution. I think part of the reason is that one can sneak past most enemies. Another reason is the amount of energy Adam has right of the bat. There are also a lot of energy recharging items to find. In DX:HR I never had more than 10 maybe and I'd use them all for the bosses and the saving Malik bit. Here I had like 25 and enogh crafting parts to make another 20. Meant I was able to stay cloaked for the last mission, save enough for the last opponent (the only boss in the game) and still didn't run out. Also lots of multitools. Never used them and stopped counting after a while. I think the game could've been harder. An optional really difficult bit like saving Malik was in HR. Or even just a room full of enemies that you couldn't simply sneak past.

I also think the aug menu looks worse that in HR, it doesn't look like Adam can see it like that because they use scenes from later in the game to illustrate what his powers can do , even though the story suggest he does see it.

A few augs work differently than in HR. The Cloak works better; it now used less energy when standing still and more when moving. The CASIE aug now gives more information, I personally think it makes conversations too easy now, but I always held off using it even in HR so ymmv.
The hacking was improved though, with more options. Stealth is easier, too, players no longer have to hold down the right mouse button to take cover they just have to press F. Makes aiming with the tranq rifle out of cover more convenient.
The gameplay in general is either similar or better compared to HR. I especially like the option of a non-lethal Typhoon aug and the additional non-lethal options in general.
The characters are interesting and I would like to see more of them, Samizdat, Eliza and the case of Adams mystery augs need follow up I think.
It's a shame, the things they did to maximise profit from this franchise, because the game itself is really good even though it's not as great as HR (what with the unfinished story and all).
Overall an excellent game. The performance is hit or miss, but they've been improving it a lot with timely patches. I love the new mechanics, better graphics and more expansive world.

This game had some nice features. I liked the idea of zombies not seeing in the dark, especially when you had to walk amongst them to turn a valve. Or when walking in the narrow tunnel with zombies on your path. It was good that they didn't react when you touched them, else that would've made it to hard.
I also liked the theme. It was darker than the original HL-Series and turning around a corner or walking in a (very) dark tunnel not knowing what to expect when you pointed your flashlight into the dark was very immersive and thrilling.
The last "mission"/fight was kind difficult again due to the mechanics of the Gravity Defying-Weapon (GD-W). However the mission was very well built. By placing the rockets in places where you had to use your GD-W to reach the player had to start thinking in terms of: "hmm what walls could I destory" or "what rooftops or other simmilar platforms could I reach with the GD-W". While doing the thinking and looking arround we also had to dodge the fire from the enemies. Be that, sneaking around or rushing.
The story behind the GD-W and about the area/lab was short (ofc due to the short game) but managed to immerse the player alot. We wanted to know more about the people working on the GD-W and we kinda got to know alot both by notes, text on walls, and other graphical hints. Short story but very well put together. Never did I think that anything was strange in a sense that it wasn't possible. The story managed to convince me about the GD-W and all the other feutres in the game using minimalistic methods to do so. Very easy to follow along the storyline.
The grapics looked good and the HL theme was caputed perfectly. The sequences were crative and highly engaging managing to capture the horror that the set period of time bring. Resulting in a highly action packed game.
In all, the game succeded into making me want more by the time it ended just like the HL-Series. The ending scene where G-man shows up was short but very cool. And the quote from G-man brought the question: Will there be more?

I bought this during the steam sale with no previous knowledge of the original game, something to be noted.
The game itself, in one word is "fun" or "amusing".
It is a parody of the 80's sci-fi cyberpunk genre, probably a re-skin of the original game from what I've heard of the original's gameplay.
The narrative can be either funny or it feels like it tries too hard to be, which can be a hit or miss.
The game has a story mode with objectives in an open world filled with "Garrisons" which you "liberate" giving you exp and access to sidequests that grant you attachments and upgrades for your guns.
Speaking of guns, they feel great and doing the side quests and collecting items earning the upgrades feel very rewarding, for example: Explosive rounds for your sniper, laser rounds for your rifles and so on.
This is one of the few games in which you can buy a loot map to find the collector items which is rather important as they grant you access to the weapon mods.
The soundtrack by power glove is the cyber platter that holds this chunk of juicy cyber hearts together, the awesome 80's sci-fi vibe is propagated throughout the game with their immersive synths and tunes.
I highly recommend this game for the price I bought it for which was about 4 USD, The game can be charged at least 15 and it will still be worth it.

What is this otherworldly, obscure and weird game about? What's up with that title anyway?
This is something I asked myself at first when I took a glance at the storepage of 3089. At first I was pretty pessimistic but then it piqued my interest because the premise just seemed extremely compelling to me. But that is coming from a person who genuinely enjoys elusive and perhaps unconventional games.
In 3089 you play the role as an android trapped on a planet which finds itself in a eternal war between two robot faction. You automatically ally with one of them and start doing quests for them. This game has an absolutely boring standard rpg formula to it. You fulfill generic and randomly generated quests in a procedurally generated world. Your character gains experience and loot over the course of the game which allows him to become stronger. What really sets this game apart for me is the visual aesthetics and audio, it has a very mysterious feeling to it. Furthermore you can find a lot of unique weapons and have to craft them. This game has a crafting system and also some special abilities for your character. The player can also control space crafts and delve into the eternal warfare while during quests.
It's a pretty open sandbox game where you basically just fulfill quests on a random map where the AI dukes it out. The shooting is a bit unusual and needs some improvement but it's solid enough. There is not much variety in the gameplay itself but still it's nice to play the game from time to time and see what it has in store for you.
I cannot fully recommend it but only for those who just like those oddball gems in the steam store. It's really interesting and quite enjoyable.

Dawn of War® - Soulstorm is a game I love, hate, and love to hate - I just can't make heads or tails of it. The gameplay is both really good and really terrible.
What makes it good is the diversity available - this is the first strategy game I've ever played that has a staggering count of NINE playable races, but what counters that is that they're all extremely complex and hard to understand. The actual gameplay of resource points and what not, though, is kind of puzzling, and I would have honestly preferred to just stay with the traditional resource gathering. In many ways, it sort of reminds me of Tiberian Twilight; the less said about that game the better.
So since Steam forces me with a "black or white" option with "yes or no", I'll recommend this game with a "yes", though it's probably not for everybody.

As someone who is no stranger to the RTS genre, I'll admit, this one threw me for a loop at first!
The most interesting thing here is the campaign.  Typically, your average RTS is either a survival game where you build up forces to withstand assault or it's a level-by-level progression, where you complete sequential missions.  This was the first time I actually felt like I was playing both at once.  The campaign mode of this game is odd, but in a good way; it's a refreshing way to bridge the two different styles of RTS into a unique gameplay system.
Another interesting mechanic is the different races in the game.  Usually, different races will have a general build order that all follow the same way, or there are a few radically different races.  With this game, each race has a unique build style to explore!  The Imperial Guard have garrisonable buildings, the Eldar can Teleport, the Battle Sisters have Holy Relics... it's like each race is it's own unique game!
(P.S.: If you're a bigtime RTS player like I am, and you're just now getting into this game, then I recommend starting as the Tau when you first play this game; their build order is more familiar to folks coming from a Starcraft or CiV background.)
The only downside to this "expansion"/game, I would say, is the lack of a story.  I mean, there is one, but it's very underplayed in this expansion.  It takes a bit of RP to really get into the story; not like Winter Assault or Dark Crusade, where there's a very obvious storyline to follow.  Still, this isn't really a big issue with the game itself; if you're already a big 40K fan, then you might not even notice it at all.
All in all, a wonderful spin on the RTS games.  9/10.  Looking to get the other DoW1 titles, to experience the other stories in this game series.

I cannot tell you how many hours I've played this Relic epic of an RTS prior to Steam.  What I will say is that Relic and Steam were completely awesome in providing me with a new software key to download the game through Steam (with proof of purchase of the hard CD some years ago) and keep playing.
While now dated, I must say the entire Dawn of War series, with Soulstorm as the final game in the first DoW series, was nothing but one of the finest RTS games I ever played.  I cut my teeth on the old Red Alert series, Dune 2000, and others and never really cared for the genre until Relic's classic Homeworld.  DoW brought that level of RTS to the ground in the 40K universe.  While hardcore 40K fans have far too many complaints, I think DoW's strenghts have outstripped any weaknesses.
Gameplay can be repetitive however.  DoW:Dark Crusade and Soulstorm are extremely similar in campaign play.  While Dark Crusade only covers a planet, the solar system covered in Soulstorm is only slightly larger.  The usual strategy employed in Dark Crusade of entering a  new territory and base building until you have enough of a force to conquer the enemy base is repeated with little exceptions except for the capture the flag battles for webway gates territory.
I do not think the weaknesses detract from campaign play too much.  Followers of the WH40K lore are likely to enjoy playing each race through the end of their respective end game content.  It is enjoyable just for that alone.  Then there is multiplayer....

This game has TONS of things going with it.
First, lets talk about the graphics.
They are, as Adam Sessler would say "Punch you in the balls fantastic".
The graphics are similar to that of a comic book - a professionally drawn,
well tailored comic. A lot of love went into making this game look visually stunning.
On to the Music.
The Music is all right. I mean is does add to the ambiance of the stages, but some of
it doesn't stand out all that much. It's not annoying, but it's also not outstanding.
either way, it really doesn't hurt the gameplay.
Speaking of Gameplay -
The controls do have a small bit of a learning curve, but the game does a grand job
of making sure that you can get the handle of it easily. The default controller setup can be adapted
in about 4 minutes, and any special moves are added and combined with the gameplay as you progress
in the game, The Difficulty also increases with the stages - monsters get harder to kill, and you have to fight more waves of them as you go along. It forces you to think about how to kill the bad guys with the different combos and powerups you get along the way. Even the boss battles are epic and fun to play. I've died quite a number of times playing the bosses, and it made me want more.
The storyline is well laid out, and the theme is very engrossing. I won't spoil it for newcomers, but it's great.
If you are a fan of Rayne, like I am, and you have been disappointed by the movies and the up in the air from BloodRayne 2 (like I have), this game does a great job of making up for that.

Trine and its sequel, Trine 2, are both incredible games, both visually and mechanically. The artwork and animation is beautiful, especially in the sequel with the water bubbles and surrounding plant material absolutely glistening even on the lower graphics card on my Mac. While the story isn't incredibly fleshed out in the sequel (in my opinion, I could be wrong), the character voices and little quirks which show up throughout the game make for an absorbing game experience, and it's very easy to choose a favourite out of the three characters you can change between.
Speaking of the game mechanic, the idea of switching between characters to fulfil certain tasks is rather original, and I think really sets this apart. However Trine and its sequel really shine when you play in multiplayer mode - I find it much more fun to play with friends, and there is still a need to switch between characters depending on where you have walked off to in the game, etc. It's a perfect game for working together to solve puzzles (and fighting with the knight ain't half bad - actually its my favourite bit [I'm such a tank haha]). Similarly, I really love the XP building system, where you can build up your abilities over the course of the game, allowing you to accomplish much greater tasks and fight more monsters in different ways.
I would definitely recommend this game for casual or hardcore gamers alike - it's great solo or on multiplayer (co-op can be played locally too) and the animation and graphics are just awesome!

A bite-sized chunk of satire, DLC Quest will make you laugh, question the state of the industry... and then cry a bit (in that order).
The author pokes fun at most of today's trends in a very thoughtful and engaging way - from filler NPCs to "necessary" zombies, nothing is left untouched! Of course, as the title implies, the main focus is acquiring DLCs - this is accomplished by platforming and obtaining coins, then visiting the friendly shopkeeper. Everything from background music to the character animations is initially locked, so you have to work a bit before everything falls into place and you can finally start advancing the "story". Luckily, the progression is perfect and the platforming decent, with a nostalgic, retro feel. Controls feel responsive, the secrets are abundant, but keep in mind the platforming is just a means to an end. So, don't expect to be challenged, that's not the point.
The game is split up in two parts (the second story was created after launch and is bundled for free and accessible from the main menu):
- The original
which tackles the subject of the landslides of DLCs made available for modern games, the morality of the practice and how we, as both gamers and game protagonists deal with the trend;
- A sort of expansion,
that continues the story and deals with other, current industry trends like day one patches, sub-par optimization and so on.
Both of these are treated in a satirical manner and placed on an overaching storyline that left me, at least, chuckling.
Throughout the game there isn't one moment where the 4th wall is left standing or when the game takes itself seriously (even the achievements and trading cards reflect that). Adding to the absurdity and humor are the NPCs you encounter and the situations you are forced into, all of them tropes from modern gaming trends, executed flawlessly. You fill find yourself saying "I see what you did there!" and having a laugh more often than not. If you're into game design, DLC Quest makes for a perfect dissection piece - it's fun and easy to understand how, why and when each mechanic is introduced, the map design, the intended game progression and so on.
Overall, it's a funny, entertaining ride; a discourse on the modern gaming industry, a mirror for both it and ourselves to look into.
Saying more or going into detail would spoil the experience, so you own it to yourself to try it out. Even though there's not much replay value it doesn't overstay its welcome, nor recycle its ideas - each DLC, NPC, line of dialogue or encounter reflects something very specific and it's up to you to recognize and understand what... and why. It will give as much as you are willing to put into it.
The fact that it approaches a mature and so-close-to-home subject in such a hilarious way, all the while sparking dialogue and introspection is worth the entry price alone.

“What had transpired here tonight was a rather complex chain of events, but I was going to explain everything as best as I could… So that they, too, would be able to understand the tragic truth behind it all. “
-Raiko Shinpuku
--------------------
SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair is a murder mystery visual novel and first in the SHINRAI series, as well as the first game developed by indie German video game developer “Gosatsu”, a duo consisting of core members Gospel and Natsu. As a visual novel, gameplay in SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair consists primarily of reading, with interactivity delegated to segments wherein the player is prompted to present evidence in order to prove or disprove character deductions. Through a series of just such segments, the player progressively pieces together the identity of an anonymous killer and reveals the truth behind an otherwise seemingly straightforward death.
A secluded mountain resort, 10 friends, 1 murderer. Investigate, interrogate and present evidence as you solve various mysteries throughout the night. Will you be able to reach the truth and uncover the culprit’s identity? Or will your deductions lead you to blame someone completely innocent…? (Steam/Itch.io synopses)
----------------
All too often is it said that “first impressions last forever” and that what defines your opinion of a person or thing is your very first, very basest of experiences with it. Quite the opposite, however, SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair establishes an identity for itself that would be somewhat unbecoming to one giving it a cursory look-over or a relatively noncommittal playthrough, and one that betrays the sheer quality of what SHINRAI eventually grows into.
SHINRAI’s introductory scene found itself, when measured against everything following it, comparatively unwelcoming: juvenile humor and a somewhat uninspired setting saved just barely by a colorful ensemble of charmingly eccentric characters. Nonetheless, as banal as it may be, it was paced expertly and fluidly presented an array of details and information that make the scene nothing short of essential.
Succeeding the opening segment, however, were a series of scenes equal parts shocking and engaging. In a number of ways, Gosatsu prove themselves masters of detail and suspense, utilizing the closed-circuit setting to create a wonderfully nonlinear mystery with a number of conclusions, all equally distinctive and convincing, bar the very truest of them, the one you’d least expect. In allowing the player to pursue any of the prospective murderers, Gosatsu creates a truly interactive murder mystery that rightly forces the player to make sense of the dizzying phantasmagoria of criminal activity they experienced throughout the night.
SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair, to the most superficial of an audience, would initially seem unappealing or generic. It is worth it, though, to read SHINRAI in its entirety, as the mystery presented rivals perhaps some of the best in the genre. Any with experience with murder mysteries and/or the visual novel genre will feel right at home with SHINRAI, as would any who just wish to read an intelligent and thoroughly thought-out story in the ilk of Ace Attorney or Danganronpa.

As a fan of the Danganronpa franchise, I figured SHINRAI would be worth a go, and it did not disappoint. The overarching mystery was well crafted, abetted by charming characters, colorful artwork, and an atmospheric sound track. On the negative side, the story is very slow to build, with key revelations and motivations unfolding in a large exposition dump at the end. Further, the writing is rather stilted at points, which wrecks player immersion a bit.
Overall, though, SHINRAI's virtues far outweigh its vices. It's an enjoyable romp, and I look forward to seeing the creators develop this world and its characters further.

I will start by saying that this review contains minor spoilers about the characters and story.
SHINRAI - Broken Beyond Despair is an indie mystery visual novel that has some elements similar to the Danganronpa series which I also am a big fan of.
The story circulates around 10 classmates that decide to hold a halloween party in a secluded mountain resort:
Raiko - Main character. Girl that doesn't show many emotions. Appears to be unfriendly towards others
Nobara - Raiko's best friend. Laid-back personality but very gullible
Rie - Host of the party. Tends to act before she thinks. Chaotic and forgetful
Runa - Rie's best friend. Caring and kindhearted. Sophisticated
Mika - Troublemaker. Always pranking people. Goal is to scare Raiko
Momoko - Popular girl in the school. Introverted and shy
Hiro - Momoko's boyfriend. Arrogant and loves to glorify himself
Kamen - Momoko's best friend. Honest person that never holds back. Doesn't like Raiko.
Kotoba - The most hated one in the group as he's considered a creepy pervert.
Taiko - Kotoba's best friend. Kind and reliable guy. Rie's crush.
When the resort suddenly gets affected by a power outage, the 10 friends split up in groups. After the power comes back on, the friends find a dead body in one of the guest rooms. The base-story is what you would call a classic murder mystery, and is not a creative one in any way. However, just as in most murder mysteries, the characters play a very big part in the storytelling and is a crucial element in every part of the story. The characters of importance have a decent and realistic backstory which in turn also builds up the story.
Story: 6/10
The characters in SHINRAI have different personalities that are relatively realistic. However, most of them don't really stand out and they aren't really likable as characters. There weren't any conversation scenes where one of the characters did a stupid pun that was surprisingly fun, any scenes where one of the characters steps in to protect the main character, any scenes where one of the characters turns out to be a psychopath, or anything that makes them unique to the others. My favourite character was Kotoba as his perverted nature made him clearly different from the others and fun to talk to due to his stupid puns.
Characters: 5/10
The gameplay in SHINRAI is one of its stengths in my opinion. Instead of having a game where you only would read and click next, like most visual novels, the developers decided to add an investigation mode, similar to Danganronpa's. This investigation mode is a point and click mode where you investigate objects of interest, as well as talk to witnesses in order to find clues and evidence. There were also choices that you could actively pick between, resulting in several routes and results, the VN is made so that you as a player is able to deduct and think WITH the main character. The crime is interesting and complex, but it's described so that you would be able to try figure out what happened instead of just letting the main character explain everything at the end (which she later does though). The investigation mode could need some polishing and it was frustrating how you aren't able to save before making the choices.
Something that was really bothering me though, was the fact that all characters except 4 had alibis instantly and it kind of removed the suspense of trying to figure out who the culprit could be.
Gameplay: 7/10
The art is very unique to this game. It's not very polished but it's to be expected, as it was actually the developer who drew it. It was bothering me at first when playing the game as I'm used to more anime-like art like most visual novels use, but as you play the game, you'll eventually get used to it. Even though the art works relatively well for its purpose, more facial expressions could have been added as the characters tended to look the same almost always and I never saw any significant changes except for when they were crying. Though my opinion may differ from others playing the game, I'm certain that the game would have looked a lot better with anime-like art similar to danganronpa.
Art: 4/10
Even though the game had its bad points, and the fact that it was quite short a game, it was still very enjoyable to read. I had a great time trying to figure out the puzzle in my head, while changing theories left and right. As an indie game, I personally believe that they did a great job, and I would recommend it to people who love murder mysteries that allow you to think and solve the crime by yourself.
Total score: 6/10
Game was well developed mystery that allows for multiple suspects to keep deduction compelling.

A surprisingly good visual novel. Going into it I wasn't expecting too much but I feel like it was a very well done visual novel despite maybe coming off as being low budget. The mystery kept me guessing, the characters were cliche but I still liked them and the art style fit the visual novel. Overall I would recommend it, it is a little short so if you are looking for a visual novel you will get a lot of hours out of this probably isn't it.

Brawlhalla il a very simple game, using only 4 mechanics : light attack, signatures attack (basically strong attacks), dodge, and throwing items.
From these 4 mechanics, the game actually becomes quite complexe.
Your characters have 2 weapons each, they get one of them by grabbing an item.
Basically, it allows you to enjoy 3 moveset per characters (your two weapons and the bare-handed moveset).
All characters share the same-sih moveset. Light attack with any weapons are the same across the board, however, the signatures attacks are entirely unique. It allows you to simply choose 2 favorite weapons then pick the character that has them both, as well as being able to handle other characters more simply if they use weapons you know.
The game is casual friendly, you can win free for all and get to a decent ranked state simply by spamming heavy attacks (I actually think it's a good thing, most versus fightings game are very very elitists). This way, you can learn to play with your friends very quickly.
However, the game also has a lot of depth if you are willing to see through the spamfest.
Lore-wise, the game has a biography for each character wich is usually hilarious. Most characters are incredibly overpowered (a pirate beat the Devil with his own fake coin, a knight was destined to valhalla but nobody could kill him in battle so his valkyrie litteraly punch him to death so he dies in battle and can get in Valhalla).

A well done but clearly indie VN with a solid mystery.  Starts a little slow with a long expository / introduction phase but is worth taking the time to get into.  It's somewhat short in its entirety but the bonus is that nothing is overly drawn out, it's all tight.
I'd say it's kind of like playing one of the long cases of a Phoenix Wright game but with more of the darker vibes of a Danganrompa title.  If you like either/both of those, give this a shot, especially if it goes on sale.

Pros
-Decent mystery and nice plot twist (not a super intricate mystery but not bad either, fun to puzzle out)
-Bad Ends and True End ; I actually liked the Bad End mechanic in that I didn't even realize I had named the wrong culprit until I had gone on to accuse them for ten minutes and actually believed my suspect was the killer until the Bad End screen came up and told me how wrong I was
-OST is pretty decent
-Notebook and Diary etc is helpful for noting down what happens in the game
-Butterfly Effect kinda?
Cons
-Kinda short
-Characters are a bit stereotypical IMO, with only a few small exceptions
-Weird gender imbalance? There are 7 girls and only 3 guys, and 2 of those 3 guys have almost no redeeming qualities whatsoever and are the two main "jerk" characters in the cast.
-One character
is completely irrelevant to the story in that they can be removed from it and the general flow of the story really isn't affected much, if at all
TL;DR - I recommend the game highly if it's on sale. If not, it depends on how much you really want it but not really $15 for me

SHINRAI deserves your love.
As most of us do, you probably judge a book by its cover, or, in case of VNs, its art. The art in Shinrai is actually drawn by its main writer and developer and is probably not what you would call professional. However after finishing the game I think the art feels just right in context, and it doesn't hurt the joy of the story even a little bit. There are lots of sprites, lots of expressions and outfits, and a lot of characters including extras. All of them may not be AAA quality, but in this game, they definitely don't need to be. It does what it has to - you grow to like the characters and their funny quirks.
Now, onto the story. What surprised and pleased me the most is that SHINRAI is an actual fair play mystery. Which is something incredibly rare in our age of detective fiction's decline. The main "case" is not something the writer made up in three minutes and then explained with five deus ex machinaes, it's an actual well constructed fair mystery that you are challenged to solve. If you're a fan of Agatha Christie, you know what a joy this can be. There are hints, red herrings, timelines, clues, diary to keep track, suspect interviews, everything you need for your grumpy little detective kit. A must have for any serious mystery fan.
You may say that the story is nothing new and you'll be probably right. But it's an old story told in a pleasing new way, with a cast of lovely characters.
The characters are mostly well developed and written well enough to gain your sympathy and empathy. Generally I would describe them as "very cute but quite realistic". You won't hear any NYAAAA or see over the top stuff - they behave as normal people would and talk like real people do, which is something that usually separates english VNs from japanese ones. There is quite enough of good humour too.
Overall, if I had to describe the game in three words, I'd say Shinrai is: Indie, Cute, Smart.
Last of all, frankly I don't write reviews often, but in this case I believe it's justified, because Shinrai is very promising and deserves more public recognition - and the public deserves more fair play mystery VNs!

I fell in love with this game within the first few minutes!
Your experience is so open ended and unique, there's always something you can do, and the quests are fun (and pretty funny when you start to think about it).
My favorite part about it is the customization of the items, it's super engaging. Every component to a weapon or armor has it's own stats so when you find a new piece you can create a better item, which I prefer over the mechanic to "unlocking" better equipment with either achievements or money.
The environment is incredible, I just love that classic retroness to it. I also like that it's an active environment, changing from day to night, raining, foggy, and meteor showers! These environments can also help you to completing your quests, a very neat detail I appreciate.
If you are a SciFi lover, RPG enthusiast, or retro nerd, no question this is the game for you!

Brawlhalla il a very simple game, using only 4 mechanics : light attack, signatures attack (basically strong attacks), dodge, and throwing items.
From these 4 mechanics, the game actually becomes quite complexe.
Your characters have 2 weapons each, they get one of them by grabbing an item.
Basically, it allows you to enjoy 3 moveset per characters (your two weapons and the bare-handed moveset).
All characters share the same-sih moveset. Light attack with any weapons are the same across the board, however, the signatures attacks are entirely unique. It allows you to simply choose 2 favorite weapons then pick the character that has them both, as well as being able to handle other characters more simply if they use weapons you know.
The game is casual friendly, you can win free for all and get to a decent ranked state simply by spamming heavy attacks (I actually think it's a good thing, most versus fightings game are very very elitists). This way, you can learn to play with your friends very quickly.
However, the game also has a lot of depth if you are willing to see through the spamfest.
Lore-wise, the game has a biography for each character wich is usually hilarious. Most characters are incredibly overpowered (a pirate beat the Devil with his own fake coin, a knight was destined to valhalla but nobody could kill him in battle so his valkyrie litteraly punch him to death so he dies in battle and can get in Valhalla).
TL DR :
-The game is very simple and fun, yet has a lot of depth if you best the spammers.

After playing it for some time I'd like to share my thoughts on this game.
These pros were keeping me playing this game.
+ Good game concept - battlefield with infantry, tanks, snipers, planes,
+ Realistically designed maps
+ Ability to use various tactics (hide in grass/bush, flank...)
+ Everything is available to buy with in-game credits
+ Gold doesn't give you much advantage, to bypass grind you'll need lots of it
+ No (almost no) cheaters
+ War mode (strategy game, which affects specific battles)
+ Ability to take enemy weapons
+ Good spawning system (spawns between checkpoints, mobile spawns, tickets for everything -infantry, tanks, jeeps etc. for both defenders and attackers)
Now cons (why I don't recommend it)
- 1st HUGE con - No valid matchmaking
- MM can put veterans with ~1k hrs played against players who just finished installation
- MM can put infantry only against balaced team of tanks, planes, and snipers (and feels good, when it looks like one team is from Cod 2  Multiplayer and the other from World of Tanks/Warplanes). And ofcourse, infantry gets slaughtered again and again.
- MM can put you in game, that is about to end in 2-3 minutes
- 2nd HUGE con - Very unbalaced factions - I thought,OK, this game is from german developers, so Germany might have slightly upper hand, but I was wrong. Germany has best medium tanks, heavy tanks, LMGs, assault rifles, etc., resulting in Germany being very overpopulated, while Soviet union being underpopulated (US is something between)
- Horribly long and hard grind for anything (be it a tank, scope for rifle, AT mines, or just credits)
- Spawnkilling - when you spawn, you are invisible and invicible, until you shoot or leave the spawn, but ... when you leave the spawn, most of the times you'll be in open area, ready for optimal torture from tanks, snipers, planes etc. (which are often already waiting for you)
- Tanks are able to load HE round, resulting in tanks camping around the map, blasting helpless infantry (especially when unbalanced MM kicks in) from safe distance
Overall I don't recommend playing this game for anything else than Germany (maybe US also), otherwise your gaming experience will detoriate very rapidly. I played for all factions, but as a Soviet infantry/tank, this game (especially staged battles) is pure pain most of the time, with W/L ratio 0.2 or worse (although no matter how your team is bad, you're still able to keep good K/D ... that's at least something).

It occurs to me at the time of this review how few really good 40k video games exist. Dawn of War 2 was a solid game, but pared down the scale even more than this game did in order to focus on squad tactics. While it takes a mod such as Ultimate Apocalypse to scale this game up to its source material's size (and add Titans), or even use a simple mod to double the cap and tweak unit limits - this is one of the few games in existence where you can slaughter the IG as Orks, or butcher others as the reaving Dark Eldar. It's immensely satisfying and still holds up pretty well all these years later. I highly recommend to anyone who loves 40k and/or RTS games. If you only like one or the other this game may be a gateway drug to the others. Don't forget to check out mods as well to expand your over all experience, and a Persistent bases mod is a must to get the most out of the Soulstorm campaign.

This is an amazing little adventure game for those who love fantasy settings and casual puzzle platformers following a wizard, a warrior and a rogue thief placed on a surprising journey to save their kingdom (very much like in Trine 1). I have completed this game probably about 6 or 7 times now with friends online and on my own. The one thing this game lacks is a decent story, to me it seemed quite basic and forgetful, but it's a nice little adventure none the less.
Trine 2 improves on the original with beautiful graphics, more abilities (even though there are still a few from 1 on there) and is also a longer game with much more unique levels. The soundtrack is also brilliant, with many many songs, all unique and original for each level too.
I definitely recommend buying this, I haven't played the goblin menace DLC however, yet i've seen it adds even more unique environments and mechanics,  but it is a brilliant game for casual puzzle platformer lovers who like fantasy and adventure. I also highly recommend playing with others on the co-op modes as it's also a ton of fun.

Brief Introduction: allow me to start off saying this is my first review here on Steam. The reason I decided to write one was because, at the time of writing this review, the game has been out for a little over a year but has only 25 reviews. I thought I'd contribute to that number.
Now for the game:
The game is of the Visual Novel genre, which, for those that don't know, means that it has a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of dialogue with a few interactive bits thrown in. The art might seem weird at first, but I got used to it pretty fast, and I thought it looked quite decent. Like other have mentioned, the characters have a few different poses, and at some points change outfits, so it's not bad at all.
The characters are pretty anime-ish at first (which means their personalities tend to be somewhat exaggerated), but as the story progresses and you find out more about them, they can really grow on you.
The soundtrack I did find a bit lackluster though, and I kept wondering if it was a problem with my notebook, but I could always notice the music/sound effects looping, and it broke the immersion a little bit.
The story, though, is where the game does shine. Once again, like others have mentioned, the action takes a couple of hours to get started, but once it does, it's pretty easy to want to play through the game in a single session. The mystery is a very interesting one, and I found myself trying to guess what actually took place until the very end, when I had that spark in my mind and things seemed to make sense. And so, along with the protagonist and everyone else, I managed to correctly deduce the true culprit of the events that transpired. The reason I'm saying this is to show that, if you pay enough attention and keep throwing theories around your head to see what makes sense and what doesn't, it is very possible to correctly solve the mystery in your first run, as the game gives you all the tools needed to do it. The mystery in the game is very coherent (no bizarre logic leaps) and makes a lot of sense, so I think this is a huge plus.
So, for the conclusion:
-Do you enjoy visual novels/games that are like interactive books?
-Do you enjoy/not mind anime-ish characters with a somewhat exaggerated personality (that does get a bit of development)?
-Do you enjoy (actually solvable) murder mysteries?
If your answer to those questions is yes, then, by all means, give this game a go. It's very likely you'll enjoy it. If I were to rate my personal enjoyment of the game, I think I'd give it a solid 9/10, well worth it's full price.

3) Dialogue isn't English.
"Too short." This is an indie title, so I'm not sure why people are expecting an epic they can sink hundreds of hours into. In terms of quality-to-length ratio I'd say this game ranks very high. Think more people need to check back into MMO rehab. Or just keep snorting it.
"Too easy." For someone like me who's really bad with puzzles, the difficulty felt just right. The game flows very well as a result and I never had to stop playing and feel like a complete moron. If puzzle games are only made for geniuses, they wouldn't be very marketable.
"OMG gibberish!" For awhile I just assumed it was some eastern European language, until I read that it's "gibberish." It actually sounds pretty good and will quickly grow on you. It's not like you can't understand what's going on in the story. The "gibberish" also saves them translation costs. Don't see a problem here.

So, you're reading a review; that's good, as it means you're giving this some consideration.
At this point in time, you're quite possibly thinking "Well, the art looks
, but I'm not sure if I want to spend my money on a VN that's just
".
Which is a fair point.  I don't like wasting my money, either. So I'll say it here - this is well worth picking up.
No, the art's not the best ever seen in a VN - but it's perfectly serviceable; there are a lot of characters, and a lot of facial expressions, and you're never in any doubt as to which character you're looking at.
And it does start out somewhat slowly (slice-of-lifey, I guess) - but then that gives you time to settle in and learn a bit about each character in turn, rather than having the fairly large cast (ten main characters) all thrown at you at once.  While some of the characters are, shall we say, a little *excessive* with aspects of their personality (hello, Kotoba!), they're all well characterised and individual; you won't find yourself struggling to remember which character is which.
What it does deliver is a plot with plenty clues scattered through it, which add together towards a satisfying conclusion - things make sense and there're no bizarre leaps of logic required (no stupid puzzles where you wonder how the hell you were meant to work out the significance of a purple rubber duck or anything!). Though it's entirely possible (or even probable) that you'll finger the wrong culprit the first time through, when you do work out what happened and why, everything falls into place logically.
And working everything out will unlock several bonus scenes, which add further depth and insight.
In conclusion - is it the best VN in the history of ever? No, it's not.  But it's a very enjoyable read, at a fair price. If you enjoy a good story where you can solve a mystery, you're missing out if you don't grab this.

I have to recommend SHINRAI for one big, important reason: It's actually a good, fair mystery.  I have to admit that I got tricked by a red herring, but only because I'd underestimated the writing and failed to put things together correctly.  The core puzzle is very well constructed, and the plot around it is well paced.  The largest problem is that so much of the key MOTIVES are released in a big rush after you already solve the crime and aren't hinted well enough in advacnce, but it's not a terrible flaw.
The writing is largely good... the designers got pretty cutesy shoving movie and video game quotes into the dialogue, but the characters are well-drawn and likeable (especially good ol' Kamen).  I have to admit to not seeing much point to the parent characters, and cutting them would have helped speed up the slow beginning.
The game's mechanics are fine; the "room search" feature doesn't get much chance to be used, and it's a bit too easy to know what objects are important while searching (unlike in the dialogue and cut-scenes, where close eye for detail is required).
The graphics are pretty pedestrian, but they certainly do their job: there's nothing more shocking than a violent mystery starring adorable anime characters.   The music is fine, but repetitive.
In sum, SHINRAI is a well-made mystery with charming characters; I definitely recommend it, and I look forward to a longer, more ambitious game the designers might be able to do next.

3089 is an procedurally generated, open-world, action RPG where you play a robot. You are sent to the planet Xax and given various tasks.

I had to watch an LP to figure out what to do. After that initial bump, the game opened up, and I really started enjoying the game. One of the best moments I had was running across the terrain and finding myself at the top of a very tall mountain. I thought I was at ground level, but I was actually above the clouds. This is a game I will continue to play.
Verdict: This game is worth getting. The graphics, music, and procedural nature of the game work together to provide a unique and interesting experience.

The 4th game in the series, 3089 has the player take control of an experimental combat droid, placed amongst a perpetual war on the planet Xax that serves as a testing ground for your efforts.
Gameplay involves traversing an open world, completing "quests" & challenges, getting into fights with enemy robots, collecting loot, and increasing skills. The world itself is procedurally generated, and the further from the starting point the player travels the higher in level enemies & items are. There are also no boundaries to the world map; as long as you can survive, you can keep travelling further out.
Quests are randomly generated and are effectively infinite in number. Because your role is to test an experimental combat technology, the quests are very straight-forward and - occasionally - don't make sense. This isn't an issue as there aren't any real lives going on here. Completing set challenges will unlock new enemies; these challenges can be thought of as the main quest-line as they (usually) lead to an end-game scenario.
The robots themselves (your character included) are assigned to either the red team or blue team. Your robot is assigned to the red team, and you'll start in a red base along with various other red robots and buildings. Other red robots can be befriended if the player's Prestige is high enough, with no limit on the number of followers you can have.
Items are modular in design; all weapons & armours are built from segments that can be interchanged at a Workstation. This allows - for example - upgrading a "favourite" gun, building a better sword from 2 others that have good parts, or just simply replacing an existing rifle with a better one. There are also utility devices such as grappling hooks, telelocators (weapon-style teleporter), hoverboards, decoy generators, and building tools. Various things can be built, from a simple wall, to a teleporter.
The player's character has various skills (including Agility, Energy, Stealth, Melee) which are increased by assigning points gained by completing quests, challenges, or clearing enemy towers. There is no limit to how high a skill may be, and if you so wish, every point can be added to a single skill. The skill-set is diverse enough to specialise as a sniper, commander, pilot, tank, sword-bot, etc., as well as developing a more balanced robot.
Another ability the player has access to is "time-ripping". When this is turned on, the entire world stops except for you; even new projectiles you generate (from firing your gun) will remain stationary until time-ripping ceases. Grappling hooks will still function as normal though. The player's robot can store up to 15 seconds of time-rip; this can be replenished by collecting donut-shaped pick-ups scattered around the landscape.
Pros:
*Open world; virtually unlimited in size
*No skill limits
*Diverse abilities & items
*AI is challenging
*Game's source code can be altered for advanced modding
*Playable on 8 year old laptops
Cons:
*Multi-play is limited to 2-player co-op
*Main quest-line is very short

I've been playing Sims all of my life, I have every single Sims 2 game in existence and I told myself I was going to just stick to those, but now I've gotten into this game and it's fun and interesting with the new stuff they added. It's a never ending game with no real goal other then to just have fun. I would recommend this game if you like any Sims game and maybe I'll even get into Sims 4 someday when I get all of these.

The Sims 3:
+ Purchase a house for your family or build and design your own with hundreds of customisation options. Buy pools, decorative garden plants, televisions, computers, exercise machines, kitchen appliances, cars, toys for toddlers, sculptures, pet animals (DLC)....the list is huge!
+ Work as a master criminal, a journalist, celebrity or even a detective + more! Attend University to further your studies and become a video game designer, sports agent or arts appraiser (DLC). Go travelling to Egypt, France and China (DLC). This game is packed with plenty to do.
+ Many different skills for your sims to level up, science, cooking, athleticism, logic, charisma etc, so you can have a very diverse gameplay experience.
+ Optional quests or objectives will become available from schooling, work and elsewhere, allowing you to participate in one-off opportunities with rewards.
+ Several neighbourhoods to play in, each with a unique layout.
+ There's a large amount of playtime in the Sims 3 for players of all sorts. I managed to get over 100 hours out of it.
- Micromanagement is very unresponsive, Sims refuse to complete workplace objectives over and over and decide what they want to do themselves, instead of what you've told them. High free will means Sims react to basic needs problems like feeding a baby or bathing themselves, but it also results in ignoring your human commands repeatedly, which gets infuriating after a few hours.
- While I acknowledge graphics aren't a major focus of Sims gameplay, it could definitely be improved. Aesthetically, this game is disappointing.
- The game is quite expensive, even though it's now 8 years old (as of 20/02/2017). DLC is also pricey, so make sure you absolutely want this game before paying in full, or wait for a sale.
- Bad pathing by Sims, they don't interact with the environment well and get stuck in certain spots. Could be much smoother.
- Despite the vastness of Sims 3, it can become boring after awhile. Once you build a mansion filled with the most luxurious objects money can buy and had a family, there's really not much else to do. This game has a cycle of repetition, whereby you continue to do the same tasks over and over, just in different ways and styles. Sure, the kids in your family grow up and you're able to control their lives, but it's like starting from scratch again, where's the sense of accomplishment in that? It's the balance between fun and repetitive content which the Sims 3 suffers from. There's a real conflict here, with the many facets of variability trying to shine, but then a monotonous feeling sometimes overshadowing it.
Overall Score: 7.5/10

This game is only 10 dollars, so for that price I can kinda almost recommend it, but I won't, because I feel it's an extremely lazy attempt at a video game. The start of the game feels ok, the combat is more or less enjoyable at first, but after the first few levels it gets extremely repetitive. You will be presented with quite a few different enemies over the course of the game, some of them bosses. Those fights are somewhat cool, though you can feel overwhelmed by what is going on on the screen at first. You literally only have 2 attacks. Press X for melee combos and RT for a gun shot. You have limited ammo, but there are usually enough drops. You can also bite other vampires and either suck their blood for health (which I found extremely necessary and which makes you invulnerable for the duration) or infect them and detonate them with Y. That's about all you get with the combat. You can also jump and dash through most attacks, which is also required to survive.
Let's just say this game is not for casuals. I'm not bad at brawlers, but this one is just boring, because all combos are simply "press x". You can vary things up with the direction pad, but that's it. And at times you even need to to solve a "puzzle" (juggle an enemy and launch him into a grinder for example). I find it extremely boring. What's worse is that you can't dash out of a combo, meaning you mash the x button to kill enemies, but you can easily get hit by another attack, because your character does not accept the dash command while hitting someone, instead of cancelling the attack or transitioning to the dash action. Combine this with the fact that you fall to the ground when you get hit and that you can die really easily once you're on the ground since there does not seem to be any "quick get up" mechanic (or I've missed it) and you can quickly lose a battle against multiple foes.
The save points are also weirdly positioned. Often they are ok, but sometimes you have to complete a difficult fight and then complete an even more difficult platforming section or the other way around. And when you die, it's back to last checkpoint. That can be quite frustrating. That being said I am not at level 12 or 13 (of 15 I think), so you will get through sooner or later if you're not a hopeless case, but the amount of unncecessary frustration is high.
Platforming: Whoever designed the controls for this game needs to be punished. They are unprecise and the required backflip is executed by first running in one direction, quickly turning and pressing the jump button. This is infuriating throughout the game, because not only do you need some space to do this properly, you also need to judge where you will land. It is even a required mechanic during a boss fight, which can screw you over hard. You can also wall jump and dash in midair.
Later on there is also Flappy Bird in the game. Great. Just what I was looking for.
Oh and let's not forget the poison. The ♥♥♥♥ing poison, which kills you instantly and sends you back several minutes.
The art style looks pretty at first, but it gets so boring after a while, because you're only in this one big castle, going down, then up, then down again...the setting never really changes.
The story is presented in boring chat bubbles in game...the little there is of it. Meh. Forgettable. You can't skip that♥♥♥♥♥♥either, so if you die at some point it can happen that you have to watch the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ "cutscenes" over and over again.
How one is supposed to get a good score in the game is beyond me. It rates you at the end of the level. I have never even come close to even getting one extra point for time or health. I dunno. I'm apparently just "worm chow", yet worm chow can apparently beat the game. Meh.
There are also skulls to collect. You can upgrade health or ammo with them. Most of them I didn't even find, some I didn't try to reach, because the risk reward system is severely misjudged.
Conclusion: If you love Bloodrayne and 2D Brawlers and want a quick fix you may want to get this. Everyone else should stay clear...it's not expensive, but it's also not very good.

A game about lesbian anime schoolgirls fighting zombies? What could possibly go wrong?
A lot of things, actually. While the main series are RPG games this one is just a button mashing Hack ‘n Slash game in which your character is placed in an arena and need to defeat hordes of enemies. Some of the arenas are just circles and others have a few corridors leading to some open areas but there isn’t anything to explore at all. Just go after the zombies and that’s it. While at the first glance the combat system seems to be somewhat interesting in the end you will end up only spamming the same moves over and over again because the game doesn’t really encourage you to change combos and try something new. Just spam the moves you think are more powerful and that’s it. That said, the game gets repetitive fast and the story doesn’t help much. While some of the dialogues are actually fun the whole thing isn’t something that make you want to pay attention because it is actually poor. The game, just like in the original series, works with the level up system but now this time you actually need to distribute the points in the attributes you want to upgrade the most. And well… the balancing of this thing isn’t really good since if you just spend all your points and max out the defense attribute your character will be almost immune to damage, something that is a game breaking feature that should not exist outside the cheats (that you unlock after beating the game) That said you can make this game be painfully easy, just making things even more boring. Just like in the main games there's an item shop where you can buy new weapons and well… just buy the strongest one and that’s it. You don’t really need to plan anything since in this game, unlike in the main series, the weapon you wield don’t really changes your combos in any way. If there’s something in this game that I think it was a nice addition to the series is the customization. At the same time it is a bit too simple the game allows to resize the accessories and place them wherever the heck you wish. Like, literally. If you, for whatever reason, want to place a wrist watch inside the character's head, you can. If you want to shove something into their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, you can also do that. If you want your character to have a giant hat flying upon their head, take a guess. YOU CAN! You can even pretend to be in TF2 and make a towering pillar of hats. But the customization isn’t only limited to accessories, you can also unlock different variations of the characters main outfit and, if you want, you can also use a torn-up version of their main set of clothing so they will fit more to the zombie apocalypse scenario. (We all know you will actually make your characters wear that for other reasons) The graphics are ok when it comes to the playable characters but the scenery is way too bland. Ahh, whatever, nobody plays Neptunia games for the graphics anyway. The soundtrack is mediocre at the best, you might just want to put something else to play on Spotify. There aren't many glitches to mention but one thing that is annoying is that the game sometimes stop working when you boot it up on full screen. I really recommend you to play the game in windowed mode so this problem won’t annoy you.
In an overall this is just a mediocre Hack ‘n Slash game that can only please Neptunia fans since it features a lot of different characters from different games and if you don’t even know who they are I don’t really think you’ll enjoy the game at all. And I can only recommend this game if it’s part of some sale since it doesn’t worth its full price.

When I first started hearing about the Hyperdimension Neptunia side games, at first I was looking forward to them as a fan of the series and everything about it. Then felt rather disappointed when I started seeing the content of games like Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed or Hyperdevotion Noire: Goddess Black Heart. I felt like all they had to deliver was either over the top fanservice, which I'm not really okay with, in the series (I don't mind fanservice as long as it's not over the top, in this case) and... I don't think that having a tsundere character as a protagonist is a good idea. I feel like there's little to go with. And I really love Noire as a character. But like... particularly with Neptunia U. The way I see it is the following: "Ripping clothes in combat? Really? What am I playing? A Hyperdimension Neptunia game or a Senran Kagura game?"
What I can say is that my view on the Neptunia side games I'm aware of changed when I heard, saw and played MegaTagmension Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies. This game ACTUALLY has something more to deliver, even if it's not much.
The game was released in 2015 in Japan and at the time, only for the PS Vita. Then a year later in North America and Europe. And got its Steam release that same year, in October 3rd.
**SPOILERS AHEAD**:
The story in itself... is nothing really special. It's not something memorable, but not something forgettable either, taking around 19-21 hours to complete.
: If you've played Neptunia U or some of the Senran Kagura games, you won't spot that many differences. If you didn't, then here's how it is. Unlike the main Hyperdimension Neptunia games, this game is pretty much a hack and slash. You have a total of 14 different characters to play as which are unlocked as you progress through the story and their transformed forms make it a total of 28 characters, which you get after you beat the story. Each with their own style of gameplay and special moves, some requiring more dexterity than others. But once you get the hang of their combos, the gameplay turns out to be what's probably the best part of the game. Though don't get used to having every action assigned to a single button press. Certain actions require small button combinations, so read the tutorials carefully.
This is also the very first Neptunia game to feature Multiplayer. Co-op, in this case. So if you got three more friends with the game, gather round, set up a room and have fun. It's worth it if you're hunting collectibles, which unlock mostly just outfits for the characters.
: For a port of the PS Vita, I'd say the graphics look rather decent. It retains the art style that has always been used for the series and I never really encountered any graphical glitches in the game.
Lastly, I should mention the sountrack, which is a mixed bag. Not in a bad sense, though. While it re-uses tracks from previous games, MegaTagmension also has a few tracks of its own. But nevertheless, the music is always really enjoyable.
So with that taken care of, it's time for the final score. Which, in my opinion, is a 6/10. It's slightly above average. I honestly wish I could give this game a higher score, but I can't. One aspect cannot carry the whole game on its own, no matter how good the gameplay is. While the graphics are decent, those don't make the game perfect. And the story could be a lot more memorable than it is. Even so, that shouldn't be a reason to not grab this game. If you're able to, get it and give it a shot. You won't regret it!

Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon
Explosive visuals. Neon colours everywhere. "Is this the real life? Is this just fantasy?"
Featuring an OST entirely composed by the australian music duo Power Glove, the sound is infused with electronic nostalgia that brings to mind many popular 80s film moments. It is one of the most memorable OST and I guarantee it will stay with you for days to come.
The gameplay is almost identical to that of Far Cry 3, but with a few tweaks and simplifications. Being a game influenced by films such as Robocop, Terminator, Rocky, Tron, Commando etc, the main hero is a cybernetic super-soldier that obliterates everything in his way with the use of his "little friend". Also, there is a dedicated key for giving your enemies the middle finger.
Keeping in mind that the game is supposed to be an hommage to the 80s films, the story, while being a massive cliche, has several exciting moments and is downright amusing. However, it's only there as an excuse for the gameplay.
Extremely fun to play and doesn't drag on with only 5-7 hours of gameplay.
Michael Biehn as the protagonist's voice, one of the best soundtracks ever made and that perfect 80's vibe.

Warning: Requires Uplay.
What is Uplay? An Ubisoft DRM service similar to Steam, only not as good in my experience (you will need an account). This game can be bought on Steam, but will open up Uplay in order to start, so you'll be running both Uplay and Steam at the same time. I found the Uplay client to run -much- smoother when launched separately rather than through Steam. You may run into problems with Steam tracking game hours (the game save will record playtime if you want a record) and card drops (try using SAM, but don't have any VAC-secured games running).
The actual review:
Blood Dragon runs very well and looks great with my Windows Vista 64-bit and my Radeon HD 6850. Even on medium-high the game will look quite decent, partially due to the video monitor filter. Blood Dragon is an 80's throwback with a better plot than its main game parent. More believable anyway, since Far Cry 3 goes from "I've never killed anymore before." to mass murderer within an hour.
Expect a bunch of sidequests, three kinds of collectables, fast-paced 80's action, cheesy plot, expertly well-executed awful one-liners, silly gun customization, humor, and explosions. If you move fast like I did, you can expect about 5.3 hours of game time with most collectibles collected. I expect normal people to take around 6-8 hours with this title. It's fun enough to consider replaying and short enough to be able to do so. The game doesn't waste your time by padding things out. It's as long as it needs to be.
In conclusion, Blood Dragon is a surprisingly entertaining and solid title hampered by the Uplay client. No one should have to run two DRM services to run one game. It's irritating, but if you decide to go through with it, expect a fun lil' adventure.

That's just it, though.  It's spread so thin.  There are so many cool individual ideas and mechanics in this game, but not a single one of them is done well.  The "action" is slow, piloting an aircraft somehow manages to be just as uninteresting as walking, the rpg mechanics are boring and uninspired, the stealth is crap, the fps mechanics are crap, and the big world you're given to explore lacks anything worth exploring.  Obviously, having only played 1.3 hours, I can't tell you how the late game plays.  I can, however, tell you that the first 1.3 hours are astonishingly dull.  Even the base being bombarded with meteors was boring, all it means is you have to sit in a tastelessly coloured "house" for a while.
That's another thing, the visuals.  Obviously I wasn't expecting anything gorgeous, I saw the screenshots.  Keep in mind, however, that what you see in the screenshots is the best that the game has to offer in the visual department.  The environments are woefully underpopulated with any kind of visually interesting scenery.  Every other aspect of the fluff is equally lacking: missions have no flavour, enemies and allies alike lack even a slight amount of personality, etc.
TL;DR:
Describing the environment is, perhaps, one of the best ways of describing the game on a whole: an ambitiously vast expanse of nothing.

I rate the game Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War - Soulstorm 4/5. Good.
Far from being just a mere expansion, this game is more than large enough to be an entire game in its own right with multiple factions and a different ending for each faction. This game lets you play full single player campaigns as The Imperial Guard, The Blood Ravens Space Marines, The Adeptus Sorroritas chapter of The Bloody Rose (AKA the Bolter ♥♥♥♥♥es), The forces of Chaos Undivided, The Dark Eldar, The Eldar, the Orks, The Necrons or as The Tau Empire.
Of course, I played a single player campaign through as The Tau Empire (my favorite Warhammer 40k faction) and even when played (fairly leisurely though) on easy difficulty my campaign lasted for about 33 hours. There is also an extensive skirmish mode which can be played against the computer or, with the right software (such as Tunngle), with other people over the Internet. Because of all the factions you can possibly choose to play as, this is a very replayable game (and the skirmish mode has a LOT of maps to play on including all the old maps from previous Dawn of War add-ons and expansions) but this game can, at times, suffer from a sense of severe repetition and of course, it helps a lot of you like Command and Conquer style "RTS" (Real time Strategy as they are called) games. RTS games are not really my main thing and I'm honestly not that great at them.
The (Greater) Good:
+This game has all the benefits and most of the weaknesses of Warhammer 40k Dark Crusade. For the most part, this game is simply longer. If you wanted to play a Dawn of War game which is like Dark Crusade this is the game for you. The wonderful options and strategic freedom provided by the global tactical map featured in Dark Crusade returns in Soulstorm. All RTS games should give you the excellent degree of strategic freedom of choosing which battles to fight and in what order which this game gives you. The global tactical map which you use between battles also does a wonderful job of giving you a star-system wide understanding of what is going on in the war. If only Command and Conquer or Homeworld had given me this degree of choice. (I loved the Homeworld games but the degree of strategic choice offered in Soulstorm (and Dark Crusade for that matter) blows the linear campaigns of other RTS games away and ideally should set a whole new standard of freedom).
+The controls are fairly intuitive and standard for a RTS game making it easy to learn.
+Just as in Dark Crusade, Soulstorm reminds you to save it whenever you quit and never seems to freeze up. Indeed, I found very, very few bugs (other than units with long range being able to shoot through solid walls and a few basic path-finding problems in certain maps). This game never froze up for me.
+The multiplayer mode options included in this game are truly extensive and there are a wide variety of multiplayer battlefields to fight on for 2 to 8 players at a time (Just like in Dark Crusade).
+The game menus are very well designed and the "cute" little imperial thoughts for the day persist in this game on the main menu and on the game exit menu.
Mediocre stuff:
+/- The game has certain "honor guard" units which can be taken with you from battle to battle in a somewhat persistent manner. I love persistent armies in RTS games as they offer a whole extra degree of realistic tactical complexity. The armies in Soulstorm (and Dark Crusade) are only mildly persistent from one battle to another. Only certain squads are retained and brought with you into the next offensive. Most other units you "created" or called in during the battle vanish completely causing you to need to go through the process of "creating" the units command and conquer style all over gain during the next battle. This is totally unrealistic and I have begun to hate this common gameplay element in RTS increasingly as time goes by. I could understand that early computers might not have been able to keep track of every single unit you made from one battle to the next (MAYBE) but now games should remember every unit you ever called in or created and put those units to use in the next battle to lower the game's feeling of repetition. I want armies which have units which persist from one battle to another (or at least an option for the game to allow this).
+/-The Adeptus Sorroritas and the Dark Eldar factions and the new "air" units (though they control just like ground units and even hover in place and don't act at all like actual air units should) are welcome additions. The "air" units however are a disappointment. When I think of air power I think of massive airstrikes or aircraft units which make continual strafing and bombing runs and so forth, not little hovering vehicles (like helicopters at best) which I can send here or there like any other light tank.
+/- The soundtrack is adequate (the Tau theme is very fitting and probably the best new piece of music in this game) but as before it is largely boring and derivative (but not obnoxious, unless an Adeptus Sorroritas theme is playing) and sets the mood well).
Bad stuff:
-As is true in any other part of Dawn of War I, the graphics, especially by today's standards are adequate but mediocre and the color scheme seems a bit bland, including a wide range of beige and gray colors. It's odd to try to describe but the colors in this game tend towards faded colors as if they were being filtered through parchment. This might have been done on purpose but it does not suit some factions very well (like the Necrons or the Tau). The landscapes are particularly drab. The camera can be zoomed very far in and re-angled to any perspective but dense fog prevents you from being able to see anything approaching the whole battlefield in the main viewscreen.
-Like in any other Dawn of War I game or expansion the view can never be zoomed out very far which can make selecting large numbers of units at a time (which is something I love to do to ensure that different types of units properly reinforce one another when I have a large army) pretty problematic. The perspective issues come together to severely limit how epic the battles can feel and instead make them feel more like a table-top RPG than I think a videogame should. As in Dawn of War, In Dark Crusade you always feel as though every battle is just a minor skirmish in the overall war because graphically, it always looks that way. This is a common problem in most RTS games however, even to this day. Perhaps this was remedied in Supreme Commander (and I know it was Remedied in the Homeworld games) but most RTS games definitely have this problem.
-Like in Dark Crusade each faction has but one victorious single-player campaign ending. If your faction is defeated in the campaign you are essentially asked if you want to be booted out to the main menu. There is no bad ending, no final monologue showing what happens because you failed. Just a menu.
-You cannot play through the single-player campaign mode either cooperatively or otherwise which is really too bad because this would have made for a great, ongoing, persistent multiplayer mode (Just like in Dark Crusade).
-This game's battles, being very similar to battles found in most Command and Conquer games, are fairly repetitious. You need to get your little infantry units out and capture strategic points (or supplies as the case may be) early or else you will lose. There is no other really viable way to play and as a result your tactical options are always limited and unrealistic. In real life, well...a lot of things are different but its is ludicrous to have to capture resources during a battle to decide what forces you will get during that same battle. The forces you have and the resources you have access to in one battle should be primarily decided based on what occurred in the battle which occurred previously, NOT the battle you are playing now.
