A very nifty action/RPG game with graphics that give me a warm and fuzzy PS1 feeling. It's nice to be in a world of triangles vs. all of the procedural boxy voxel games out there. The procedural generation makes exploring your world interesting, and even when things don't line up -quite- right, I never ran in to very many situations where a mission couldn't be completed. Combat works well, and scrounging for gun parts adds to the fun. The soundtrack fits well and never felt repetitive. Other pluses are low system requirements, multi-player, and the ability to build your own bases (kinda). Now for critiques; the procedural side missions can become repetitive after a time, and the procedural world can make it difficult to remember land marks. Still, I think the positives outweigh in my opinion. If you like the cartoon Reboot, you will probably like this game.

After I saw this game for the first time, I knew I had to get it; it looked brilliant. Due to my limited resources, I managed to buy it one month later. Didn't mind the waiting time, I was happy I finally got it.
I pressed the button and excitingly waited to get into the game, but then....BAM! Some kind of "Java error". The game recommends me to update Java. I update it, but the game keeps opening the Java fils with WinRar and not with Java application. I fix it. The game shows no errors anymore and the launcher throws me in, but then...BAM! The game crashes. I put some research into it and find out that it runs poorly on Intel HD Graphics. So I mess around with the settings and finally manage to get it working by disabling anti-aliasing. I also had to keep the ambient occlusion off because it caused crashes, too.
I finally create my character and read the textual intro. I'm thrown into this weird♥♥♥♥♥city. The game only tells me I need to go to the house where various stations are placed (Quest station, Weapons station, etc.). I find the house and get some equipment. My adventures begin!
To keep this review somewhat short, I'll skip the descriptive nature of it - the game feels incomplete. You virtually have no tutorials or ANYTHING that might give you a hint about some of the game's features (there aren't many). There are no main quests or goals, there are just some random bosses that you can kill to get some clue about the game's poor storyline. And then you get the location of a new boss. Rinse and repeat. "Side quests" are always the same, either you have to kill someone, protect someone, escort him to some other place, bring him a disk that you find in a defusable bomb crate, plant some "bug" behind their back or stalk them. There you go, I just listed most of the quests you'll face. You can only have one quest active at a time, so you need to go back and forth to get new ones all the time. The game doesn't explain the crafting system to you at all - basically, if you find an item that says "incomplete", it's actually an item part that you can use with other parts to create that kind of weapon. The first gun I bought looked like a whole gun in its icon, but it was actually a part, so I was unable to equip it. You also don't level up in a traditional way, every quest grants you a certain number of skill points which you can directly apply to improve your stats. And the art style is pretty bad even though it looked kinda cool in the screenshots. The camera is badly placed so you always feel like you're stuck to the ground.
There are some redeeming qualities but there aren't many - hoverboards and ships are cool, there's a time-ripping ability which slows the time but you remain fast, and you can gather random robots as followers to help you on your quest. But the game falls short on delivering a satisfying experience, mostly you're just wondering why you're still playing. So, my suggestion is, skip this game completely. It isn't worth those 10 euros. If you really have to get it, at least buy it in a bundle.

I never thought I'd be doing this for GTA V of all things.
I spent a lot of time on the Xbox 360 version, just messing around with my friends and enjoying the updates as they came.  We moved to PC, hearing about the better graphics and more content.  Our characters looked great, the world was awesome, and we thought this would be a great time.
Big mistake.
While the Single Player is great (only played it once), the Online is one of the most enjoyable games I've ever played... barring the ever-present hackers, constant threat of random bans with no appeal process, rich jerks with jet bikes and fighter jets.  Trust no-one online.  You will never escape these threats, and going into invite-only sessions locks content off to you.
The deck has been stacked to incredible levels against the player; Rockstar's decision to make the CEO/Biker/Gunrunner DLC businesses only accessible in public sessions (with aforementioned hackers and rich jerks) shows a distinct hostility towards anyone not willing to buy fake money for real money.  Do any amount of research on "solo public sessions" and you will see a great deal of players creating ways to get a session where they can just PLAY THE GAME without losing their time/money investments in 10 seconds.  There are in-game groups (known as crews) dedicated to just making a safe session for all involved, vote-kicking anyone not with the crew and policing their members to let everyone run their shipments.  Let this show how a decent number of players are rebelling against this pointless public session only nonsense.
There is no good reason for the DLC businesses to be restricted to public sessions, while broadcasting your shipments within 10 seconds to the whole gameworld.  The worst reason is shameless greed.  The most insulting thing is that anyone who actually destroys these shipments only gets $2,000 and minor experience boosts for the whole shipment.  It's not even worth it for people to bother (you can easily spend $2,000 on just buying more ammo and armor), but you can bet your firstborn child that they will blow it up out of pure spite.
There are other reviews that express the many glaring problems with Online better, but I needed to throw my 2 cents in.  I can't recommend this beautiful game to new players.  This game where the design is now glaringly biased towards microtransactions, relying on its own toxic community to frustrate you into giving in to said microtransactions.  Where each DLC increases the in-game prices for its content, making a clear attack on your real money versus your limited time to earn the money doing missions.  This game where you can get randomly banned for playing by the rules, with a very real possibility of your progress being totally wiped.
I didn't think I'd be doing this for GTA V.

This is another review I would set as "neutral" instead of only thumbs up or down, but this time the negative review is mostly not about the game at its core. Let me explain why.
Regardless of its flaws, the game is still fun and it's got some original and interesting gamemodes... but since there are few people playing it (it was in a bundle recently, but the playercount is not drastically increased), I was only able to play a few matches. As for any multiplayer-only games, I fear that the playerbase will come back to zero again sometime in the future, this is why features like AI bots should be in every game.
Now, here's a little rant: I don't understand why most gamers disagree with me and most developers (both indie and AAA) don't realize this, but AI bots are important even in multiplayer-centered games! They could fill up all empty slots if there's less people in a server, and they could still let you enjoy the game's content even without a playerbase... but since the game doesn't have them and online is rarely active, that made me sadly regret my purchase (pretty much the reason why I rarely buy multiplayer-only games: it's like renting them temporarily). Which is why you should think twice before spending your money on something you probably won't be able to play unless a big group of friends is willing to get the game too and play some matches with you (in this case, go for it).
Singleplayer lasts forever, multiplayer doesn't. And that's a fact.
In conclusion:
+ Good concept
+ Fast-paced, "pick up and play" game with a decent variety of guns
+ Interesting gamemodes and maps
- No AI bots
- No server browser
- Minor flaws: can't voice chat on steam while you're playing, moving the ball in the soccer gamemode can be a little laggy, inability to disable "hitmarkers" and to manually choose the character models.

There is but one thing that I must disagree with in this game, and that is the incredibly low perspective. It nearly leaves my eyes sore staring at my screen too long, and yet I still find myself pouring hours into the game. There is just something so captivating to me about painting an army to my specific tastes, then sending them to battle against a cornucopia of different enemies, be it the long-range Tau or the resilient and slow moving Necrons, the game does well to offer variety in nearly every regard. There are nine seperate factions to play as, each is very independant of the other, and rarely is something ever copied or re-used. The voice acting is especially well done, and be it the cry for help or a taunt thrown towards the enemy, each line is spoken with skill and care for the character they are representing. I do, in fact, prefer the previous DLC, Dawn of War: The Dark Crusade's campaign, but then the multiplayer in any RTS game I have ever played has never felt quite as different as this specific title. Finally, I must say that if you are looking for an strategy game with serious a range of different factions with recognizable similarities, then there may be no better title that Dawn of War: Soulstorm.

Remember APB:Reloaded? That game where you would get completely screwed if you didn't put 20$ here and there for awesome vehicule and OP weapons? You see, one of the great things about GTA:O is that it's getting updated once every 3 to 6 months which is okay I guess? Where's the downside? Well, every updates content is locked behind a paywall that is unreachable for any new player, casual gamer and people who don't have a dedicated group of friend to efficiently spam the Heist missions, which gives you about 250 000$ per hour on a solid run. 250k can't be that bad right? well nah,
-every major updates comes with a new ''organisation'' which is a worst investment for making money than just farming heist at the cost of 1m to 5m $
-every new vehicules, which is like the only thing to spend money on, can cost from 1M for a normal, pimped out vehicules to 5m for the special vehicules that came out with the last update.
So now, we are at about 4 hours of farming heists with maximum efficiency to buy ONE new item from an update. Or you can spend like 20$ of microtransaction to get 1.25M dollar.
Where's the outrage? Most of the updates can total up to 40 MILLION DOLLAR IN ITEM if you want to own everything, which with the 8m/100$ card, sums up a 500$ Bill or 160 hours of non-stop farming heists since remember, it's the most efficient way of farming money.
Honestly as a new player, you are beyond screwed at this point since most of the player nowaday got everything from hacker who dropped money on them and/or are level 100 which means they have all the weapons that can obliterate a fresh character.

Almost nobody plays the missions, you saw that trailer with like 20 people parachuting down a mountain? well you're never gonna experience that. period. All the 3 organization missions, which luckily are more rewarding than just spamming the vanilla missions, require you to pay at least 1 million $ to make and player can destroy your progress if they feel like it. Every lobby is either composed of 1 or multiple hacker or some no-life who play since the beginning of time with a fighter jet(hydra) and just goes around, killing everybody without anything you can do, no matter if you are level 1 or level 100 with every weapons in the game, the jet guy will just outsmart you.

So yeah, this game is dying, everything in multiplayer is so outrageously out priced that you're better off buying microtransaction(but if I was you, I wouldn't buy the game at all). half of the community are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, most of the time when you try to join a MP lobby, you will get below 10 person lobby and when you join a full, 30 people lobby, either there's a hacker or everyone speak a language that you don't understand(half of the time it's mandarin, the other half it's either russian, french and sometime german). you will get completely destroyed by anyone who wants to mess with you and no matter how good you are at gaming, you won't be able to fight back because of the underpowered weapons from under level 80.

(This is a review for GTA Online).
TL;DR broken garbage with little to no customer support, genuinely disgraceful title, move on.
GTA Online is riddled with game-breaking bugs. You WILL lose your♥♥♥♥♥♥ whether it's hundreds of thousands of dollars mysteriously being eaten by the void or your precious business shipments lost due to crashes. When that happens, you have to fight for days to get the support team to even read your messages instead of sending you an automated reply and the chances of them refunding your property, EVEN WITH A VIDEO, are extremely slim.
The following is one of many examples from personal experience. This particular bug, along with Rockstar's refusal to reimburse hundreds of thousands of lost dollars, has happened to me twice.
You spend an hour retrieving four top-range cars for your vehicle export business. That'll net you about $500,000, enough to buy that armored car you've been eyeing up! You get a group of four players to export them all at once and you pay up the $80,000 to fully upgrade the cars to maximise your profits. You start the sale, but wait! GTA has decided that you don't get to sell your cars today. Your screen goes dark, then it comes back and the map disappears. You float in blue hell for a while. Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ you think. The game crashed! But this is GTA Online -- the most unpredictable AAA title you've ever played -- and to your relief, the game recovers a few seconds later. It seems your hundreds of thousands of dollars are saved; you and your friends have loaded in outside your garage, ready to export the vehicles. Except you can't move. Your friends can't move. Everything looks normal, other players drive past you, but you can't move. You can't drive or get out of the car or answer your phone or interact with the world in any way. You spend a few minutes struggling with the game, trying to get the cars to move with no success, but you're a smart guy. You had Shadowplay enabled, so you record the bug in its entirety and then you close the game. Confident that this AAA title has competent support, you send the recording to Rockstar, politely requesting that your cars be returned so that you can retry the sale (hopefully without the game having another meltdown).
"We are unable to verify your claim."
"What? Which part of my claim aren't you able to verify? It's all on the video."
"We apologise for any inconvenience. We are unable to verify your claim."
You're in disbelief at this point. It's hard to wrap your head around the idea that a company with as much money as Rockstar cannot afford to set up competent customer service.
"Seriously? I lose hours of work and hundreds of thousands of dollars, and all you'll give me is "We are unable to verify your claim?" This isn't customer support at all. Can you at least tell me what aspect of my claim you are unable to verify?"
"We apologise deeply for any inconvenience. We will escalate your claim to the proper department"
You experience some relief, hoping that you'll get passed to a thinking, breathing human rather than an underpaid customer support drone who clearly barely speaks English.
... 1 day later ...
"Hello. We apologise for any inconvenience. We are unable to verify your claim."

What to say. What to say. When one first delves into the world of torchlight 2, they are reminded a bit of the diablo series in certain ways, such as the health and mana bars. It is your basic hack and slash dungeon crawler with its various rpg aspects of course. The graphics kind of remind me of borderlands with its cartoony look as well. The storyline of torchlight 2 is okay, but not too in depth. Where it really shines, is when it comes to combat and that is what has had me hooked for hours on end. When you start out you get to choose between 4 different classes of characters and each one with its own sense of uniqueness as well as fun to play. My personal favorite was the engineer, seeing as this class could summon a few varying creatures to heal and do damage in battle. Another thing about torchlight 2 is the fact that no matter what class you are, you get to have a pet to accompany you into battle. Pets level with you and you can even teach them what abilities you want them to learn with spell scrolls. A few other things about this game that I'd like to point out is that it supports 6 player co-op and even supports 8 player co-op with the right mod of course. That's right! It supports mods as well, and they fit flawlessly into the game. I run a few mods on my game such as a class compilation mod which bundles a bunch of community based classes into one bundle that fit seamlessly into the game. And there's even a little bit of pvp action for the player that wants to duke it out with another. Fact of the matter is, if you want a game that surpasses diablo 3 in every aspect but the storyline, this is the game to get. Not to mention it s a lot cheaper than diablo 3 even when it's not on sale. This is a great game, and I really wish the developers would have made some dlc content for it, because I would have paid for it as well.

3089 is an interesting concept and is fairly well executed with the exception that there could be more content. Basically, you're a robot thrown onto this alien world that is inhabited by only other robots. It's always Red vs Blue with you being on Red's side. You start with nothing and have to go buy your own guns and armor. You can also obtain parts by killing other robots or by stealing off of your teammates. This allows you to come up with different combinations that can increase your stats in different ways. One piece of armor might give you increased health, defense, and flying skills, while another can give you gun, melee, and agility.
Another thing is the quest system. It allows you to pick your own quests from these stations in buildings. There are always 13 quests at one time, and they increase in level as you filter through them. The further out you go from the starting point also increases the level of the quest, but also the reward. You can earn credits and skill points through these. While the quests are pretty basic, e.g. go here and disarm this bomb, spy on this robot without being detected, and go kill these robots. The problem with this as thats about the extent of the quests.
Aside from that there are the occasional bosses that show up on your map. They provide a substantial challenge and unless you have some other robots following you around, it can be almost impossible. There's also a building aspect to the game but it's pretty hard to understand. Sometimes you'll build a teleporter and it won't work. You can also build storage boxes to keep some of your things in.
All in all though, I would say it's a fairly fun game to just play for a bit. It's nothing spectacular graphics wise, but it makes up for it by just being fun and interesting in general. I think the developer is working on a sequel, 4089 is what I believe it's called and I hope he'll expand on the already implemented ideas.

Got it in a recent humblebundle as I thought it was a nice looking bonus to the BTA tier.
So after playing a couple of matches I just feel like the movement is not fluid enough, half of the few weapons are mostly useless and there are way too many locations for enemy to shoot at you.
So about movement first. You can't properly jump on most things in certain levels even though there are so many objects that are almost at the jump height (or are at the jump height, but require you to stop and do concentrated jump because of how jumping on objects works), making  jumps feel clunky. In close range face-to-face combat a player can move around objects so much that it's hard to get hit by an enemy or hit them as they run around the objects.
Then the weapons. Flamethrower has a very short range and it takes many hits to kill someone with it. Sniper can be shot quite accurately with or without a scope and when using it anywhere except long bridges/high ground, it's very hard to find someone to shoot with all the objects around. Half the time your deaths come from not being able to see your enemy who is camping in the shadows, sides or holes of multiple objects so that they can't be seen, flanking or just simply killing you from behind. Some places are just so dark that you can't even see an enemy jumping over you without squinting. I think the rifle, shotgun, grenade and rocket launcher are well balanced considering how many sides/corners you have to look out for when you move.
Some maps are just chaotic and full of obstacles so you can't even properly hit enemies.
The graphics and level design looks great, but I can't say I'm enjoying the game with this kind of gameplay design.

I honestly have very mixed feelings about this game. It can be fun but it can also be absolutely rage endusing. I can't say that I would play money on this game ever, even though thats how the developers made the game. You may be wondering how that is. Well you have seperate unlock trees for the factions. It does not sound that bad right? Well for each character you need to level them up seperately. So that means you can get a character on the German side up to level 40 and then decide to use a different character to see what a Paratrooper is like vs a Tank Crew. Well have fun starting from the begging again. Youll have to level up all over again on that character that is in the same faction, so that means using the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ starter weapons, the most notably ♥♥♥♥♥♥ is the M1 on the American side.
Lets talk about the weapons and the overall balance since I'm already on the topic. Long story short, there is little weapon balance. There are clearly better weapons than others. Using the starting weapon for the factions is actually the worst experience. They have a low rate of fire and are surprisingly inacurate for marksman rifles. I have gotten longer range kills with SMGs, which seem to have a longer effective range than the starting rifles. It doesnt help that the gunplay in general is just terrible. The guns sway and kick unrealisticly. If you fire rapidly, youll have better luck at getting a kill than firing slowly while trying to be accurate.
Accuracy seems to be a minor factor in kills, because it all comes down to who can get a headshot. You may be thinking then, "Oh just aim for their head". While in any other game youd be right, however in this one its random, or at least feels that way. I've gotten more headshots from spraying and praying than actually trying to line one up. This problem isnt just with me though, Ive talked to people in game that have the same experiences.
Now you may be thinking, "He must hate this game". No, I dont. I feel like this game has so much potential and it sucks that the systems in this game, like gunplay and weapon balance, are so underdeveloped. There are other things that I did not talk about, like how ineffective the AA guns are, and how certain factions feel stronger than others. If there was a rating of "Give it some time" or something alonf the lines of that, I would choose it, but I cant. So with that I cant say I recomend it. The only saving grace for this game in my eyes is that the developers had the sense to make it free to play. Hopefully they will try and improve on the issues I talked about. I hope this game can turn itself around.

- High production values
- Fantastic sound, music & ambience
- Good, stylish, detailed graphics
- Controls are smooth and work well (I used keyboard)
- Quite immersive
- Well thought-through game design
- Fluid gameplay (no bugs)
- Graphics "vibrate" a little when you move left/right off the screen
- No concrete story; just fragments
- No real "adventure" components; just mostly jumping around and activating objects

Have a relaxing, meditative playthrough and indulge your senses.

(This is a review for GTA Online).
TL;DR broken garbage with little to no customer support, genuinely disgraceful title, move on.
GTA Online is riddled with game-breaking bugs. You WILL lose your♥♥♥♥♥♥ whether it's hundreds of thousands of dollars mysteriously being eaten by the void or your precious business shipments lost due to crashes. When that happens, you have to fight for days to get the support team to even read your messages instead of sending you an automated reply and the chances of them refunding your property, EVEN WITH A VIDEO, are extremely slim.
The following is one of many examples from personal experience. This particular bug, along with Rockstar's refusal to reimburse hundreds of thousands of lost dollars, has happened to me twice.
You spend an hour retrieving four top-range cars for your vehicle export business. That'll net you about $500,000, enough to buy that armored car you've been eyeing up! You get a group of four players to export them all at once and you pay up the $80,000 to fully upgrade the cars to maximise your profits. You start the sale, but wait! GTA has decided that you don't get to sell your cars today. Your screen goes dark, then it comes back and the map disappears. You float in blue hell for a while. Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ you think. The game crashed! But this is GTA Online -- the most unpredictable AAA title you've ever played -- and to your relief, the game recovers a few seconds later. It seems your hundreds of thousands of dollars are saved; you and your friends have loaded in outside your garage, ready to export the vehicles. Except you can't move. Your friends can't move. Everything looks normal, other players drive past you, but you can't move. You can't drive or get out of the car or answer your phone or interact with the world in any way. You spend a few minutes struggling with the game, trying to get the cars to move with no success, but you're a smart guy. You had Shadowplay enabled, so you record the bug in its entirety and then you close the game. Confident that this AAA title has competent support, you send the recording to Rockstar, politely requesting that your cars be returned so that you can retry the sale (hopefully without the game having another meltdown).
"We are unable to verify your claim."
"What? Which part of my claim aren't you able to verify? It's all on the video."
"We apologise for any inconvenience. We are unable to verify your claim."
You're in disbelief at this point. It's hard to wrap your head around the idea that a company with as much money as Rockstar cannot afford to set up competent customer service.
"Seriously? I lose hours of work and hundreds of thousands of dollars, and all you'll give me is "We are unable to verify your claim?" This isn't customer support at all. Can you at least tell me what aspect of my claim you are unable to verify?"
"We apologise deeply for any inconvenience. We will escalate your claim to the proper department"
You experience some relief, hoping that you'll get passed to a thinking, breathing human rather than an underpaid customer support drone who clearly barely speaks English.
... 1 day later ...
"Hello. We apologise for any inconvenience. We are unable to verify your claim."

Do you like action? Do you like violence? Do you enjoy sadistically forcing people to fight for your pleasure?
Then look no forward than the American government!
Cough, er, I mean Brawlhalla.
But for real, if you enjoy fighting, fast paced games, this is for you. And it's free. And it's not resource demanding. And it's free. And it's fast to load. And it's free.
This is a F2P game, but I can tell they were heavily inspired by league of legends cash shop. You buy skins and cosmetic items for your characters, weapons, and other stuff like that. You can also pay to buy champions faster. This isn't pay to win, just is convienent. For me personally, I can't play games for hours on end, as I have work and school. So they offer a very good deal where you can pay $20 and get every champion now and forever. But I didn't just buy it because it was a good offer, but because this is an amazing indie studio.
I purchased that pack 30 minutes after downloading the game. Not even joking. After 30 minutes, I just wanted to help the team who put the time and energy into making such a great game and offering it for free.
Combat is fast and skillful. This is like league where it's easy to learn but very hard to master. So many different skills and strategies.  The art direction is beatiful, it runs well, and it feels good. Additionally, load times are incredibly quick, and you can play multiple games an hour. This is a good, quick game to play before you need to leave for school but it also lends itself well to hour long play sessions.
I haven't invested to much time yet, but I feel confident to say that anyone who is enjoys multiplayer games, fighter games, or high action games will enjoy this. And it's free.
If you loved playing any of the smash brothers, I recommend playing this game. It's a lot like Super Smash Bros. Melee but with an even better formula.

What to say, what to say.  I started a few characters in 2014/15 early release stage.  I remember several bugs and the grind cost for weapons, so I stopped playing.  Then the game was "officially" released but I didn't start playing again until Aprilish 2017.  Here's my point of view from what I've noticed upon my return.  The credit cost is still high.
1. I don't play war games, often.  They're great and challenging when you have a group of friends against another organized group.  Problem is you never know when that'll happen.  Depending on the resources spend in a war battle, it could be a massacre or evenly matched so fun will vary in the eyes of the player.  When you play as a general and spend war bonds then play as a hero in the FPS, it can be engaging.
2. All I hear people say is that the "end" guns are not balanced.  That holds water, but the skills of the "player" also play a part in the "fairness."  Why would you run into the fray of automatic weapons without one?  Holding a M1 garand?  Play your role and strike at a distance, then steal their weapon and go on a rampage.  That's how I get to use the German Sturmgewehr.  Never forget that all the weapons and vehicles are based off of the actual ones used in WW2.  Some nations held technological advantages before other caught up.  Remember a head shot counts the same for all weapons.
3. Don't play this game like Call of Duty (modern  series) or Battlefield.  I don't feel like this game was designed like that.  Not to mention you'll just get sniped from recon or tanks when in the open.
4.  Without teamwork the games aren't very fun.  It tends to be like this often but, such is the nature of humans.  Individuality...
So if you like try and find a clan to team up with.  Increases fun, in my opinion but it's not for everyone.
5. The number of &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; or "trolls" are increasing.  The need to whistle/teabag what ever, will destroy the enjoyment of playing.  If you're not good at FPS, then all the deaths you'll acquire and the need to grind for credits will keep you at the bottom.  Don't play war matches.  Tends to draw the better players.
6.  I haven't noticed long queue times recently.  Tankers yes but infantry is quite fast.  Add some AUX seats and you can mix it up.  Of course you have to grind and level up your Infantry man to get AUX seats.  (AUX seats allow the player to change roles in game for new players.  Start as infantry, you can switch to tanker.)
7.  Finally, I hope the Devs add more maps.  They dropped a lot of the graphics when they increased the players per game/server.  Sadly it sounds like people are steering clear but I actually enjoy this game.  Remember it's free so what do you have to lose but time.  This game is in the hands of the developers and the players.  Play your characters' role and you will have a better time.  Want to change your style then choose a different character.
8. Biggest downside is cost for in game stuff.  Even changing your name cost credits.  Squad names too.
Playing devils advocate; maybe the repair costs exist so players don't waster resources as much.  If you lose 10 medium planes and 0 kills, it's gonna cost you.  If you shoot a bazooka to destroy a light tank, it'll cost you.  Lots of things to think about but I feel if you stick to the role of your character then the overall game will improve.  I say give this game a try.  When you get fed up, it's easy to stop playing.

The atmosphere, music, style etc all are A+. I could not wait to play, and enjoyed the first half of the game.
Now for the bad. The game eats inputs. For a platforming game that eats your jump inputs when holding right half the time is unacceptable and becomes completely unplayable towards the end of the game when timing multiple jumps becomes necessary to complete the level. For the first half missing a jump isnt the end of the world, but still can be frustrating.
Second major issue is hitbox detection. Getting hit by things not touching your characters image, being able to stand half into spinning saws without being hurt, falling through platforms that you jump on, or even taking spike damage from the top edge of the platform, but not the spike part you can jump off of...
Third some of the abilities/moves not intuitive. The game also does not say a controller is recommended. I would argue its STRONGLY recommended. I may purchase on psn to see if using a controller solves this.  Now doing a high jump involves running, releasing ALL keys, then pushing jump, but only if Rayne is sliding, if she just comes to a stop she will only do a regular jump. This mechanic is balls.

text:
With the artwork it has, this is effectively BloodRayne The Anime. And for some reason, it works so well to the point it might be even better than the actual BloodRayne games that came out years ago. BloodRayne Betrayal is not for the casual gamer, with its all balls-out approach to platform difficulty, you would have a frustrating time just trying to get a better score in each level and the action comes fast and hard. Very quickly, to the point that Dark Souls almost looks kind in some respect. This is truly a homage to the platform games of old like Castlevania, which seems to be the main inspiration here.
The soundtrack is lovely. There's no voice-acting but the music is exciting and really gets you pumping as you get killing through each level of the game. Graphics are nice and controls seem to work fine. Fine, but not a 100% perfect. BloodRayne looks hot, as usual and she has all kinds of ways to kill the numerous types of enemies that come her way. There's not much of a story here which probably won't do much anyway as you'll be literally killing non-stop.
If you're one for the difficult platform games of old, then this would be a good buy. If you're not the type that can withstand the frustration of getting hit and killed over and over again, then stay away at all cost. It'll take everything from your hand-eye coordination and memory of combos to get the work done.

TL;DR: This game is bad. Only get it to play with your friends a few times. Be warned that the lag is immense even after a year of 'patches' and that BMG don't know how hitboxes are supposed to work.
I personally depise this game for 3 main reasons that I'll describe in more detail later.
- Community
- Devs
- Balancing
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I'll start out with the pros of this game to get them out of the way.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. It's free.
2. It's fun to play with a few friends.
3. They handle replays well so it's easy to share them with most people.
4. The Discord communities are good.
5. There's a 'GG' button at the end of every match which is handy.
6. There's a lot of variety in weapons so there's something to fit everybody's playstyle.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now here are the cons.
----------------------------------
1. The community in-game is indescribably bad. People you play against can be some of the most ignorant, whiny, childish, disgusting scum you've ever seen outside of LoL. I can't play in any lobbies because people always insult me then immediately ban me for NO REASON. Everybody spams taunts and behaves like a brat after the match no matter how nice I am to them (giving them weapons, saving them from silly mistakes they make, giving a thumb's up when they kill me in a skillful way, saying 'gg wp' after every match, etc.).
2. All of the characters are the exact same except for 6 attacks (6 out of a character's 30 attacks are unique), 2 weapons and stats (that don't even matter or barely affect the gameplay).
3. Lag is a huge issue. I've had countless times when a match would start and everybody would immediately teleport uncontrollably off the edge, die, then the game would freeze until the actual match ended meaning that I literally couldn't do anything and lose. Teleporting is the biggest problem and after an entire year of playing, it still hasn't been fixed.
4. The devs at BMG don't listen to community feedback outside of test features. I've went to their discord and requested 3 times, in the place where the devs are meant to listen to feedback, for them to nerf, 'fix' or atleast discourage passive play (Which is ruining the game for all of my friends because it's not fun to play against, has no counters unless they're a terrible player and is rewarded). All 3 times they've either ignored me, told me to just get better (Which is not how you fix a broken playstyle that is uncounterable and is making people hate your game), or even just made fun of me and shrugged me off because i 'missed the salt-pit'. They update the game every week which would be good if it wasn't just for minor tweaks to singular frames, 2 skins (That cost aproximately £4.50 each) and a chest (the equivalent of a lootbox where you give about £3 up front and they give you a random skin from the chest's list).
5. Matchmaking is god awful! I go on ranked and get matched with someone who's 200+ elo above me (The equivalent of 2 or 3 ranks) which means that I'm guaranteed to lose and lose 10 elo. This also happens to other people. I get matched with someone who's 200+ elo under me, they lose, get mad at this game for good reason and go on a losing streak. Don't even get me started on Experimental or Strikeout matchmaking. I, a Diamond player with over 850 hours of experience, get matched with a Silver player who has about 100 - 200 hours. What. The. F*ck?
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I could keep going on and on but I think I'll stop it here. Don't get this game. Only get this game if you want a few hours of local fun with friends then don't pick it up again.

At the time of writing this review, the game is on sale for half-price, which is why I'm comfortable recommending it. Because it feels like it's only half a game.
The story, while good, ends abruptly with very little closure, and even goes out of its way to remind you of all the unresolved plot threads. It feels exactly like "part 1" of a two-part movie, which would be fine if they had, at any point, advertised it as such.
The overwhelming majority of the game takes place on the same two maps, which left me feeling like I never actually left the "starter zone". As a massive fan of the original Deus Ex AND Human Revolution -- both of which sent you all over the world and never stayed too long in one place -- this was a huge disappointment.
The less said about the pointless, tacked-on microtransactions and pointless, tacked-on multiplayer, the better.
BUT, if you can get past all that garbage, there's a really decent game underneath, and it's certainly worth paying half-price for.
But at full-price, this is a definite pass.

Crush Crush. I genuinely can't state anything, this game is immaculate for the area it targets.
Let's start with the easy bits:
The music and sound effects are cheeky and admirable, succulent and sweet. The mere rhythm of it gets my heart singing, and is quite reminiscent to the music of Phoenix Wright Ace Attorney surprisingly, despite being in different genres. A small song is composed, about 1-2 minutes long, and is looped. As a music nerd, it fits the setting; running around chasing the girls. 8/10
Art design is astounding; the characters and icons are all wonderfully designed, and years for me to click it. It might come off as slightly blurred once in a while, but you need to appreciate the dev's hard work of designing the sprites. 8/10
Right, time for the hard bits:
Stroyline. It comes to happen that you, as the main protagonist, 'crush' into eash individual girl as you meet them. By annihilating their plans, of course they thoroughly dislike the idea of your presence in the first place. However, by providing gifts and talking, you are able to increase their friendship levels to the limit. Of course it's not realistic; it's a video game! But quite imaginative one, and I personally found it pretty comedic. 9/10
Gameplay. Your completely average clicker game, but with quite the twist. You may click, or gift depending on the depth of your pockets or your endurance to click. Personally, the 'girl' clicker game has been taught of multiple times ago, but with a different setting (a.k.a Sakura series). But coming from an Early Access game? There's already so much content that's already been unlocked with the gift system, prestige system, hobby system and job system all being well thought out from hobbies increasing in time duration as and when your level gets higher, to actual promotions in-game based on the amoutn of times you've been 'credited' with in-game currency. And offline capabilities? 7 days? Count me in.
In this week alone, I've played 10 hours of this game. And if there's criticism to be made, it's the fact that there's some text grammatically incorrect, hobbies may take way too long to level-up and girls' demands are quite unbalanced. Iro asks for 2 shoes; approximately 118 million in-game currency at Awkward Besties, when Bonnibel asks for a mere cake at 'Crush' level.
To conclude, despite the flaws, Crush Crush is simply quite the masterpiece for an Early Access and FREE! game. A mixture of cookie clicker and Huniepop, it simply hits the spot for me. Absolute marvel of clicker games.
And if you've come this far, you should know one thing
My waifu is Bonnibel. Touch her, and I'll go Yuno Gasai on you XD

A desperate old-school aesthetic without actual old-school substance. The profuse stupidity and half-considered sci-fi tropes are there, the challenge and deliberate balance are not. The noisy, interlaced, "shades-of-pink," VHS aesthetic is simply a distraction from how little is actually going on. The gunfights are all immensely easy, made worse by the fact that the enemies simply throw themselves at the player without ever posing any actual threat or attempting any defensive tactics. The level-up system is completely unnecessary due to the game's abject linearity and lack of variation and simply serves to slowly buff the player out of control. Aside from the upgrade system and the visuals, the game's mechanics are mostly identical to Far Cry 3's, except that Far Cry 3's enemy layouts actually created situations which required some consideration, especially when going for a stealthy approach. Here, the best strategy is almost always to stand is a narrow corridor -- and there are plenty -- and wait for all of a level's enemies to come rushing to their deaths. For a game that prides itself so much on "old school action," Blood Dragon is surprisingly braindead, even by modern standards.
This is an old-school game for people who have neither experience with old-school games nor the skills necessary for them. I'd like to see one of the people who praised this game -- just one! -- one-credit-clear Metal Slug.

text:
Soulstorm is the last expansion to the first Dawn of War game. The game takes place in the Warhammer 40k universe, where humanity is led by the undying corpse of their god in a future that knows only war. The game has nine factions, two being added in this expansion, the Sisters of Battle and the Dark Eldar.
It is a real-time strategy game in the classic sense where you build and upgrade a base, but unlike other games, resources are spread across the map in the form of nodes that you must capture. This means that defensive strategies like turtling are generally discouraged, and large battles between forces converging on these crucial nodes occur often.
The single player campaign has you choosing a faction to play, and traveling on a risk-like strategic map of several planets. You select where you wish to go, and a battle begins over the territory, the victor getting the spoils, which can include veteran units and special wargear for your commander. The campaign plays similarly to the one in the Dark Crusade expansion, although that one felt slightly more polished.
The Dark Eldar and the Sisters of Battle are both perfectly fine additions to the game, although the powers system unique to the Dark Eldar is somewhat lacking and the Sisters feel as if they have nothing exactly special about them. I generally find myself playing Space Marines, Chaos, and Imperial Guard.
Soulstorm isn't bad exactly, but it's certainly not the best expansion for Dawn of War. It is a great game to play still, whether it's single or multi player.

This game is beautiful and moving. The music fits wonderfully. The graphics are amazing, and the world is atmospherical and magical. The fact that the characters do not speak a coherent language did not detract from this amazing story at all; if anything, it really did help take me to another world. I felt closer to the characters just through their gestures, moreso than I would have if they were speaking English or another known language. The lack of a coherent language reminds me of Shadow of the Colossus and Ico. Similarly to Ico, this game involves solving puzzles and helping a second character get around, but what makes it so different and unique is the fact that you control both characters; I have never played a game quite like this.
Highly recommended. Warning: it will throw an emotional curve ball at you.

Lord of the Rings Online.. Is it good or bad? I would have to say this is a generally good game. This game is very much your typical mmorpg game. The controls are very simple and easily understood. You spend most of your time in third person observing your character, combat involves locking onto a target, then clicking (or using a hotkey) to trigger the different attacks that are displayed on your action bar. Area attacks do exist, and generally the physics play out reasonably well.
The World: The world is big. There is plenty of places to explore, and the graphical level is pleasing to look at. While it will not match up in freedom of movement, or detail to Skyrim, it is definitely a fun place to view and explore. At first the world will seem pretty small, it is only as you go along that the distances between locations grow to the point where it is unpleasant to travel there by foot. They did, however, do a good job of matching up when distances get long, with when you your character can get a horse. In summary: medium-big world that is aesthetically very pleasing to look at.
Questing: The questing system is very closed. You progress through them, some of them are voiced, most only have one or two lines of voiced dialogue the rest you have to read on your own, you rarely have any options. They do not support the player choosing to be evil or good, or making choices that will have impacts upon how the quest will progress. Despite the limited nature of it, they did a fairly good job of making stories that are interesting, and that fit with the lore of Middle Earth. Summary: lack of player options, but decently entertaining anyhow.
Characters: Character setup is highly limited. You can choose from four races (Dwarf, Elf, Hobbit Man). Then you have a group of Classes;[some titles may be wrong] Guardian, Champion, Burglar, Warden, Rune-Keeper, Hunter, Captain and Lore Master. The races share the classes, with a few classes being disabled for each race (for example no Dwarf Burglars, or Human Rune Keepers. Each class also has three 'paths' that they can follow, those will effect what kinds of weapons they will be good at, and how well your character is at solo play. In general, there is almost no cross-over between classes, and no way to change once you make your character, so research well before you make a choice.
Crafting: There is almost nothing to talk about here. You choose a craft that contains three skills. Some skills let you gather, others let you craft. No single craft you can choose is completely self-reliant, so you will need the help of friends or the general world market to level up all of your skills. Crafted weapons are, however, well worth the effort of getting. They are on average far better than what you can find through loot for your level.
General play: While this game is termed a "role-playing game", there is very little actual role-playing to be found on it. The role-playing servers rarely have players who actually actively try to take on their character's roles. There are some good communities that you can join in with, but if you are on your own do not expect players to be particularly sociable or in character. Outside of role-playing the community is very open and helpful. Questions are typically answered quickly and nicely, and there are almost always players around who are willing to help you out. There are also plenty of player friendly guilds/factions out there to join if you enjoy that kind of play.
tl;dr, generic mmorpg, with its biggest highlight being that it is based in Middle Earth.

Far away from the teenage romance novels and goofy Dracula renditions that have come to be associated with vampires, Bloodrayne explores a darker take on the age old monsters, its titular femme fatale being something of a female counterpart to Van Helsing out to rid the world of the demons that threaten to destroy it. Betrayal from WayForward acts as a departure from prior games in the series and stands as a rather polarizing title from every angle; as instantly dismissible as it is alluring.
I won’t get into any story details because it’s entirely forgettable and even the little emphasis placed on it is more than it deserves, but in essence you are Rayne called in to deal with a demon infestation that’s been terrorizing the local towns people. That’s about all the story I needed and could have done without the melodramatic text bubbles, but as it stands it allows for a lot of people to die by your hand, which is ultimately the entire point of the game.
Betrayal is structured like a typical side scrolling brawler. You move from screen to screen clearing out hoards of monsters, taking part in occasional platforming segments or a larger than life boss fight. You have a modest but well rounded collection of moves, with nice touches like sucking blood from enemies to restore health or Rayne’s trademark pistol add a nice amount of personality to the otherwise routine fights.
On paper, Betrayal has everything in place for an excellent brawler, but when you actually get your hands on it it’s immediately clear that a lot has gone wrong in the translation to an actual game. Most unforgivable, WayForward commits a cardinal sin by constantly locking your character into animations. What this means in practice is combat feels slow and unresponsive, causing you to continually fail because it’s impossible to dodge mid-attack, and getting knocked down leaves you open for more attacks as you’re entirely helpless for a handful of seconds before you pick yourself back up (which as you can imagine creates a circle of falling down and getting kicked to death with no retaliation possible).
Even when you aren’t trapped in a string of animations, controlling Rayne is excessively clunky and unintuitive. Moves require precise inputs to execute, but these are commonly misread or ignored making anything beyond a basic attack unpredictable and more dangerous to attempt with a constant swarm of enemies around you than it’s worth.
What I’m getting at with all of this is Betrayal is a frustrating game; a VERY frustrating game, and one that shouldn’t be anywhere near as difficult as it is. It’s a contrived challenge, the combined result of poor controls, animation lockouts, and checkpoints that are placed almost intentionally to cause you to quit from having to replay huge chunks of a level each time you die (which will be often). It starts off hard and by the end raises the bar to an outrageous degree, to where I was gritting my teeth and praying I’d get through it so the game would finally end.
I wanted to love Betrayal, and for all its flaws I don’t regret playing it and even enjoyed portions of it a great deal, but any recommendation I could give it comes with so many connotations that I find it hard to say with any sincerity that it’s something you should spend your time with. Aside from its slick, hard drawn art style that looks absolutely stunning (especially in the dark, when all you can see are silhouettes against the background), it stumbles all the way from the start and had me questioning if it was really worth continuing with.  In the end, I’m still not sure of my answer.

DLC Quest is a very short game. My total playtime for both game modes was only 2 hours. In spite of its short duration, it's definitely worth playing. It's a fun retro platformer with smooth clean graphics and varied, interesting environments.
The game is pure satire on the state of downloadable content in video games today. You unlock everything as you progress: music, npcs, new areas, zombies (because all games need zombies these days), etc. by using coins you collect in-game. There's even a point where you walk into a zone and it's not there because it was content left out of the game at launch to be sold as DLC later. The game doesn't actually have any real DLC to purchase with real money.
This game is not difficult for a platformer. You don't need twitch reflexes. You won't throw anything at the screen for missing some insane jump 300 times in a row. The gameplay is simple. Just running and jumping, doing RPG-style questing, but that's all this game needs. It delivers on this simple mechanic well. The short nature of the game preseves its charm. It's just a fun and silly romp that says all the things gamers think about the current DLC model.
I definitely think it's worth $3 and it's usually only $1 on sale.

3089 -- Futuristic Action RPG is the sequal to 3079 -- Block Action RPG.  It's the same procedurally generated content idea, but we've moved from giant pixel graphics (ala Minecraft) to a more triangular approach.  So a big graphics improvement from the previous title, and there were many other engine tweaks and fixes that went into this sequal that are new and improved.  There are a few kinks to iron out yet (the map is one of them, very finicky) but overall there is a lot of improvements to like here.
However, two things of note that I like more in the previous title are the music and the grappling hook.  While the music isn't bad in 3089, the music in 3079 was *really* good.  In addition, the grappling hook in 3089 has weight restrictions and is slowed down compared to its brother in 3079 - it's like the pistol in Halo 2 compared to Halo 1 - yeah it works, but it's not nearly as awesome as its younger brother was.
With the above said what it really boils down to is this a good "game" and would I recommend playing it.  Unlike my "unrecommended" for 3079 I think 3089 is a perfectly playable, procedurally generated game, rather than a sandbox tech demo.  Even with that said, I still think the developer needs to implement a few more tweaks regarding general gameplay before I'd recommend it to the average gamer.  However, if you're into this sort of real sandboxy, do anything you like sort of title with procedurally generated content then 3089 is probably worth a look for you.  Otherwise the recycled quests and lack of real story-based content make me recommend passing on 3089 with another real cudos to the developer for their engine improvement.  I'm looking forward to the next iteration of this series and anticipate that (with a few more gameplay tweaks) this developer will drop gold.

The Sims 3 is really fun and addictive! Still, it is important that buyers be aware of what they're actually getting prior to investing in this game. If you do not do a little research ahead of time, you may end up feeling disappointed once you begin to play.
The Sims has always been a franchise built around DLC. If you are trying out Sims for the first time and you decide to only purchase the base game (to experiment and save some money), keep in mind that you will not be able to do many of the things you probably have seen in player videos and previews. That being said - I would suggest reading through the descriptions of the available DLC prior to making your purchase. Choose what might be worth investing in based upon what you hoped to get out of this game.
For instance - are you simply looking to play around with one character - walk him/her through their daily life, get a job, climb the career ladder, etc? If so, the base game may work out just fine for you. If you're looking for more, you may want to choose a bundle, or purchase the game with some DLC, right away. Still, think carefully before spending your money. DLC for The Sims is relatively costly. If you know you would enjoy playing with cats, dogs, and horses, and engaging in outdoor seasonal activities - the main bundle (with generations, pets, and seasons) may be worth the expense. But, if you're more interested in traveling the world, creating vampires and witches, or living the college life, you're probably better off skipping the bundle and just buying The Sims 3 plus one additional DLC that meets your needs.
In short - The Sims 3 is a great game - but you may be disappointed, or end up spending more than you'd like for content you do not need or care about, if you do not do some research before making your purchase.

G1 is a testament to how a well-written story will outlast graphical advancements any day, because while graphics become more outdated with time, a good story will last forever. G1 hits you with a curious but well-executed medieval Sci-Fi story, that's simultaneously thoughtful, memorable, and well before it's time. There are no real low points to it either; from start to finish, it remains strong and consistent. You are also very much the master of your own destiny in the game; unlike the future games, which place you into a specific sect as soon as you start the game, G1 has zero hand holding. Beyond the vague reputation of your kind, you're free to do whatever you want, and you can very easily play without allying yourself with the numerous factions presented to you. There's also the option to go completely mad with power, which I personally have a big preference for, and very much appreciate and recommend.
As a small segue from the storyline point, from a graphics perspective, this game is very primitive. That's not to say it's bad by any means; it's very simplistic spritework (which you can actually view frame-by-frame from files in the main data section), which I personally like a lot. But emphasis should be made that it's VERY simplistic, as even when the game first came out, the graphics were considered primitive. If you're someone who prioritizes prettier graphics over storyline, the Geneforge series will not be for you.
Exploration also plays a large role in this game. Beyond finding enemies to kill for XP & loot, and hidden vendors to sell loot too (as vendors have a static amount of buying currency, and you'll very quickly exhaust the main city buyers), you'll find a surprisingly dense amount of lore scattered strategically throughout each map. Enemies are placed in smart locations, traps are both smart & fair, and neither is so oppressive that they cancel each other out; you can very easily do everything and go everywhere in this game, despite what some of the ingame text tries to tell you. I would very much recommend exploring everywhere you find interesting or worthwhile; beyond the aforementioned points about loot & XP, G1 has some of the most memorable map areas of any game I've played to date (Hill of Jars, Shaper Crypt, and Valley of the Wind, to name a few). With that said, you will reach certain level caps where lower-level areas are no longer rewarding enough to explore, which is completely fine, as you can always prioritize them in another playthrough.
Combat is generally simple and well balanced, with positioning and terrain usage/awareness playing key roles in your success or failure (especially on the higher difficulties). Your choice of Shaper (creation user & support mage), Guardian (physical DPS with some creation support), or Agent (magic DPS with some physical options and very limited creation support) will very drastically affect the way you play, with some options being more user friendly than others (in my opinion, Shapers are the easiest to play as, Guardians in the middle, and Agents as the hardest, almost solely due to how well creations do). Unlike some of the future Geneforge games, every class is viable on every difficulty.
With that said, perhaps one of the very few minorly-negative points I have about G1 is that it's a very offensive-oriented game, though do take in mind that this is most from the perspective of someone that plays solely on Torment difficulty, where taking 2 hits kills you at pretty much every stage of the game. There are no defensive spells, and only one defensive buff exists, which can only be applied with a very rare item set. Furthermore, Anatomy replaces Parry from the future games, so the only option is to pump points into Endurance (which give limited returns), or focus entirely on offensive DPS. As such, melee is theoretically usable but entirely nonviable, and ranging is king. You will live and die on your DPS, positioning, and combat priority. This is also why creations are so good, as they can help supplement in damage (as your own damage will start falling off later on), and tank damage that'd otherwise kill you. With that said, it is entirely natural do die several times during a run, which makes mistakes more forgiving, but kills immersion a bit, as you can run straight into an enemy stronghold to scout out their defenders, than reload and strategically start picking them off (with knowledge you shouldn't have if you were doing everything in one go). With that said, none of these are a real deal breaker, but it does encourage similar play-styles between characters.
As a small aside, I'd like to point out that, while this game uses a die/%-to-hit system, which I find very easy to despise if implemented improperly, G1 executes it well enough that I'm comfortable liking it. Hits can be a bit more variable in the later stages, as several die are cast for attacks & can lead to a 40% variance in damage sometimes, but the game's forgiving enough that it becomes less of a factor (so you don't get the FTL paradox of losing a run because a series of rolls didn't go your way). It also, mercifully, does away with the 95% to-hit cap from the Avernum series games of the same era.
A few veteran tips; if you can handle the responsibility (and not be tempted to exploit the game), holding down Shift + D, and then typing "exitzone" can be used to warp out of towns and dungeons instantly, and hence save a lot of time that'd otherwise be spent backtracking. Likewise, "clearthisarea" can be used to a similar effect. Again though, use these responsibly, as both can break game progression. Secondly, G1 has hands down the best secret of the series, which I think every player should get to experience. Without spoiling the secret itself, start at the special totem in Drake's Vale, than work your way clockwise around the mountain, touching each level's special totem in order (you'll know when you've hit the last one). The rest I'll let you experience for yourself.
In conclusion, Geneforge 1 is one of the closest examples of a perfect game I can think of. It flawlessly merges simple graphics with well-balanced gameplay, and a deep, complex narrative. It offers players with a large, vibrant world to explore, and rewards their efforts with fun challenges & chunks of extra lore.

TL;DR - A breathtakingly original, open ended, nuanced, ahead of its time, extremely well written sci-fi yarn about people meddling with overwhelming power and the fallout of using it to create living (intelligent and self-aware) tools of servitude wrapped inside a horribly paced, convoluted, imbalanced, frustratingly buggy, puke green shell.
Pacing and balance is the main problem with Geneforge: it takes way too long before anything interesting happens, locations become stale before you get anywhere relevant to the story, enemies and obstacles are painfully repetitious (and lazy- how many freaking maps are nothing but endless turrents/mines put behind every corner and bend)...  the list goes on... talent trees are unforgiving, leveling up is far too grindy (especially after the game stops rewarding you exp for completing quests), core abilites level up purely on random exploration, inventory management is painful, towns are far too big, most abilities are pointless, enemy difficulty goes from too easy to downright stupid so fast you can't even see it, looking for specific quest or story NPCs in the sea of identical NPCs is annoying, save/rest scumming is a core mechanic... you get the idea.
The one redeeming element of Geneforge- and it's pretty bright considering- is the extremely sharp and hauntingly subtle storyline.  The idea of the shaper knowledge changing your persona as you grow in power, putting you on top of several groups all vying for their own freedom in a hopeless situation is expressed with efficient detail (not a word too few or too many).  All the major factions rest in grey areas where you're simultaneously intrigued and repulsed.  Getting the second hand story of everything else happening on Sucia island mirrors your own journey with surreal flavor; you can't help but be taken aback and become invested in the various outcomes.
Unfortunately, even the brightest parts of Geneforge are not without serious issues.  Allying with the different groups doesn't alter the general game in any real way, there are too many strange side factions introduced so late you can't really care, there is way too much back and forth running around, the Geneforge itself is haphazardly shoehorned into the story, the main antagonist is fun to read about but doesn't make an appearance until the end of the game, and again, everything takes way too long.  It might sound as if I'm nit-picking or being overly critical but due to the amount of wasted, pointless time in Geneforge, little annoyances become overwhelming.
I am familiar with Spiderweb Software and yes, such a huge game is an achievement for such a small dev team (in the early 2000's no less).  Moreover, I don't necessarily wish to tarnish Geneforge's positive Steam reception, but reviewing the game has to take into account both the time it was released as well as the time it's currently being played in.  While Geneforge has a wealth of content (something to be noted and prized in the early 2000s) most of it feels stretched thin like too little butter across too much toast.
If you're a fan of early PC western RPGs (ie. Fallout, Baldur's gate, or other Spiderweb games), and you've got the patience, you will most likely enjoy Geneforge (especially for it's story).  If you're not (regardless of what age group you're in), you may not find much to compel you here.

As a longtime fan of Spiderweb games in general, I have to say that Geneforge is by far my favorite. While the gameplay itself is pretty simple, and (let's be honest) quite repetitive. The heart of this game is in its story. Most notably in the moral crux that it presents, which pretty much boils down to:
If you have the power to create and end life with the literal wave of a hand, are you morally obligated to grant your creations any rights that you yourself cannot take away?
Some creations treat you as a god, some see you as an equal, and some hate you because they never asked to be created. It's an interesting and thought-provoking concept that's well worth the price. It feels more like a book than a video game, and that's not a bad thing.

I've played this game for 26 minutes. That is enough for me to say that this game is going to be criminally short, and absolutely spectacular. This review won't be the most informational, but trust me when I say that the other positive reviews have reason to be there. This is marvelous and I can't give the creator enough credit for atmosphere, surprisingly functional stealth elements, and the main item from this mod. I thought it might be kinda gimmicky, but again,. it's been 26 minutes and I can't see this thing getting even the slightest bit old.
EDIT:
Unfortunately that's... exactly how long the game was. I was assuming that I had been taking my time and had at least a decent amount ahead, but no. 30 minutes is what you're looking at. I whimpered as the credits came up, because this little experience is like a morsel of delectible half-life 2 mixed with such a well implimented idea- TWO, well implimented ideas... no, three. Maybe even four. Yeah I'm going with four. No wait, five. Five. Well... Six if you count the atmosphere in general, but I guess that's not really a big idea as much as just well executed game design.
The gimmic:
Isn't really gimicky. It feels great. It's simple, easy to use ,easy to get the hang of, and otherwise is implimented flawlessly. If HL3 ever was to come out, I'd be remiss if this thing didn't get used somehow.
The stealth:
Yeah, they actually added stealth. It ain't Metal Gear Solid, but it's simple, it's effective, and it's a wonderful addition to what this mod seemed to be going for. In a situation like this, where trying to go all out with it could result in a sloppy mess of a mechanic, simplicity is preferable. And, it's not bad. It works cleanly. That's the most I could ask.
The lore/reading:
While this mod isn't long enough to have "Lore" that people would want to heavily scrutinize, it's got enough to make it feel like a true part of HL's canon. On top of that, the lore is entirely communicated through writing, in game. Papers that actually have writing on their in game model that you can pick up and read, light willing- and oddly enough, QR codes. Using the Z key lets you zoom in, and if held on a QR code, will decode it and show what's written. Brilliant idea, and again, I would pray HL3 would adopt it if it existed.
The breachers:
I don't know what to call them, but I've started calling them doorknockers or breachers. They're this unique and delightfully modeled piece of resistance tech that can be attached to those obnoxious Combine doorlock thingies and then used to open the sealed door. It's slow, but effective, and it gave the game a nice feeling of possibility. Sealed doors now have an in-game resolution... So it doesn't feel uncomfortable seeing them everywhere, even though you know you still can't open those things unless the modder wanted.
The ammo/pacing:
I'll put these together because I consider both to be half of an idea that compliment one another. Firstly, the weapon pacing is fast and hard. While I understand that the reason is because this mod is so short, it felt nice not to feel stuck in a rut with one or two dull weapons to use. You got a pistol, had time to appreciate it, then got a shotgun, had time to appreciate it... you get the idea. It was fast, but not too fast. As for the ammunition, you're not given much, and you can only hold a little bit. That means that you're heavily encouraged to switch weapons often, to be smart with your ammo, and to use all of what you have at your disposal.
Addendum, the atmosphere:
This atmosphere is really nice. I'm not gonna act like it's the best I could want, but dang if it wasn't great. Very satisfying. Tense, creepy, enriched. The lore/reading bits only added to this.
All in all, this is GREAT. I can't recommend it highly enough. I wish with my whole being that it was longer. Kudos, modder. Kudos.

Transmisssions: Element 120 is a fanmade mod for Half Life 2 that focuses on a small adventure set in the HM universe. The games "plot", if you wish to call it that, is small and mostly told through enviromental storytelling and the occastional discarded note lying around. The game  is split into four main chapters, the first is spent doing some clever puzzles involving darkness and the effect it has on enemies, the second is finding and learning how to use the games main new mechanic, the third inolves a fight for survival against waves of head-crab zombies and the fourth and final chapter is a fantastic large scale battle against a small army of combine soliders.
The gameplay is your typical HL affair, you explore the enviroment while collecting new weapons and getting into both combat and puzzle based setpieces. However, the introduction of the previously meantioned new mechanic does change things up somewhat; the Zero Point Energy Projector, which is kind of like the cousin of the gravity gun. It shoots out a ball of energy which knocks away anything around it and if you aim it at your feet and fire while jumping it sets you flying up into the air. This new weapon is used well both in combat and puzzles and is just fun to use.
There is one issue with this game howover, the time it takes to complete it. I'm of the mindset that a game being too short is better than a game being too long and the fact that i'm even complaining about it shows that the game is good enough for me to want more, but at less then an hour you can't help but feel saddened by how little there is on offer here. But, that being said, the game is completely free, so you won't lose anything by giving it a shot.

Very interesting little game here. Took me around 20 minutes to beat, but over the course of the game, I realized a few neat things about it. I believe there's around 24 total sages to talk to. This directly correlates to the Dharma wheel. You play a totem, but in looking at the character itself, it seems like you actually play a hungry ghost rather than a totem. There are six tablets you have to get, which translates into the six different groups within the Bardo. Later on, you see three Buddhas lit up, which could correlate to the Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, and Nirmanakaya, or the three bodies of Buddha.  I also find it quite enjoyable that you meet Avalokiteśvara, a bodhisattva who embodies the compassion of all Buddhas. Even more truly, it's kind of enjoyable that they placed this bodhisattva above you, because their name literally means Lord Who Looks Down. Although, in their depiction, it could be the emanation, Mahakala. I'm not sure what sect of Tibetan Buddhism they're basing from, but oh well! Great job. I enjoyed it.

This is a 2D sidescrolling game that can be compared to Castlevania 1/3 on the NES. A controller is highly suggested for this.
This seems to be a perfect port from consoles as I own it on PS3 and have beaten it several times. I was very glad they brought it to Steam. It's nice to see the game up close and that's always enjoyable. The controls for this game may not seem responsive, but they are. It's not like Strider where you can press attack repeatedly and get results. Think of it more like the response of controlling a character from a fighting game. You'll have to learn the difference on how to execute a toe-tap vs a down-stomp after jumping. Once you launch an enemy in to the air, you can either jump up and pound on them, or you can send them flying. You have all the basic moves from the beginning, so you won't have to worry about learning them as you progress. There are, however, a couple of powers you do acquire later on in the game.
I've seen a couple reviews for this game on major gaming sites and they are overly harsh. This stems mostly from complaining about the difficulty. I can tell you right now that this isn't anywhere near as difficult as a lot of other games out there. At the same time, I can say that it'll only be easier while being enjoyable if you learn how to properly control BloodRayne.
The graphic style goes perfect with this game. The music is superb. The brain behind the music is Jake Kaufman. I highly recommend you google for him. The options screen has just about enough video options due to this being a 2D game. You only have resolution size, windowed/borderless/full screen, and vsync.
I highly recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of 2D side scrolling games.

DLC Quest shares a premise with earlier indie game Evoland (take an abstract concept of commentary on the video game industry and turn it into a game itself) and unfortunately suffers the same fatal flaw: abstract concepts of commentary on the video game industry make terrible game premises. DLC Quest, however, manages to be even WORSE in this regard, because its core premise has no progression even built in; it's literally one overextended joke about how much AAA publishers contempt for the consumer comes out in their handling of Downloadable Content for published titles, and in fact it's not even that sophisticated. Much as the game itself is only £2 (65p at time of writing) the fact is that without charging actual money for DLC the game loses any real investment a player could have in the satire it's peddling because there's an absence of the actual tangible effect of the relatable concept; but it can't do that because doing so would undermine its stated political standpoint. The idea was doomed from the start and in terms of realisation of that foretold failure DLC Quest, like Evoland before it, does not disappoint.
