I'll keep it sweet and short.  I'm not much of a puzzle enthusiast but what the hell, I hear words echoing around from many Trine franchise supporters that this is an excuisitely beautiful puzzle platformer that one cannot help but be pulled into her gravitational embrace.
Almost all of those rumblings were almost true.  Sure, it's straightforward platforming but the nuances and choices made by its creators really stretch into an appropriately lengthed simple story allowing a knight, an archer, and a magician to join forces and retriece the Trine.  Cutscenes are oldschool, not dissertations on melodramatics; this game is to be played not digested.
Your 3 heroes set off on their journey and tricks, traps, simple puzzles ensue.  Since some of your triumvirate may die (don't worry, then return at checkpoints which reside between most puzzles so there's not much restart necessary) nut some of the more interesting fun can be had when you're down a wizard and have lost his conjuring skill to get you up to that balcony.... hmmm, think about it another way and... your archer can grapple hook to the ceiling then swing herself up to the balcony.  Tada! Magic!
And that's alot of how the game plays.  Three heroes, three styles, plug them in, experiment and your puzzle will be solved.  They weren't challenging in the sense that they may take a few minutes each and then few may take a bit longer, but it never delivers a sesnse of defeat encouraging you to abandon the game in frustration.
Highly recommend, and with Steam Sales going on this is priced ridiculously low at 2 bucks. You should be ashamed not buying it at $2.  I just don't believe anyone buy a troll could not take so genuine joy for 2 bucks.

Transmissions - Element 120 is a fun, albeit short, action-packed experience that can be enjoyed for free in its entirety, lasting about less than an hour, total. Set in the half-life universe, developed entirely by a fan, the little that IS here is quite impressive.
Quality remains consistently high throughout. Level design is well paced, and nothing feels rushed. You're left wanting more by the end of your journey. The soundtrack is great, art-style/ambience consistently astonishing, and gameplay enjoyable.
In the 1.2 hours that I played this game, I've done everything it has to offer. There are achievements to hunt for if you're into that sort of thing.
I really can't stress this point enough, but the game is REALLY short. However, that doesn't stop it from outshining a lot of the other free games offered on Steam, simply because the heart is there. This was accomplished by ONE DUDE. And that's cool!
Transmissions - Element 120 captures the essence of what made Half-Life 2 neat. It stands as a reminder to just how much we're missing out on Half-Life 3, which will probably never see the light of day. That said, it's fitting that Transmissions is so gloomy.
The gameplay's great. Plenty of enemies to shoot up, the bulk of them being the headcrab-zombies that littered the Ravenholm levels in Half-Life 2. There's a fun new take on the gravity gun that lets you fire yourself into the sky, or simply tear combine-soldiers apart.
The finale has you going head to head against waves of enemy soldiers. It's a fitting lid on the whole package that seals up the journey, nicely.
It's a nice little adventure that'll keep you entertained for about an hour or so, including achievement hunting. The quality of what's offered here is impressive, enough so that you're reminded of what Half-Life 3 could have been.

It's a great game. But I honestly wouldn't recommend it to people who aren't majorly in to hack and slash games or want to play a more casual game. Since there are some annoyances which I think takes away some of the enjoyment of the game.
For example, the difficulty can vary greatly. At one point I was strolling through a level without having any problems with the combat or the platforming, that suddenly changed when I came to a bunch of platforms that I had to jump across, those platforms would disappear if I stayed on them for too long. If I fell down from the platforms I would end up in acid which would kill me in one hit and I would have to start over from a checkpoint. There was also missiles flying around in random patterns, as well as enemies who would throw bombs at me. Since the platforms were so small, I would fall to my death if I ended up getting hit by a missile or a bomb.
This required way more skill and luck than what was previously required of me. Varying difficulty can be a great thing, but I don't think it's so great when it happens in the middle of a level.
The combat itself isn't really hard, in fact it's pretty easy and the enemies only do a few types of attack with little variance. However, the game with often require you to be very precise with your actions and will also often feel unresponsive when you try and do certain actions. You get knocked to the ground extremely easy. The weakest attack will knock you down if you're mid-air. Enemies will often hit you while you're getting up from the ground, which will cause you to get knocked down again.
It is also sometimes very very hard to tell things apart, especially what's in the background and foreground. This is espeically prominent in chapter 15.
But besides that, it's a great game. It's easily worth 10€ and really enjoyable if you're able to look past those things I listed.

*sigh* You know I am actually a huge fan of the Hyperdimension series, even the spin-offs like Hyperdimension U: Action Unleashed were great! I was a bit disappointed by this game. Promised to me was a procedurally generated shooter, with procedurally generated missions, weapons/equipment, NPCs, difficulty, and a world that is generated on the fly as you explore it. And, to be fair, all of these things were delivered. However, I was hoping for an exciting and dynamic experience high in variety, which is not quite what eventuated. The problem with so much procedural generation is that it makes the game a little bland.
The missions are particularly so. The missions are made up of about 2-6 objectives to be completed in order, and are made up of a set list of about 8 different kinds of tasks, like "Fight a gang of 4 robots", "Protect Sylvia Dee for 1:15", or simply "Talk to Derek". All the missions are made up from these objectives, over and over again, just with different numbers, names, and times. These missions make little contribution to the minimal overarching story, and the content of their objectives is completely irrelevant; only whether you completed them or not.
However, all of that said, despite my expectations being far higher than what was offered, I can still recommend 3089. Essentially, I was expecting 3089 to be a procedurally generated RPG, and it simply is not. It is, however, a challenging and reasonably fun shooter, with additional replay value because the world is never the same for any two characters. The missions, even there 's little incentive with respect to the story to complete them, are still fun from a gameplay perspective, and the large number of points you get to upgrade your character are a lovely bonus! Exploring the world into higher difficulty areas, to access more powerful items, is good fun too, and the world generation is actually pretty decent. I did enjoy the number of floating islands, chunky low polygon trees, impressive peaks and valleys, caverns and crags. While the missions, NPCs and weaponry all felt completely characterless, the worlds are somewhat interesting to explore.
It took me a while, but eventually I started enjoying myself. If you approach it with a mind more open than mine was, I think you'll be in for a good time.

I played all of Geneforge 1 in 2005 or 2006, right around there.  More recently, I bought the game on Steam about 4 years ago and played some of the beginning.  What do I think of it?  It's a good game--I can't deny this.
But in many ways it doesn't even come close when compared with some of the titles I feel to be truly great.  When I played it I compared it specifically to Final Fantasy 6 and Chrono Trigger, and the first Dungeon Siege, which were basically the only RPG's I'd played.  Like most typical RPG's your character increases in strength and abilities by killing enemies and completing quests.  But the classes differ vastly.
Your character can be one of three classes: a Shaper, who specializes in creating living creatures directly from magic; an Agent, who is far more focused on using magic spells to inflict the actual damage; and a Guardian, whose specialty is dealing direct physical damage, mostly with swords.  I tested Shaper and Agent, but in the end enjoyed Guardian much more--the other classes seemed playable, but I think Guardian is easiest from my recollection, and didn't require as much micromanagement.  The gameplay is good, and in combat your character gets action points you can spend to move, fight, and use items and abilities.
Combat makes up a lot of Geneforge, though you'll probably also spend lot of time talking to characters in the game, picking up items and selling them and trying to amass enough money to purchase the best items.
But the best part of the game is the story.  You will learn more about magic, and the Geneforge in particular, a powerful piece of magical machinery that can greatly enhance those who use it properly.  You'll learn about the different magical creations in the game, learn about the different factions in the game (four of them IIRC), and learn about the history of the land you've been stranded in.  And much of the heart of Geneforge is freedom to choose--your character build, your faction, your ending.  If you sufficiently improve your character, you will be able to roll over most enemies.
Anyway . . . if this review sounds a little bland, perhaps it's because the game itself is kind of bland as well.  There are people who absolutely adore the whole idea of turn-based strategy, the idea of tactically micromanaging the actions of each of your party members, and carefully choosing their equipments and stats.  I used to be one of those people, when I first started playing RPG's, but less so today.  And if you are one of those people--I suspect that you will LOVE Geneforge.
But these days, I suppose I feel I need more from a game.  I think all the micromanagement has gotten to me over the years.  But also, Geneforge has very little atmosphere or enjoyable character.  It has virtually no music, though it does have atmospheric sounds.  I can't remember the name of a single character from Geneforge--whereas I can remember the names of all the main characters from Final Fantasy VI and Chrono Trigger, even though it's been even longer since I played them.  Geneforge's environments are mostly brown--deserts and dirt, though there is some variety thrown in.  And--while the ability to create life in Geneforge is quite awesome--I didn't even feel that this aspect of gameplay was very fleshed-out.  The story in Geneforge is definitely interesting, and there is a huge volume of writing in the game, so if you're a big fan of reading in your games, I can see it appealing to you.  But frankly, I still feel that both FF6 and CT have significantly more interesting stories, characters, environments, and of course excellent music.
Geneforge is a good game.  Some people love it.  You may.  Someday, I may go through and play the others in the series.  But . . . I didn't find a whole lot be excited by in this title, and I feel its impact is far less than it would have been than if, for example, the creator had even expended minimal effort to create a few characters that are really memorable.

Do you know when you truly love a game?
When almost 12 years after it's launch, the giddy excitement of running home from work to play it never actually wore off.
Don't let my playtime fool you, I owned the boxed versions of these games loooong before they were in my Steam account and have invested literally THOUSANDS of hours into this game. I was always kind of interested in 40K, having roomates who played the tabletop when I was younger and reading the odd comic here and there, but THIS was the game that turned me into a 40K fanboy and opened me up to the whole universe.
Now before I go any further, if you want the definitive version of Dawn of War for its best balance in both mutliplayer and a better designed single player campaign then buy Dark Crusade. It was the pinnacle of the series.
There are two reasons why I play Soulstorm more than Dark Crusade, the first is that the multiplayer community seems to be much more active on SS than it is on DC, the second and infinitely more important reason is what the games community simply refers to by two letters......UA.
The "Ultimate Apocalypse" mod for Soul Storm or "UA" for short, has become the absolute best Warhammer 40k game ever made.
The following are just the things that I personally like about the mod, but doesn't even tip the iceburg for what it encompasses :
-expands the maps and removes level caps so the truly epic 40K battles can expand in scope
-introduces new races including Inquisition, Chaos Daemons, Tyranids and more...
-introduced tons of new untis for exsiting races
-new buildings, superweapons and tech trees to explore for all races
-better balancing than vanilla for multiplayer
-constant updates and new content all the time
and of course......
TITANS!!!!
The only thing I can hope for (because lets not kid ourselves, Relic is working on DoW 3) is that they make the next game much more like UA in design and get away from the smaller tactical stuff they did with DoW 2.
All in all this is my favorite game of all time and the first and to date ONLY time I will score a game with a perfect 10/10.
Bravo Relic and the UA team,  everyone's got a fave....and you made mine.

Brawlhalla is an epic platform fighter for up to 8 players online or locally. And it's free. Join casual free-for-alls, queue for ranked matches, or make a custom room with your friends. Millions of players. Frequent updates. Over twenty-five unique legends. Come fight for glory in the halls of Valhalla!
Graphics- the game has got cartoony graphics and is not trying to look hyper realistic. The graphics are simple but still very nice to look at. Nothing amazing or special just some nice graphics
Soundtrack- the soundtrack is very good and really gets you into the game you are playing. It makes sure you are fully immersed in the match you are fighting and want to win!
Game play- game play is very good and fun. Characters are balanced and each character plays differently. You have your bare hands and 2 main weapons you can pick up. Each character has different weapons and makes it so that no character feels the same as another! As said before the game is balanced and very fair which is a major part in all games that some games fail to do.
Characters- the characters have a page of lore which comes with them which can be very interesting and cool to read. All the characters look different and play different and are very fun. It is fun to play them all and find your favourite (mine is Hattori).
Customisation- as well as choosing a character you can unlock different colours that your character can wear. You can also unlock different setups where you will have different things such as damage or speed increased or decreased and have a overall different play to suit your play style.
Online- online works very well and I have never had an issue with anything apart from the occasional lag which cannot be helped.
Controls- the controls are very simple and easy to learn. this is really good as you have some people who will have been playing for a lot longer than you but it evens the playing field a little bit.
Ranked- ranked is very fun and very fair. You can look at the lead boards and see exactly where you are online at a website. You can do a 1v1 or 2v2 ranked and increase your elo rating and hopefully climb the leader board.
Clans- clans have been implemented very well and are an amazing addition to an already great game. They have done them perfectly and will be adding more to clans which is amazing. I love how all of your clan can work to get xp to level the clan up! You can all work together to create an amazing clan. They are going to keep adding to this already successful feature which is great.
In game purchases- one flaw is that it has in game purchases to get mammoth coins so you can buy things that you can only buy with mammoths coins. it is not pay to win as the only thigns you can buy are skins so that is good but it is still a bit annoying that you can only get skins by buying the coins.
Community- I believe reviewing the community is a bit unfair as you cannot help a bad community but this community is very friendly and good fun! There are some rotten apples like always but most players are fun and good sports and will always help!
overall, this game is nowhere near finished but is already an amazing game and has a bright future ahead I will give it an 8.4/10

The game does so many things right- 'addicting' is an understatement. But this doesn't offset the many things it does wrong and frankly, Its really a shame the problems are as bad as they are.
In my review, I will be covering what is mostly wrong with multiplayer and not much else.
Singleplayer? Its good. almost no noteworthy complaints. you can mod it up a-...

Multiplayer does barely enough to say it isn't a 'pay-to-win' game. Yes, You can get in the same place as a sharkcard user- no gear is specifically off-limits to non-sharkcard users. It will only take like, a f---ing year to reach the same spot as them, but sure, you can get there.
If you want to get ANYTHING nice without buying sharkcards you have to grind.
.
I wouldn't have played as long as I had if hackers hadn't superleveled me and threw 11 million dollars at me. But I also made the mistake of spending ALL of that cash on a bunker, an office and supplies so i could be a gun runner. I haven't been able to make any money back Because me and my crew get absolutely Wrecked by the other crews- who have flying motorcyles with F---ING ROCKET LAUNCHERS. Every single time. Across multiple different sessions.
Seriously, whoever the hell thought it was a good Idea to add the 'Oppressor' into the game should be fisted by Edward Scissorhands.
Its impossible for weaker gangs/CEOs to win against hackers/Sharkcard Users with the best gear.
I  F---ing get it, the entire theme of the game is that You can do anything you want when you have enough money- but, how exactly, is this balanced or even fun to the people below you?
It just doesn't matter wether or not you're playing PvE, PvP or just work as hired muscle; You will make
for money. A reliable Income outside of sharkcards is basically non-existant.
if you are somehow tempted to consider buying a sharkcard,
. You're just telling companies- like Rockstar- that you tolerate this system and you are willing to
them for adding
.
Everyone has a GPS tracker implanted in their brain. Just Forget about beind discrete or sneaky because everything you do is
on the map anyway. Its *Very* easy to stalk other players and harass them in a moments notice.
Sure, You could just go into passive mode so they can't attack you, but then you can't do anything worthwhile. Passive mode seems to only exist to end spawncamping (which, should it exist in any open world game, you are doing somthing wrong).
I don't want to be forced to find a new session because some random guy looked at me and said 'Wow, F--k that guy. Lets kill him untill he goes passive, then follow him around and shoot the cashier of every store he tries to visit.'.
They have really have nothing better to do aside from the tedious money grinding.
The community itself is pretty toxic; Some of them are really petty, aggressive and sometimes downright cringy. whenever im online i feel like im playing with a bunch of 12 year olds who think playing a game with explosions and ♥♥♥♥♥♥s makes them a big kid.
Allow me to paint you a shining example: I was once invited to join somones CEO buisness. I happened to ignore the invite because i was helping a friend out. a couple minutes later, The
f---ing CEO hunts me down with an APC (SAM launcher variant) and a couple of his 'associates' and spawncamps me and my friends taunting us the entire time untill we enabled passive.
At the end they said, 'They've had enough, boys. lets hope the name sticks.' and continued to follow me and spam invites untill we left and found a new session. Im not making this sh*t up.
and now, we finally address the spawn system. Why is the respawn system so bad? Its fairly common to respawn only a block away in the middle of an intersection so you can get sniped immediately by the same guy who did a driveby on you about 12 seconds ago. Why they are allowed to spawn camp you until you are forced to resign your CEO/Club status is beyond me.
PvE mission/heists promote Elitism. mission are instantly failed if someone dies or fails to do their designated job (which is bound to happen) and you get 0-2 spare lives for the entire team to share depending on the difficulty.
Designated jobs are stupid and completely unnecessary- if division of labor needs to get done, people can just open chat and talk about who does what (as a matter of fact, nearly all of the heists would be so much easier if they allowed players to formulate their own plan instead of being spoon fed a preset plan).
If somone fails to deliver thier job, noone else can pick up the slack and the mission is failed, end of discussion. Sometimes it isn't so bad, most of the time it is.
Aside from the current problems that already exist, this Dramatically damages relations between Newbies and Pros because the total payout for a mission decreases the more you restart it- in addition to being fairly small to start with.
Lets not forget that if a single person disconnects during a job/hiest, you are all placed back into matchmaking. Usually everyone else will leave too,  leaving the host incredibly frustrated and alone, waiting for up to 10 minutes to form a new crew.
I don't know If the kick function can be used during a heist/job, but if it does i imagine it hasn't ever been used for this exact same reason.
--------------------------
Alright. Multiplayer is out of the way. Lets move on to the other things.
Weapon/car stats are NOT displayed in numerical values and can be a bit vague. for the most part you won't need it, but it sure as hell would be nice. I still don't know if changing my tires actually does anything.
The UI kind of sucks. You seriously have to open up a menu mid-firefight to use healing items. Granted it would be kind of stupid to mash a button to heal, but it wouldn't be any worse than mashing the menu button to heal. That just comes down to how the actual firefights work.
Indicators of being damaged or having low health can be easily overlooked. The health bar is fairly tiny and is stuffed in the corner, making you have to look away to check your health.
NPC's are pushovers like, 70% of the time. None of them use explosives or even flanking tactics. they do not pose a threat to better-geared players most of the time. If you are undergeared, stay in cover and you'll be fine (usually). They mostly overwhelm with numbers.
Racing is 'meh'. Maybe its because i suck at racing in the first place, but i find it typically boils down to who has the best car. When everyone has roughly the same car, it instead comes down to starting out in front and not making any mistakes. You will not regain the lead unless they also make a mistake.
End of review.

Cons:

The community itself is pretty toxic; Some of them are really petty, aggressive and sometimes downright cringy. whenever im online i feel like im playing with a bunch of 12 year olds who think playing a game with explosions and ♥♥♥♥♥♥s makes them a big kid.
Allow me to paint you a shining example: I was once invited to join somones CEO buisness. I happened to ignore the invite because i was helping a friend out. a couple minutes later, The
f---ing CEO hunts me down with an APC (SAM launcher variant) and a couple of his 'associates' and spawncamps me and my friends taunting us the entire time untill we enabled passive.
At the end they said, 'They've had enough, boys. lets hope the name sticks.' and continued to follow me and spam invites untill we left and found a new session. Im not making this sh*t up.
and now, we finally address the spawn system. Why is the respawn system so bad? Its fairly common to respawn only a block away in the middle of an intersection so you can get sniped immediately by the same guy who did a driveby on you about 12 seconds ago. Why they are allowed to spawn camp you until you are forced to resign your CEO/Club status is beyond me.
PvE mission/heists promote Elitism. mission are instantly failed if someone dies or fails to do their designated job (which is bound to happen) and you get 0-2 spare lives for the entire team to share depending on the difficulty.
Designated jobs are stupid and completely unnecessary- if division of labor needs to get done, people can just open chat and talk about who does what (as a matter of fact, nearly all of the heists would be so much easier if they allowed players to formulate their own plan instead of being spoon fed a preset plan).
If somone fails to deliver thier job, noone else can pick up the slack and the mission is failed, end of discussion. Sometimes it isn't so bad, most of the time it is.
Aside from the current problems that already exist, this Dramatically damages relations between Newbies and Pros because the total payout for a mission decreases the more you restart it- in addition to being fairly small to start with.
Lets not forget that if a single person disconnects during a job/hiest, you are all placed back into matchmaking. Usually everyone else will leave too,  leaving the host incredibly frustrated and alone, waiting for up to 10 minutes to form a new crew.
I don't know If the kick function can be used during a heist/job, but if it does i imagine it hasn't ever been used for this exact same reason.
--------------------------
Alright. Multiplayer is out of the way. Lets move on to the other things.
Weapon/car stats are NOT displayed in numerical values and can be a bit vague. for the most part you won't need it, but it sure as hell would be nice. I still don't know if changing my tires actually does anything.
The UI kind of sucks. You seriously have to open up a menu mid-firefight to use healing items. Granted it would be kind of stupid to mash a button to heal, but it wouldn't be any worse than mashing the menu button to heal. That just comes down to how the actual firefights work.
Indicators of being damaged or having low health can be easily overlooked. The health bar is fairly tiny and is stuffed in the corner, making you have to look away to check your health.
NPC's are pushovers like, 70% of the time. None of them use explosives or even flanking tactics. they do not pose a threat to better-geared players most of the time. If you are undergeared, stay in cover and you'll be fine (usually). They mostly overwhelm with numbers.
Racing is 'meh'. Maybe its because i suck at racing in the first place, but i find it typically boils down to who has the best car. When everyone has roughly the same car, it instead comes down to starting out in front and not making any mistakes. You will not regain the lead unless they also make a mistake.
End of review.

This review comes from years of gameplay and extensive gameplay from the recent Gunrunning Update. Before reading, I do warn, that my preference to Rockstar removing all mods from GTA V will not hinder the views I present in this review.
Overall, the game is an amazing showcase of Rockstars talent of game development. The single player (if you haven't already) is a must! It carries through the heritage and the loveable gameplay from previous GTA games but with new characters, hours of endless gameplay and good, quality graphics.
GTA online as a whole is extremely enjoyable. With friends, it has been some of the most enjoyable gameplay I have joined in on easily in the past 5 years. However, I do have to raise my hands against Rockstar for the way in which money is earned in online. If you don't mind grinding missions for stupidly expensive items, you're safe. However, I do object to the inflation of in game prices and the decrease in money earned from missions and jobs. Before the recent updates of late-2016 and 2017, the games financial system was very balanced and also featured some expensive items but nothing too stupid. Now though however, the finance has been hijacked by Rockstars lust for people to spend on the in-game currency through Shark Cards. Even so, I wouldn't object to it. However, paying similar amounts to the games retail price for $8 million in-game is pathetic.
Lastly, the games aim for players is very scewed. It was in the past very balanced and low-level players had access to the tools to prevent the high-level players from killing them endlessly. However, with the introduction of Gunrunning, it has posed issued with low-level players getting destroyed and pushing them away due to the Rocket Bike and other such vehicles which are virtually impossible to destroy if you're new to the game. With these sorts of vehicles, it does promote a lot of GTA players to go around and kill endlessly (which is not necessarily a bad thing and is what the game is about). But it does push away a lot of new players which are trying to do what they can to level up and earn money.
Overall, I would say it is worth buying the game, but I would also say prepare yourself for the endless grinding, the rocket bikes going around killing you constantly, and the shark cards being forced down your throat.

Brawlhalla is a F2P fighting game. More specifically, it's a Platform Fighter game in the same vein as Smash Brothers. Anyone familiar with the Super Smash Brothers series should be able to hop into this game with relative ease, and anyone who doesn't have experience with ANY games like these shouldn't have a hard time either. It's relatively straightforward, but the key difference that sets it apart from Smash is that it's item-based.
In Brawlhalla, your default weapon is your fists. You suck with your fists. You have barely any range, your attacks come out slow, and you don't do a lot of damage. Every character in the game has the exact same moveset with their fists. What you're supposed to do is pick up the weapons strewn about the battlefield. Once you get a weapon pickup, you'll randomly be assigned one of two different weapons depending on your character. Lord Vraxx for example can get Guns or a Rocket Lance. Thatch can get a Sword or a Gun. With a weapon, your moveset changes accordingly. Everyone's basic attacks with a weapon are the same (two different characters who both use guns will have similar base movesets) but there is a strong attack button that gives you access to your Signatures, which are like Smash attacks. Every character has 6 signatures (down, side, and neutral - three for each weapon). Using your regular attacks to rack up damage on the opponent and finishing them off with your signature techniques is the key to success here.
The fact that all the same weapons have the same basic attacks regardless of who you're playing as means that characters do initially feel much less unique than the rosters in other games like Rivals of Aether, but as a result the game is noticeably more balanced than most and there's more emphasis on individual player skill over the character you're playing. The weapons actually all feel really satisfying to use, and in the right hands you can pull off some pretty insane stuff with them. Feel free to pick a character with weapons you like. There's a viking, a rock dude, a monk, a pirate, and an alien overlord, among others. Gameplay is fluid and tight, and the netcode is surprisingly good.
The soundtrack is actually pretty tight too. Nothing's AMAZING but the music is pretty enjoyable to listen to, and the sound effects for each attack feel good, really sound like they hit hard and seriously add to the overall experience
The game itself is free to play, with a free rotation of heroes each week. You can earn coins through regular play to unlock heroes permanently, but you can easily play and enjoy it all without spending a dime. Compared to games like League and Smite the like, unlocking characters with coins is pretty generous because you'll likely only dedicate yourself to 2 characters at a time (unlike a MOBA where you'd need to learn several so you can fit into a team comp)
In addition there's a huge assortment of cosmetic items which you can purchase with real money if you desire. Weirdly enough I openly welcome the amount of cosmetic content there is. Every hero has at least 3 skins, and then there's alternate weapon skins you can get, KO effects, taunts, and sidekicks. The extra customization is nice for anyone who's willing to shell out for it, but if you don't then you're at no more of a disadvantage than anybody else (at least unless you feel like looking ugly is disadvantageous).
Partly due to it being F2P, the playerbase is surprisingly healthy. Casual online modes consist of Free For All (4 player brawls) and 1v1 Strikeout (three lives, but each life is a different character). For those who are a little more competitive, there's 1v1 Ranked and 2v2 Ranked. 2v2 in particular is a nice addition, as I find climbing with a friend and being able to wombo combo the enemy into oblivion to be immensely satisfying. I faced some toxicity at lower levels of play (Bronze to low Silver, really) but as I climbed I've met some really cool people. Much like any other fighting game, this requires some quick reflexes and split-second decision making, which may not be present in everyone and if you're not used to this sort of thing it may not be for you. Luckily there's a training mode which lets you work on certain things and gives analysis on attacks, framedata and hitbox info.
My only problem would be the art, and it's more like a personal preference than anything else. The art isn't bad, but it resembles something seen from a Facebook game and makes it seem kind of...cheap? The game itself thankfully has a lot of value to it but the art style may turn some people away. The developers are luckily very open and transparent, and take feedback from the community on many internet discussion boards.

I have never written a review on here, but considering this is one of the best games and one of the most underated games ive ever played, ive decided to try my hand at it. Starting off, i know it may say i only have a couple hours on record with the game, but id like to stamp that out now. I played this game years back off an old game engine before steam was a thing, buying it again now is more comfort and support for me, like buying an old book that you read years ago. I have well over 200 hours in the game, and about a thousand in the series. So let me dive in, and let you know what this game is about.
Geneforge is more than a game, its a book, an experiance, a choice, and a beautiful combat system all in one. It cries out to the imaginiative, the 3 am readers, the DnD players, the indie game searchers. What it lacks in graphics, it makes up 10 fold in story. The game puts you in the middle of an entire world and has you influence the outcome of it. In the first game, you find yourself in this estranged world, where the game gives you a brief history of it, then immediately tears that away. It isolates you, shows you that you must survive, and asks you what to do to survive. But that is only the first part. once you gather your bearings, you have to forge a path. At first the paths seem clear, good or evil, but the more you progress the more you realize there is no good. there is no evil. This game makes you question everything, with the only clear progression being that of power. You single handedly experiance the start of a world rebellion, and reitre as a god or a soldier by the end. The same picks up in each consquensial title later on, each putting you, a young shaper, smack dab in the middle of the biggest points in history of this new world. The hours, weeks, months of text painstakingly put into this game alone makes it a solid game, but the combat is fantastic too. You play a tactics style turn based micromanaging comabt system, sort of like fallout: tactics or final fantasy: tactics. But instead of pre determined abilities, like everything else you determine your path. Conjure up an army to fight for you, use magic and objects to trick your opponets and take them out one by one, or don a helmet and sword and slash your way through hoards, the choice is yous. My by far favorite part of it however, has to be the fact that nothing is safe in this game from you. It emphasizes that your choices can change the entire reality. No npc cannot be killed, although it may be hard. The world will form to what you want it to, if you are brave enough to undergo the task. Dont take this as you cannot lose, for the wrong desicion will put you in a spot where you cannot escape. But understand that you are free to make that deicion, you are free to make any desicion. This is the closest i have ever come to DnD Freeplay.
Pro's: Excellent story line, worth of a novel of the highest value.
Freerealm as hell, you are free to make any desicion you want, nothing stops you, you shape the future and history alike.
LOTS and LOTS of content, as said earlieri  have over 1000 hours in the series as a whole. thats a lot for a single player non grind game.

Air neutral/up heavy attacks make you go up. Air down attacks make you go down. It's just more of the same with each character.
Not a whole lot of variety, but I suppose that's fine for some folks. I'd recommend if you don't really care about dextrous fighting, otherwise, not my thing.

It was Wednesday afternoon. The air was quite humid, leading me to be fairly discontent with the current weather situation. I walked around while the air deceived me into believing I was surrounded by thousands of wee salamanders-- all quietly feasting on my flesh. Not in a way that they could do any damage to it, of course, but feasting as salamanders often do on their human comrades... with gentle laps of the tongue. After sustaining adequate mental degredation from the intense heat and offputting humidity, I decided to return back to the inner recesses of my humble cave, and turn on my computer.
I was not certain what I would be doing on this machine... researching the life cycle of salamanders, salamander fun facts, or even the possibility that salamanders as both the creators and destroyers of the universe. Eventually, after meditating on the beauty of these amphibians for what seemed like seven lifetimes (but was actually four seconds) I launched Steam and downloaded this game. And I must say, I am glad I did.
Sounds - 9/10.
Reminded me of the sweet mating call of the Iranian Baldnosed Salamander that I owned once in a dream (I could never own one of these in real life, as their sweet songs often cause any nearby organism to go completely insane and partake in autocannibalism until said organism is nothing more than a bloodied sack of semi-digested organs).
Visuals - 10/10.
I actually blinded myself two years ago so that I could live as the Texas blind salamander (Eurycea rathbuni) does. I am certain if I was able to see this game for myself, though, I would fall in love with it. Something just tells me this game takes wonderful advantage of a multi-layered stage to present an awe-inspiring masterpiece complete with meticulously crafted sprites.
Story - 5/10.
Less one-line Dr. "Edgelord" Seuss quotes that you would find in a horror game sponsored by box tops. My daughter's lungs filled with blood? As if I would allow my daughter to go swim in our corpse-filled pool without her blood snorkel! Add more salamanders and you'd get 10/10.
Gameplay - 9/10.
For a free game, I was impressed by all of the things there were to do. After I completed quest #57, I realized seven days had passed and my body had become host to a local colony of parasitic moths. The moths were quickly removed from the deep nests they bore into my flesh, however there is something I will never be able to remove: the peace and tranqulity this game afforded me in my playthrough of it. Thank you, dear developers.

So. This game is very very fun. Its basically The Thing merged with Aliens merged with Garrys mod TTT. It has four different classes, Cultist, Scientist, Engineer, and Soldier, all with different abilities. For example, the Scientist can conduct experiments in the labratory and give the humans, or the aliens, speed or health buffs, and the Cultist can place down protective symbols to help protect the humans from the Aliens. Speaking of the aliens, one of the players will spawn as an alien in human form, and what you can do is middle mouse click to transform into your true form, or you can right click to infect humans with a huge chest spike. The aliens will try and infect all of the humans, and the humans will attempt to complete special objectives to stop the map exploding. If worst comes to worst there is a escape shuttle in the hanger which one human can escape in. Keep in mind you have unlimited respawns, but if you kill a human with guns as an alien or a human you will be given a penalty to stop mass murders. The storys not so bad either, its basically the humans were drilling in the ground, found an alien artifact that grants unlimited respawns which the cultists worship, and a weird alien tree thing that infects humans.
But, there are a few problems with the game. The main one is the playerbase. There isnt much of one, infact if you go onto the server list you will probably find all empty servers. The devs have worked around that though, they have made a discord area where you can find matches with other people, and the community is great fun to play with. There are a few glitches and bugs, but that is to be expedcted from an early access game, but its a very fun experience none the less.
Would I reccomend this? Yes, yes I would but discord is a must. Without the discord, its nearly impossible to find a game. Go join it. The game is extremely fun, espiecally when your a lesser alien and climbing on the ceiling

3089 is a highly ambitious delightfully quirky game.
When I first bought this game I expected it to be a fun way to spend an evening and then to never play it again. This proved not to be the case as I was sucked in by the interesting world, free form character generation and the equipment customization. What expected to be a shallow RPG experience turned into a vast world of option surrounded by a procedurally generated landscape.
While it’s lack of direction is daunting at first it soon revealed a degree of freedom seldom seen in videogames. Despite this freedom the game does not lack content, the procedurally generated quests, while sometimes strange and nonsensical create there own little stories. You could build your character as a mercenary and take the quests where you kill groups of bots, or you could make a spy, sneaking around planting bugs and eavesdropping on the robotic citizens of Xax. Perhaps you want to build a pilot and fly around the world. Or you could be a leader and get other bots to do your dirty work for you.
What I’m trying to say is that 3089 is an amazingly deep and enjoyable experience that anyone who enjoys action RPG’s should give a shot.

On paper, 3089 is an amazing game: An open world FPS/RPG with procedurally generated weapons, terrain, and quests. The implementation of it leaves much to be desired. It lacks good gunplay (you shoot like you're coming out of a Rainbow Six game, while the enemies shoot like Quake 3 aimbots, meaning you lack the time to get a good shot at them), good leveling mechanics (your skill in guns is completely irrelevant if you don't have a gun on the level of the enemies, your level of agility doesn't mean your grappling hook or teleporter gun can support that much weight), drops are pathetic (every enemy drops something, but it's usually an incomplete item, and items can only be completed at workstations back at base), shops aren't guaranteed to have, say, a level 5 grappling hook, so if your level 1 hook can't support your weight, you're just unable to use that mechanic, flat out, and the quests are completely and totally random. It's not even on the level of "This one guy stole my book. Either talk him into handing over the book or kill him, then return it to me." It's "Get the disc from the person. Then, spy on this person for 1:32 without being seen. Then, kill 3 robots. Then, defuse a bomb without being seen or killing anyone. Then, remove some ghosts. Then, hand over the disc to this other person without being seen." There's no attempt to make your actions seem worthwhile, to give them any context. Your only reward is a handful of skill points. There is no way to visually tell level 1 enemies from level 5 enemies, you simply have to infer it from how they're doing slightly under a third of your health with each of their perfectly accurate shots while you fumble around trying to shoot them at point-blank range with your wildly inaccurate weapon. If it's 3099 improves by the same amount that this did from 3079, then I could recommend that game, but ultimately, I can't 3089.

When the kickstarter was announced for this game, I was intregued.  There hadn't been a Wipeout game for PC since the original Wipeout 2049 (also called XL in the US), but this generally was unplayable on modern hardware due to the speed it ran at.
So having a Wipeout styled game for PC being developed by former staff from the original Wipeout team was something to jump at.  So how does it fair?
Graphically Formula Fusion has retained the style and settings familiar to Wipeoput 2049, but updating to a much higher resolution to make modern gamers happy.  The tracks have lots of detail packed into them and are visually quite a treat - from the neon city lights of New York, to the misty water haze as your fly behind the waterfall on the Niagra track.
AI can be a little hit and miss, sometimes being nowhere to be seen once you have taken the lead (more true on the earlier tracks of the FF4000 campaign).  Once you start progressing into the higher classed races, they can be more challenging to get past and stay in front of.
This brings us onto the weapons in the game.   If you expect a wipeout styled weapon experience, this is the one place you may feel let down.  While you can select from several styles of ship from the onset, and earn credits to be able to upgrade them in your garage, the ships are pre-loaded with a set of default weapons (typically one offensive and one defensive).
While you can change the weapon loadout in your garage before starting a race, this does leave you with less enjoyment than could be found in the manic random weapons provided in the Wipeout series of games.  It also leaves you with a less strategic playthrough as in Wipeout you could be waiting for a specific weapon to help you  or to hold on to for those final seconds before the finish line.
And the weapons themselves in FF don't seem to be as impactful as you would get in Wipeout.  The mines especially would not be a recomended choice generally in FF as a primary weapon.
The music while does fit in well enough with the game - although the original Wipeout game music still ranks as some of the best for this style of game - that even 2049 players would often substitute the default music for (The Prodigy's Firestarter was still the ultimate track to play that game to).
There have been people complaining as to the lack of perceived speed when playing compared to the original Wipeout series, or some of the newer antigravity games like Redout or Ballistic NG.  While FF may not whizz the scenery past at the same velocity of Redout, it is by no means a slouch.  Controls can feel a little less tight when compared to the Wipeout games, but they have been revised since the early betas of FF to give a familiar feel with a bit of weight behind them.
As with all games, there are learning curves, and once you start to get used to the handling physics in FF, you can navigate the tracks without too much trouble.   The biggest problem lies in the narrowness of some parts of tracks, which are a pain if you do not turn off sterring assist (as it will slow down when approaching bends costing you dearly when approaching these tighter bendy areas of the tracks).
The game does still have some issues which are constantly being worked on and patched out by the developers, and they do have good feedback in the forums and community area.
Overall the game shows a lot of promise and is constantly still being improved by the developer.  It is a worthy addition for any antigravity racer fan who enjoyed Wipeout in any form.

Geneforge is one of those gems that sat in my games library forever that I swore I'd get around to eventually.  I'm glad I finally did.  When I first tried to play it, the graphics and sound and simplistic gameplay turned me off, and I put off playing the game.  However, having picked it back up, I can happily say that the game makes up for the lack of graphics and sound with excellent gamplay and a cool new world to explore.  I was surprised that such a simple design could give so much freedom to the player in how they interact with the world.
The fact that it's so simple actually works in the game's favor.  Gameplay is straightforward and challenging, but not because the controls are clunky, but because every situation requires careful planning.  The plot is good enough to keep you invested, and at least for me, the gameplay was entertaining enough that I kept playing long after I could have ended the main plotline just because I wanted to explore the world more.
If you have trouble with games that rely on text to tell the story, this might not be for you.  If you have trouble with older looking games, I'd encourage you to give it a shot.  I'm glad I managed to look past the graphics long enough to let the game grow on me.  And this game has sold me on playing the other four as well.
Just remember to save.

If this review is too long for you, you probably aren't going to enjoy this text-heavy game.  But you can skip to the summary at the end.
REVIEW
Go back to the very early stages of this millenium (when this game was released), and you might remember two things:  (1) fascination with emerging medical technologies surrounding genetic modification and (2) the Infinity Engine at its zenith.  Both of these influences can be found in Geneforge, which takes genetic modification as its theme, and uses a Baldur's Gate-like mechanic for its gameplay (although shorn of D&D rules and a conventional fantasy setting).
Like the Infinity Engine games, Geneforge is an isometric, story-driven RPG which actually respects the *R*.  It takes place in several discrete zones spread out over a world map.  It is text-heavy.  The basic mechanics are much simpler here, however--simpler, but complicated enough to admit of sophisticated strategy.  It is also quite robust, giving many hours of gameplay to anyone interested in exploring everything.
As an indie game, however, it is graphically ugly.  Much of the text exists to describe what more graphically advanced games would show without words.  The interface is sometimes incovenient, and you'll naturally find yourself irritated with some of the aspects of inventory management--although my own irritation might have a lot to do with my neurotic hoarding/organizing addiction.  (For a reference, check out some of the screenshots posted in the Steam community to get a sense of how loot can get away with you.)
The open-endedness of the world can also be a curse as much as a blessing:  about halfway through the game, it's easy to lose focus on where you ought to be going.  (
If nothing else, check out the Matt P's numeric rating of the difficulty of each zone--this can give you a sense of what areas are best to tackle next.)
To my mind, there are two main selling points to this game: (1) the novelty of creating and modifying creatures to aid you as you go about, and more importantly (2) the story.  But the attractiveness of the story needs some unpacking.
The story is open-ended, and it involves you responding to some events on an island surrounding competing factions with conflicting motivations vying for power.  That's nice and all--although you can get that kind of fare elsewhere.  That's not where the real juice of this game lies.  The best part of the story isn't the plot proper, which concerns your character.  It's what has already happened in the *past*, and which you discover incrementally as you proceed.
Think of yourself as a kind of archeologist, doing a dig.  You dig at a site, and discover what a certain society was like.  But if you dig a bit deeper, you might see the remains of a civilization that existed at an even earlier time.  Dig even deeper and...you get the idea.  The way I counted, there were *four* layers of history contained in this game, from the truly ancient to the recent past, and you fill in the pieces of this rich puzzle of what has happened on Sucia Island as you proceed.  (Incidentally, I have no idea if this pattern continues for other games in this saga, although I suspect not.)
If the idea of playing the role of archeologist sounds like your cup of tea, pick up this game.  (You might also want to pick up Steven Erikson's fantasy novels, but I digress.)
One final note:  This is the first of a long saga of 5 Geneforge games.  I haven't played those other games, but GF1 is quite satisfactory all on its own as a standalone title.  So, don't feel that you *need* to get drawn into the larger saga to enjoy GF.
SUMMARY
+ Open-ended, with interesting moral themes
+ Simple but sophisticated gameplay
+ Great story
+ The novelty of shaping/creating your allies
- Ugly
- Lacks direction at times
- Interface can be clunky
I'd recommend this game to anyone who can appreciate its intellectual flavor and doesn't mind primitive graphics.

Into the Future allowing you to play in a futuristic scenario along with the addition and customization of robot companions. I'd avoid World Adventures, Island Paradise, and any of those "Stuff" packs.

This 2D platformer fighting game is well executed technically. The art style, animations, and hitboxes are all very clean. However, the game failes to have a strong hook of its own. The different game modes change the number of players and how they get assigned to matches, rather than changing the objectives of the matches themselves. And this wouldn't be so bad if the game didn't start feeling monotonous so quickly.
Character attack styles change with what weapon they're equipped, but every character uses the same style when equipped with the same weapon. Because of this, characters become more of set of weapons they can equip than anything really individually interesting. Further, there isn't a very wide variety of attack types, with hitboxes via weapon swipes being the vast majority of attacks (I was surpised to not find any projectile attacks despite guns being an equippable weapon). Finally, with the only defensive option that feels powerful being "not be in range of enemy attacks" the game is lopsided towards offense, which causes competitive play to usually devolve into keep away and doesn't allow real mind games.

This is the first game I have ever regretted getting on sale.  I sincerely wish I had paid full price because it was worth it.
A review of a few aspects of this game follows with some light spoilers (no leaks about plot).  The spoilers will be in the paragraphs with headings.  If you don't want to read anything and experience the game completely fresh (which I heartily reccommend) then buy it now, regardless of whether its on sale.
Summary: I purchased this for just over $2 and it was very much worth it.  I would have paid full price ($14) if I had known it would be such a great game, but I didn't. So I am telling you it is good enough to pay at least as much as you would for a movie ticket.  Because you don't really play this game, you experience it.  I will be very
disappointed if this does not spawn some kind of follow on work because there is so much room for the ideas presented here to grow.  I can only think of one reason that any person should NOT play this game, and that is due to it requiring a controller (as indicated in the Gameplay section below). Get it,  you will not be disappointed.
SETTING
I wont comment much here because it needs to be appreciated from a fresh perspective.  But right from the beginning there is more there than you might think.  And this is definitely a game where it is good to stop and just look around.  The only regret I have here is that there is not more to see.  The world is beautiful and just so.....you have to see it to understand.  But its far greater than you would expect out of a 3hr game.
GAMEPLAY
This requires a controller, and that fact may screw with your head for a while.  I know that even towards the end there were moments where I confused with how to make which brother do what.  And just when you think you have it down, it gets harder and you feel like you are playing with one arm tied behind your back.  And then it just clicks and you get it.  This adds to the uniqueness of the experience and is a plus (even though it might seem like a slight minus).
TONE
This game reminds me of a certain tv show (which I won't name) regarding to how it opens.  And then it continues to present other things.  Metaphorically speaking, its like a song with no chorus: it changes as it progresses but not so much that you feel like you are listening to a different song at the end.  For reference, there was a definitive moment when I went "ok. But how is this going to end?"  Shortly afterward I answered my own question with a "Wow.  Yeah, ok."  While I'm sure that sounds cryptic, the point is that the game does not fail to continue to surprise you until the end (although surprise is not exactly the best word to use to describe it I think).
MUSIC
That noise in the background.  Thats how I treat everygame I play, but this one is different.  The music has no bearing on your gameplay (i.e. it doesnt give you a clue of what to do), but it is just as much a part of the story as the visuals and gameplay are. I have tried three times to explain this further in words, but I just can't do it.  I think you will understand when you listen for yourself.
If you are still reading, I will just end with the following two statements:
- What is presented in this 3hr game/story/experience could easily be expanded to something that could take as many as 20-30hrs in my opinion.  And that makes this beginning chapter so much more potent, even if a sequel never comes.
- This game earns a legitimate high score because it accomplishes what it sets out to do very well indeed.
10/10 MUST PLAY

Hey! How's it going everybody, and welcome, to the first Squishy review. Today we've got Brawlhalla.
First, a description. Brawlhalla is an online multiplayer game, which can also be played offline in couch party. It's developed by indie studio blue Mammoth Games. In case you haven't noticed, this game takes a few pages from Super Smash Bros. It's really hard to take that formula and make it your own without the comparison being made. Fortunately, unlike other clones, this is a solid fix for anyone looking for an experience like said game on PC. So I'll be going through pros, cons, and subjective things that could be pros or cons. Also, for the devs, I'll give some ways the game can improve.
(Disclaimer: I am only gold rank, so this is not the full game experience. I'll update the review as I go.)
+ Really fun gameplay.
+Easy to pick up, hard to master, just like Smash.
+Great sound. It's crisp, satisfying, and does it's job, giving you feedback.
+NOT P2W. Instead, you spend money on Mammoth coins to buy cosmetic items.
+A good amount of tutorials to help you get better at the game. You can find them on Reddit, the wiki, and YouTube.
+A great competitive scene. I would say Gravy Cancel offers the best tournaments right now, but official Brawlhalla tournaments aren't bad either.
+Really easy to master all characters movesets. All legends have two weapons, where the majority of moves come from, and an unarmed moveset, which is also the same.
+The graphics are really charming. Unlike most other indie games, it's not pixelated, and isn't made to wow you with it's style. It's basically a cartoon. I love it!
+Will run on almost any computer, unless you have a Commodore 64.
+A well balanced game. No legends are blatantly more powerful than others.
+Plenty of modes to play. There is singleplayer arcade, but also ranked, team ranked, custom games, strikeout, and couch co-op.
+Devs constantly update, adding new legends, tweaking the game, fixing bugs, and adding new test features.
+/-Not the most tight controls. It's actually kind of floaty. I found these controls to be easier to pick up than Smash, but some Smash veterans may not like it.
+/-Music. I like it, but it never leaves the background.
+/-I feel some people won't like the amount of characters available. Don't know how you couldn't. Really, I think this is a good amount of characters.
+/-No story. It doesn't really matter anyways in this game, but maybe some people want to know more about this world they're fighting in. The closest thing to story you'll get is tidbits of lore about the legends.
+/-No singleplayer campaign. I don't care whatsoever, but some people may want a little bit of experience playing the game before going online.
+/-Like any fighting game, you'll need to invest quite a bit of time to get good at the game. I've seen quite a few people complaining about how they can't beat a certain combo or string, or they can't beat spammers. While balancing does need to be done in those areas, there's also a matter of you can't beat those people because you're not experienced enough, or you don't know how. My advice? Look at some guides, practice, know what moves to use when, and use the opponent's predictability to your advantage.
+/-The community is a bit iffy. On the one hand, you have some great people that you can become friends with that are actually good at the game and can help you. On the other hand, you have a lot of salt sprinkled around the community in the form of people who think the game sucks because they can't win against a spammer, and then there's the spammers themselves, which tend to be extremely toxic, and will rage at you when they lose. That's not the case for everybody, but it seems to be the norm. Overall, just be nice.
+/-You won't get all the legends right away. There's a free weekly rotation of legends with each patch, and you can buy the legends with in game currency you earn by logging in, leveling up, and completing quests.
-Lag. Now, if you play with a wired connection, you should be fine. But, a wireless connection is dreadful to play with. Now I play with a wireless connection so some of this may not be true, but I think there's also issues with the servers from time to time. Devs, I mean no offense if you read this, and this may just be me, but there may be issues with the servers. I say this because sometimes online performs better than other times. Luckily, there's a way to report lag if you're struggling.
-Not the same amount of depth as Smash Bros Melee. This may or may not matter to people, but anybody expecting the same amount of depth as Melee in this game is going to be sorely disappointed. There are definetely advanced concepts and techniques, and some of them different than Smash, but overall, not as much.
-Exploits and balance issues. This is going to be the biggest problem for new players, and what makes most people quit. Some of them are worse than others. These are extremely annoying to deal with at first, but there are definitely ways to get around them, you just gotta stick with it. I constantly see people complaining about the exploits, but it's still your fault you lost, not the game or your opponent. You can use these for yourself as well but people won't love you for it. If you don't want to use exploits, these will severly♥♥♥♥♥♥you off at first. However, if you're learning from your mistakes, you'll beat them eventually. Basically, stick with it, practice, and learn the best way to circumvent these. There are guides if you need help!
You don't have to get rid of the exploits, but make them a bit harder to use. Also, find a way to stop edge camping. Sometimes, you can edge camp on a map and then run away when your opponent starts chasing after you. Find a way to get rid of this! It's almost impossible to beat. Also, find some way to reward the aggressive players against the evasive players. Maybe attacking makes your character move slightly faster for a little bit. Thank you guys for being awesome, and I can't wait for the future!
5/5: What the Hell are you doing get this game!
Overall, this is still a great game for anyone looking for a casual, fun Smash fix on PC. Not for anyone looking for ludicrous amounts of depth, or for anyone who blames their losses on the game or opponents. If you are the latter, GTFO RIGHT NOW. Also, make friends and join a clan. It's much funner playing with friends. Thanks for reading, and give it a thumbs up if it was helpful. I really want the devs to see this review so help will be appreciated.

I would recommend this game to anyone interested and have really enjoyed what it has to offer so far.
There is more depth to it than originally appears, that said we've been fortunate enough to get eight friends to get it so we've had some really great games.
+ Classes are good fun and prove different approaches
+ Inclusion of items such as the radio helps identify aliens (although I don't think players should start with one) and add depth
+ classes still useful as aliens- can research tech to improve aliens like the humans can
+ Aliens can sabotage systems- this is huge and really adds to the tension! We particularly like that they can take out the lights
+ varied objectives keep most matches fresh
+ the two levels are fairly fun and different from each other although the Aurora has much more tension and tactical possibility.
+ Fun with friends as long as you're all on mics.
+ Aliens can crawl on walls and ceilings (as long as they aren't the prime)
-Dying resets skills- it takes far too long as an engineer or scientist to do what you need, and one death resets all of this. Friendly fire counts too, very hard to make progress as an engineer or scientist.
-Not enough of a penalty for killing humans as a human. I've seen others say they want less, but it's possible to kill a few players and carry on playing
- Not enough tutorials or tooltips. After 6 hours we still don't understand the alien abilities!
- Objectives are still not clear (but this is early access) and can result in player death until you've understood it all.
- Not enough areas on maps where there are backdoors- too many places where humans can just camp an entrance and force the aliens to try to rush them.
Despite the cons, I would suggest that as long as you can get a group of people together, this game is well worth the cost and as long as the Devs keep working on it, will continue to be excellent!

3089 -- Futuristic Action RPG - yes, the 'futuristic action RPG' bit actually is in the title, is a game by phr00t's Software that found it's way on Steam by way of Greenlight.  I can hear the groan already, with the reputation for shovelware and drek that Greenlight has garnered for itself.  It's not entirely undeserved, both in the terms of Greenlight and in terms of this game specifically.  To sum up my thoughts, 3089 (yeah, I'm just going to call it 3089 from hereon out), is a game I feel delivers a lot of promise but not a lot of content.  Mechanically, it's sound - and yet, it feels like it doesn't really do anything particularly interesting with those mechanics.
Let me just add as an aside before I get too much into the meatier bits of review that I looked at both 3079 and 3089 and 3089 is the one that seemed to offer anything at all, really, in terms of meaningful content, so that is the one I am reviewing now.  I may return to 3079 at a later date, perhaps after a content update, if it ever receives one.
The game is obviously largely Minecraft-inspired in it's visual aesthetic.  It's .. fairly well implemented, and I feel it kind of gives it a bit of a unique bent.  However I feel it really doesn't add to the game in any meaningful way, and in fact makes it look very 'budget'.  The thing with the sort of 'voxel' look that Minecraft gives is that it is very difficult to pull off that visual style without looking like you're doing the style out of a lack of being able to do something better.  In this case, it's less that, and more an obvious attempt at aping something very Minecraft, which I'm very 'eh' about.  I'm not a fan of Minecraft's visual aesthetic to begin with, so something to improve upon that style wouldn't be looked down upon, but I feel that the ways in which the aesthetic varies actually adds a sort of visual inconguence.  The models for the androids, fighters, and usable objects are much higher poly-count than the world itself, and it makes it feel as if they do not belong in the same world.  It is rather inconsistent in that way.  Several textures in the game world become hugely distorted or over-sized by trying to stretch them over one large face rather than simply properly tiling them, as well.
The gameworld itself is procedurally-generated, like many roguelike games, and it seems to have a decent variety to it.  It's .. fairly sparse however, and crossing from one area to another can be onerous.  Put yourself in mind of going cross-country in Skyrim, and then imagine all the flora and fauna on the way aren't there.  Some of the 'biomes' for lack of a better description are better than others, but they all seem kind of empty.  Most of what you'll encounter are .. crates and other androids.  And the occasional building or town with merchant stations, crafting stations, or quest stations.  It makes the gameplay seem padded and very dry, to end up spending so much of it just in transit.  Most importantly, it just isn't fun to have to spend that much time trekking, and the game doesn't offer any passing scenery that would capture your interest.
The gameplay mechanics are similar to many games with roguelike elements.  You have a procedurally-generated quests system, a crafting system, and related things such as health stations and energy stations.  The mechanics of these are fairly well-implemented, just bland.  None of the items I came across seemed particularly inspired or interesting and many weapons are simply better versions of existing ones, rather than ones with unique mechanics.
The gunplay itself is fairly unsatisfying, and that's what leaves me ultimately unsatisfied with the game, I think.  Guns ungratifyingly plink-plink-plink enemies and don't have any feeling of weight or power behind them.
As a final note, I did want to add one solid positive and say that I really dug the soundtrack and general sound design.  I found it pretty context appropriate and that's a common stumbling block for many independent developers.
Ultimately, the onerous exploration and the unsatisfying gameplay coupled with the long periods of essentially doing nothing interesting, and I can't really recommend 3089.  It has potential though, so I may revisit the game if it receives a content update.  I think that's the biggest disappointment here, it's a bunch of things really well-implemented that just don't seem to get realised to it's potential.  And I hate to say that, I really do, because it's quite obvious this developer cares about their game and they have put a lot of work into it.  Perhaps with some more work on the polish, it'll improve.

Formula Fusion was supposed to be a worthy successor to Wipeout. They had the staff, the design, the concept, and the music all right. But, as is often the case with these things, they failed at the execution.
The biggest issue with this game is one of the worst for a racing game: the physics and controls are just not fun. It feels less like an anti-gravity racer and more like trying (and failing) to control a bobsled running down a track. What's worse, one of the biggest defining features of these types of games, the air brakes, don't feel like they do anything helpful at all. Using them doesn't help you make better turns, but still slows you down. It just doesn't feel like you have control over your vehicle. Even if you did, though, the feel of the physics is disappointing. It simply doesn't have the depth or immersion of the games that came before.
That isn't where the problems end, though. Some others include:
-Confusing UI/player feedback
-Weapons system is confusing and over-complicated for how little it adds to the game (useless compared to Wipeout)
-Narrow track design that doesn't pair well with the lack of control of your vehicle
-Generic locations/world
-Muddy graphics, making it hard to learn tracks and see what is ahead of you
-Garage system is presented poorly, and makes it hard for anyone who just wants to get into a race
-Poor optimization/framerate
-Promised music was never added to the game
Many of these problems may have not been nearly as big of a deal if previous games hadn't gotten them so incredibly right. But, as it stands, I cannot recommend Formula Fusion, especially to any fan of Wipeout. You most likely will NOT enjoy it.
Instead, I'd recommend trying BallisticNG, a fantastic free fan game based much more closely on the Wipeout formula.

The Neptunia Games have always been a matter of whether you love the games or just straight up hate them. I'm more in the middle but that's for another topic.
Let's get this review out of the way: How did this game came to be you may ask? Simple answer - take Hyperdimesion Neptuina U, give a zombie makeover with a zombie story, add the schoolgirl genre because it wouldn't be Japanese enough right and take everything that made U fun and throw it all away and you get this. A fast paced hack and slash that's quite slow to be honest especially compared to Senran Kagura and Hyperdimension Neptunia U which are much faster paced and are actually fun to play.
The story is about as ordinary as any zombie based story is: the school is infested with zombies(it's actually a play but who's paying attention to this badly written story)and it's up to the Neptunia Cast to stop them(Loose sense of the word). And that's where all the problems begin - the zombie thing has been done to death(pun intended)by the Western World to the point all you need is zombies and BAM! Instant money(coughcough The Walking Dead coughcough). So the makers of this game(must be on something high)thought they can input their ideas into the genre and added the most cliche thing ever: schoolgirls(because it wouldn't be Japanese if it didn't have them). The game has crashing problems when changing the screen size or just changing the screen to full size which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as hell. This game is utterly amazing: a different take on CRPG where you are the Shaper and you create your party members through your own abilities.  It is a Fatasy setting with a twist of science fiction blended into a story that is both moving and fantastic. It will lead you into various adventure quests as the story is non-linear.  It has a ton of maps to explore especially when you find that lone canister hidden in a locked away room and you click on it to alter your shapers genetic code--what surprises will the canister yield upon your Shaper--you never know.
The game is old, the graphics may not appeal to some, especially to those younger gamers who are accustomed to high fidelity graphics and game play.  This is a turn base combat style game and should not be mistaken as a Diablo clone just because it has an isometric perspective, it is far from a Diablo style game.  If you're new to CRPG and you have purchased this game or had gotten it for free I would suggest playing it on easy mode it can still be quite challenging at times.  The other modes are much too difficult for someone new this format of gaming, once you get the feel of the mechanics, feel free to set your challenges higher: Normal, Tricky , and Torment-- frustration and delight awaits you in those modes.
Overall, this is one of my favorite games next to Planescape: Torment, Ultima 7, and System Shock 2, in fact, I bought the entire saga and am looking forward to playing all five games.
