Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a good game, but it ultimately falls short of greatness, which is unfortunate because it does improve on some of the aspects of Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
In terms of the good, DE:MD expands the "choose-your-own-playstyle" freedom that's the hallmark of the Deus Ex universe. For instance, combat-based playthroughs (both lethal and non-lethal) are equally viable with a sneaky, hacker ghost. (In particular, the possibility of a weapons-blazing, non-lethal combat style is pretty unique.) Most missions have dozens of ways to get to your goal, and this is the best thing about DE:MD--you can really play how you want to.  There are other great things, too--the black and gold aesthetics continue to visually set Deus Ex apart from other generic sci-fi titles.
The dystopian world building is amazing, with the tragic fallout from DE:HR permeating everything, from the apartheid of Prague's police state to the snippets of loss picked up in passing conversation. But, paradoxically, this leads to my biggest critque of the game: the nuances invested in the world seem to have come at the cost of the characters and story. Adam Jensen, the protagonist, is ever the gruff, moralizing hero. The main characters are barely given much to say other than mission objectives, with each conspicuously having one "Humanizing Backstory Conversation." Unfortunately, that's not enough to care--even though I wanted to.
Further, the story seems strangely small for a Deus Ex game. Without giving away too much, your taske is to find out who's behind a terrorist attack and, of course, that leads to a slightly bigger conspiracy. The plot is about as sophisticated as a made-for-TV sci-fi movie, which seems like a waste, especially in comparison to the convoluted, conspiracy-filled narrative twists that the series is known for. This might be excusable if DE:MD used the space to do some interesting character building, but it doesn't.
So, I liked my time with DE:MD. I got to cruise around as a god-like stealth master, which was pretty fun. Did I end up really caring about either the plot or the people? Not really. I would've liked to, though, since the series shows so much promise.
7.5 / 10
PS: Other small gripes that minorly impacted my enjoyment:
1) In DE:HR, I liked the epic "persuade" conversations with the number of choices and timely interrupts, but DE:MD generally has fewer and less difficult ones--which seems directly related to the character-building problem stated earlier.
2) The AI seems kind of silly. For instance, if I walk into the LOS of a guard in a restricted area, they get suspicious, but if I move several inches over into a non-restricted area, they don't.
3) If you are doing a stealthy playthrough, the game pretty much stops being hard less than halfway through. The enemies don't get any increased ability to detect you--the security devices and patrols just become more numerous. But, once you can cloak and have a full battery, you can basically just speed run through the game by walking past everyone.

I've been playing this game for ages, longer than I've had Steam, and I still come back to it nearly every week. Obviously, this game isn't nearly as interesting for people who don't know the 40k universe as it is to fans of it, but it is still a very enjoyable game with lots of replayability, and is a solid game with or without the 40k setting.
The replayability only really comes from the skirmish and multiplayer, as I find the campaign to be a bit repetitive and quite franky not very interesting. Plus, while there is a good selection of units in this installment in the series, I always find the there is always a couple of units for every race that I seldom use unless I specifically work them into my strategy. My only other real complaint is that there is sometimes annoying pathing issues with units moving in a large group, and if you are playing with AI it can become quite tedious.
Other than that, i absolutely love these games, mainly due to the awesome unit models and animations etc. The army painter is also a really nice feature that allows you to create your own armies or recreate known ones from the 40k universe (to some degree - it is a bit simple for some designs). The aesthetic and overall art style ties in very well with the setting aswell, including all the viscera and crater holes that are left behind from bloody combat. The maps are also varied and are good sizes for the most part. The game itself also makes you feel like your part of the battle, and the strategic point based gameplay is a nice spin on traditional RTS.
Overall, it's a solid game with some fun features, but it is the setting and the aesthetic that keeps me playing, probably because I am a big fan of the 40k universe. So to conclude, if you are into 40k, it is a very worthwhile purchase, but if you aren't... eh, I'd still buy the game.

I have been playing Lords of the Rings Online (LOTRO) since it went to free to play in 2010.  I just loaded LOTRO from Steam recently.   LOTRO has been my favorite MMORPG, since City of Heroes was closed.  I have bought all the quest packs, expansions and many unlocks for my one account. I only play on the Gladden server.
LOTRO is called a "Free to Play" MMORPG in the description, but if you want to reach level cap in LOTRO, you will have to pay some real money.  Free to Play accounts are limited on purpose, of course. Free to Play only have the landscape enemies, all the epic story quests, few instances, some instant action quests, 3 starter areas and 1 area lvl 20 to 30, and can make 2 characters which have to buy trait powers, bags, swift travel, gold cap unlock, etc. The Devs are quite generous with awarding store points for just playing LOTRO and the game is more Free To Play friendly than others.  You can grind for store points by completing deeds on each character on your account, but you would have to work very hard to earn enough just to buy 1 quest pack.  You can also Google for guides to show you how to earn enough store points to Play for Free, check the Steam guides also.
I suggest you try it out from Steam as Free to Play only, up to level 32. Then if you really want to pay, go to the in-game store to set up credit card payments. The best way to play LOTRO, imho, is to pay for the all the Expansions and Quest packs, then take VIP for 1 month, then create all your characters, then play for free as Premium account.   Expansions have to be bought separately, even for VIP players, but can be bought with store points in-game.  Paying for VIP for 1 month will unlock all the stuff for each character you open that you would have to buy separately.  With store points, you are able to unlock alot of things that VIP players get for free, and are in premium and free accounts to annoy them. Get the account Wallet also. The LOTRO store has a lot of sales on points bundles and items in store.  Don't expect payments from the Steam wallet to work, but it has worked at one time.
If you have problems running this game while loaded from Steam, then download it straight from the LOTRO dot com website.  If you are a Mac user, and have problems playing this game then switch to a Windows OS computer.
There is no pvp servers, just special pvp maps for level 105 subscribers to fight player controlled monsters.  You get a Orc Warrior (Reaver) for free with any character on that server reaching level 10.  The rest of the Creep classes are buyable using store points.  You can pvp on the same side by sparring but there is no rewards for that.
LOTRO is a massively multiplayer online role-playing game set in a fantasy universe based upon J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-Earth novels. It takes place during the time period of The Lord of the Rings movies. The graphics and controls are good still.  The level cap currently is 105 and there is plans for more expansions. The game like all other MMORPGs that has it's faults but it is better than the other games out there currently still, imho.  There are still plenty of hardcore and new players on the remaining open servers, after there has been a server consolidation in 2016. Standing Stone games is the original development team and have shifted producer to Daybreak game in 2017.  Has a great Crafting system. There are plenty of raids, dungeons and instant action content.
Try this game out if you like fantasy MMORPGs.

The game is still receiving big updates (Dev hinted at vehicles soon, and I think they're still trying to balance the weapons out) but the basic mechanics are all here.  The game is funny, has great music, and the levels are all very unique.
The basic premise of the gameplay is that it is online only, (no bots, no story) and each level has a unique goal.  So it isn't like other shooters where you pick the game mode (death match, capture the flag) and then apply that game mode to your map.  In this game there is one free for all level, a couple capture the flag levels, a couple base domination levels, etc.  My favorite level is Barnyard Ball, where the soldiers are fighting on a foozball table and must push a giant ball into the goal.
On the downside, some the levels lack any kind of spawn protection, so you can run into situations where you spawn and die, spawn and die, spawn and die.  This is typically less of a problem when there are more players at a time.
But as other reviewers have noted, there don't seem to be that many people playing the game right now.  Hopefully  with the steam summer sale, the server population will increase.  The game tends to be more active on weekends.
Mean Greens is at its most fun when the teams are evenly matched with a lot of players.  It is meant to be a hectic game.  Death counts for great players can still be pretty high.  So don't feel bad if you die alot.
The combat itself is basic in a good way.  There is no cover mechanic, there are no smoke grenades or flashbangs, you don't have to bust down doors.  This isn't Rainbow Six.  And that's a good thing.  It's meant for a broad audience, it makes me laugh, and for the most part the regular community is good natured and fair.
I want you to buy this game, mainly because I want more people to play it with.

I wanted to like this game. I'm sure that the game had many interesting choices to make that led to different stories. I didn't mind the poor graphics one bit, and I'm normally a fan of games like Baldur's Gate.
In the end, though, I just couldn't get used to the terrible combat. It's infuriating. Make and ugprade a few meat shield creatures coupled with a few ranged ones and you're good to go. Just charge forward and hope that you don't die. And I say hope because it all really does hinge on luck. In games like X-COM, you might need to rely on a few lucky hits, but for the most part, some dumb mistake you made is responsible for your deaths. Your choices matter in games like X-COM. Too bad Geneforge isn't like that.
In Geneforge, there are a-holes that can instakill your main character everywhere. Seriously, there are areas where more than 75% of the monsters can bring your main character from 100% HP to 0% HP. Even the second hostile monster in the game, the Thahd, can one-shot your main character. All any of those instakilling a-holes have to do is attack your main character, get a decent damage value from the RNG, and land the hit to trigger the game over screen. All you can do about it is pray that their AI picks on your creations rather than your main character or get bad RNG numbers if they do attack your main character. Too bad the AI doesn't always pick on your creatures. Sometimes, they just arbitrarily walk past your meat shield and give your main character a lethal smack, and that's it. And all of that happens on normal difficulty. On harder difficulties like torment, the monsters get better hit chance and damage, which means more one-shots on your main character. That's half the combat: just hoping that some monster doesn't one-shot your main character.
If you can get over that hurdle, you'll have a good time. I personally couldn't ignore this problem though.

Old school western RPG.
If you have played anything like Fallout 1-2, or maybe Baldur's Gate, you should feel right at home here. Although it's an early 2000 game, the interface feels like it's from the mid 90s - makes sense, Jeff Vogel is essentially a one man development team.
But why do I recommend this game? Because Jeff Vogel creates wide open worlds with large amounts of content, alternate paths, and meaningful quests. Throughout my ~35 hours of play, the only parts that felt like a grind/chore were a few specific areas (<1 hour, because I chose to ignore them) that had large swarms of mobs roaming the map, or environmental damaging effects that were too annoying to deal with. The only quests that felt like the reason of being given as "because ♥♥♥♥ you, that's why" were few, played for good effect, and completely optional. Speaking of optional quests and really open worlds, it is technically possible to beat it by performing the only quest that you get at the very beginning - Get Off Sucia Island. Of course, you miss out on a fair amount of treats Geneforge will offer you.
Combat is alright, but hardly optimal. Pathfinding is trash - you gotta manually path out a lot of movement or face the consequences of letting the pathfinding handle it. RNG can be somewhat harsh - 50 max hp, take 8 damage, take 6 damage, take 41 damage, dead. Frequent saving and/or high risk aversity can negate this. Despite all of that, there is a variety of playstyles, builds, and spells that make combat entertaining enough.
In summary, if you are willing to overlook the flaws associated with an aged genre, you will find world building and open-ended questing/exploration strong enough to rival the best of titles in that category.

Geneforge from Spiderweb Software is a old school indie RPG Game. It is dated, sure, but it still has a lot of charm.
The first part of the game introduces the player into the world of Geneforge, the Island Sucia was abandoned 200 years ago and you are stranded on the Island. You have to make a choice which of three selectable classes you will take, later in the game you'll also be member of one of the factions (sects) each with benefits and codex.
The selection you make during the game will change the outcome of the game, and this long before the genre of visual novels was envisioned. The area of this game isn't exceptionaly large but it has good stories to tell, and a lot of hard obstacles to overcome. The difficulty of the game can at times be misleading, but that isn't a drawback, it is in fact a virtue of the game.
The game is not a high end graphical game which might come to some as a bad thing, but graphics often don't play such a great role in RPG games, at least not in the elder games. Of course the game still had potential to be even better than what was achieved, but you can play this game and still have a lot of fun, or get utterly frustrated by a random encounter with too many foes that were too strong for you and your creations.
I can recomend this game based alone on the RPG virtues of the time when it was created.

Give this game a shot based on the gameplay it offers rather than the graphical presentation. Personally, I enjoy the simple graphics as it adds a somewhat nostalgic feel to the game's environment. Also, all graphical elements are moddable through the .jar file and the ease of modding the game is highly encouraged by the game's developer.
It combines the addictiveness of Diablo/Borderlands' weapon and armor randomization with the procedurally generated terrain such as in Minecraft and achieves it very successfully. In addition, you can break and combine parts of armor and weapons.
Yes, there are grappling hooks, gravity guns, and teleportation devices. As well as decoy guns, turrets, and other interesting devices.
The limitless terrain is awesome and lets you take any path you wish for as long as you want. You can choose to just explore at your own will or take upon randomized quests with varying lengths and failure conditions. There are randomly generated battles between robots (NPCs), "dungeons", terrestrial anomalies, biomes, weather and it all flows really smoothly.
You will find very quickly that enemies will shred you apart if you do not make good use of cover and later on, if you neglect defensive stats (stealth or armor/hp). The enemies provide the right amount of challenge while not being too ridiculously powerful or weak.
Death penalty is currently losing one random item in your inventory, equipped or not. So don't yolo without keeping a storage of important items (requires a building tool, unlocked during the story quests).
Make sure you find all the "back-up" nodes inside buildings and save at a location where you'll be spending alot of time at. You do not want to painstakingly go all the way back to where you were from the starting location.
You might not see or think much any level of character customization until you open up your character stats then it hits you like a truck.
There are plenty of ways to build your character in terms of gameplay style (of course you can mix and match all of these as you wish...or just master them all):
recruiting masses of robots
guns (pistols, rifles, launchers) (Energy and ballistic)
melee (sword and dagger)
stealth
piloting aircraft
pickpocketting (!)
There are also improvable supplementary stats such as consumable efficiency, reprogramming chip equipment and the standard health, armor, energy.
Weapons can come with a plethora of effects such as a corrosion effect (damage over time), homing, explosive radius, shot speed, shot distance, varying ammo consumpion, ammo per reload, stat boosts and more.
Most of your additional stats will come from armor, as well as protection from radiation.
Also, hoverboards. ReBoot ANYONE?
Super-short summary: You are a test subject robot dropped into a world to see if "emotion" is capable of overcoming regular robot odds.
The story fits quite nicely with the theme of the game and serves as a great guiding tool for those less inclined to randomly stroll about the world with no direct feedback. You will need to advance a bit into the story to gain access to one of the more interesting features of this game: the building tool.
Be careful about advancing through the story too quickly, you may find yourself in the middle of a big...surprise.
Currently the game supports two player co-op which I have yet to try. You may have to open port 3089 on your firewall and/or router. Games hosted will be announced on the dev's twitter if public is set to on.

(NB: I've had this game since before it was on Steam)
Let's get this over first, the graphics are appropriate and fitting to the game's purpose. Yes, they are not the best graphics in the world.. it's not a Crysis engine game etc etc etc..  I actually quite like the graphics to be perfectly honest.
The game is a first person shooter with a story that runs throughout but does not force you to play a certain way to achieve storyline progression. Sure, there are bosses to beat in combat but how you defeat the bosses is completely up to you. It's a freeform game and you may choose to never actually play the storyline sections of the game at all. There are quests, there are skills that you choose to upgrade individually to suit your playstyle, there are multiple weapon and armor types with randomly generated stats that you can use to upgrade your character suit your playstyle, you can even break down the weapons and armors into components that you can combine with other components to suit your needs etc
The music is great too and very fitting. All in all, it's a great indie developed game that is well worth your time and attention. If you can look past the graphics, which again aren't all that terrible, and realise that some gameplay footage and screenshots can't ever do any game justice... look past them enough to try the demo.. you might find a great game, overflowing with old-school gameplay mechanics, hiding away within this game.

A fun loot-based 3D action RPG with lots of customisation and options. What worries me about it, though, is that it lacks the atmosphere or mood that other RPGs have. While other RPGs can feel moody, calm or hectic, this one's world feels like a toybox much of the time. Granted, it is a toybox you can get completely wrecked in, but the whole aesthetic of the game, plus the fact that the main storyline is off the beaten path makes it all a bit goofy if you aren't willing to go through the main storyline (which is good, by the way). For the record, I have about 10 more hours on this game than is let on, because of how easy it is to not have Steam record your hours for this game.

Although it pains me to say this, I can't at this time recomend this game. It's over shadowed by many game breaking problems that bring me out of the good points. I'll say it simply:
Cons:
-The combat systems feels like it is over thinking itself. The game's floaty space mechanics allow for a fun fast shooter, but it encourages you to take cover by having overly accurate AI who sometimes have homing projectiles. Even when you do make it to cover you will often find yourself being bombarded by enemies in space ships.
-the stealth system is an interesting attempt in a game like this, but the seemingly random AI of the mobs make it unsatisfying and unintuitive.
-The quests are repetitive and not very rewarding.
-Although it is teaming with robots, the world seems sparse, and it is easy to wander off into the distance to find nothing interesting and get instantly killed by a ton of robots.
Pros:
-combat related: The time manipulation and innacuracy of the guns makes combat very satisfying once mastered.
-Recruiting mobs to fight for you is made taking out bosses incredibly satisfying, and really gave an advantage to every fight.
-The stats system was fairly robust for an action rpg, and the integration of random drop items really gave it a borderlands feel.
Overall I do not recommend this game unless you are simply looking for a fun way to kill time without much in return. I see a lot of possibility in future updates.

3089, a futuristic, open-world action RPG. Everything in the game is randomly generated. This includes terrain, weapons, quests, enemies, items, etc.
I had absolutely no idea what I was doing for a solid amount of time when I first tried the game, it was very, very confusing. I could tell the terrain was randomly generated, as it was ridiculous how high some of the cliffs in the game could be, especially when there's a house hanging over the edge.
The game has some rather low-res graphics, but it feels strangely fitting to the game's atmosphere. There's so many things to do in 3089. I spent most of my time looting and killing all of the robot NPCs around, dying a couple of times in the process, but ultimately having a good time whilst doing so. 3089 has plenty of replayability, and I give it my recommendation!

tldr; Good value at $20. More content (tracks, ships, and modes) will be added for free for people who buy it now. Price will increase for new buyers as these features are added. Ultimately whether or not this is a good purchase comes down to how much you like the ship handling physics they chose.
---INTRO---
WipEout clone?! Not really. Formula Fusion has opted for a handling model which is a departure from WipEout. It executes that model well, but whether or not you enjoy it will depend on your preferences. This decision to deviate from the physics in WipEout HD/Fury has pros and cons. The cons are obvious. If you love WipEout handling then you may be disappointed at how different Formula Fusion's model feels. I certainly was at first. At the same time, there are also pros to this choice -- namely, variety. If I want a game that feels like WipEout, I can still go play WipEout. However, now I have the option to play Formula Fusion if I want a different feel.
---HANDLING---
So how does FF handling differ? After going back and forth between the two my conclusion is that FF has a better sense of speed at the highest class but at the expense of AG "floatiness" and pitch management. The loss of this element of precision control on your craft feels like somewhat of a missed opportunity. You don't fly off bumps on the track as often as WipEout which means that pitching doesn't play as much of a role (although this could be changed somewhat depending on the nature of the tracks R8 releases in the future). You also don't have side shifts or barrel rolls which could be a pro or con depending on how you see it. Finally, airbreaks and turning slow the craft down more in FF than later WipEout entries like Pulse/HD/2048. The breaking/turning physics are more akin to the original games in the WipEout series which makes cornering feel more like drifting. Pro or con? Again, down to preferences.
At the end of the day, FF does things differently but it feels like an intentional difference. They are not trying to replicate WipEout and as long as you don't treat this as WipEout HD 2.0, there is still fun to be had in R8's interpretation of the AG racing genre.
---POLISH---
When it comes to polish outside of racing, FF has some work to do. The menu interface, especially for Garage Customization is clunky. Many parts are lacking a meaningful description which makes it difficult to make informed decisions on what you're buying.
A good example highlighting the level of UI polish is in loadout managing. When managing your loadouts you cannot see a list of all saved loadouts and edit them. Instead, to update a loadout you give it the same name and then save. Technically it works but it's certainly not the most elegant solution. When it comes to UI polish this is the general rule; Everything "works" but it could be better.
---FEATURES---
FF does feel a little lacking when it comes to content at the moment. However, for $20 it feels more than fair. Especially since free tracks, ships, and modes are on the way. Currently there are 8 tracks and 5 ships. Each track has a forward and reverse layout as well as the option to toggle between day and night.
---PERFORMANCE ISSUES ON LAUNCH---
As far as performance issues go, the developers have done a great job monitoring the situation and patching problems quickly. At release I had an abysmal 20 FPS but after the latest patch I now have a consistent 60 FPS on max settings. The way the devs have quickly handled the situation inspires confidence in the future of Formula Fusion. I have no doubt that any remaining issues will be resolved.

***updated  Dec 2017***
Dev has kept plugging away and is getting game into good shape. Still framerate drops are still present on a couple of tracks that happen consistly at the same places without any obvious cause (ie complax visible geometry). Music has improved considerably with a couple of quiet decent tracks added. Still a little bugger though and stops playing sometime during race. Overall a good enjoyable gravity racer, if you dont mind the occasional fps drops. You will need a solid system to run at max setting and an awesome one to run 4K maxed out.
***updated review based upon second patch***
After the second patch I've had a noticeable improvement in framerate and better frametimes as well. I'm still seeing odd missed frames but overall much smoother. If you're not particularly sensitive to dropped frames you might not even notice all.
The racing is good and there is an appropriate sensation of speed. The style is very reminescent of the first Wipeout games so that is a plus, they are not the 'virtual reality' tracks of Redout. The wind/engine/hover noise is quite satisfying as you fly around the track. AI is challenging perhaps a tad too hard. One racer tends to consistently get way out in front which means you need to string together a bunch of near perfect laps to win rather than pick up second.
The game seems a little barren of content but considering the genre it's OK, I really don't need an excess of filler in a Wipeout clone. Unreal engine since the beginning has suffered from visible texture popping and it's showcased here, particularly in the track demos that open each race. The graphic settings also don't save between sessions even after the second patch. Whenever I start the game they default back to 'EPIC'. I've worked around this by directly editing the .ini file.
Music and some sound effects also frequently dropout. The music is 'meh' and really just consists of a techno beat. A little disappointing considering the music of the original Wipeout games. It would be nice if you could use your own tracks.
The UI and in game messages could definitely do with a lot more pizzaz, instead of plain text dialog boxes poping up while your racing.
Overall, addictive and definitely gets the pulse going. The core of the game is very good though the presentation is a little rough. Some of it feels of being placeholders to get the game out the door. Nevertheless well worth the entry price though I would have paid more to get a game that felt more finished. At this point the developer seems committed to the game so things are likely to improve.

So, what is this game? A hack'em slash'em with neptunia characters. HDN:U with Multiplayer. That's the gist of it. It Plays a bit more like Senran Kagura Shinovi Versus than U, as the game will spawn it's enemies only from spawn points close to you, and despawn them if you go too far from them. Unlike the "Follow the Path" of SK, or the "Continue on the only obvious path"/"stay in the small arena killing things until the objective is completed" of U, most of the time you go on maps hunting for bosses, who are even denoted on your minimap!
Now, for the enemies changed from U:
Aztec Golems have a jump attack, and are more aggressive.
Kupokitties are less hyperactive.
No robot enemies
Zombies that throw their head as boomerangs
"Flying disco zombies" that shoot hellfire rockets at you, very slowly.
New Large bosses:
-Temdinkale is a one-handed sword fighter with okay mobility and a fun to fight moveset
-Megadonkale is a red dual-wielder with TONS of mobility, a pain to melee, since even his dodges damage you
-Doomkale wields a hammer, is slow as hell, and is badass.
-Undead Cannoneer lugs around two huge guns, and has spectral gauntlets to slap you around with in close range.
-the two Mariwogus-types are large fenrir-type dogs with launchable frisbee weapons, four per doggy. They have high mobility.
-Truenail and it's clone type are big walking birds with a glowy tail ending in a christmas tree light.
Unlike Nep U, you no longer map your skills to specific buttons, but instead always have four skills available.
Like Nep U, and SK, the camera control is abysmal, and needs a specific autohotkey script to be convenient with a mouse.
The multiplayer is a pathetic joke, no real communication (no chat, there is picking up phrases from a phrasebook), no real steam integration, dead game is dead tier lobbies, few games, often someone's either playing with a low-level character who dies in two hits, or a high level murdermachine kitted out in invincibility patches, high def, keep patch, life steal patch, who can steamroll bosses without thinking... Best of all, enemies scale up in HP and Damage with more players, so playing solo mp is easier. Go figure!
And as usual with IF, the game is a buggy wreck. It can lock up when looking for multiplayer servers, it can lock up before the menu, it WILL lock up (not responding) if any application asks for permission to change things in the computer.
The missions are no brainers in story mode, loading times are large.
So all in all I can't wholeheartedly recommend this game. Get it if you are interested in playing with one character or another (I've come for plutia, and you know how she doesn't leave anyone until she's satisfied :D ), get it if it's in the bargain bin, don't get it for full price.
And if you really need some action hack'em slash'em and you haven't played diablo 2 yet, do yourself a favor and get that game. For two thirds of the price you get the base game and the expansion. The ability to play in either classic mode or expansion mode, which are two wholly different experiences. Deep itemization and high amount of character customization allow you to play the way you want (Aside from a few caveats).

Damn, I've just finished the game and I feel like sh*t. I was holding back manly tears all through the last 15 minutes of the game, and the ending just devastated me. I was just a seconds away from breaking down like a little girl. What an emotional journey.
Ahem. OK, here's the review. The game follows the story of two brothers who go on an adventure to save their father, who has a serious disease and the cure is literally on the other side of the world. They overcome lots of different problems (mostly platforming) on their journey and they even escape some life-threatening situations.
The developers managed to create an incredible world filled with hundreds of little bits of lore, something even some AAA titles, with huge budgets and an army of lore-masters, cannot manage. The atmosphere just pulls you in and never lets you go until the end. I really regret that I had to play this game in multiple sessions instead of in just one sitting. I suppose the atmosphere, the satisfaction I felt after I finished the game would be much more profound that way.
The soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal. The game has one of the most goosebump-inducing soundtracks I've ever listened to. It suits the mood, the story so well that you'd think they made the game for the song, not the other way around.
The game is made with Unity engine (I think) and the graphics are very nice. I mean, it's not like they are cutting edge but the style they used for the game is incredibly atmospheric. A photorealistic game engine would really ruin the mood instead of enhancing it.
I played the game with an Xbox controller, and I have to admit, even with the controller the game was sometimes really difficult, some puzzles difficult to coordinate. Still, I had no real trouble. I really, really suggest a controller though; the game would probably be impossible to play with a keyboard.
All in all, I haven't felt this emotional thanks to a game since To the Moon. If you're looking for a game with an emotional story, perfect soundtrack and a cathartic ending, this is it.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a good game, but it ultimately falls short of greatness, which is unfortunate because it does improve on some of the aspects of Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
In terms of the good, DE:MD expands the "choose-your-own-playstyle" freedom that's the hallmark of the Deus Ex universe. For instance, combat-based playthroughs (both lethal and non-lethal) are equally viable with a sneaky, hacker ghost. (In particular, the possibility of a weapons-blazing, non-lethal combat style is pretty unique.) Most missions have dozens of ways to get to your goal, and this is the best thing about DE:MD--you can really play how you want to.  There are other great things, too--the black and gold aesthetics continue to visually set Deus Ex apart from other generic sci-fi titles.
The dystopian world building is amazing, with the tragic fallout from DE:HR permeating everything, from the apartheid of Prague's police state to the snippets of loss picked up in passing conversation. But, paradoxically, this leads to my biggest critque of the game: the nuances invested in the world seem to have come at the cost of the characters and story. Adam Jensen, the protagonist, is ever the gruff, moralizing hero. The main characters are barely given much to say other than mission objectives, with each conspicuously having one "Humanizing Backstory Conversation." Unfortunately, that's not enough to care--even though I wanted to.
Further, the story seems strangely small for a Deus Ex game. Without giving away too much, your taske is to find out who's behind a terrorist attack and, of course, that leads to a slightly bigger conspiracy. The plot is about as sophisticated as a made-for-TV sci-fi movie, which seems like a waste, especially in comparison to the convoluted, conspiracy-filled narrative twists that the series is known for. This might be excusable if DE:MD used the space to do some interesting character building, but it doesn't.
So, I liked my time with DE:MD. I got to cruise around as a god-like stealth master, which was pretty fun. Did I end up really caring about either the plot or the people? Not really. I would've liked to, though, since the series shows so much promise.
7.5 / 10
PS: Other small gripes that minorly impacted my enjoyment:
1) In DE:HR, I liked the epic "persuade" conversations with the number of choices and timely interrupts, but DE:MD generally has fewer and less difficult ones--which seems directly related to the character-building problem stated earlier.
2) The AI seems kind of silly. For instance, if I walk into the LOS of a guard in a restricted area, they get suspicious, but if I move several inches over into a non-restricted area, they don't.
3) If you are doing a stealthy playthrough, the game pretty much stops being hard less than halfway through. The enemies don't get any increased ability to detect you--the security devices and patrols just become more numerous. But, once you can cloak and have a full battery, you can basically just speed run through the game by walking past everyone.

I've really enjoyed DX:Mankind Divided. I felt like it gave me an interesting story and fun gameplay. I also enjoyed DX:Human Revolution, so I was looking forward to MD. The story and its take on society and its prejudices and fears was pretty cool, and in a very real way speaks to the times we are living in now. There were a lot of options as far as unlockable abilities (augmentations), but I couldn't get to all of them during my first playthrough. I liked the hidden triangle pieces (can't remember what they were called). Whenever you find them you can use the Deus Ex mobile app to scan them and get access to a short audio or video clip with the developers, or other people invlolved in the game, discussing behind the scenes info about the development of the game. I thought that was pretty cool. At any rate, I definitely recommend this game...especially if you are coming into it as a Deus Ex fan!

First things first, it took me >6< hours to not hate this game. Those first 6 were rough and I considered bailing several times. I hated Human Revolution for what it's worth. A clunky UI, some strange gameplay elements with an odd weapon/ special selection process... But once I sunk into the game as presented and played as intended, something happened. Now 30 hours into the game I LOVE IT! I'm still very nostalgic for the first Deus Ex and while this certainly isn't that, this is a very good game, despite the overwhelming negative response here.
Chasing the events of a bombing is ho hum as a story line but I don't really care, it's a good ride with plenty of interest. Honestly the side story is more interesting than the main one. Amazing visuals in imaginative settings where there are ALWAYS more than 1 way to achieve a goal, always more than 1 path. Go in blasting or take the stealth route, the game rewards the latter which is also a much more satisfying way to play. If you play this game as a traditional shooter you will be disappointed. This isn't COD! Never was, never will be, if that's what you're looking for this is the wrong title!
Many have complained about specific nuances of the game like micro-transactions which at 30 hours and counting I've still not encountered. If you follow the main story line only maybe it's a shorter play through. Using stealth and cunning to get through the game is much more challenging and will keep you engaged for a much longer time. I use the parts I find to craft and the praxis I earn to aug, nothing more, nothing to buy with real money. There are loads of side missions that take you through all kinds of interesting situations. I do every available mission per the chapter I'm on and am nowhere near bored yet.
Now the things I don't like. Adam just isn't "badass" enough, or surely doesn't look badass. The character design tries way too hard to be cool. The voice acting is reminiscent of Clint Eastwood, who I don't like and really grates on me. The game seems to want you to focus more on your augs and stealth stun/kill attacks. Switching weapons is a labor that pauses gameplay which is disruptive. Modifying weapons is a chore as is organizing and using your items. The aug tree is fairly robust but organization can be a hunt peck sometimes.

To sum, this is truly a great game underneath it all. It is not your traditional shooter so for max experience I recommend not playing it like one. Uncovering secrets, hidden paths/vents, hacking computers/safes/bots, uncovering information, sneaking in and out of areas undetected and not killing unless you have to. Very different game play than what you're probably used to in this genre.

You get to play as the leader - for this solar system anyhow - for one of the iconic Warhammer 40K armies and battle the eight other factions for the dominance of the Kaurava system. The sinister Dark Eldar and saintly Sisters of Battle are the newest factions in Soulstorm; while they're both welcome, I can't help but feel that they're a little underpowered, although fitting with the Dark Eldar, the Reaver Rush can take some of the challenge out of the game.
While it doesn't bring as much to the table as the previous installment, Dark Crusade, this will still whet the gaming appetite for those who have fond memories of painting figures, rolling dice, or arguing with friends over unit spacing.

I've been playing this game for quite a while, Shadows of Angmar days in 2008.
I have stopped with this game quite a few times. Yet I still comeback and play it.
It's like the classic MMO but with the LOTR lore, sounds awesome.
The game plays great, even though they use target-tabbin, I have yet to see such fluid combat in other MMO.
It feels great. You really feel like you're hitting or being hit. This is one of the reasons I keep coming back.
The PVP can be freaking awesome and incredibly tedious.
Questing can actually be fun, but to get from 1 to 100 should take so long that I'd doubt it feels fun after a while.
PVE used to be really great, but the old content is abandoned and they haven't released a new raid in a while now.
The community is one of the best assets of the game, I have made quite a few friends for life over here.
Finally, with all the great things I had to say, and that keep me coming back, I must say:
This is Free-To-Play until some point. You can always play it, but you'll eventually need to take some money off your pocket to unlock later content. The currency you buy, Turbine Points, can be gathered through gameplay, but to get enough would take over a thousand hours.
P.S.: This isn't a P2W game. They surely sell a lot of convenience, and people who pay can really get to that point with less effort, but they don't really sell advantage (anymore).

I promised that after 300 hours played, I would write a review. So almost 400 hours in, here we go:
First of all, I started playing LotRO, when it was still pay by month, so the hours do not refelct my actual game time :)
I do not agree with the haters hitting on the pay per use aspect of the game. Players can still get a decent experience without dropping a dime. Of course the experience gets better with money invested, but compared to spending 15 or 20 bucks a month, it is a steal.
The game experience itself is great, as the epic story drops you right in the middle of the actual story. You get a feeling of actually helping the fellowship move forward. The narrative is very deep and many of the extra characters are just as likeable as Tolkien's cast. Some of the quests can be a bit boring (go to guy a, then go to guy b, then go to guy c etc), but it is a MMORPG after all. Time flies when you are playing, and that is the most important part.
Visuals and sounds are maybe a bit dated (it is from 2006, you know), but I still often just wander around Rivendell, Bree or the Shire enjoying the scenery. So I guess it is good,
So would I recommend the game? Heck yes!

what to say about Geneforge? To put it simply: It's an oddly fantastic game.
Having never heard of the series, I purchased a bundle with all 5 Geneforge games. I really enjoyed my playthough of Geneforge 1, despite the difficulty and dated feel of its isometric graphics. Many of the sound effects are terrible and yet somehow memorable and enjoyable. The entire gameworld is immersive, and the creators succeed at inviting the player into a curious world unlike anything I've found elsewhere.
The turn-based combat is unique and seamless with world exploration; no cutscenes to a battlefield. Feel free to disagree, but this games combat feels a lot like what Dragon Age would have been (without the dragons) in 2001. You set your party into a formation (some strategy), you scout bad guys, you draw them into battle and then the turn-based system engages right where the characters are standing, based on the players/enemies speed as determined by stats. The balancing is steeped against the player and pots/items/spells saved my creations several times. Oh yeah, did I forget to mention?
If you want to know more, or about what the Geneforge is, buy the game!
Aside from combat, content-wise it's pretty dense. I was able to get up to 50hrs in a single playthrough, although I explored just about every square inch of map and tried multiple different endings. The story is pushed by text-narration as opposed to characters rendered in 3D, animated w/ voice acting. This makes it impenetrable to many spoilt by games such as Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, and Bioshock, but nevertheless it has it all. Political intrigue, factions, tons of choices that shape the world and your standing within it, hundreds of items and creatures, and dungeon after dungeon to crawl through.
I can't speak to the whole series, although I may play them through in the future, but IMO Geneforge 1 is worth your time for anything under $3. I think I got it for a buck in the bundle and was pleasantly surprised.
Ultimately, I give "Geneforge 1" 7/10, would genetically modify self again.

All of Spiderweb Software's titles are low on graphics and, as the oldest title available on Steam, Geneforge 1 is no exception; however, it was never built for that. Regardless of what year you play this game, the amount of raw depth and story is outstanding. It has been ten years since I first played this game, the Geneforge series remains one of my favorite games of all time, and I can't recommend it without advising players to start at the beginning.
Geneforge offers what I would personally feel is the goal of all RPGs: to create a story and setting that is compelling in its mystery, intriguing in its, theme, and captivating in its storytelling. The game begins with your character washed up on an island that was barred by the administration of your legendary and powerful magic order. You aren't allowed to be there, and the story is about why that is, what made it that way, and how do you interact with the inhabitants left behind, all while learning more about what your order is about, what they're like, and how you're going to resolve it all when you go back.
I have absolutely never played another game where I wanted to know more strongly what came next, except for its sequel, perhaps. It's something about the setting and the theming that really clicked with both my curiosity and deep fascination with a fictional, magic world. Although the graphics may age and the user-interface be abundantly clunky, the story and writing will always remain the same.
My recommendation is positive. Highly positive.

Early in development, it looked like a fun, casual platform fighter that would be free and enjoyable for anyone who didn't want to spend money on a fighting game, and still play online versus with friends. +800 hours in the game, a couple dozen hours watching developer and competitive livestreams, and a look into the in-game store, and you'll see it's a cash grab. You don't actually need to have done all the things that I've done to see this, but for those who don't believe me, this is my experience with the game.
Not all the characters are viable - less than half I would say - and you can see for yourself by playing a few hours of the ranked mode at higher ranks, and less than a few hours watching livestreams of competitions. Which ones are viable changes season to season - first three Seasons, Hattori was played by more than 50% of the winners per game (BM even made an infographic in 2015, see for yourself). Season 7, gauntlet Legends Kor and Wu Shang and Katar Legends Asuri and Lucien have by far the most priority.
Though all the purchasable items are completely aesthetic, and do not add substantial and necessary content, their prices are absurdly high. Developers are constantly pushing things out way too early and unfinished because of upcoming conventions, competitions and live events, and what they
getting out very timely - on a weekly scheduled basis - is purchasable, aesthetic content that has inconsistent quality and consistently increasing prices.
And the servers are awful, you will be matched up with people from the other side of the planet despite selecting to only play within your region. Even if it did match you up with people from your region, most people have such an awful connection that the game can hardly support them getting into the match, let alone both of you (or all four of you, if you have the stones to play 2v2); the herds of sheep who cry about the game being peer-to-peer will say that they have a "degree in internet studies" (actual quote), yet not actually be able to tell you what kind of network Blue Mammoth has built to run Brawlhalla's online components. All that combined leads me to believe that this game is truly only for one kind of person, and that is the kind of person who spends there life in "e-sports", seeks out sponsors, and can give Brawlhalla and its developers at Blue Mammoth Games more publicity, and eventually, more cash. With all this said, feel free to call my review rude or abrasive. But know that the developers are most likely not making the game for
to enjoy.
Update: 12/21/17
TL;DR - It's one over-ambitious mess right now, use a time machine to go back to September if you want an okay game, or better yet, go back two and a half years if you want a halfway decent game.
One massive step forward back when dash was added; chain dodging, or as the hint text during loading screens called it, "chase dodging" (even though that's never what it was used for), was an absolute joke.
Twelve massive steps backwards since. You've got your "netcode improvements" in version 3.02 which only have made connection worse since. I've never seen the frames drop, not once, since I started playing this game, my issues have always been with getting instantly disconnected from matches and with rollbacks. But behold, 3.02 introduced actual drop in framerate. Huge ones.
And cannon. Were you guys really that out of ideas that you had to make cannons? No nunchuks, magic, boomerang/shuriken/chakram, flail, mace, two-handed sword, sword & shield combo, rifle, sling/slingshot, halberd, or crossbow. Cannons. Like, the ones on a ship. Obviously the first character you release is a pirate, you clearly made the weapon with her in mind. You're going to run out of ideas fast with cannons, though, things are going to get ridiculous pretty soon. This might be the closest thing to an ad hominem against the game or the creativity of ideas as I get, I know, but I'm just confused as to why the devs had to add cannons so soon.
And speaking of devs. The team now has to take on developing for the PS4 as well. And the platforms are not compatible currently, meaning the game is developed separately from the PC version. Meaning less time to bug fix, test for balance, and take care of server maintenance.
Things were looking like they were improving around official release. And now, we're back to "good" old Brawlhalla.

This game feels like its weapon customization feature: it took the things I most loved on a videogame (procedurally-generated open world; weapon and item customization; base-building; vehicles) and put them together, making something that may not look very pretty, but it doesn't need to, as it already serves it's purpose very well.
After beating it's campaign, I must confess I expected it to be something that would make me explore (even) more the infinite world, but who needs more story when you can make your own? Even better: Why can't I make a story with a friend? What stops us from making an hoverboard race shooting some blue bots along the way? What stops us from scaling a mountain with a grappling hook? What stops us from racing to the top of the mountain, implusing ourselves up with grappling hooks (so awesome on singleplayer)? (Unfortunately its online component didn't work for me, so I was only able to do this on SP :P), but on all cases, I assure you as what you can call, someone who plays LOTS of videogames, that this is a very good game that should not be overlooked because of its graphical presentation.

Gave the demo a try and was intrigued by what I played. Snatched it up and was surprised with the potential of the game. After two hours I'm finally going to delve into the "building" gameplay but I'm very satisfied with the combat and variety of items.
The parts system is genius and even more fun than buying better weapons; assemble your own!
EDIT: Try out the demo here:
EDIT 2: While this game has a lot of potential, it is essentially a grindfest with a story wrapping the experience. I also have a few "dealbreakers" to add (from my perspective).
There are balance changes that are either pending or need to be considered such as the usefulness of vehicles (they don't really do damage, don't bother being a pilot at the moment) and the frustration induced by a gang of 3+ bots all with stun launchers that leave you crying helplessly as you watch your character inevitably die (you can't turn, attack, or use items from what I experienced, regardless of level since there is no "stun resist") and lose a piece of your equipment.
I wanted to like this game, but with one developer it'll be a bit more time before it's balanced enough to make me want to play again. That stun-lock was really discouraging and is a huge turn-off (sorry, Phroot).
Feel free to pick this game up, though! It still has its merits and is something I'm still proud to own. Quite a feat for an indie game that relies on procedural generation. Good luck in the future, Phroot. You've got the idea, keep running with it!

DLC Quest isn't so much a game as it is a parody. That said, it's a quirky and satirical journey across two small campaigns packed with jokes and references that poke fun at the all too familiar concepts of downloadable content, pay-to-play, preorder exclusives, and freemium. The campaigns themselves are very, VERY short, myself finishing both of them and clocking in at about 2.5 hours, but this game isn't meant to be a huge adventure. Despite the length, its got a decent amount of humor put into it, and the platformer mechanics and gameplay are simple enough for anyone to pick up. Good for the two hours I spent, granted I also acquired it on sale for $0.98. If you're looking to kill a few hours with something simple and witty, then this is a game I would consider.

tl;dr:
- Fantastic visuals
- Physics which scratch that Wipeout itch
- Good performance; great performance after the first patch
- Good multiplayer when you can find it
- Confusing UI
- OK music
- If you can't progress in the campaign, use the garage!
- There *are* multiple weapons & items. Again, use the garage.
- If you suddenly notice your shield/health steadily dropping for "no reason", it's probably not a bug; you're probably in an endurance event
- If your position jumps suddenly at the end of a lap, having been static the whole way round, that is probably also not a bug; you're in a "speed lap" event
- Read the game description on the store page for an overview of the mechanics. An in-game tutorial, guide, or manual would be great
- Seriously, use the garage
- I assume more content is coming, as only one team's campaign is available, and only the first craft type is available in campaign mode
I've been playing this since early access, and was not always been convinced, but the end result is pretty good - especially considering the price. As a veteran of the early Wipeouts, I must admit that this does have some rough edges, but it comes far closer to scratching the old itch than anything else I've played recently. There are ways in which it is its own beast, too, for better or for worse.
First off, the soundtrack isn't a patch on the old licensed tracks; but I must admit the end result sounds better in-game than expected, and it's growing on me. Realistically, budgetary and other issues probably made a licensed soundtrack on the scale of the old ones infeasible for a new, small studio. Secondly, tDR are on board, so expect top-notch team branding and track-side billboards, but the overall feel is let down by a somewhat incoherent UI, with issues like settings not always saving and missing item descriptions in the garage.
The main problem, though, is that certain elements of the game & how to get the most out of it are inscrutable to newcomers. Some kind of manual or tutorial is sorely needed - it's so bad that it's hurting reviews, with people posting negatively simply because they don't understand it.
Instead of the old Wipeout model of one craft per team, FF instead has four base craft types (available to all teams) with different starting characteristics, each of which can be customised with "cards" in the "garage". The UI for this really needs an overhaul:
- Many cards have a title but no description
- The stats shown don't seem to have a 1:1 relationship with craft performance (good for experimenting with load-outs, bad for predictability)
- Load-outs conflate weapon & utility item choices with performance & handling tweaks (would prefer to be able to choose weapons/utilities without going in to the garage to create a whole new load-out)
That said, the different performance & handling cards really do make a noticeable difference to how a craft feels, and are absolutely necessary to progressing through the campaign. With just the initial canned load-outs, I struggled to get anywhere in the campaign's second speed class; but now, I've made load-outs which turn the first craft into something fast & floaty, slower but twitchy, and average but well shielded, and switch between them based on track and event type to great effect. I'm now playing through the third speed class, and starting to feel the challenge - but it feels like a fair challenge, which will be overcome with further tweaking & practice. Better card descriptions, a way to jump quickly onto a test track to preview the feel of a load-out, and weapon & utility selection outside the garage would make things so much better.
Finally, performance. I have an i7-5820K and a 4GB R9 290, so a mid-range rig by today's standards, and can happily play at 1080p with all bells & whistles enabled (including TAA; exclusing v-sync). Things are even better following the first patch. With everything turned up, it looks fantastic in motion.

First up: I liked it, its pretty good stuff :)
Brothers a Tale of Two Sons is about 2 things:
1. The Story
2. The rather unique gameplay.
Story:
The story really is not all that special, its about the journey your main characters undertake.
Its a real adventure the two brothers have and it feels like it, like an old childrens novel.
I say old because the story does not pull (m)any punches, its pretty dark at times like fairytales of old used to be.
I do whoever have some reservations for the writing, I dont want to spoil anything so ill just say that the reason for the adventure, is one that is ill advised which, for me personally, did hurt the experience a bit in the end.
Gameplay:
The reason its rather unique is because you control both brothers at the same time.
This is very different from pretty much any ga,e I have ever played before and it really takes some getting used to.
You would expect puzzles from a game like this, puzzles where you need to work with the two brothers individually to solve them, like for example Portal 2 except you control both players/robots, but this is sadly not the case.
Everything is straight forward and the challenge comes indeed purely from controlling both characters at the same time, the controles are the challenge which is I guess both good and bad.
However, that there is not much of any puzzle solving helps move everything forward which perhaps adds more to the sense of adventuring, you need a bit of pace for it.
The game has a 90/100 on average which I find way too high.
I guess the grade was taking into account what type of game it is and what price was asked for it on release but a 90/100 is reaaaally high and to me should only be reserved for the best of the best and nearly unforgettable experiences and that, this game, does not offer.
Its fun, its emotional, its artistic...its good, but a 90 goes a bit far.
I would give it more like a healthy 75 myself if I would have to grade it.
Do I recommend it?
Yeah I guess I do, its not a must own/must play title but if you can get it on a deal it will be good to do a playthrough of.
It is after all only 3 - 4 hours long.
(oh yeah and some of the achievements are ♥♥♥♥ed up man)

As a fan of the very first Deus Ex, I was always going to play this one unless it turned out to be thoroughly miserable.  DEx and Thief were so dramatically different from anything else I played at the time, and so satisfying - lurking in a shadow or just around a corner, right under the enemy's nose, watching them while they go about their business, totally oblivious to my presence, thrilled me like nothing else.  I'm right here, but you don't even know.  I looted your secret treasure room, I ransacked your armory, and you have no idea.  Your elite guard and elaborate security are powerless because you cannot see me.
I spent a lot of time on both games, but that only made me crave more.
In this regard, Mankind Divided delivers.  It still uses the cover stealth found in Human Revolution, though less overtly - there are fewer right angles, and more importantly, fewer blatant cover walls.  Its world is broad and deep and
and full of nooks and crannies (and air vents).  It offers a wide variety of tools and toys and is only seldom linear.
However, MD is not only its world and how you navigate it.  As ever, there are conspiracies afoot, and would-be puppeteers hiding backstage, fighting amongst themselves for power.  HR's plot was generally self-contained, but MD has obviously tried to begin connecting the dots, and the price is closure (that is, this game doesn't have it).  If you're familiar with DEx, it becomes even more apparent that the closest MD could get would still be like the end of Empire Strikes Back.
This aspect of the story didn't really bother me.  I wanted to see how the dots connect.
What did bother me was the surface-level conflict of augmented people being demonized and segregated in response to events at the end of HR.  State police are everywhere in this game, constantly complaining about and harassing them, and you, the player.  I think there is some potential for a game (or games) to examine and explore the real prejudices that plainly inspired this aspect of the story, but sincerely, and without whitewashing their nature or inventing reasons to let people think both sides are bad.
MD is not that game.  In this game, it is out of place, it is overbearing, it is tasteless.
Aside from the main game, there is also a side story called Breach mode.  Its existence is frankly insulting.
The way it's framed, you're breaking into corporate severs to steal data, but it's essentially identical to that section of the main game where you run around in the NSN for five minutes, though with the full suite of augs and weapons and with actual enemies on patrol.  It is a series of these five minute nothing levels stretched across a web that resembles the hacking interface in the main game.  Choose a level that you will inevitably see again, only marked elsewhere on the map, download some amount of data/pick up fragments/defeat enemies, then exit.
Instead of finding and buying equipment, you find nothing, and you use cash earned by completing servers to buy booster packs full of random stuff (
).  You get your guns reloaded with standard ammo every time you return to the map, and you can buy more of it for whatever specific gun, but heaven help you if you need a special ammo type ie EMP rounds to destroy the exosuits that pop up far more often in this mode.
Eventually the game will drop a server in your way that requires you to fight a boss, with your very limited ammo, because everybody liked those so much in HR, right? (
)
What makes the inclusion of this mode extra frustrating for me is that some of its ideas, taken separately from the chaff, form the shape of a potential successor to Thief - a cyberpunk game of breaking and entering in a 3D visualization of computer structures that isn't constrained by meatspace concepts like gravity and solidity.  I hope someday that game will exist.
DExMD, the game we got, is good - if you can endure its ham-handed appropriation, if you stay far away from Breach mode.

Trine 2 is the definition of what a plaformer should be.  The graphics are top notch with great lighting.  The fluidity of the animation and controls are perfect so that while some of the puzzle sections may be difficult at times they are never blamed on the slick controls.  The levels are long enough to be enjoyable and not too long where they get boring.  Each level offers a variety of landscapes and scenery, all of which are beautiful.  The storyline is forgettable, but still sets up a good reason for why you are playing the game.  The three different characters offer very different ways of playing and each offer different ways to solve the puzzles.  Think of it as an action only version of Quest for Glory where each character has a different solution to each puzzle.  The addition of the Goblin Menace, the Dwarven Carverns and now the Workshop has helped expand and continue the gameplay of this fabulous series.  The best part of this game is the multiplayer offering.  Now with online multiplayer, this game truly shines when playing with two or more players.
The price for this game, when on sale is typically under $4 for the entire complete story.  Take advantage and don't miss this great game.  Bound to be a classic in gaming history.

State of the Game July 2017
Performance
The game performs well on hardware that was popular at the time of release, it's entirely possible to maintain 60fps with very reasonable graphics options if you avoid some of the GPU hogs. The Audio engine contains bugs that cause the GTA to crash on a wide range of hardware due to discrepancies in settings, some Audio hardware allows for high bit-rates, GTA runs at 16 Bit 44.1KHz. Higher settings will make the game crash after some arbitrary amount of time.
Options
Many, only notably lacking direct support for extended mouse buttons, which have to be configured by mapping to keys in some instances.
Relevance & DLC
GTA V has remained semi-relevant with help from its online multi-player updates, some have been excellent, some interim fluff. Notably story mode has been neglected with the exception of adding a few cars here and there.
Overall Game-play
The mechanics and physics are excellent when they work, often humorous when they don't. Lag between players can cause a host of physics anomalies especially with traffic, something dedicated servers would help fix.
PvP
With the latest update comes in my opinion the death of PvP in GTAO, Explosive rounds have positively affected the ability to get rid of Hydra Trolls, but also transformed how cancerous players now spread around their play style. There's little to no skill in a normal gun vs thermal scope and explosive rounds battle. An alternative could have been airborne Merryweather strike called in by phone with the precision of the jet that attacks by the airport. GTAO Lacks any credible ranking system, or ability to enter sessions with rules sets such as disabling near blips, if tracking people down meant completing objectives for brief intel on peoples activites vs simply looking at the map & throwing explosives at them during PvP missions, the activites would perhaps be more satisfying for all parties involved
Exploits, netcode and controversies
The Achilles Heel of GTAO. There are few that will tell a truthful story about the modding scene as it relates to GTA. In essence the netcode is essentially born of a lan game further developed from how it was in GTA IV that now routes player actions through a server acting essentially as a router to hide actual IP addresses and coordinate basic session duties. There is still no in-session detection of exploits, only RockStar's feeble attempts to scan the many stats they collect combined with reports that can be cleared/blocked. And a system that attempts to scan memory for known exploit code. Yet with each update the hacks return in just a few days. Many who blindly support modding, leaving negative reviews on all Rockstar's games will state that TakeTwo's action against OpenIV was wrong. Supporters of the OpenIV community who have developed software to catalogue game assets and function hooks fail to understand that this knowledge is a large contributing factor in the creation of the mods by less responsible developers subsequently used for creating an unfair advantage in PvP, or generally being abrasive. Thus what we really have is an awkward situation for Rockstar. We have OpenIV who don't make software that affects online play, and we have people who build on that work to be asses. Resulting in people who actually play rarely playing in open sessions with random people, this further amplifies the remaining pool of lavatory waste in the remaining open sessions who actively want to be in open sessions to cause chaos. Having said that, I'm not against the modding scene, if GTAO had a place, or specific sessions modders could do what they wanted, I'd welcome that. Combined with better team building tools (max members <100? team chat when not in session, team events, team session settings, in-team factions/gangs.
Lastly, perhaps the worst of the modders are not those who blow people up without engaging and attach eggs to your head, but those who subtly add a small amount of weapon damage, regenerative health, or targeting / bounding box aids to give skill-free advantages.
PvE
The standard cash grinding missions while plentiful at launch have been neglected in favor of multi-player missions, that still offer little cash reward but offer some entertainment value.
Recommended? yes definitely… play with friends.

For me,
is one of the series that represents a hybrid of old school and new for RPG, a transition that came around at a time when developers not only relied on certain conventions (such as the heavy use of textual description in games) but embraced these over the flash and thunder of visual & audio spectacle that would inevitably supplant them in mainstream gaming.  This review is for Geneforge 1 through 5, the complete series.
Mr. Jeff Vogel and his
are involved not just in the Geneforge IP but also the
series which is enjoyable.  Geneforge was developed in five installments from 2001 to 2008.  Graphics were never a priority with this IP, and in my opinion like most games developed by this company, its greatest strength is story.
Some things that must be talked about when discussing Geneforge:
Understand that these games feel old by any standard.  People who didn't grow up playing MUDs or other types of games in high school will likely be frustrated by the high amount of text here: it's how you get the dialogue, interact with people and objects, and absorb specific information about every new area you come across in addition to most of the situations that dynamically arise in the game world.  The pace of the game is necessarily slowed down by this feature and many players either don't have the patience or simply aren't inclined to sit through so much content when presented in this format.  Yeah, you have to stop and read.  I urge you to take that time and effort, since the reading provides great detail and insight into the lore, characters and story --not to mention you'll be completely lost on what to do next if you skip through it!
Combat can be very fun and is especially rewarding after you've repeated an encounter that initially punished you but discovered a viable path to victory.  "Shaping," the act of creating life via magic, is the central theme of Geneforge and translates into an "essence" mechanic, a second mana pool the player character spends to summon a host of little minions (or a handful of stronger ones, or a single powerful one; it varies based on the demands of each encounter).  There are a few types of shaping that each come with their own creations (magical, melee, ranged, control, etcetera).  Even on the casual difficulty you need to be smart about how you invest skill points upon leveling up.  Support skills like Leadership and Mechanics are great; they can supposedly be used to beat the game without a combat-viable character.  Melee and ranged specializations are available too, of course, if you aren't into the magic system.  I found the most success with a bit of everything, emphasizing survivability + stats over armor in my gear choices.  Be prepared for some trial and error (or look up some cheats online...but really, don't do that).  There are a couple of succinct and helpful guides out there, though.
The third item on that list just further drives home the importance of realizing it's a long game with lots of text.  You have very little indication of where to go or what to do even when given a quest.  You'll forge out into the world and earn every inch of progress with meticulous interrogation of NPCs in towns and navigation of treacherous, trap-filled monster infested wildlands in equal measure.  If you skip that text, eventually you'll be having to consult a guide or just roam randomly until you get lucky.  I did not explore every area, complete every quest, hunt down every rare item or talk to everyone I met.  In fact, at times I followed the main questline as closely as is possible in my eagerness to see the main plot play out.
Technically the game is very simple but runs without any issue.  It started as demoware on the Mac.  Everything runs fine but looks extremely dated and perhaps feels clunky.
The themes dealt with in this story are ones I liked and would enjoy seeing more of in future games.  I found it very pleasing that the story unfolded in episodic manner from one game to the next, especially regarding the recurring characters who I'd grown attached to.  The only criticism I'd level against the story is that it is delivered almost too arbitrarily; I felt at times I would have been better served experiencing the story through my actions rather than being told what to think with a text box.  Overall however, it was an excellent delivery.  Of the cRPGs I've played, this series isn't my favorite but it's up there, although...
I can only recommend Geneforge to players who have considerable patience and time on their hands for the experience I've described above, and who are craving an "old school" game.  It's challenging but good fun.  Defeating your enemies to reach the ending and see how everything wraps up based on your choices is so rewarding.
TIP: Be thorough in exploring, talking, and reading the text for each area.  It'll help in various ways, not just the extra experience points.
TIP: Guides exist online if you find yourself in an unbeatable fight or unsure of where to go next.

Finally, Someone made a Concing game.
I bought this game simply because i was informed that two of the old JS (Janus Syndicate) members were involved in the development behind ConcPerfect 2017. And i have to say: What an awesome game it is! If you already don't know what "Concing" is, Concing is a skill based movement by usually throwing a Concussion gernade on the ground which is used to push the player forward in a direction of the player's choice. It was pretty common around the early 2000s in the old days of Team Fortress Classic. Concing isn't exactly around anymore and the TFC days are long gone, But, This little indie game brings that back. You will concussion your way to victory by jumping platform to platform until you reach the very end of the level, Along with a timer that keeps track of your score. I would say it's more fun to play with others but sadly this has to be one of the most underrated games on Steam and barely has even a community, And that would be one of my complaints with this game. There is nobody playing it and it really deserves more players. Another thing is that i put a little over 2 hours in game and i've already had beaten most, If not all the levels, There simply isn't enough content. But, The game is new and the developers are always coming out with new updates, So hopefully they'll add more levels and content into the game. I would also say the walking animations aren't really that good and i think they really need to be improved but that isn't really a problem. But at the end of the day, I really look forward to the future for ConcPerfect 2017 and i think it'll be a great game. The gameplay is solid, The Conc physics are spot on, The level design is really impressive, The graphics are really good and sort of cartoon-ish and most importantly, It's fun to play especially with your friends! I highly suggest this to newcomers who have no history with Concing who want to get into it and i recommend to oldschool Concer's who are still interested in Concing. It's really worth it especially for 2.99$!
