Ready for a second serving of Neptunia and Tamsoft? Idea Factory's ready to serve you more with MegaTagmension Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies (what a mouthful!)!
This is a spiritual successor to Hyperdimension Neptunia U Action Unleashed, but this time, you're brought to the Light Novel universe known as Gamicademi, where you take control of schoolgirls fighting zombies. Yep, schoolgirls, zombies, AND Neptunia, an epic casserole we have here. Now I'm sure we've all modded Left 4 Dead 2 to include Neptunia characters and go on 4 player zombie slaying havok. This here is the real deal, you're getting the actual Nep girls fighting zombies (which are zombified monsters of Neptunia lore like the Dogoo and Super Otaku).
Just like Neptunia U, the story is rather silly, but it's a lot more interesting as it progresses. The story is that Gamicademi is closing, and as a means of saving the school, the girls must film a movie about their school, and believe it or not, zombies appear and the girls use the opportunity to make a zombie movie featuring their school. Both the movie in the making and the game's story all prove to be very silly and hilarious. It's even funnier when some of the girls go into crazy antics.
Meanwhile the gameplay is a lot like Neptunia U, but the moveset has been nerfed and reworked. The new attacks take time to get used to since now you can charge attacks and in turn makes combo stringing a lot more challenging (good luck getting 9,999 combos). You still have your horde of enemies with dumb AI at least, so they can make things more or less easy. It takes time getting used to the new schemes especially with 14 characters (another 14 with their HDD/transformed state), but it still feels fast paced and easy to pick up and play.
Missions are much shorter as well. As this is a Vita game, this was a perfect way to get your Nep on the go. And if you're using a laptop, then you'll get about the same amount of portablility and accessibility. Now the missions may be shorter, but sometimes they can be difficult especially at lower levels. At least you retain the EXP gained if you die in the apocalypse.
Another thing I like about this game is how you can put accessories in JUST ABOUT ANYWHERE. I repeat, JUST ABOUT ANYWHERE. What is this, Garry's Mod? I can cram two stackable plushies onto the same head, headphones, hats, all in the same spot. Clearly someone wanted this to be the next Hat Simulator since Team Fortress 2.
When you're done playing the singleplayer, you can tackle the game's biggest focus, the multiplayer. It's 4 player hack and slash goodness as you take on various quests like it's Monster Hunter and God Eater. I'm surprised at how stable the game's servers are in my view especially with lag free input (a friend of mine told me Tamsoft makes excellent netcoding and their Steamworks are just as good as the Vita). I sure could use a handy button to invite friends over. There's private servers that you can secure with a password, so it's something. And if you wanted to cross-platforms with Vita, no dice. Just Steam servers. But hey, Multiplayer is very fun.
In the end, this takes a lot of the fun things about Neptunia U and made it quirkier, and more fun to play. It's also zombies and schoolgirls mashed in. It seemed to me that Idea Factory saw how many L4D2 and GMOD players loved playing with Neptunia mods and wanted to make a game of its own. I had a lot of fun playing this game, and since it's the Halloween season, what a perfect time for them to bring this game to Steam. Now if only Uni learned how to do Rule No. 2: Double Tap.

Looking at some of the other reviews, you'd think the game was an absolute mess. And they weren't wrong, it launched in a terrible state. However, 2 days later a patch has drastically improved the performance for most players. It now runs flawlessly for me at 1080p medium-high settings, and i have a lower spec PC (AMD FX 4130, GTX 770) so i'm sure it's perfect for others.
The gameplay feels very good for the most part. I think that aspects of craft handling could do with some polish (e.g. crashing into a wall makes you stick to it a bit when flying heavier ships) but in my opinion the flaws aren't major and the gameplay is fun regardless. Furthermore, the devs are committed to improving the game with updates so it is likely that this will continue to improve.
Asethetically the game looks brilliant (even, as i said, on medium settings) and easily rivals other racing games. The soundtrack is fitting, but could do with some more variety. As I understand, this was due to some issues regarding licensing songs in time for launch, but it is possible that more music will be added to the game in future.
In terms of content offering, Formula Fusion boasts 8 tracks, each of which have reverse and night variants. This will take a long time to master at the elite speed class, so the size of the roster isn't an issue at all. The game includes 5 ships, each of which can be upgraded with a variety of loadouts so you can tune them to your liking. Additionally - and I hate to keep bringing up future updates instead of the base game but it needs to be said - future track and ship DLC will provide even more content, and should all be free.
Overall, I think the game did launch too soon, but it has a great amount of potential. It currently has enough value to be worth a purchase for avid fans of wipeout-esque games, and i would suggest to anyone that they at least keep an eye on how development progresses.
In need of more polish, performance optimisation and more tracks, but it's already enjoyable. In a few months, this will be a worthy successor to Wipeout.

First off, I want to make it clear that 3089 is NOTHING like Minecraft. Where 3089 lacks in visual esthetics, the game play is really captivating.
3089 is a very unique RPG that can allow you to not only customize your character, but most (if not all) your gear and weapons as well. There are a bunch of cool abilities like teleportation, building, cloak, bullet time, vehicles, hover boards and grappling hooks. It makes the game extra fun to combine some of these abilities and tackle some missions or engage in a epic boss battle.
The architecture and the planet of 3089 really reminds me of the classic Starsiege Tribes and that goes double for the construction system. As I started to toy around with the building tool, it felt like I was playing "Construction Mod" for Tribes 2. I don't want to keep comparing, but there are a lot of qualities of 3089 that reminds me of the Tribes Series. I'm an old Tribes vet so I absolutely love that familiarity.
The planet XaX has a lot of different hazards such as lighting storms, rain and lakes that can cause corrosion, and an epic meteor shower that can kill almost anything. 3089 has a smooth transition of day and night thought the days don't seem to last long. I've put in 10 hours and from what I can tell, there is nothing significant of the day and night cycle unfortunately.
3089 can be a little overwhelming at first but once you get familiar with the world, that's when the game blossoms.

This game is not finished. Extremely poor performance on my i5 6600k and 980ti, not to mention the missing features. The handling is

Instead of bumping back onto the track with considerably less speed like in the classic games, you kind of just get...stuck to the wall. This was fine in HD/Fury thanks to the side-shift mechanic, but it really feels awkward here.
If this game were feature complete and didn't suffer from
poor performance. Would I recommend it? Probably not. It's not a bad game by any means, but it feels kind of dull compared to just about any other AG racer on the market nowadays. I regret buying into Early Access, but this is largely due to my being bitter over the claim that R8 games consists of former Studio Liverpool devs (a highly dubious claim).
Don't recommend. Look elsewhere for your AG fix.

Edit (7/6/17): After some recent performance patches it seems to run perfectly now, I haven't played much yet but I'd recommend it in its current state. R8 seem to have been quite on the ball with fixing the performance but it does beg the question why they didn't just delay the launch by a week so it didn't have these issues on day one? I guess they wanted to get it out before Wipeout Omega Edition, but that's a PS4 exclusive and this is currently only out on PC, so I'm not sure what they hoped to gain from beating it to market.
Anyway, it's still a poor man's Wipeout but it is still fun in its own right, I look forward to seeing where they go with it.
Original review: I
want to recommend Formula Fusion, but honestly, if I told a friend they should buy it I'd feel bad, so I won't.
I personally don't dislike it, I think the handling has improved greatly over what it used to be to the point where it's quite intuitive, the graphics are nice, the AI seems... Maybe competent but not unfair? There are 'only' eight circuits (each with forward and reverse and day and night versions of both directions), five or six ships and five difficulties, but I think that's about right for a £15 price point.
What I don't like is the (well documented) poor performance and the overall 'bargain bin' presentation to most things. Part of what made Wipeout so memorable was the slick UI, licensed music that fit it perfectly (and in some ways came to represent the game better than the gameplay itself), attention to detail and the awesome design language that The Designers Republic came up with, sadly Formula Fusion doesn't have any of that, or at least if it does, it's not anywhere as obvious.
So what you're left with is a Wipeout-like but without the bits that made Wipeout special, meaning if it had released around the time of 2097 it would've been one of those more forgettable also-rans. I mean, there's a reason why we're not comparing this to F-Zero X or Rollcage. As great as those games were, Wipeout was the one to beat - and it's still the best.
That said, for £15, if they fixed the performance and the more obvious bugs I'd happily recommend it.

The story advances a little bit every time you track down and defeat a boss.  Boss battles aren't easy, so you need to train and level-up a bit beforehand.
The quest system is pretty lame, though.  Quests are randomly generated; they have no story; they don't effect the larger game world in any meaningful way.  Quests just give you skill points to improve your character.  Some people will compare this game to Borderlands, which is fair up to a point.  However, Borderlands goes far beyond this game in terms of character customization, special abilities, cool features, etc.

This is an interesting one, although not really a great one.
The world and lore it establishes are well-done and interesting. You get to encounter different sects, and you can ally yourself with them, betray them later, and then change your mind and do what they probably would have wanted if you hadn't already massacred their town. All of these actions have consequences within the world and how that world reacts to you. Those consequences follow through all the way to the ending of the game, which has a pretty impressive variety of outcomes. This is probably the strongest part of the game and what makes it worth playing through.
The growth and progression of your character is also well done. You can choose to play Geneforge as three quite different "classes". Every level up you get a set of skill points that you can apportion as you wish. The class you choose doesn't dictate what you can do, but it does make it easier/harder to level up certain skills. Skills range from physical combat, magic spells, the ability to "shape" creatures to fight for you. General skills, such as Leadership and Mechanics, are also available. Pleasantly, these are actually very useful to find non-combat methods to progress through the game.
Again all of these things are well done, and are what make the game worth playing. Where it falls apart a bit, is in the interface and to a certain degree, the combat.
Combat is turn-based, and on the surface, can be quite tactical. Timing, and awareness of the positions of both your allies and your enemies are all quite important. Particularly, when you do have allies (such as the creatures you can "shape"), you do have to take into account whether or not you or your creatures are blocking a path forward. You can use this both to your benefit and your detriment, by funneling enemies down a corridor into one of your stronger creatures.
In theory anyway.
The problem is that, at least in my experience, the game is rather easy. So, tactics more or less go out the window, when you can just click-click-click your way to victory. Positioning at that point becomes more of an annoyance, as you try to coax the pathing algorithms to make sure that you don't waste a turn because you clicked slightly to the left of something, so it paths all the way around and your turn is wasted. And it's even worse that the punishment for this is not death, but a test of your patience, more often than not.
Towards the end of the game, the challenge is upped, but by presenting annoyances, like poisoned areas that do damage to you and your creatures for just being in them. There is an optional area towards the end that serves as a pretty robust challenge, but again, the tactics aren't really that interesting at the end of it. It's more a battle of attrition that you just need to push through.
Overall, the combat side of this game seems like it would be great on paper, but it ends up being boring most of the time, and annoying some of the time. Very rarely is it actually much fun.
I should mention that the presentation of the game is quite old-school, and to top it off, there is no music aside from the title screen of the game. You just get some ambient noise in towns, and sound effects for all the actions. That's it. Honestly, some music would have made some of the more annoying slog parts of the game much more palatable. I mean, it helped a lot when I was just listening to a podcast or some music when I was doing it.
That being said, despite all the gripes, I would still totally recommend the game. Normally, I'm a gameplay over story/presentation guy, but in this case I can overlook it. What it does right, it does very well.
From what I've heard, the series just continues to build on itself as it goes on. Based on what I played, I'm very much looking forward to eventually going through the following games in the series.

This series is a good example of classic-style open world RPGs like Fallout. The story does moral ambiguity very well, particularly as the series goes on. Compare that to a lot of modern games where your only options are "Barf rainbows and friendship" or "Be a complete psychopath." And as the type of person who can't seem to choose anything other than rainbows and friendship, this series made me feel
uncomfortable. (Which is good; stories should make you feel things.)
While the gameplay is good, it can sometimes fall victim to the "Dominant Strategy" trope. Dungeon too dangerous for your squishy wizard? Just have your creations scout ahead while you hide in a pantry! Character building isn't
open, but it's done in a way that makes sense. Playing as someone specializing in the magical arts? They aren't exactly going be become Conan overnight.
All in all, I'd recommend this series to anyone who enjoys classic PC RPGs, or anyone who enjoys a good (soul-crushing) story.

Before I clarify my thoughts on Geneforge, I must ask a question. What, to you, makes a good game? There are many potential answers to that question, all of them valid. If, however, you rely on graphics for the sake of immersion you will not enjoy Geneforge. Its graphics are rather primitive, even considering their age. If you cannot bring yourself to overlook the game's presentation, that's understandable. But if you can see past the rough edges, you will find an RPG with a lot to offer.
If graphics are the lowest point of Geneforge, story is the highest. The game takes place in a creative and well-realized world where science and magic combine into an entire discipline based on creating life. Those who wield this power, called shapers,  hold immense social and political influence over the setting. Entire species owe their existence to these mad scientists of the magic world, and the shapers are quick to bring that up and exploit it.
On the island where the plot is set, long-abandoned creations get these quaint ideas like "free will" and "fair compensation". It's up to the player to decide to what extent they support the rights of the created beings, if at all. Choices like that are common in Geneforge, and railroading the player's decisions is refreshingly rare. None of the story paths is presented as the absolute most ethical--each faction has flaws and benefits, both to the NPCs and to the player. Not allying yourself to any of them is possible but more difficult.
The game play itself is adequate, but personally I only saw it as a vehicle to access more of the plot. Make of that what you will.
In summary: Geneforge is a game that must be viewed with certain expectations in mind. There are a number of obvious budget and technical constraints at work, which may turn away those with little tolerance fo such things. Those who can endure despite its flaws will find a game with immense personality, well worth the effort required to uncover its riches. Give it a shot.

Finally something pretty unique in the RPG genre. A game that's not just about seeing how many goblins you can bop on the head or how much gold you've shamelessly stolen by the end of the adventure.
The Geneforge series is all about story, strategy and whether or not, you're willing to sacrifice Binky (your sadly under-leveled Fyora) for a brand spanking new, just off the line, Terror Vlish (you might name him Keith). Now in any other RPG this is an easy choice - Binky doesn't even have time to say goodbye to his best friend Crispin (a dependable Clawbug), before you've reabsorbed him and used his essence to create Keith.
But this is the bit that makes Geneforge different - Keith might be better in every possible way, but you two haven't taken a journey together from the Bandit Woods, through the Thorny Fen, and down into the (horrific) Mines. You and Binky have a partnership and you're not about to give him up, not even for Keith (with his awesome name).
Eventually you'll either decide to give up Binky (Crispin still gets a far off look in his eyes whenever he smells roasted Ornk) or you'll keep Binky and find another way to survive the Labs. It'll take more healing, planning, tools and a fair bit of luck, but Crispin won't be crying himself to sleep every night.
And that's what Geneforge is about. At its core, it's game where you create creatures to fight for you, that you actually weirdly start caring about (sorry Jiggly Puff). It's a journey, both plot and game mechanic wise of hard decisions. At the end you'll never feel completely happy with the choices you've made and that's the sign of a good game. There's no right or wrong in Geneforge, only things you did because you followed your gut.

Very similar to the Sims 2, except with more options, freedom, and things to do and buy. Moving around between properties (either residential or community) without any loading screens is by far the best aspect of the game. You can also roam the neighborhood without going to any specific lot.

Pros:

Cons:
Loading times. I have a fast SSD and an unlocked 5th gen i5. Want to hop in and play with your friends? Click on GTA V. A minute or two later, you can choose GTA V or online. Choosing singleplayer will take a minute or two to load. Choosing multiplayer will take a couple minutes as it loads the singleplayer anyway, then a couple more as it loads you into a multiplayer session. Then add a couple more to join your friends' private session. Almost ten minutes to get into a server, easily. At least now you can play GTA. Unless...
Stability issues occur. The game crashes consistently with no reason on my PC and my friend's machine. Which wouldn't be so bad if I didn't have to wait for so long to play.
But when it's working, you get to explore the wonderful world of Los Santos. Unfortunately, every way of interacting with said world is infuriatingly bad.
Player movement on foot: unusable, will get you killed frequently due to your character running into gunfire or off a cliff 20 feet away, despite you instructing them to go elsewhere.
Cameras: default to an angle which is far too low. If you move your mouse to fix them, they auto reset every 2 seconds anyway, even if this is turned off in settings.
Flying: autocenters controls, even when disabled in settings. Do you like scrolling your mouse all the way forwards across your desk, picking it up, and doing it again and agin, just to fly a helicopter in a straight line? Buy this game!
Driving: surprisingly good mechanics actually. Unfortunately, PC players can't use a wheel... so you can only use the brute force of arrow keys. Oh well. The driving mechanics have issues- hit curbs to gain speed, pedestrians interfering in races, etc, but nothing compares to arrow keys.
User Interface: Again, terrible. A user interface designed for consoles hasn't even been changed for PC. Not going into detail. If you play you'll see what I mean. Add to this the game's tendency to remove clicks, or only count a map vote/setting change/etc after 3+ clicks, or the left/right selectors tendency to not respond properly after a change in the width of the content.
Shooting mechanics: Not so much that they are bad, it's that they're nonexistent. Recoil hardly matters. All automatic weapons feel inaccurate and put far too much luck into already chaotic conflict. The AP pistol and heavy sniper make all other weapons irrelevant anyway(except explosives).
And then finally, we have Rockstar's updates.
This game(which is already expensive 4 years after release) is, even after you buy in, essentially a grind or pay2win game. like a free2play title. Rockstar prefers to put out the newest supercars(that take several hours of grinding to get just one of) instead of making actual content. But that's not too bad. More concerning are the armored cars, APCs, etc that completely change the combat and add a huge tax to GTA combat. Either have 8+ million for the gunrunning DLC content, and more for the included APC and rocket bike and their ilk, or die to those who do. Public GTA combat has been completely ruined by this cash grab update.

I was genuinely surprised by this movie.  I went in expecting a pretty poorly made horror/gore filled indie movie, and came out fairly impressed by what I had just watched.  Except for the last 30 minutes or so.  I honestly felt that the last 30 minutes were complete and utter trash (including the ending) and if I were to judge this movie based on that alone I would never recommend this to anyone.  Let me explain briefly.
The majority of the movie has good character and story build up.  It draws you into the situation and provides an interesting backstory explaining the main character's ailment and what led up to that point.  Things seem plausible and I found myself genuinely interested in how our protagonist was going to get out of his current situation alive.
And then the last 30 minutes happened.
Up to that point I was very much into this film.  But those last 30 minutes constitute some of the dumbest, corniest, and overall baffling scenes I've ever encountered in a movie.  For starters, the choices made by the intruders are literally some of the most unrealistic, and downright stupid decisions ever made by any criminal in almost any movie ever.  I almost stopped watching just to savor the memory of what was, up to that point, a pretty decent movie.  I won't ruin anything, just watch and you'll see all of the things I'm talking about.
Second, the fight scenes were friggin god awful.  I read the reviews before watching and I was looking forward to the fight scenes, given all of the praise that was given to them in some of them, only to be insanely disappointed through every second.  Think of the worst YouTube video you've watched of someone trying to "show off" their martial arts move, and you'll be pretty close to the fight scenes here.
Lastly, the ending may have been the biggest pile of garbage I've ever witnessed in a movie.  Yet another thing that received praise in the reviews, and I could not have been more disappointed with it.  Now I know little about the biblical context upon which this movie seems to be based, but I do know that a movie with an ending such as this may as well not have an ending at all.  I thought up about five different possible endings while watching this movie, which I'm sure most people who watch this will consider while watching, only to be shown an ending which I couldn't have possibly conceived due to how dull and anti-climatic it is.
Despite all of those criticisms, the first 70-80 percent of the movie is actually pretty good, and it would be wrong to give this film a bad rating based on the disaster that is the last 20 percent.  Maybe I'm an outlier, and the last part was great to most people.  Maybe I've seen too many fight scenes, kung fu movies, and all of the Ip Man movies and so I'm biased against what is a good and bad fight scene.  All I can say is watch it for yourself.  Most of it is enjoyable, and you can judge for yourself whether the last 30 minutes was acceptable or not.

I must confess that I stoped playing those games since MK 3 and only now decided to go back to them. Seems like Mortal Kombat 9 got criticized for its cartoonish character models, especially the female ones, so this time in MKX they tried a more realist approach, making characters look more like real people, with men looking not that buff and women looking not that busty. The result is that now the carnage has a real gory feeling, like if you are taking part in some kind of slasher movie, especially whe you perform one of the infamous fatalities and do crazy gory stuff with the opponent's body, like ripping their heart, cutting their head off and other even more macabre stuff.
There's a bunch of single player modes, so even if you don't play online you still gonna find the game fun anyways. The story mode in this game is kinda good, I mean, it makes sense and is entertaining enough without being too dumb. Thumbs up to Netherrealm for making a fighter with a decent story mode. The other single player modes are usually variations of the traditional "towers" found in usual Mortal Kombat games, and here you have a huge amout of those towers. The most fun are the so called "living towers" which provide you some kind of challege to increase the fight difficulty, like fighting while the screen is shaking or with lasers blasting both opponents and so on.
The only is kinda dead now, so you will only find random people to fight on weekends and such. Usually, to find an online partner, you have to call up someone on you friend list. That's how most of the online activity happens.
It seems like when game was released, the netcode was broken and Netherrealm simply stopped caring about the PC version at all. Now all these problems were solved and the game runs fine on PC with all the content included.
The problems with this game are only two, both gameplay releated:
1- Fireballs and long ranged attacks are too overpowered. You can pick up certain characters and keep basically running away while apamming fireballs and the opponent can do little about it. Unfortunately, this seems to be a recurrent problem in all Netherrealm recent fighters. See Injustice 1 and 2, for exemple.
2- The controls for the special moves are really messed up. Some follow the traditional MK style, like down, up + button, while others follow a more Street Fighter style, with quarter circle + button. I thinks it's time for MK to adopt only one style and get rid of this mess.

This is actually quite fun. I've spent many enjoyable hours playing 3089 and 100% recommend it (even if it sounds like I don't!).
Positives:
The screen shots are far worse than the game graphics. I cranked it up to x16 AA and everything is crisp and clean on the edges. (Unlike the SS's) Quests keep you occupied. The ability to build stuff like a radar, skill buffer, and teleporter (more on the teleporter later). Your weight affects how well you can move. Hundreds of pounds over your max and you won't be sprinting but movement won't stop alltogether or even slow you down that much. BUT if you want to go fast with a hoverboard, the hoverboard will not move if you exceed it's weight limit.  Translocators shoot a sphere and warp to it's location grappling hooks shoot a line out and if it strikes an object you will be pulled up and gravity guns for moving stuff around like boxes all add to the game.
It's fun building your weapon. Rifle has a stock.. barrel.. mag.. silencer.. scope. Stock determines number of shots. Single shot will be more accurate and powerful (per round typically) while increases in the number of rounds fired with each trigger pull (think shotgun) will decrease the damage of the individual rounds, as well as accuracy of the weapon. In addition there can be effects.. like a percentage of dmg translating into an explosion or rounds homing in on targets.
Barrel determines base accuracy, range, damage and speed the round travels. Mag determines how often the weapon can fire, and how much ammo is consumed per shot. Silencer silences the weapon. You're less likely to be noticed. I haven't noticed a decrease in damage. As with any piece there can be additional stat buffs so less noise are more stats are always a good thing. The scope well.. duh.
I play a sniper. I had a 220 range barrel but the accuracy and bullet speed were a bit low and swapped out for a 160 range with a 10% accuracy increase and almost double the speed. As you can see this single weapon had MANY options.
The launcher's are just like they sound. Can be lob based, but also add additional effects like corosion (DoT) or Leech. Fire slower, fewer rounds before a reload and consume more ammo.
Negatives:
This is going to sound like I'm being picky.. and I am. These are things that just irritated me a bit.
3 Types of guns. Period. Pistol, Rifle and Launcher. Each of those come in the normal ammo using version and the "Energy" version. I've never tried the pistols so won't be talking about them. The rifle vs launcher, i've tried them in both normal and energy versions. Energy seems to simply use your "energy" as a different kind of ammo. That will regenerate to 25% on it's own. You can recharge at a station or use items to boost it up to 100% (or higher if you equip an item with high energy, recharge, then remove it). Ex: I have over 1500% energy because I have a hoverboard that grants me ~360 energy. I've used items while on it to recharge it to 100% (while on the board). As soon as I get off the board I loose the 360 energy stat bonus but I keep the pool of energy. That said. I don't use energy weapons.
Why not? I don't see a point. It seems to use a % of your energy per shot. So at 5 energy or 500 energy skill, each shot from that level 7 rifle will consume the percentage listed on the mag.
While there are many ways to build a weapon, there are really only 3 ranged. I'm trying to build a bit of a shotgun rifle for close quarters but the most i've found so far is 3 rounds. Keeping it non explosive so i don't damamge myself. These numbers may increase later but it just feels like i'm hammered into a specific type of weapon due to lack of variance in the earlier part of the game.
Followers: Don't plan on doing any damage if you want an army following you. They will run around you, in front of you, and everywhere. They'll die to the daily meteor showers and screw up quests. It's a great concept and thats how I started out, till i realized i couldn't do anything at all as a ranged character with an Army. If a stray round hits one of your followers they'll ALL turn against you instantly.
Building a base: You can construct walls. Cool! But when I tried to set up a base inside the blue base, it was a bit disappointing. I had my gear like boxes, teleporter, radar all setup way in the back. I had created a maze on the 3rd floor with low walls for fall back points if I had to retreat further in. Every other time I go on a quest though I return to a bunch of bots already set up shop all throughout the maze just wandering around. Turrets and all. The enemy has always ignored my structures.. and are more of a bother than anything significant.
Quests:
I can't stand the "don't be detected" type quests. I try to avoid them but every now and then one slips in. The "kill" without being detected by target isn't bad since i'm a sniper, but "no additional detection" and the "spy" ones where you have to sit there and watch or avoid all detection can be brutal.
The World:
Now, the fact that the world is generated each time is good.. and terrible. After my first "leadership" attempt the 2nd world I got was surrounded on all sides by an ocean. A good 300m straight down. I kept getting quests in the water. While you can go into the water.. it makes it far more difficult (at least in early stages) to deal with enemies that can come from any direction.. up.. down.. sides.. everywhere inbetween. Also, not a lot of cover in the middle of the ocean. Ever try protecting a bot? It's not easy. Now do that with zero cover and any direction of approach in a 3 dimensional plane. To get back again (this was before I had unlocked teleporters.. which.. charge money) was a 10 min swim to the nearest ledge that had a ramp.
What i'm saying is, once you start a game, look at your map. You may be in for a really difficult challenge starting out.
Other:
Surveryors: Don't kill them unless you have a plan for dying a lot. They die EASY. At around level 6 area I decided to try my hand at them. I killed a few dozen and got some great gear, including a level 90 hoverboard. But for every one you kill, 2 more are sent to kill YOU. And they go up 10 levels every time they do. By the time they were up to level 110 I was dying WAY too much. They lock on at a long range and 1 shot me. So how do you get all those ones to stop coming after you? Each time you die to one, it despawns. You have to let each one kill you so that it despawns. Remember if you kill it, 2 more will spawn. (I'm pretty sure about the 2 spawning to kill you, I was kinda busy killing and looting to count each one. In the end I had to suffer around 12 deaths to make them stop attacking).
Held items. They have stats yes. But they do not apply unless you have them selected. If you have a rilfe and dagger equipped but have the rifle out, the dagger's stats will not apply until you swap from the rifle to dagger. So don't load yourself down with a bunch of stat based weapons. I go with my primary weapon which uses ammo, and a backup that uses energy (in case I ever run out of ammo.. which.. hasn't happened yet).
Wishes:
I wish there were doors, or something to prevent things from simply spawning wherever they want. I wish turrets you placed were not temporary. What's the point of gathering all the materals to defend your base if the enemy can simply spawn inside  and your turrets just go "poof" over time? I wish there were some other options for rifles to make them more like a shotgun or sniper instead of a middle of the road rifle. I wish grapplers, translocators and hoverboards held WAY more than each level currently allows. I'm always over what they can handle in the level range i'm questing. I've accepted that fact since i'm a sniper/tank type with high agility. I can run crazy fast, carry a bunch etc.. but i'm not going to be able to translocate across a gap, or grapple my way up a cliff.

This is a game that really surprised me. At first glance I didn't really think much of it, and to be fair it is not much to look at. However, the gameplay is actually quite entertaining. Some of the more pronounced strengths of the game to me, in no particualr order, is:
1: The randomly generated world. It creates diversity, and the terrain generator is quite capable of creating interesting terrain.
2: The loot comes in parts than can be picked apart and reassembled at workstations, making you at least somewhat interested in what you pick up. It could use a little bit more weapon type variety though, especially in the melee department.
3: The Time Rip ability. When you wander the world, there are little clocks to collect that spawn all over the place. It fills up a meter you can use to stop time for at max 15 seconds. I don't think I have to say how useful this is if something goes wrong.
4: As you advance in the main quest, more enemy variety is introduced, which helps keep up the interest. And you do indeed notice the difference...
5: Unlimited skillpoints. The quests from quest stations are randomly generated and provide skillpoints, so you are allowed to waste points in stats that don't promote your ability to fight.
6: And lastly, the special weapons category. Hoverboards, grappling hooks, blink tech, decoys. ect. It really makes it more fun to move about, which is a huge plus! Especially when a meteor shower starts and you have to rush to a place with a roof. Tip: If one player has a hoverboard, the other player can request to be a gunner, combining the two players so that both can make use of the hoverboard. It's hilarious.
All in all, I was really surpised I liked it as much as I did, and even the graphics have really grown on me. I am looking forward to what other things this game has in store for me. Fingers crossed for more weapon variety and some more special items!

3089 is a fun game. If you like fps rpgs like borderlands and fallout 3/NV you should not have to much of a problem getting into 3089. In 3089 you are an android droped on to the mysterious and randomly generated planet Xax, You are one of the few androids with emotion codes giving you the ability to do quest and fight robot at your pleasure instead of taking commands from the Overlord.
You start off in a friendly base where you can buy weapons, armor, consumables, and other forms of transportation, take quest, and recruit other androids for help and all of it is randomly generated. The weapons, armor and specials are all made on a parts system where you have say three parts to an energy pistol all with their own effect on you and your guns ability's. The amount of options this system gives you along with the normal rpg system of adding points to certain skills to better your self gives you a lot of flexibility in how you mold your android. If you want to be a pilot that fly's ships and shoots guns, go ahead. A stealth focused melee character that teleports and can turn invisible, fine. A commander that recruits androids to fight for you and steals all of his items, no problem. The gun play is serviceable and fun but does not have the most kick to it, but that does not mean the combat is lackluster because of all the ways to move in combat you have a lot of choice in how you fight a battle, you can use a grappling hook and hover bored in conjunction to get crazy height and speed and drop on an enemy with a sword. I have heard some criticism on the graphics and while they are not the best and even I someone that does not really care about graphics when looking at screen shots thought "wow this does not look good" am glad that I took the time to watch some videos on it first, but the graphics do grow on you and seeing as the game is made in java it should be very modible. Anyway a videoGAME is about game play, that is why they are not called videographics. Another complaint I have heard is that the character is slow and sluggish and this I find laughable either the person does not understand encumbrance and is carrying to much thus making them slow or they have not payed attention to the specials terminal where you can buy many items to increase your speed and maneuverability. So while there are a few problems like the graphics and the AI not being the brightest it is nowhere near enough to make this an un-enjoyable game. Seeing as it is made by only one person is pretty crazy, and the game is cheap being only 10 bucks at most, definitely recommend.

I know this game has been getting it's fair share of lashings. Understandable and even I agree with some of the key points people are not approving of.
I just finished a 36 hour playthrough including all side missions and POIs. Though I have yet to play either of the two standalone missions or Breach Mode.
Do I feel that it was ended a little soon with a more "anti-climatic" ending? Yeah actually. That's the largest fault for me with this game. The villians are built up nice and strongly, just to wither out into almost nothing. I feel like the setup to the final stage was rushed and the actual ending was poorly executed. Personally, I think they could have easily fleshed out the main story more and given this game a true ending worthy of what they built. I also wish we had more places to go rather than be confined to a rather small main map area. I know it was packed with content (which is nice, really adds to the reality of drawing the player in), but It felt kind of clausterphobic.
Why am I recommending this game anyways with these flaws?
It's because I still enjoyed it. The ending was really my only major gripe with Mankind Divided. Some other minor issues with game crashes here and there. Which only happened twice throughout my 36 hours (Honestly isn't bad. There are other major titles that crash before you can say "I never asked for this".) I also really enjoyed the side missions and POIs. Some of those were really clever and a lot of fun. Some of the new augs were really fun to play around with. My favorites being Remote Hacking and P.E.P.S. Also liked the reworked Social Enhancer aug as well.
The graphics are nice. I was able to push a mix of High and Very High settings and get a good solid 60fps @ 1080p w/ my GTX 970, 16GB ram, and my dated (soon to be replaced) Phenom II X6 1045t. I was more than pleased with the aesthetical value presented as well as the art direction. Part of the biggest draws for me in this franchise is the amazing art direction. The sound design was enjoyable too with the music. It really set the atmosphere. As well as the improved aspect of verticality that was added into this game. It really gave it a nice boost.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game despite it's flaws. It added another enjoyable story to the franchise and sets it up for a next one. Which I'll be eagerly waiting for. I've been a long time fan of this franchise and love to see it continue.
I recommend this game honestly. It may not be worth full price to many. But hey, you can get this game for $30 from some places online. (Which is what I did. I paid $34 after tax). I think this game is worth at least that price if not a little bit more.
Cons:
Story overall could have been fleshed out a little bit more

Poorly executed/rushed ending itself
Small overall map size despite it's density. Gave off a clausterphobic vibe

Story was engaging despite being thin in some parts

Overall atmospere

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided feels like an incomplete product made solely to stretch out a franchise by setting up an even later sequel, but I'll get to it later.
THE GOOD:
* The actual, moment-to-moment gameplay is the best we've had from a Deus Ex game yet. The cover mechanics were smoothed over, movement feels a bit more responsive (being able to grab onto ledges feels good). The stealth system seems to have gotten just that little bit better.
* The range of augmentations is once again expanded to the point that there is an over-abundance of tools that you'll probably never use. Still, it's a good thing you have the option to. If you're not shy about maximizing your XP gains, you will probably have access to all augmentations you could want by the end of the game, and then some.
* The story is full of references to previous and upcoming games in the DX chronology, if you know where to look and are the kind that gets excited about little nods to continuity.
THE BAD:
* The game is incomplete, maybe purposefully so, ending just as things are finally picking up. As it is, the plot goes precisely nowhere, and when the inevitable sequel comes out, I wouldn't say that you needed to play Mankind Divided to understand it. By the end of the game, all that gets done is Adam is made aware of a couple important names(Bob Page and Joseph Manderley are Illuminati, whoop-de-bucking-doo), and an upcoming decision (The Human Restoration Act) is influenced but never made. I think it's deeply frustrating because the player, who at this point should have played the original game, already knows all of this and how it turns out, and so the events of this game feel devoid of meaning.
There are painfully obvious sequel and DLC hooks already in place.
* As a side-note to the previous point, the fact that the plot's events are largely inconsequential leads one to believe that Adam's choices do not matter at all in the game, and that the eventual sequel will render them, and the characters they influence, moot.
* The UI is plain bad. It's clearly made for consoles, and is most apparent in the hacking minigame, where you'll be baffled that you cannot pan the camera with your mouse at all. Special mention to every shop interface, that has you jumping through hoops just to get to the right screen.
* The load times are excessive, especially when trying to cross from one side of Prague to the next.
* The release of Deus Ex: Breach and Deus Ex: Go alongside this game makes me wonder if those side-games took time and resources away from the developement of Mankind Divided. I can't know for sure, but stuffing your game full of collectibles for DIFFERENT GAMES and demanding you play them to enjoy everything MD has to offer feels like Square Enix didn't have confidence in it's own product. And that stinks.
* Let's not even talk about the single-player micro-transactions. At the very least, I can confidently state that selling you PRAXIS Kits for real money, although scummy, didn't seem to affect the availability of PRAXIS points in the actual game - there are more than enough, although the first couple hours can make it seem otherwise.
* It's subjective, but I really enjoyed the yellow and black Human Revolution aesthetic. People complain about ♥♥♥♥♥♥filters', but I think it gave HR memorable visuals, as well as helping to set the tone. Everything in Mankind Divided is more washed out and colorless.
* The game really tries to sell you on it's 'cast of colorful characters', but the truth is, -characters- were never a core strength of DX, it's always more story-driven. The characters felt - to me - like they were trying too hard to be memorable, including some ridiculous designs like Valclav Koeller, who looks like he belongs in a Shadowrun game, whilst being hastily introduced as an important being part of Jensen's life, a fact that the character seems to know, but the player doesn't. This feed into a larger problem of trying to -make- Deus Ex into a character-driven game, which I think is a huge mistake. I like Adam Jenses well enough, but we didn't need to be the protagonist for this game, much less a sequel. If even Deus Ex has some really bad games under it's belt, so far at least it's tried to keep things fresh by introducing new protagonists at every turn, something that's happened even in Invisible War and The Fall.
IN CONCLUSION
It could've been an excellent game, but is weighed down by many flaws, and as such, is merely 'good'. It stands firmly in the middle of the other games, being better than the disasters that were The Fall and Invisible War, but falling short of truly great titles such as Human Revolution and, of course, the original.
I still recommend it if you're into Deus Ex, or just first-person stealth games in general. Just don't expect to be blown away.

Make no mistake. The scenery and attention to detail is stunning but, at times I felt that no real progress was being made. Also, a sense of 'reuse, rinse and repeat' were often on my mind. Vastly superior were the grand locales of Deus Ex Human Revolution. I was hoping for more of the same yet, while two other locales did come along, they were very short lived.
Graphically, the game follows closely with DE:HR. A host of tweaks and updates certainly added to the new adventure however, in some cases [Hacking, for example]. Why fix something that was never broken?
New experimental augs - Well, I have no plans to ruin things with spoilers but, WOW. One aug in particular came to mind but, as we all play differently, I'll let you decide the best of the best.
MD is somewhat linear is style, offering few genuine 'choices' that affect gameplay. Certainly in the latter part of the game, the choices you had were irrelevant as ultimately, you wound up following both regardless and of course, as a 'nod' to my fellow reviewers, I must conceed that the lack of choice at the end of the game was very dissapointing. From the original Deus Ex, every fan has relished in the triple whammy that has been iconic of the DE universe and, to abandon this without question is, in this reviewers opinion a critical error in judgement and one I believe will haunt the developers for years to come yet, if the game ending is a 'tease' of things to come, then we may already be leading into a 'part 3' of Deus ex 3 here... Time will tell.
Overall, I have played game that are worse by FAR, and for the same money. "Wait for the sales" people cry. Well, I didn't and have no regrets however, I am a true DE fan and, unless I am willing to give up my current career and learn to code my very own DE game, I am content to accept this latest offering, with high hopes for a future release.
And, a final word on those micro transactions. Suffice to say, I do not plan to use them, nor did I feel ANY need to use them even while in game so, consider them as a luxury if you happen to have some spare cash laying about and nothing much at all to spend it on. The 'buyable' content is by no means a must have.
Overall - 7/10

I was seriously excited for this game.  I even did a fresh playthrough of human revolution to refresh myself on the story and gameplay. That only got me more excited and I ended up preordering, but like so many others, I regret my purchase.
No matter what I do, I cannot maintain a steady 60 frames per second. SE claims that this is by design, and that at the "high" preset, meeting the reccomended specs, you should be able to maintain an average 60fps at 1080p. I have tried this on multiple systems, and on each of them I struggle get over an average 40 at that preset (gtx 1060 at 1080p; gtx 1070 at 21:9 1440p).
Turning off contact shadows and volumetric lighting does not provide a big enough performance boost to hit that steady 60. The result is a stuttery experience.
Very dissapointing, especially given the incredible performance of its predecessor, and the performance of games  like DOOM and Battlefield 1, which look, in my opinion, far better than what is on show here.
I planned to give it another try today after hearing about the directx 12 patch, but if anything, performance is worse.
I'm not sure that I really wish to continue playing at all having heard how abruptly the story cuts off, and how intrusive the singleplayer microtransactions are. Others complain of preorder bonuses being save locked, meaning that any DLC you may buy, should you choose to do so, will be locked to an individual save. This means that if you purchase praxis kits, you will need to re-buy more to use them in a fresh playthrough.
I've given it almost 2 months now, but I feel like the performance issues will not be addressed. Even if they are at this point, the experience has truly been soured, and the steam reviews are in the toilet. If you have not yet played human revolution, definitely grab that one, it's the better experience and far cheaper.

I have been playing GTA for a long time, and an full-blown MMO capability is something I was waiting for almost just as long. I love the concept of being able to build an empire in LA. The game requires one of two things though; heavy PVP focus or consistant "squading" as it were. I will say this though, the online portion is one hell of a grind, and it will take you a while to build the empire. However, Rome was not built in a day. So why should the Roman empire? I love that Rockstar constantly comes out with new updates to keep the game feeling fresh, but I also feel like they should work on bettering what is already present. Which leads me to the cons below.
The main issues I have are the repetativeness of the jobs, and the people online who are too lazy to actually put effort into the game so they mod. It does not matter how many updates come out, the jobs/races/whatever they entail will get boring quickly. To that end, I feel like they should add more contact jobs as well as normal races.
As far as the modders go...scum of the earth. There is no limit to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t they do; from placing impossible bounties that do not exist (such as 500000, that no one can claim but them), to dropping cars on people out of no where, to auto-ejecting people from helicopers or planes, to dropping exploded airplanes or dead bodies that look like a person's character with clown hair, to spawning money on people (that will get removed next time the game is patched), or RPGs that do more damage than they are supposed to. The list goes on.
In closing I feel that if they update/add new jobs, and keep working on weeding out the modders, and undoing the damage done by them, the game will only get better. It's not supposed to be easy to rack up millions of dollars while paying for assets, but you don't live in your house for free, and the company you work for has to pay to keep it running and you working.
Notes
1: As far as the complaints about Shark Card prices...here's an idea; how about you stop complaining about them? The shark cards are there for people who -are- too lazy to play the game. Of course they are going to be pricey, your not supposed to rely on them to get ahead in the game. You're supposed to friggin' play it. If you cannot handle the grind, stop playing.
2: If you do mod or grief I hope your account gets found out and banned. You ruin the game for people who want to go into public lobbies for PVP and to move supplies. It is one thing to fairly take out an enemy and claim the spoils, it's another thing to cheat to do so or keep targeting 1 player or a group of players when the lobby is full of others.
3: Lastly, I am hopping for a Gunrunning II, or a Cops and Robbers update. I think the latter would add a perspective to the game most people overlook. A fun perspective at that.

It's a good game, riddled with ridiculous weaponised vehicles and items that never needed to be added, and bugs that have never been fixed, some since release.
Nobody ever asked for an orbital cannon, either. Its literally like paid, first party mods for players with actual modded money. It costs 750k to fire once. One time. One target. 4-8 hours of grinding for me, and that's money wasted on something that can be done with a single sticky bomb and a 4km trip in most cases.
750k can buy a top of the range sports car and all of its performance mods. 750k can buy an MC. 750k can buy like 5 high end apartments. It used to take me an entire week to grind to get the Kuruma armored on the Xbox 360 version.
The base game was great. Import export was a great dlc. Gunrunning, smugglers run, and Doomsday DLC was some of the worst dlc to ever come to this game. These DLC's make it harder to do NORMAL CEO/MC free mode missions.
The amount of bugs sometimes makes this game unplayable, sometimes forcing me to restart the game, and wait about 4 minutes to get back into a good low population lobby where I can be safe from modders (there's about 2 per 20 pllayers in a public session on PC)
I also enjoy this game most of the time, and I enjoy import/export missions, and it really sucks that some idiot in a flying car or motorcycle can lock on to me and destroy 80k worth of car. The risk is too much sometimes. I've actually been so angry from playing this game sometimes. It's the masochistic sadists at rockstar to blame, not my bad driving or defensive tactics, or the 10 year old on the chrome oppressor, it's rockstars greed. Absolute disgust for most of their employees.
The thing I really enjoy though is the amount of pure vehicle customization. There's no licensing of vehicles or vehicle parts, so they can literally put any (non weaponised) car in that they feel the community would enjoy. The Elegy retro is my favourite car. The manchez is my favourite motorcycle.
It's like driving a really nice car covered in feces. There's something good under all of it.
I hope GTA 6 does not include ANY weaponised vehicles, unless they are about as powerful as a normal tank or hydra, with the same Pegasus delivery style. That's how much I could tolerate. GTA 6 should ONLY be focused on what this game is about. Stealing cars, and driving cars. But they let the greed take over with GTA V, but only after 2 or 3 years.

I would first off like to say that if this you are about to buy the game for about $20-$30 and are mostly interested in the singleplayer, then go right ahead because the singleplayer mode is actaully not bad. That being said the main draw to this game is the multiplayer which is frankly a joke...
I got this game on sale for around $60 and that included a megalodon shark card with the game. To put that into perspective that means that I entered into this "groundbreaking" and "revolutionary" multiplayer with a $100 real world boost and I was still unable to fight against the tide of griefers nor was I able to even establish a way to make real money. The entirety of the game feels like it designed simply for you to buy shark cards, which are uproariously expensive (I mean c'mon, $100 for 8 mil GTA$ is nothing when considering that 8 mil gets you nowhere).
Doing any kind of legitimate money producing activities will take you about an hour to earn 200,000 GTA$ and feels like a chore, like you're going to work. Video games are about escapism and this is quite the opposite. Now to support the analogy about this game being work I'm gonna do some math here (scary I know). If 8mil GTA$ = $100 and working in this game for 1 hour gets you 200,000 GTA$, then it would take you 40 hours of "playing" this game doing nothing but grinding out bunker missions or CEO missions (assuming you have ammased the minimum of 1 mil GTA$ is takes to aquire the cheapest of those things). To clarify, this is the equivalent of working for $2.50/hr.
Moving on from that note, apart from being designed to make you buy shark cards it is designed for you not to be able to play solo. No, not designed for you to play with other people, but simply to be unable to play solo. Most things in this game have tight time limits and lots of AI enemies to deal with, but nobody has the incentive to help you out because the only way to pay them is by hiring them as associates, which still pays them MINIMAL amounts.
After all is said and done, you buy that car you've really wanted, or you buy that new apartment or warehouse or whatever only to finddddddd that the car feels and sound just like every other, that the apartment is interesting for only about 10 minutes, or that the warehouse is only useful if you spend more money to do something with it.
TL;DR: The game feels like a chore and takes forever to get anywhere, when you finally do get somewhere it is painfully unrewarding after the first 10 minutes, and there is little incentive for anyone to help you out whilst playing solo simply isnt an option.

I was quite impressed by this. The art direction is incredible and more than anything else, it's very good at giving you a sense of adventure. That's mostly what won me over.
You're not actively invested in the adventure like in a Zelda-like action-adventure game or even a point-and-click adventure game, this being more like what I would describe as an interactive experience with a bit more gameplay than a "walking simulator".
The sense of adventure all comes from how the world is presented and the limited ways you interact with it and to achieve it so successfully just with that is no small feat.
Sure, I am now left just a bit disappointed that this wasn't more gameplay-oriented since I liked the foundations of this adventure so much. I'm sure I could have liked it better as it describes a lot more what I personally want, but that doesn't even slightly impact my recommendation for something that is moderately low-priced and even for the type of gamer I am,
worth the trip at least once.
(Side note, I strangely did not feel anything for any characters in the game and it's not like it doesn't work for me usually, I'm not a total psychopath. It worked in The Last of Us, Life Is Strange, Telltale's The Walking Dead, many JRPGs and story-focused games I played through many many years of gaming. I don't quite know if it's because I rely mostly on dialogues for emotions. But it just proves even more how good this game's art direction and exciting looking world are that they totally won me over on their own.)

I picked up this game yesterday, heading into the experience without any previous time playing Phr00t's other game(s), and this how I feel, concerning graphics:
While I understand that people are entitled to their opinions, I'm getting fairly frustrated with the back-and-forth I've seen on the forums (just in the past few days, since finding this title). While I am not at all new to the steam forums, the level of aggression about the graphics really perked my interest in trying this 'Crappy-looking polygonal game', if only to see for myself. After all, it gets old hearing people who believe they are speaking for the entire gaming community, when they are really only repeating the same comments on many indie discussion boards-> graphics suck (which may simply be to the artistic vision of the game), too expensive (Less than a pack of cigarettes in many states), Lots of bugs (let us not think on how many brand new AAA release titles are patched heavily on the first few days, and they have massive teams of coders, devs, and so on), etc.
Steeling myself against my own initial misgivings about the game, I hesitantly opened my wallet, and spent less than an hour's worth of minimum wage work, for a functional game. Think about that for a moment...Technically, you, as an individual, are paying the lone developer less than minimum wage for all his work- However many hours that was spent producing this game, and the individual pays seven whole smackers. Phr00t sure pulled one over on us, huh? ...Now then, moving on.
Stop the presses. The gameplay is actually really well done! While the older-style graphics may be a distraction, I was mainly interested in the deeper aspects of the game itself, and soon found myself overlooking any graphical shortcomings without complaint.
I will state this, rather flatly at that:
If you are looking for Modern Warfare type games, you're barking up the wrong tree. Those games exist already, so you may find your time better spent there.
Speaking only for myself, I find the retro graphics really endearing, reminding me of many games I played in the past as a kid (The original Starfox on the SNES, for example). They 'fit' the word well, and while I'd LOVE to see modern graphics on something like this, it is easily played and enjoyed as is. We'll see how things move along, and how the community develops.
TL;DR- The graphics are basic, yet functional. There is room for improvement, either by the dev or by the individual (See: Minecraft texture packs / High-Res packs). If you feel that you cannot get past the graphics, move on to another title. If you can still use the innate human ability for minimal imagination and suspension of disbelief, you might really find that you enjoy it.

UPDATE: They pretty much fixed most of the performance issues, so other than the price point there's no reason to not get this if you're into WO or AG racing altogether.
If you're like me and the Wipeout series ended with 3 (with the Ballistic NG DLC,) this is the game you've been waiting for all these years. First, DR is behind this again which is the No.1 thing I was really wanting since to me WO is just as much about the aesthetic as it is about the racing.
Second, the game itself feels like an evolution on the ideas they had back then. The gameplay is pretty much what you'd expect from wipeout and doesn't really favor so much "omg speed!!!1" like other AG games but instead focuses on tracks that have a lot more variety and are far more memorable as a result. Sure, you can also go really, really, fast but only if you're really, really good. Which, to me, feels that much more satisfying. The handling itself was an issue during the EA period but I feel like they managed to strike a balance now through the card system, so it feels pretty good as a result.
With that said, the game has some rough edges which I hope they smooth out over time such as the interface being unhelpful in explaining things like what tuning cards exactly do and which ones do you need in order to be competitive in certain tracks. Some for example favor a low AG setup so your craft is lower to the track surface, this depends on the way the elevation changes happen because you can bottom out if you're not careful. It would've been great if this was all explained in a tutorial or using the interface itself as I think it's an interesting and welcome change to the formula.
The most important thing they forget to tell you is that the mod card system is not about "upgrading" anything, it's about modifying performance to suit a track/race type. Hence no card is "better" than other, it depends on what you need them for and how they affect the race. In this regard the stupid stat bars on side make absolutely no sense and should be removed entirely. This is the reason many people are finding the AI so hard, they're not tuning their craft properly for the race but the game doesn't help you at all with this so it's trial and error until you find the right combination.
In terms of content the game right now is similar to WO3 as well, 8 tracks in all plus various standard modes. It's a little bare but if the developers keep adding content as they said they would this is not going to be a problem at all.
As for the music, this is something I was quite disappointed with as the tracks are quite unmemorable, but then again competing with the WO1,2,3 soundtracks is a nearly impossible task. Still, can't help but feel like they could've done much better.
All in all, for 20 euros it's a little steep for the amount of content at the moment, but this will probably be a different story later down the line.

On paper this game should be great. Its another AG racer in crazy technocity race tracks, with staff/designers from previous successful racers, a giant demand from kickstarter and Early Access, with online multiplayer and customisable ships to boot. What could go wrong?
Simply, this is not ready for release yet. The earlier versions we're better too, or at least they didn't have as MANY problems, so I'm not too sure what happened here.
The first problem you will encounter is a unrelentingly huge FPS drop during all gameplay. It won't matter what you change your settings to - minimum and epic both get between 15 to 25 FPS. This is not a hardware problem, and catagorically ruins the entire game right off the bat. Its the main problem that needs fixing, because "What's the most important part of any game? Well, being able to ♥♥♥♥ing play it".
Secondly, the weapons and powerups feel weak. I'm not sure if they have any effect on your opposition at all to be honest.
Thirdly, don't use steering assist. It will become impossible to maintain your momentum during slightly thinner parts of the track as the assist kicks in to slow you down. Dumb, useless feature.
Fourth,  the AI is pretty brutal to start out with. The lowest class should be easy R8. This is not easy.
Fifth, there is ♥♥♥♥ing NO INSTRUCTION ANYWHERE. No infomation on powerups, no tutorial mode, nothing. Dumb.
Lastly the game, kinda in general, is unfinished. There needs to be some serious quality control here. If you change your settings to minimum at the menu screen, you can barely read the menu text afterwards - that's such a simple thing that has been overlooked. It also lacks the high-speed feel of a decent AG racer, and as mentioned before the weapons and powerups suck♥♥♥♥♥
It does have some positive points - the aesthics of the game are 10/10, the tracks are fairly decent to race with no major problems (other than they lack loops and jumps, and there is nothing stand out about any of them), and the music for the game is decent if a little low energy for a high speed game.
Many features are still missing (such as cockpit view, which has vanished now?), and as it stands the game is a shell of what it wants to be. This COULD be a great game - but its just not there yet.
There's a console release planned, so hopefully we are going to see some patches fix some of these problems. But terrible launches do nothing for your game and company's reputation, and shouldn't be the standard for games released. I wish patching things was not seen as a good thing in industry, it SHOULD mean you ♥♥♥♥ed up and have to fix it. But what do we know right? We're only the ones who want it to be good after all.

Pros:
Best large open world
Good graphics for 2013
Cons:
Loading times. I have a fast SSD and an unlocked 5th gen i5. Want to hop in and play with your friends? Click on GTA V. A minute or two later, you can choose GTA V or online. Choosing singleplayer will take a minute or two to load. Choosing multiplayer will take a couple minutes as it loads the singleplayer anyway, then a couple more as it loads you into a multiplayer session. Then add a couple more to join your friends' private session. Almost ten minutes to get into a server, easily. At least now you can play GTA. Unless...
Stability issues occur. The game crashes consistently with no reason on my PC and my friend's machine. Which wouldn't be so bad if I didn't have to wait for so long to play.
But when it's working, you get to explore the wonderful world of Los Santos. Unfortunately, every way of interacting with said world is infuriatingly bad.
Player movement on foot: unusable, will get you killed frequently due to your character running into gunfire or off a cliff 20 feet away, despite you instructing them to go elsewhere.
Cameras: default to an angle which is far too low. If you move your mouse to fix them, they auto reset every 2 seconds anyway, even if this is turned off in settings.
Flying: autocenters controls, even when disabled in settings. Do you like scrolling your mouse all the way forwards across your desk, picking it up, and doing it again and agin, just to fly a helicopter in a straight line? Buy this game!
Driving: surprisingly good mechanics actually. Unfortunately, PC players can't use a wheel... so you can only use the brute force of arrow keys. Oh well. The driving mechanics have issues- hit curbs to gain speed, pedestrians interfering in races, etc, but nothing compares to arrow keys.
User Interface: Again, terrible. A user interface designed for consoles hasn't even been changed for PC. Not going into detail. If you play you'll see what I mean. Add to this the game's tendency to remove clicks, or only count a map vote/setting change/etc after 3+ clicks, or the left/right selectors tendency to not respond properly after a change in the width of the content.
Shooting mechanics: Not so much that they are bad, it's that they're nonexistent. Recoil hardly matters. All automatic weapons feel inaccurate and put far too much luck into already chaotic conflict. The AP pistol and heavy sniper make all other weapons irrelevant anyway(except explosives).
And then finally, we have Rockstar's updates.
This game(which is already expensive 4 years after release) is, even after you buy in, essentially a grind or pay2win game. like a free2play title. Rockstar prefers to put out the newest supercars(that take several hours of grinding to get just one of) instead of making actual content. But that's not too bad. More concerning are the armored cars, APCs, etc that completely change the combat and add a huge tax to GTA combat. Either have 8+ million for the gunrunning DLC content, and more for the included APC and rocket bike and their ilk, or die to those who do. Public GTA combat has been completely ruined by this cash grab update.
This is the only game I've ever regretted buying.

I've had this since it was first released to the "Test Pilot" crowd way back in the day, and it's amazing to see how far its progressed!

First thing I noticed: the AI is incredibly brutal, and I really have to work for wins, even in the lowest class! Once you get a bit of money from some wins, it does become a bit easier.
Second thing I noticed is that it's lacking any kind of instruction beyond what's listed on the store page. I have a feeling this will be fixed eventually, but you'll have to explore your options and make some guess work! As someone who's used to old DOS games this felt like a major throwback since older games tended to do this.
And finally: It's fun! The craft handle incredibly well and certainly feel like they have some weight behind them. Any time I crashed I didn't feel that it was unfair, and it was instead a lack of my own skills. The AI is indeed brutal, but also pretty stupid when it comes to dealing with human interaction. Sneak right behind them and they'll just keep racing, letting you focus on taking them out one by one (which is actually a little fun). Dodging is something they don't do.
It feels a bit lightweight right now but given R8s hardcore dedication to driving this through I know they'll be expanding upon it in short order! Even in its current state it's a blast to play and reminds me of the old Wipeout days of the PS1 era.

No matter what I do, I cannot maintain a steady 60 frames per second. SE claims that this is by design, and that at the "high" preset, meeting the reccomended specs, you should be able to maintain an average 60fps at 1080p. Turning off contact shadows and volumetric lighting does not provide a big enough performance boost to hit that steady 60. The result is a stuttery experience.
Very dissapointing, especially given the incredible performance of its predecessor, and the performance of games  like DOOM and Battlefield 1, which look, in my opinion, far better than what is on show here.

I've given it almost 2 months now, but I feel like the performance issues will not be addressed. If you have not yet played human revolution, definitely grab that one, it's the better experience and far cheaper.
