I feel like I should qualify this review by first stating that I'm a massive,
fanboy of Human Revolution. I recognize that that game has some flaws but the ambiance is second to none, the stealth gameplay is satisfying, and the way the plot drives you forward to its conclusion makes you loathe to put it down. It's one of the few games in which I've gotten 100% of its Steam achievements. Deus Ex Human Revolution is one of the best games of the 2010s in my own humble opinion.
This game just fails to live up to pretty much every level set by the previous game.
The gameplay is returned more or less unchanged from the first game. The only real difference is that Jensen is given several new tools to use, justified by some cheesy in-plot explanation as someone having altered his augmentations while he was comatose after the first game. The problem here is that not enough has changed from the first game. And while that doesn't seem like much of a problem given how much I enjoyed Human Revolution, it's starting to feel quite dated and lacks any further development over the past 5 years.
I'll approach this mostly from a stealth angle since that's how I play the game.
The most glaring issue here is that there's a core problem with the energy system that regulates your use of augments. Jensen has some awesome tools to use to maneuver around the environment undetected, but the problem is how overpowered these tools are. To solve the issue of being an absolute god, the devs chose to reign these in by using the same battery meter from the first, which is replenished by consumables when it gets low. This is a problem simply because you end up playing the game without ever using them, instead choosing to save them for when you really need them. Now that's not a problem by itself, but it is when you realize you're sneaking through entire areas trial-and-error and never actually using the majority of your augmentations. This was a weakness in Human Revolution, and it was greatly disappointing not to see it rectified in this game. There
to be a better way to balance these powers than resorting to consumables. Perhaps a smaller battery meter that recharges more slowly? The battery meter refueled by consumables feels archaic and clumsy in a game that features otherwise interesting stealth puzzles to overcome.
And on top of that, the new augments present aren't actually all that useful. Aside from remote hacking I never used any of them, instead relying on the vanilla mods from Human Revolution. This could have been dealt with by having a new playable character, or a second one like the route Dishonored 2 went. Anything would have been more interesting than the same exact skillset from Human Revolution with the addition of a half-dozen augmentations that aren't even particularly useful. The fact that Jensen is back reeks of the studio's unwillingness to take a risk, or perhaps it was dictated to them by their publisher that coverboy Adam Jensen needed to be present in the game. I suppose we'll never know. But a new protagonist or at least
kind of change to keep things fresh would have added a lot more flavor to the now-stale gameplay present here.
Ambiance was something that Human Revolution did amazingly well. There were complaints about the gold filter but I really thought it added to the game's ambiance and I never had a problem with it. On top of that, the Michael McCann's absolutely mindblowing score changed the entire feel of the game and was arguably the single best part of it. Mankind Divided instead goes for a more realistic feel, and the score, while at times comes close to the high bar set in Human Revolution, is far more inconsistent and settles for more subtle, less noticeable score. I didn't feel nearly as blown away by the sense that I was in a different world in Mankind Divided that I did when I played through Human Revolution, and for me that was a real disappointment.
Don't get me wrong; the world in Mankind Divided is good. Very good, in fact. The environmental design and level design is the only aspect of this game aside from its graphical prowess that is clearly better than Human Revolution. But I really missed the blatant, heavyhandedness of Human Revolution's ambiance in this title. In going for more realism they lost some of the weight of Human Revolution's atmosphere. It's now less cyberpunk-comic-book, more hard-science-fiction-thriller. I suppose it depends on what you prefer, but I was disappointed. I'm typically more a fan of subtlety, but I loved the chronically overdone atmosphere that Human Revolution featured.
Lastly, and perhaps most glaringly: The plotting of this game is a cruel joke. It starts off with a bang then slows to a crawl, with hours of exposition and environmental narrative introducing plot points that are barely touched upon later, if even ever mentioned again at all. There are several interesting threads kicked along only to be left completely unresolved while we instead focus on investigating a terrorist bombing. Jensen's mods, the group he's working for, etc. are all left unresolved in an egregious example of sequel baiting. Finishing this game is wholly unsatisfying; I was left completely undriven by the frankly boring plot, and although the level design is great, the dated gameplay itself does nowhere near enough to carry the game on its own. As you can see from my achievements, I got right up to the end and never even finished the game. The side quests were far, far more compelling than the main plot. And once I was done with them I felt like I was grinding out the rest of the game until I decided just to stop and move on to something I'd actually enjoy.
All of these flaws might be passable if only to experience what this game does well: Interesting, well crafted environments, excellent level design, great side quest writing, solid voice acting. But this game, unfortunately, runs like absolute garbage.
I have zero issues running most games in 1440p at 60 fps, however this title barely broke 40 fps in most places with low to medium settings. Turning off SLI actually
my framerate by 5 fps or so. Not a great sign. Even after turning off SLI and running it on my 1080p monitor I still experienced frame drops to around 50 fps on medium settings. This is simply unacceptable, and had I known the majority of the game ran like this then I'd have refunded it within 2 hours. But, interestingly enough, the entire first area runs quite well and it's only once you get to Prague that the problems start.
Interesting how games are shipping with more polished early areas ever since Valve adopted its refund policy. Quite interesting. And infuriating.
There are also several graphical and physics bugs present, and the game didn't even ship with DX12 (though it was later patched in and is now active). This is a title that clearly needed a few more months of polish, but with Square Enix's dumpster-tier publisher reputation it's not a surprise that it was forced out early. MegaTagmenion Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies. A new spin-off game of the Neptunia franchise, based on the same system as Neptunia U and of course develloped by the same team. Just like Noire got her own game, this one has Blanc as a main character, even though Neptune is present throughout the entire game. When will a Vert-only game come out?
But let's now evaluate the game.
The gameplay :
If you have played Nep U and got the mechanics right, it will not be hard to play MegaTagmension, as it is also a Hack-N-Slash. Although, a few changes are visible. The commands are a little bit different, and if you play with a keyboard you might wanna go through the settings to re-assignate some keys. Goodbye to the torn-off duds caused by the monsters, and goodbye to the Nepbull released by monsters. Now, if you wanna heal during battle, you have to buy items and equip them. New ennemies, and a new way to improve your characters using "Ability points" that you gain through leveling. No medals anymore, but instead treasure pieces (in fact consoles) that let you unlock new outfits. You can also by accessories and customize your characters, this can be helpful later. Overall, an easy-to-understand system. Also, if you're used to grinding in the Neptunia games, try not to grind too much. A lvl 70 character won't help you fight the last boss in an epic battle, as you need to be around lvl 40 to beat it. You don't want to kill it too easily.
The Story :
As I said earlier, this game's main protag is Blanc, our Justice goddess (No, Blanc, that was a praise, put that hammer down! ). Our 8 Gamindustri rulers (Yes, I put the Candidates as rulers) have enrolled in Gamicademy, a school situated on an island in the center of Gamindustri, so that anybody from any country can join. They have joined this school to understand humans better and help their people. But when they hear that the academy is gonna close because of a lack of students, Neptune don't hesitate to do anything she can to save it and bring more students. The story itself is pretty entertaining, our 4th-wall breaks are still here and some scenes are an hommage to the community. The time completion may depend on your will to end the game fast or not. For me, it took 8 hours, and I haven't "fully" completed the game as there are some scenes that can only be unlocked via certain conditions (But in-game hints can help you unlock them). A whole lot of characters from the different games, as well as a new character brought by the constant wish of the Devs to put themselves in the game : Tamsoft. The same way IF and Compa represents Idea Factory and Compile Heart (And don't forget our dungeon helper Stella, representing FelliStella), Tamsoft represents... Well, Tamsoft, they didn't bother trying to change the name, which is not completely a bad thing. She's a rather strong character and can become useful in some fights. (She even have a transformation).
The Multiplayer :
Remember earlier, when I told you about customizing your characters? Well, it is mainly because there's a brand-new multiplayer mode, allowing you to take on quests with up to 3 other people. The quests aren't related to the main game, and the Multiplayer has in fact it's own story, and can take some time to complete. You will even be able to play directly with the HDD form of a character, while another player uses it's normal form. (It happened to me, I was playing as Purple Heart while somebody else was playing as Neptune, and we cleared bosses with an excessive amount of Neptune Break). You can choose wether to use a save from the Story mode, keeping your lvls, or you can start with a brand-new save only for Multiplayer and work your way from lvl 1 to lvl 99.
Issues :
I have only noticed a few issues :
-Whenever I start the game, I have to wait 5-10 minutes before reaching the main menu. I suspect this is because I don't have the perfect configuration.
-Sometimes, in multiplayer, people might try to join while you're doing a quest, which may results in endlees loops of : <Player> has joined, <Player> has left, <Player> has joined, <Player> has left, etc...
So this concludes my review of this game. A rather good spin-off that doesn't deviate from the franchise, a good story, a good gameplay and very few issues. For me, I give this game a 9.5/10

I would love to recommend this because I am a big fan of the franchise, but unfortunately I cannot do that, not for the full price at least.
MegaTagmension is a musou style game (like Dynasty Warriors) while the promise and potential is good, the problem is that the whole game consists of very short scenes in which you fight just 1 pack of monsters. The most gameplay you will get in a row is about 3 minutes.  This is NOT a game in which you traverse large levels with monster packs, bosses, complete objectives etc. You load the scene, kill 20 mobs, and that's it. I haven't completed it yet, but the whole thing can probably be completed in about 3-4 hours tops. Of course there is some replayability thanks to leveling, lily ranks, treasures gathering and such.
Most of the time is spent in menus and reading dialogue cutscenes, which are funny and interesting as always in the Neptunia games, but when you have to spend 5 minutes reading dialogues to get 2 minutes of action it kind of kills the fun.
If you are a hardcore Neptunia fan, it will still be fun of course. Though I would suggest waiting for a sale. This game just isn't worth 30€.

Update 1:
Expect to reach 'end game' at some point without unlocking everything as the last few chapters with Pamu and few others are extremely grindy as you have to wait days/weeks for your hobbies to level up unless you want to pay to buy gems.
Update 2 (23 Aug 2016):
Now at Hobby level 46 going to 47 will take 26 days, this is with 16x multiplier bought with gems and 105x prestige. In other words its the end of the road for players that don't want to pay for more gems, so this kind of makes it pay-to-play rather then free-to-play which is unfortunate.
The game in its current state v0.44 has serious issues when it comes to late game progression and the time it takes to level up is badly balanced for a truly free-to-play model.
Update 3 (21 Oct 2016):  [Out of Early Access]
The overall game balance has improved a lot.
The most you will need to spend to be able to nicely and speedily progress is $5 to $10 which is perfectly fine for the ammount of entertainment the game provides.
You can still progress without paying anything, but it will take longer.

Everything by Spiderweb software is guaranteed (By me) to be a wonderful RPG experience.  The graphics are terrible (The first Geneforge game came out in 2002), but looking past them you will find an engrossing story, awesome turn-based strategic gameplay, and a ton of endings and optional locations along the way.  My favorite series by Spiderweb is Geneforge, but all of their games are worth checking out.
Sidenote: There is a HUGE deal on steam, which allows you to get all 5 Geneforge games in a bundle for only $20.  Seriously, you are doing yourself a favor by purchasing these.

I actually played this game ages ago around the time a demo was released for Geneforge 2 I think?
Anyway I do recommend this game, but only to people who are into turn based strategy style rpg combat. The game does have some things to be 'desired', one of them being companions/creations who can genuinely level and a better reason to keep around old ones.
This game has a sort of 'old style' charm to it with simple RPG leveling, stats to put points into and different classes to play. Graphics aren't amazing, but if you really want (like I did) you can go edit them a bit (not sure if you can do this with the steam version ) (I turned my shaper into a hot elf chick cuz I can).
The gameplay is solid, though it takes a bit to get used to the 'looting' system where you open the grab menu and you look at all the items around you or click containers to view what's inside. Stats and stat paths can determine if you are skilled enough to go certain ways and it's entierly possible to get through the game without REALLY fighting. I played a mixed route and tried my best to see it all and found it difficult because I wasn't specialized, but it was ok in the end since I reached a point where I felt I was 'thinking' about the combat, but also doing quite well by using some items correctly and also by positioned right, etc.
One of the best reasons to play the game though is the rich story, lore and plot. The game has 'canisters' that can enhance you throughout the game and although I don't want to ruin anything, I will just say that using them can affect the ending. So can a LOT of the actions performed. I think there is anywhere from 3 to 20ish different endings, only around 4 of which I really saw, 1 being death cuz duh it happens.
Summed up, solid game, old world charm, slow paced, good story. Definitely recommended.

Even after all of these years, Geneforge 1 is still a great RPG and worthy of being played by anyone who wants a very good story and multiple endings that change based on your actions.
If you like exploring to find every nook and cranny, and if you like learning about the game's history by talking to NPCs and reading books, and if you like pondering moral and ethical questions then check out all of Spiderweb Software's games.

I know what you're asking, is it like the Army Men games?
Well, not 100% quite. It is a good game, however. It's like the Army Men series, but a bit faster paced. There is no single player, there is no bots, and there isn't weapon pick ups or drops or the likes. You start out with all the weapons and they're poorly balanced.
The shotgun really out shines the main rifle, or all the weapons really. The flame thrower is a tad underwhelming and I find the reach is dreadful making it the worse weapon in the game. This balance can really ruin the game for some players. I also find the rocket launcher a bit too powerful as well, but it isn't like you have a whole lot of shots with it, so it isn't a strong complaint from me.
Though you will not get 5v5 games often, I did just finish a 3v3 game. I do not understand how this game got so many negative reviews for being dead when there is plenty of games being hosted occupied by players. It's not like it was designed for 32v32, you'll get a full game or near full game if you try.
The biggest complaint I have is level variety. You have a handful of levels that have, set in stone, only one mode of play. This means you can only play one level for capture the flag, only one level for free for all deathmatch, only one level for team death match, etc. The question is... why? Not only is it lacking levels, but it's lacking levels for game modes. It could easily implement the majority of modes on all the maps, but that isn't the case.
Ultimately, this is a fine game if you can get it on the cheap. It has great potential and I hope the developer can take advantage of it. It really could make a good Army Men series tribute, or reincarnation really.

This is the game I've been waiting to play, and I never even realized it until I started playing. Procedural generation... with constant renewal. Yeah, that's right, enemies keep respawning, as do boxes and missions and pretty much everything, which means there's always more stuff to do, even in the earlier portions of the game.
You can craft weapons and gear. You can build the landscape (and not just in cubic meter blocks!). You can kill robots, run missions, fly ships. Do whatever. It's cool. Turning your character into a tank is as easy as going stealth assassin. My point is, if this game bores you, it's probably because of the way you're playing.
Some have commented on the learning curve. Honestly, I'm not seeing it as that bad at all. Difficulty increases the further you leave the starting base, and every quest you complete gives you skill points. If "out there" seems too hard, just run some more lower-level quests until you're as strong as you need to be.
It doesn't have the visual polish of games like Borderlands or Skyrim, but it's got a nice pre-N64 charm regardless. And besides, it's $10 for a game made by one guy. For everything you get here, complaining about the graphics is just kind of greedy.

I have been playing GTA for a long time, and an full-blown MMO capability is something I was waiting for almost just as long. I love the concept of being able to build an empire in LA. The game requires one of two things though; heavy PVP focus or consistant "squading" as it were. I will say this though, the online portion is one hell of a grind, and it will take you a while to build the empire. However, Rome was not built in a day. So why should the Roman empire? I love that Rockstar constantly comes out with new updates to keep the game feeling fresh, but I also feel like they should work on bettering what is already present. Which leads me to the cons below.
The main issues I have are the repetativeness of the jobs, and the people online who are too lazy to actually put effort into the game so they mod. It does not matter how many updates come out, the jobs/races/whatever they entail will get boring quickly. To that end, I feel like they should add more contact jobs as well as normal races.
As far as the modders go...scum of the earth. There is no limit to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t they do; from placing impossible bounties that do not exist (such as 500000, that no one can claim but them), to dropping cars on people out of no where, to auto-ejecting people from helicopers or planes, to dropping exploded airplanes or dead bodies that look like a person's character with clown hair, to spawning money on people (that will get removed next time the game is patched), or RPGs that do more damage than they are supposed to. The list goes on.
In closing I feel that if they update/add new jobs, and keep working on weeding out the modders, and undoing the damage done by them, the game will only get better. It's not supposed to be easy to rack up millions of dollars while paying for assets, but you don't live in your house for free, and the company you work for has to pay to keep it running and you working.
Notes
1: As far as the complaints about Shark Card prices...here's an idea; how about you stop complaining about them? The shark cards are there for people who -are- too lazy to play the game. Of course they are going to be pricey, your not supposed to rely on them to get ahead in the game. You're supposed to friggin' play it. If you cannot handle the grind, stop playing.
2: If you do mod or grief I hope your account gets found out and banned. You ruin the game for people who want to go into public lobbies for PVP and to move supplies. It is one thing to fairly take out an enemy and claim the spoils, it's another thing to cheat to do so or keep targeting 1 player or a group of players when the lobby is full of others.
3: Lastly, I am hopping for a Gunrunning II, or a Cops and Robbers update. I think the latter would add a perspective to the game most people overlook. A fun perspective at that.

Finished this last night and I really enjoyed it.
It works for me on so many levels:
- Immersive near-future cyberpunk world, not so different from our own world when it comes down to it
- A fun interactive environment where you can pick up trash cans and boxes and throw them at random civilians (why not?)
- There are tons of hidden rooms, paths and items all over the game. It's fun to go exploring!
- Different ways of approaching each enemy or mission.  Lethal or non-lethal variety of weapons, or avoid combat altogether, or a combination of them, like what I did.
- Character progression happens often enough and is impactful enough to keep the character interesting
- Different ways to build your character - go loud or go quiet, adds replay value
- Branching story choices adds replay value
- Best-looking Deus Ex yet, ran at near 60 fps for me most of the time, there was room to turn up the settings if I were to get a high-end PC.
- Soundtrack is awesome, like the last game.  It's one I will continue to listen to outside of playing the game.
I think the biggest beef some folks have with this game is that it's really just a middle chapter for the series.  I think the story is fine and thoroughly enjoyable, in fact.  Some of the game's stories get resolved if you choose to do most of the side quests, but the overall story is not resolved.  I think it's okay, because I will be looking forward to whatever the next chapter has in store for us.
There was plenty of good fun (while feeling cool doing it) in this game, and I wholeheartedly recommend it.  Play it!

I feel this game falls shy of the mark in too many ways to make it worth playing, and after about 45 minutes of it, I don't really feel like picking it up ever again.
It is somewhat reminiscent of Wipeout and has an aesthetic resembling the original - unfortunately this is just about the only thing it has going for it and I feel that in attempting to copy Wipeout too closely it honestly just feels like a low budget amateur knock-off and fails to pull out the stops.
The initial user experience for me was not good - the user interfaces for this game are utterly appalling and need to be heavily redesigned; the main menu presents you with a tiny scroll-able list widget at the bottom of the screen, almost as if the designer intended for you to stare at the rendered background more than actually navigate the menus - this is a common theme across the UI. For example, when selecting a ship to compete in an event, you get a tiny 3d model of it sat in the center of the screen occupying about 15-20% of the screen premium, and a name underneath it. The rest of this space is completely empty. I can apparently scroll up and down through 3/4 'loadouts' though this is not made very clear - the 3d model for each loadout is identical and there's no description of what they actually are - you have to hold down a button on the controller to pop up a little widget that also appears in the middle of the screen occupying no more than about 20% of the screen space. Why this couldn't just be on the same screen, as well as a list of loadouts is beyond me. Generally speaking, the interfaces are unintuitive and often hard to read - for the love of God, please hire a UX designer to make sensible interfaces and overhaul this mess.
The game has no tutorial or introduction whatsoever - after diving into the first track on the first event, I found myself needing to look up the control scheme. I do have some very real questions about the physical anatomy of the person(s) responsible for the default control scheme, as it makes no sense whatsoever. Steering is the left analogue stick, throttle is on A, air brakes are on the left / right triggers respectively, and there are offensive / defensive powerups (tied to your loadout) on your shoulder buttons, and a boost ability on X - this all seems good so far, except that this is a racing game in 2017 and by putting the throttle on the A button I don't have real control over it - when there are perfectly good triggers that are instead occupied by air breaks that also do not seem to be pressure sensitive. Then there are things like pitching the nose upwards and downwards; For some reason pitching downwards is controlled by clicking in the left analogue stick, but pitching upwards is up on the d-pad? I'm not entirely sure how that's physically supposed to work without me removing my thumb from steering, or otherwise growing a second smaller thumb to help out.
Racing itself is okay-ish - the game is acceptable but it has a distinct lack of finesse and never really feels like it comes together. The handling and physics on the vehicle is largely functional but it doesn't feel particularly great. I did at one point get rammed from behind, which catapulted me through the scenery and killed me instantly - I'm not really sure what that's about. The loadout options seem to be honestly quite dull and uninspired (I played two loadouts, one with a machine gun and a mine, and another with a rocket attack and a shield). The offensive weapons seemed to be largely useless and although I used the defensive options occasionally, I'm not actually sure there was any point. There is of course also a boost mechanic that does work quite well - but I have literally no idea how it works or what charges it up, I'm not sure there's any on-screen indicator of how charged you are at all (the HUD is not fantastic and hard to read when concentrating on the track - you can't glance at it because it kind of blends in).
The three tracks that I tried had decent length, but ultimately they were quite boring; the first two had very little in the way of identifiable set pieces or scenery, making it quite difficult to become familiar with the circuit. The first two were very grey which did not help, though the third was significantly better and had smatterings of colour. I feel the biggest issue is the frequency of boost pads and item pickups - they are vomited all over the courses with little or no care regarding their placement - there are so many of them that it's practically impossible *not* to hit them, and you are pretty much constantly carrying a weapon (in the case of the machine gun, you often literally cannot fire it fast enough before replenishing it's ammo).
What killed it for me though is that when racing, the game helpfully reminded me that there was an online session available at intervals of around 30-45 seconds by flashing up a message box on the right hand side of the screen. I hope there is an option to disable this buried in the settings menu somewhere, but at this point I'd honestly given up and lost interest.
As it transpires, when looking for this game on the web store, there is actually a demo you can download, but I didn't see this before purchasing. Searching for it just brings me back to this store page - I'm not sure why I can't see it but can find it in search listings.
There is a lot of potential in this game, but it needs a lot more time in the oven. It needs polish applied to it's core game mechanics, attention paid to the user experience, and reworking of the circuits to tighten them up, make them memorable and give them identity. I'm a big fan of the genre (and Wipeout), but at this point in time I just can't recommend the game even if the price is right. I would presently recommend Redout instead. Nevertheless, I'll keep my eye on the game and hope it gets the updates it's sorely needing, and maybe I'll revisit it (and this review) at that time.

Yes, I only made some races yet. This is not an in-depth review and more my first impression, so I keep it short:
1. Graphics: Awesome! you get a wonderful feeling about speed. For me, it submits the best immersion of the speed I experienced so far (Motion Blur ON / Camera Shake ON / Everything on EPIC).
2. Sounds: Well, the soundtrack is nothing special. WipeOut was much better at this. But for me its ok. Engine sound could be better. Sounds sometimes like a car. But again - not a major drawback for me as I do not concetrate so much on audio.
3. Gameplay: Some tracks are less wide as in WipeOut, so you need to practice more and I learned that customization of your craft is the key to success. So in my opinion its not the gamekiller as some others stated here.  What I am missing is some in-game documentation for e.g. in the garage and customizable controls (buts thats maybe due to the EA state). I played with an XBox Controller which works very well.
So I think the game has the potential to be a great WipeOut successor. I am looking forward to the multiplayer part. I paid 19.99€ and its fine for the current state of the product. With more content, a good multiplayer part and some tuning I think even a full price  of 40€ would be justified.

Interesting that so many people have lags :-( But not everybody seems affected. I have GTX970 and there are no lags. Everything is smooth and fast.

This game has come a long way. I bought it almost a year ago and found it barely playable. I fired it up again last week and found myself completely absorbed by the gameplay. I'm so glad to know the single-player campaign will finally be available this week. Can't wait to dig in to it.
Comparison to Redout
In my opinion, this game feels more like Wipeout than Redout does. I enjoyed Redout, but the crafts felt a little light and lacking in momentum. The Formula Fusion crafts feel weightier and more 'real' to me, which is something I appreciate. Also, since Redout went the VR route, the graphics, while cool and stylish, are a bit cartoonish for my taste. Formula Fusion presents more realism in the graphics department as well.
So if a great-looking, great-feeling Wipeout-style game is what you're looking for, then I recommend you buy Formula Fusion.

Thought I'd go through and update this review after suffering through the game a little more, the verdict? pretty much the same as before.
The big problem the game suffers from is that it claims to be a spiritual successor for a game that it is nothing alike. That game is Wipeout, and honestly if you have acess to a PS4 just get that, it's by far the better game.
This game is in a wierd place, the physics feel gross, the weapons are bad, and the customisation for the weapons actually makes the game weaker for it. Speaking of the weapons, unlike most combat racers instead of picking up a random or procedurally calculated weapon from a pool, you simply have two slots that you attach weapons or "utilities" to in the garage. The pickup pads on the track simply enable a use of your preset weapon/utility. These are customisable as I mentioned before by adding "traits" however because the game uses traits instead of preset weapons it means they are all nerfed to make the traits relevant. Which is bad because it makes the combat utterly boring.
There is craft performance customisation, again along the boring lines of pick a few cards here to slightly alter your craft. And then there's ever so slight visual customisation which is just pick some colours and skins... yaaaaay....
Then pretty much everything is locked in the singleplayer right away for the sakes of "progression" I mean, when literally 90% of the game is locked behind forced progression it's pretty easy to see there is no content to be had here. It's also a very bad first impression when you cannot experience a significant chunk of the game because it is locked away at the start.
On top of all that I personally find having the camera fixed to the track while the craft floats about all over the screen to be quite uncomfortable and unnatural of a racing game and there are no options to change it. What ever happened to a simple chase cam?
I'm gonna be plain here, the game feels like a bad indie, it feels unpolished, incomplete, and just plain bad design. Maybe I just had my hopes up because of what the game claimed to be, something it never lived up to. As I mentioned before if you have access to a PS4 just get Wipeout Omega. If not, you may be interested in Grip, the spiritual successor to Rollcage, a game similar to Wipeout, it's on Steam and it's actually very good, take a look if you haven't already.

Brawlhalla is a 2D Platform Fighter.
Personal Reveiw: I personally think this game is great for anyone intrested in indie games to try out! it doesn't require anything demanding to play and it can bring hours of fun for you and your friends.
Details: The game has a unique system of giving out 6 Characters to use and test out each week, This feature is great for finding out what characters you will might to use and when you rack up enough coins (Free In-game Currency) You can buy the legends you like. As of the time i am texting this reveiw there are 4 Diffrent legend prices: Low (2,300 Coins) , Medium (3,900 Coins) , High (5,400 Coins) and New Legend Price (7,200 Coins). Earnng coins in the game is easy once you get used to playing the game and getting knock-outs. Each legend has their own profile/background story, skill set, Weapon set and abilities! Each map is kind of simple but in a way has its own feel to it aswell. The game modes are standard (Score wise or Limited lives) and then they have fun party game modes (Ex. Bombsketball).
DLC and Supporting Devs: The Devs have stated that they have no plans on making Brawlhalla paid to play, pay to win ect., All money spent is to support the developers and get cosmetics ingame. DLC such as the All legends pack are simply just a quick way for someone who doesnt get much time to play games to get a all character to play as (Or for lazy people too). however those characters are easily unlockable. The Valhalla ($15) Pack is simply cosmetics and a support tag for players and the collectors pack ($100) is simply a huge donation to the developers and some more exclusive items that are purely cosmetic!

Made a werewolf guy (supernatural DLC) who's hot-headed, fearless, and cocky, and a vampire woman who is composed, proper, and a neat-freak live in a house together. Naturally, they clash at first: she can't stand how he leaves his dishes everywhere and runs around on all fours sometimes, while he finds her stuck up and pretentious. But over time, they start chatting more and realizing how much they have in common.
Their friendship hits a rough patch at the full moon, when he transforms and ruins a bunch of furniture, and she goes a little nuts and attacks him (apparently there's an action called a "lunatic slap" during the full moon that she did on her own). But they bond over fighting a robber together and playing lots of hopscotch, and soon their bond is stronger than ever. It pretty quickly moves to "Romantic Interest," and all of a sudden they are flirting and kissing all the time.
After a few in-game days of this, it's time for them to "woohoo" for the first time. He gives her a big dip kiss, and they go to the bed with swelling music and falling rose petals. Right as I'm wondering how birth control works in this game, since I'm not ready to raise a hybrid werewolf-vampire baby, she falls out of the bed and dies. The grim reaper shows up and takes her ghost away as I stare at my computer in shock. Apparently she died of thirst, unwilling to feed from him and not wanting to interrupt the romance to go drink.
Now he's walking around the house grieving, surrounded by walls covered in all the paintings she made. He tries desperately to resurrects her while her ghost is still haunting the place, but can't find the necessary ingredients to make the potion he needs in time. He finally moves on when he finds a puppy at the animal shelter that needs a home, and starts forming a warm friendship with the zombie next door.
8/10 would play out a young adult paranormal romance novel again if it weren't so incredibly slow and if each DLC wasn't ridiculously expensive.

Grand Theft Auto: V is a video-game triumph. The game is beyond insanly detailed and the Developers, Rockstar Games, (With the Rockstar North Devision based in Edinbrough, Scotland,) spent $3,000,000,000 on the game's making and it's clear why when you play.
Grand Theft Auto: V features 2 "games" - Grand Theft Auto V and Grand Theft Auto: Online.
We will speak about Grand Theft Auto V first.
Grand Theft Auto: V is mostly a story-based games with ~80 missions which takes alot of hours to go through - all missions make sense, good quallity and thought went into them. The harder missions are harder, the smaller missions are even easier - I think for someone who has played other games on the PC Platform and buys it on here, your first playthrough of the Story will probally be the best as you don't know whats coming and you to learn - the game teaches you so niceley. I won't brake any spoilers but it's worth playing through the Story again as it makes sense even more. Words can not describe the simple detail from the map of San Adreas (Calafornia,) and Los Santos (Los Angleas) and the surrounding areas. I mean, it really is amazing.
Grand Theft Auto: Online is based in the same Universe ~9 months before the events of the main story take place. After completing the Story, Grand Theft Auto: Online is endless. Rockstar have been providing free DLCs adding new Content since the Xbox 360 and Playstation 3 launch in October 2013. Since then all DLCs have continued to be free. Recently in the past year Rockstar have added "CEO" "VIP" & "Motorcycle Clubs" which are effictivly businesses which you can use to make money apart from doing the normal Jobs/Missions given to you on your Phone. This adds another aspect to GTA:O of which I adore, being that you need to work to grow your empire, (Being the forementioned VIP, CEO or MC businesses.) I work everyday to be able to get that true dream of everything you ever wanted. I love it to bits - whilst ofcourse meeting other players in the process and having fun.
Some downsides of GTA:O are however that there is a mild scripter-problem but Rockstar have often ban-waves and some items now cost a fair bit of money and they really urge you to buy the Micro-Transactions - Shark Cards - HOWEVER - this can be avoided by working hard enough. A Work/School week's off of GTA:O can get you a good business going with a solid income.
Both Grand Theft Auto modes have a sandbox feel, so you can do anything you ever want, ever, in the game. This is pretty much what makes GTA, GTA. Fancy robbing a bank, mowing down people, shooting up in a store and seeing how
long you last? Yeah - do it! Nothing's holding you back - it's the perfect chaos simulation!
If you haven't got Grand Theft Auto: V yet and your hardware can run it, you're missing out. It is a MUST BUY in my books!
*About the 3rd party comments: I would plead everyone to change their reviews back to positive or right a serious one in their opinion. What's all this about?
Rockstar Games' parent company, Take-2 Interactive banned "modding" (Being able to change the game,) in Grand Theft Auto - this caused an outroar in the community and the modding community. Some software named "OpenIV" was banned as it was responsable for modding - Take-2 probally banned the software as the team developing it were converting Grand Theft Auto: IV's map, Liberty City - into Grand Theft Auto: V. They don't like it when this happens, so they probally thought by taking out OpenIV they can get their way, (As they did by taking down the Red-Dead-Desert in GTA:V project,) as well as fixing the "hacker issue" in GTA:O. (I wouldn't ever call them hackers - just scripters.) However, OpenIV's team required you to own GTA:IV to be able to do the port and their software could only modify the Single-Player game - and Rockstar stated before that they were fine with this.
Since then, the software has been re-allowed to develop but their GTA:IV in GTA:V project was cancelled. So please everyone, write an Email to Take-2 and don't blame Rockstar - they had no control over this. I'd also urge you to change your reviews and upvote this so more people can see the PSA - thanks!

Will be updated as I progress through the game.
This game is a good time sink when you are bored. Nice art, ok gameplay. No need to pay to progress [in the initial stages, read updates], but as with any similar game it is a bit grindy.
Update 1:
Expect to reach 'end game' at some point without unlocking everything as the last few chapters with Pamu and few others are extremely grindy as you have to wait days/weeks for your hobbies to level up unless you want to pay to buy gems.
Update 2 (23 Aug 2016):
Now at Hobby level 46 going to 47 will take 26 days, this is with 16x multiplier bought with gems and 105x prestige. In other words its the end of the road for players that don't want to pay for more gems, so this kind of makes it pay-to-play rather then free-to-play which is unfortunate.
The game in its current state v0.44 has serious issues when it comes to late game progression and the time it takes to level up is badly balanced for a truly free-to-play model.
Update 3 (21 Oct 2016):  [Out of Early Access]
The overall game balance has improved a lot.
The most you will need to spend to be able to nicely and speedily progress is $5 to $10 which is perfectly fine for the ammount of entertainment the game provides.
You can still progress without paying anything, but it will take longer.
The overall game has been improved with lot more dialogue and new characters, and there are still others to come which should make it easier for free players to get more diamonds along the way.
Overall its a solid clicker game with really nice art style, entertaining dialogue and great support from the small dev team.

Geneforge presents an original setting, masterfully blending sci-fi with fantasy. Here “Shapers” are humans able to create and shape life through magic, raise armies of creatures to work and fight for them, and even genetically alter plants to serve as tools and weapons. Everything about the world seems exotic and well-thought, and it’s very interesting to learn about its lore and workings.
The story starts with your character being washed in the shores of a mysterious island, where rogue creations run wild over abandoned Shaper ruins. As you explore the massive island in search for a way back home, you’ll find the truth behind the abandoned ruins, and will decide the fate of the various factions that inhabit it. The writing is solid, and the game asks you to make some seriously complex decisions, without any banal morality judging you. I’ll add that Geneforge is the only game I ever played where the NPCs managed to change my mind with solid arguments (instead of bribes) after I had decided on a set course of action.
Combat is turn-based with action points, and although it has some annoying limitations (like only one attack per turn), it’s solid. There are three classes to choose from, and they give you freedom to fight any way you want, being able to create hordes of weak monster to fight for you, focus on a large and powerful creatures, cast spells like firebolt and fear, or simply hack and slash your enemies. Non-combat skills like Leadership and Mechanics are also important, as they provide unique ways to avoid conflicts and solve quests. And although it may not seem obvious at first, there’s a great deal of reactivity here as well.
When this was release, back in 2001, cRPGs fans had their mouths full, being spoiled with the release of classic such as Arcanum, BG2: Throne of Bhaal, Morrowind, Wizardry 8 and Gothic. So it is understandable that Geneforge, with its unattractive graphics and puke-green UI, went by undetected by most. But it’s a damn shame, and you should fix that now.

An amazing addition to the RPG genre it takes a turn away from party character development focusing on the world, your actions in it and the repercussions of said actions. This gem from Spiderweb allows for a multitude of choices in your actions and playstyle in and out of combat. Do you think that creatures made for the sole purpose of manual labor should stick to manual labor? Do you think that prefrabricated beings can change and evolve acquiring ideas and motivations of their own? Do you like planning out each combat turn by turn or maybe you like to fly by the seat of your pants trusting in the intelligence of your handmade monsters? All of these and many more are choices you can and will make if you choose to step into this colorful world, and I certainly hope you do. As ever the first game is the roughest but as the series continues the story and gameplay improves adding in new monsters, classes and spells which you will use alter the path of the world.
Pros
A fantastic story with moral questions relating to the inhabitants of the world as well as to yourself
A solid number of monsters to summon allowing you to customize your party for the situation at hand
(For fans of turn based) Solid turn based gameplay factoring in speed attributes and action points causing a more cautious approach to your actions
Cons*
Graphics are a bit dated which for some can be a stickler
The game's difficulty does not scale per se so if you push on too fast you will feel the pain but if you take your time you can breeze through areas unless you alter the difficulty
The Shaper/Rebel faction dynamic can be a pain at times barring you from acquiring the last rank of a spell or summon key to your personal strategy
Overall it is an extremely enjoyable series that I've spent many hours on before it came to Steam and I would suggest you pick it up if you are a fan of Turn Based RPGs in general.
*And worries for some gamers

MOST IMPORTANT - before you play, for best immersion and best deus ex 1 feeling, SWITCH OFF the following in the gameplay options: OBJECTIVE LOCATORS (very important, these destroy immersion in this game!), COVER PROMPTS and COVER TO COVER LINE, and PICKUP OUTLINE (optional). You can also switch off some bars and displays or switch some to timed fade-out, which I would also recommend.
In short: it is good, but it has a very short main story, only one city and only 3 or 4 small additional locations. I recommend getting this one on a sale, and also to wait for the directors cut or a similar edition including additional content. It performs very well, however, on gameplay, level design, music and sound - it feels like dx 1 in parts - , very good sidequests, some small interesting innovations and also well done on the conspiracy side of things, even though the story lacks length.
pro:
- if your point of comparison is mainly the atmosphere and gameplay experience of deus ex 1, i think you will like it. i think it feels much darker compared to dx 2 (which was very creative and original, but its locations always felt artificial and small to me) and 3 (which was very... yellow, less dark and felt more artifical than this one -  at least regarding the visuals)
- handles its conspiracy theories very well and includes some fairly current, up-to-date theories and story spins,
. I really like the direction they are taking with the background story and the focus on

- at least two really awesome maps, one being a very good-looking, authentic and dark feeling and atmospheric city hub (even though very cold, but that fits the story and dx in general)
- nice music that reminds me of dx 1, and good sound design
contra:
- way too easy (new powerful augs, a lot of stuff in your bag, easy levels, only one boss and so on...), even on hard. theres an additional mode in which you basically cant load save games when you die, but that is just crazy imho. maybe i try it some day ^^

- the main story is way too short (did I already mention that?)

I would like to think I went into this game with low expectations, but I still came away disappointed.
This is a basic defence game where you defend against wave after wave of enemies coming your way. Every 3 or so waves you go to an unexplained shop screen where you can upgrade your character, equipment, spells and stationary defences using the gold you acquired for getting rid of your enemies. Every 10 waves you fight a large boss, culminating into a large final boss at wave 50.
My problem with the game, or main problem I guess, is that it is very unforgiving about how you spend your gold. With only finite amounts available every shopping round, no way to replay waves to grind for gold and no progress carried over between games (you always start from scratch with a fresh character) a misclick spending money on Intelligence even though you were going for a melee run can ruin your run. Or, rather than a misclick, just trying a new approach where you save up for some stationary defences for example. Or finding yourself stuck at a boss because it is out of range of the weapons you invested in.
Combine that with rather vague explanations about what every upgrade does, unimpressive graphics, no real story and weirdly floaty jumping and the game just kind of breaks down to a tedium.
If you plan to go in with low expectations, lower them some more. Or better yet, maybe just don't.

CAUTION: This game is only actually worth it when it goes on sale because it is a short and easy game, but it still serves as fairly decent satire.
There really is not much I can say about the gameplay, replayability or graphics because the game doesn't need to look amazing considering it's puny length and you would already know what to expect from the gameplay. You cannot die, there's close to no physics and unlike the Stanley Parable; when you replay this game, you will get all the same things. However, this game does give an important message about DLC overkill in games. In most games, you will see pre-order bonuses, retailer exclusives, overpriced and stupid DLCs which don't really enhance the game so much as to justify the purchase of DLCs, they seem to serve as novelties nowadays.
This is what makes this game important. Remember the days around the PS2 era where if you bought a game, you got the whole game and not just parts of it which will be filled in with DLC. That made games more exciting and more worth paying for. That all changed with the dawn of expansion packs for the big MMOs and Horse Armour (I'm looking at you, Oblivion!) but it isn't entirely for the worst from what I have seen. The DLCs for Saints Row: The Third have added many hours to the game and are of decent quality rather than being lousy 20 minute long stories which I thought was cool.
The only real issue I have with the game is the fact that I, and many others already know that a lot of DLC is pointless on the PC unless a game doesn't have mod support and on PC, mod support is always expected and always demanded for it to constitute "a real PC game" which is fair enough knowing that mods are changing the face of the games industry, but this satire is very relevant for consoles, which don't have mods, so console gamers rely upon the release of overpriced DLC to get new stuff in their game.
It's good for a laugh, the platforming is fairly easy and it can be quite entertaining, just don't buy it for full price.

The Mean Greens is a colorful, fun third person shooter made with the unreal engine. I will list the pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
+The game is colorful and enjoying to look at, maps like "Art table" are just riddled with colors, the lighting in the game is done right too.
+It runs like butter on my pc, and on my cheap laptop, I can't really imagine anyone experiencing framedrops with a decent setup.
+The music is catchy and nice to listen too, I had a smile on my face when I first heard the song during operation birthday, or hearing ride of the valkyres during Bathtub bash.
+Everyone has all the guns at all times, there is no reason to complain being killed.
+Each map has it's own game mode, all with different varieties. Modes like team deathmatch in the Table top wars map, FFA in the art table shuffle, Attack and defend in Operation birthday cake, and one of my favorites which is bathtub bash, a mode where you must ride rubber duckys to reach flags and deliver the flags back to your ship.
Now If what I said above is convincing you to buy the game, what I say next can probably change that.
Cons:
-While there are a ton of different game modes, some quite work out. In the map Operation birthday, the objective is to assault a birthday cake and light as much candles as you can while the enemy team stops you. After around halftime, the sides switch, so if team 1 lit 10 candles, all team 2 has to do is light 11. If team 2 lights 11 within the first minute, you've already won the game, and must wait the next 3 minutes until the round ends to be declared the winner (Which I think is stupid). Some game modes just require suicide to win. In the game modes Kitchen run and Deep freeze, all you have to do is run to your objective and do the action it tells you to (such as pushing the enemy cup off the table or unfreezing your dinosaur), so you can play the game for 4 minutes in a straight up tie, but 1 enemy touched your cup just slightly, and you lost the game.
-The servers can be absolutely horrible at times, you can hit join game and be waiting up to 3 minutes just so it could tell you that you failed to connect.
-The worst one would have to be-
The game is completely empty, I hit server browser only to find out there are 10 players online in TOTAL, if you are lucky you can find a server with maybe 6 people, and people usually leave during it. The game is fun with people to play, and no one ever plays.
Conclusion: I don't see the $10 dollar price being worth it up to now, I bought the game on release and I still don't feel like it was a good buy, but I can't not recommend this game, if you have a couple of buddys that will play it with you it's an excellent choice, otherwise wait for the price to be lowered. I see this more as a game that should be free to play, it's amazing but all it needs is a community to play it, and not a lot of people will pay for a game without players already playing it.
(Sorry if this review was long, it's the first game i've reviewed and I felt like I had to tell people about this game.)

Even though i've only played this game for a little bit, i can already feel that this is a great game with quick matchmaking, a wide variety of heroes and playstiles and that for free (apart from the in-game purchases).
Pro's:
+It's free, so you can check it out without having to pay a thing!
+Quick matchmaking: within a couple of seconds after finishing the previous game, you can already jump into the next one.
+In-game purchases luckily only for cosmetic items, all heroes are unlockable for free.
+Visually pleasing artstyle.
+Lots of different characters to allow different strategies and playstyles.
+Reminds of Super Smash Bros.
+Framerate is good even on older pc's (like mine).
+Co-op
Cons
-Keyboard and mouse don't play as nicely as a controller.
-The in-game purchases are very expansive.
-Balance between certain weapons is sometimes gone.
-Gets repetitive when playing in long sessions.
Overall this is a great alternative for Super Smash Bros. on pc, which you can try for free. Not a game to be playing for hours on end, but when playing in short bursts with friends, there is a lot of fun to be had!

*I'm a Kickstarter backer so my opinion is more important*
So, in a naive move to beat Sony to launching WipEout: Omega Collection, R8 has pushed Formula Fusion out the door, in a state lacking polish and still with some bugs.
But, R8 wanted to launch, so I will treat it like a finished product.
The games pacing feels off. The tracks are not designed with the speeds of the crafts in mind, some are certainly worse than others, but none of the tracks are great. The first completed track, Mannahatta is awful. It should have been left as a test environment lost in the game files, but no, it's still here, now relegated to one of the last tracks to be unlocked. Bad game design is not good difficulty design, R8.
Vehicles and cards are unbalanced. I knew balancing was going to be something R8 struggled with. Once someone figures out the optimal loadout, it's the only one you'll ever see.
Vehicle handling feels too unresponsive for the tracks, as previously mentioned, I just cannot work out how this game wants me to play it, I can never turn early enough for sharper turns, and when I try to, the game just punishes me for such a drop in speed.
Graphically the game is, passable. R8s team is largely made up of former WipEout artists, but none of FFs tracks are really very memorable. Pretty to look at, but they don't leave a lasting impression. No landmarks, or memorable corners, all the tracks are just a jumble of little chicanes and huge turns, which feel like they lack any real interest or care in their design.
Collisions are off, too. Vehicles bounce around too much or depending on their shape, just get stuck and feel almost impossible to pull off the outside wall.
Audibly the game has both a boring soundtrack and audio bugs, that will randomly cause all or some game audio to completely stop. Fortunately, Spotify is here to save the day.
The UI is visually nice, but maddeningly unhelpful.
The garage, where you can select 'cards' to create your own vehicle behaviour loadouts, will randomly close the card selection menu. In addition, not all cards display what they actually do to vehicle stats, which would be fine, if not for the fact that only weapon upgrades actually have descriptions to explain what they do.
I want to love this game, but it has too much style and not enough substance, everything looks right but feels so wrong, so hollow. Sort of like someone trying to develop a game, based solely on photographs of a WipEout game.

When everything works out, and the servers don't lag your character off the side, and the server doesn't have a spazmattack that ruins the whole match, the ranked matches are great and they get your blood pumping.
Unfortunately, that rarely happens. With how big this game is on Steam, I had higher expectations for the network programming. The game is abysmal when it comes to handling even the most minor lagspikes and the result can throw off your whole match. Sometimes, right before your match starts, the server randomly goes into seizure mode and you have no idea what's happening, but it always results in both players somehow dying and several minutes of waiting for the server to resolve the mess it had just made.
Overall though it's a pretty good multiplayer Smash-like time killer, or you can go more competitive with it if you want.

When R8Games was finally in the shape it should be, they started Formula Fusion- a spiritual succsessor of WO games with graphics made by The Designers Republic.
The project might be succsess in the future, but I think it is already good in the EA state. It has it's flaws, it's unpolished, but it is a great base (a really playable one) of something beautiful.

As a fan of the WipEout series (WipEout HD + Fury, Pure and Pulse), this game definitely lives up to the ideal successor status. Mind you, it does if you understand the creators want to polish the game with their own view and twist. The game rapidly generates itself, it's lore and overall aesthetic world in a somewhat dim future. It is quite clear the aesthetics of the racing teams are bridging a large techno-cultural gap between itself and Formula 1. Not everything appears to be starry, spangled and utopic, however. Some tracks are marvelous city escapades, while others are industrial, gritty and flashy Blade Runner styled backdrops. The use of the Unreal engine really fleshes out the sense of speed; whether you enjoy camera shake or without camera shake, everything feels fast. The feeling of transitioning from low to high speeds is thrilling, which makes cornering all the more impactful. Finally, when one grasps the winding corriders, tunnels and corners of a track, the feeling of basic mastery is rewarding as any anti-gravity racer.

The Defenders: The Second Wave is a 2D action game where you have to survive fifty waves of enemies by whatever means necessary. You start off with a small staff that you use to whack ghosts but every third wave you are given the chance to purchase skills, equipment and even build tiny castles with AI controlled to defend you. The friendly AI is stationary and has an attack radius of when it can attack enemies so they work more like sentries than companions. They will need to be placed on castles and can not be placed on normal ground. A castle sounds very useful but remember you are fighting against ghosts so they will just effortlessly move through your walls. All this is purchased with money that you receive by defeating ghosts and are given some every 5 rounds.
Starting off you will notice how boring melee combats is. All you do is wait for a ghost to approach you, whack him and he is pushed away a bit then its right back to attacking you. It mostly gets boring due to the AI. Enemies are programmed to rush right at you so it just becomes a game of trying to whack floating giant pinatas to get the gold inside. It does become more interesting when you build a wizard character as you have to keep track of your mana instead of just mashing the attack key. Oddly enough even if you are not a wizard your abilities like a simple charged attack takes up mana so you may need to spend money on intelligence if you want to use them effectively. For some reason a healing spell requires a lot of strength which makes no sense as character with a lot of strength has more health and regains it much more quickly than a fragile wizard that desperately needs it.
The game has up to four player local coop and it does feel like a game built around coop. You have to be very careful how you build your character if you are playing solo. It is most noticeable when you are being attacked by both sides and have no way to defend your back. Your best defense is a good offense as destroying them before they reach you is the only way to avoid damage. That does make playing a pure wizard in solo much harder as you will be pretty screwed if you run out of mana and have to wait for it to recharge. Some way to dodge the enemy like the Warrior's “brutal leap” ability is needed. Stats themselves are very important. You have to be aware of  of things like weight limit and speed when buying weapons and armor, so that makes it feel like more than just a simple upgrade and makes buidling your character pretty fun.
There are 12 medals to unlock which will let you purchase special items. They range from beating the game on hard to something weird like killing a dozen butterflies or attacking the moon. If you die you will start off again right after your last boss fight so that means a checkpoint every 10 waves. Even if you start the game over you will be able to start in wave 40 with a basic character but all the money you would have made if you actually played through all the levels. That is a pretty cool way of testing character builds. One thing that really annoys me is that every time you start a third wave to shop the screen immediately pops so you don't have time to reach any of the money on the floor even if it is right in front of you. They should have at least made it so that all the money is automatically added to your character or at the very least give you a short timer to collect the money before shopping.
Some of the enemies are very annoying as well like the zombie hands that frequently pop out of the ground that will stop you dead in your tracks. Like the rest of the enemies you will not be able to dodge it as it pops up very quickly, so you will be attacking the floor when all is calm just to kill it before it can spawn. There is so much mindless clicking involved that you'd think this was a clicker genre game. The bosses are pretty huge and each are very different from another but most of their attacks are undodgeable making it a pain for wizard characters. If you are playing on easy the final boss will be a huge disappointment though. There are three difficulties which are Easy, Normal and Hard. I was barely able to beat it on easy with a wizard character yet was able to easily breeze through normal as a warrior. Moral of the story being do not expect to have a good time as a wizard while playing solo.
Graphics and animations are very poor and remind me of something like South Park. Environments are bare-bones and besides the church there is nothing else to see. It was previously an Xbox Live Indie game so these are to be expected though. Music is rather forgettable as well but it serves it's purpose well enough. And here is the technical issue that negatively effects the game the most. It is locked at 30 fps which is never appreciated in any game. Having 60fps wouldn't have helped combat at all but at 30 it feels pretty odd. There are no graphics menu but it is set at 1080p which is nice and you are able to switch to windowed mode as well as having a music and sound effects slider. I don't know if it scales higher than 1080p unfortunately. Overall it is a decent port and I have had no issues other than the whole 30fps thing.
It is a pretty entertaining game for those that can take advantage of the local coop feature but for solo it gets boring fast. Due to the awful endings you don't really feel inclined to go through 50 more waves on a higher difficulty level unless you are shooting for all the achievements. Gameplay is just not fun or varied enough to make you want to spend a lot of time with this title. I did get a few hours of entertainment out of The Defenders and the very cheap price of the game makes it a much more tempting purchase. In the end of day I feel I got my money's worth out of this title and would be tempted to put more hours if I had someone to play it with more frequently. Recommended to those that want a local coop game or just a mindless action game with rather nice character building.

MegaTagmension Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies is a great spinoff of the Neptunia series. It's very similar to Hyperdimension Neptunia U : Action Unleashed for it's hack and slash genre and that this installment features co-op multiplayer!
However, in regards to playable content, I find this one lacking compared to NepU, NepU has more quests I believe and afterwards you would have to complete the tournaments + Neptral tower if you were aiming for 100% achievements, NepU provides much more play. With MegaTagmension, after finishing the 12 acts, you'll have to resort to multiplayer to get 100% and it's pretty much more quests and luck to get certain items. A few things that I do like is the accessories in the game, all accessories are avaiable to all characters and do not require multiple purchases if multiple characters are going to wear the same thing. I also like how you can adjust the position/placements of the accessories. And of course, I liked how Uzume, Plutia and Peashy are in this game along with the new character, Tamsoft.
I do have some cons about the game. Firstly, the game's consistency. I feel as though the game may be a bit too easy especially when you decide to do a "YOLO" with a character at level 8 on a mission that recommends level 25-30 (Around there) and you are still able to beat it despite being underlevelled by almost 3-4 times, if not more. Then again, for players who love a good challenge, this may be a downside. For me, I personally don't mind.
With multiplayer, I do hope there is a patch in the future that may fix some possible issues such as players joining MP games that are password protected. I am willing to play game with another player but when I set a password protected MP, I set it because I want to do solo MP for achievements and so, it'd be nice if players would stop randomly joining my password protected rooms somehow XD

Well, what do we have here, you may ask?
What we have here is probably one of  the best indie titles I've played this past year. At the time this review is posted it may say that I have little to no hours in this game, but rest assured that I’ve had 40+ hours in this game before it came out on Steam. I got my 40+ hours using Desura, a game distribution platform not too dissimilar from Steam, where this game was published with constant updates. That being said, my 40+ hours came from playing different builds of this game, from the Alpha to the latest build, v1.0.10. And let me be frank here; every reiteration, as in every update, made this game more and more enjoyable in almost every aspect. The developer, Phroot, took the time to add new features along with many important bug fixes with every update. In other words, he knows what to do and how to take care of his game. Now on to what the game is about:
Gameplay:
The gameplay of 3089 is set in first-person, as  seen through the screenshots. Now you may be thinking, "Oh another FPS??!?" Rest assured  that even  though  the game is set in first person, the gameplay is far from your traditional FPS for many reasons:
1. Non-linear procedurally generated environment.
No two playthroughs are the same. Everything about the environment is different from where enemy bases are spawned to randomly placed towers (in a good way). Bridges, roads, buildings, and bases are randomly placed in the huge sprawling world known as Xax. The only thing constant throughout every playthrough is that you, the player, is always spawned in a friendly base (and even then, the base has randomly placed buildings). Every building, bridge, road, etc is sprawling with life as there are always friendly and enemy robots roaming about, sometimes fighting each other to the death. It's a magnificent sight to see groups of robots fighting it out while you just sit watching. The world is alive; never have I felt that I'm completely alone in this single-player game.
2. Variety of playstyles.
3089 has done a fantastic job of allowing multiple types of playstyles, such as a stealth run to a full run-and-gun experience. The game accomplishes this with skill points, and as you complete quests you can apply those skill points into a variety of different attributes, such as Stealth to avoid easier detection by enemies to Vehicles which allow you to pilot better vehicles. There's even a Leadership ability in which I can recruit a large amount of friendly robots to follow me wherever I go. It is so satisfying seeing my cadre of robots go after a group of enemies for a particular quest. In short, there are so many attributes that can be applied to your unit, and combination of each of these attributes can add to an entirely new playstyle.
3. Combat.
The combat of 3089 is familiar to other games, but still satisfying nonetheless. There are a variety of different weapons to choose from, ranging from simple pistols to swords. That's right, swords. Now I haven't used swords a lot since melee combat isn't my thing, but I can testify for the gunplay. The gunplay is solid as there are different weapons to choose from along with the extensive customization (which I'll go into detail soon). There are rifles, launchers, pistols, and energy rifles. Honestly my favorite type is rifles as they just feel so solid and powerful with the right customizations/attachments. The combat of 3089 can be challenging as you have to manage your ammo inventory and your 'Burst', which is how many shots you have before 'reloading.' You have to time your shots and make sure they hit their mark if you want to make it out unscathed. Like I said, the combat is challenging yet super rewarding. Along with the variety of weapons, there are also a large number of enemies, ranging from simple robots to giant spider bots. These spider bots are fudging huge and have powerful weapons!
4. Loot and customization.
This has got to be one of my favorite aspects of this game. Loot is acquired from killing enemies along with 'uncrating' random crates you find along the way. The loot you find is proportional to the level of the environment, so if you kill an enemy in a level 10 environment, you get an item that is level 10 (the level of a certain area is seen when you open up  the map. The level is denoted by 'Difficulty', so a difficulty of 10 of an area would house level 10 enemies and level 10 loot. The area you start in is Difficulty 1, so the farther you stray from your starting area, the higher level and more difficult the game is). The loot you find can be anything from parts of weapons to armor pieces. In 3089, you can customize your weapons to a nice degree with these parts. For example, rifle parts include barrels, magazines, bodies, scopes, and silencers. Armor parts include leggings, helmets + visors, and lower torso and chest pieces. All parts of  a particular weapon are interchangeable, so you have the ability to make a powerful weapon catered to your liking.
Graphics:
I'll be honest here; when I saw this game for the first time, I was like, "What is this???" But as I went through the screenshots on Desura, it changed my mind. The vast hills in the distance with simple buildings in the foreground from a screenshot got to me. So I gave the game a chance by downloading the demo. In short, I was amazed at the beauty of the world. Vast landscapes on this alien world with large areas full of robotic life. The aesthetics are simple, but does extremely well to show off the world. With every update, the landscape look more 'alive' with more things added to the world, like bridges and ramps and helipads. Before you pass this game off because of the graphics, please reconsider. Download the demo and see how  gorgeous this game can be. The screenshots don't do it justice.
Story:
The story is quite simple and self-explanatory, so I won't spend much time explaining what it is. What I will explain is how to get the most out of it. To get the most out of what's going on, it is best to read every data text that you come across. You get snippets of the story through these data texts, which can be acquired from completing quests and following objectives. These data texts, which are just a few sentences, explain what the fudge is going on and what you can do to maximize impact on the world.
Conclusion:
Possibly one of the best indie games I've played in a while. I find it astounding how this game made by one person with the help of others can provide me with more enjoyment than some AAA games out there. It may sound like I'm exaggerating but it's the truth for me personally. If you love exploration games with lots of freedom with a gorgeous living world, then this is the game for you!

Deus Ex is a fun, challenging and massive series. (Even Invisible War was enjoyable, I don't care what the haters say.)
Mankind Divided has some intense moments, amazing shoutouts to previous games, easter eggs from other games, new features and plenty to explore. However, this game ended way, way too quickly.
This game felt, to a point, like the original Deus Ex. I started getting the feeling that there were conspiracies. That Jensen was beginning to become more self-aware and curious as to whether he was a pawn or not. There were numerous references to characters in the rest of the series. It's just that everything was done at what feels like 50% of the potential. It's still awesome! Don't get me wrong. Mankind Divided feels like Deus Ex, just not completely like Deus Ex. (Think how Star Trek Enterprise felt compared to TNG, or Honey Nut Scooters compared to Cheerios)
This story basically boils down to a giant tease of what we already know in the series. Too much focus on the System Rift/Breach gameplay. I give Deus Ex a 7/10.

I've got quite an unusual opinion about Soulstorm compared to Dark Crusade. Most people think Dark Crusade was more balanced and was a overall better release, but I think that Soulstorm was far better designed (in terms of balance and replayability), though greatly flawed on release. In Dark Crusade, there was extremely heavy bias towards Tau and Necrons (being a Tau player myself), and unforgiving brutality to Imperial Guard players due to being extremely underpowered, though it was nice for the planet to stay persistant with what happened on it.(I.e, you defeat an ork encampment and establish a massive Eldar base, if that is then attacked, you will be returned to your base EXACTLY as you built it to retaliate).
In Soulstorm, everything (faction-wise) is perfected. It had horrific problems running on release, it's annoying that your base is basically cast aside at the end of a mission, meaning that if you are attacked you have to build your base from scratch (unless you invest funds) and the addition of flying units is a bit odd, but most (if not all) Tau units have been nerfed, as they should be, and all necron units were also nerfed. Subsequently, all Imperial Guard units were also buffed, providing an equal battleground for all of the (now) 9 factions in Soulstorm. Apart from Dark Eldar, they're like the new Imperial Guard.
But who wants to play as space emos?
If you're more into the lore and fluff of the universe, (and cringe when you see a space marine get cut down by a single guardsman), and would rather play something thats a little more faithful to the factions, I'd recommend DoW II and its expansions. It sacrifices strategic scale battles and faction choice in favour of tactical scale battles and realism (in terms of the 40k universe).
