I can't recommend this game. It's more of the same gameplay-wise, and I like that, with a few little additions here and there. But a sequel should be innovative. This isn't necessarily a bad game. I still enjoyed it. But compared to Human Revolutions, this is nothing but filler. The entire game could've just been one massive DLC. The best way I can put it is...Mankind Divided is the Attack Of The Clones of the Deus Ex series. It barely moves the story forward, there aren't any surprises that'll jump out at you, and the ending..I'm not spoiling it for you, but the ending is OBVIOUS sequel bait.
This entire game is just a set up for a sequel. If you're looking for a grand event like the Aug incident in Mankind Divided, or some kind of insane climax like in Panchea, then I'm sorry but..You'll have to wait for the inevitable threequel, assuming THAT won't just  be a set up for a future game. I also experienced a lot of bugs, such as mission icons randomly jumping from place to place on your minimap. I'd follow an objective and SUDDENLY it appears behind me, where I just came in. I'd experience sudden game crashes, or idiotic AI that doesn't notice I'm standing just a couple of inches infront of them.
HOWEVER, there are a lot more side missions in this game than in HR. I consider that a plus, although I should mention that it's at the cost of more missions to do. Whereas HR had a lot of meat on its bones story-wise, and a lot of locations, MN just doesn't. Though to the games credit, there are a lot more options regarding how to deal with ingame bosses(Which there aren't many.). I hated slipping through entire levels in HR like a ghost, only to be forced into combat. Fortunately, that isn't the case. You can either talk them down, or just go non-lethal. Though, I can only remember three instances of that. As I said, there just aren't many bosses.
Ingame achievements like ghost are very cryptic and arbritary. Sometimes you'll alert an enemy by shooting them in the back with a stun gun. Gas grenades are fun to use but..Again, you'll end up alerting everyone. Also, "ghost" doesn't count when you're doing side missions. I kept going back to saves for hours, until I read a comment online. I'm a very stealthy player. Non-lethal and ghost, in every stealth game I've ever played. Nobody ever notices me, and I always get ghost achievements at the end. I was disappointed to find that Mankind Divided only has an offical achievement just for passing ONE level unnoticed.
There's also the issue of the battery. It drains too fast, even when using smart vision. You can reprimand that with biocells, or praxis kits to extend the battery, which of course is to encourage  you to buy praxis kits. but I felt like I was being punished for playing with augments. Old habits eventually kicked in, and I learned to play Mankind Divided like an ordinary generic stealth game without any special powers. But I didn't buy Mankind Divided for generic stealth. I can enjoy generic stealth anytime I want. But I bought it for the augments, which have always been the draw and focus of Deus Ex. Don't bother with augments.
In conclusion, what you have is a buggy mediocre generic stealth game that just happens to be called Deus Ex, with more questions than answers, and if you want those questions answered, you'll have to put $60 down for the inevitable sequel. As for the ingame transaction drama, Ihave one simple solution..Just don't buy anything. You can beat the game without a zillion praxis kits. I did. I very much regret buying this game. I won't tell you how to spend your money, but if I could refund this, I'd buy Invisible Inc, Thief: Gold, Mark Of The Ninja, or a PC port of good ol' Arkham City, all four of which are much more competent stealth titles.
Oh, and did I mention that you have to rebuy all of the same augs you bought in HR? The SAME exact augs. I'm not even kidding. There's about five or six new augs, the ones that were hyped so much in the trailers..But they're all pretty gimmicky. And don't be too worried about choosing one over the other. You can pretty much buy the one you missed out on on New Game+, anyway.
TL;DR : Anti-climactic as well as predictable story, nerfed battery use, buggy AI, too few bosses.

Oct 31 is the date I finished the game with the first DLC.
The version of the game I played was already patched ~10 times on PC by devs.
It runs smooth, no bugs, no glitches except a single one with DX12 enabled. If you have any graphical glitches like weird textures or something like that - disable DX12 and try the game again. It's not GPU or drivers, I checked it myself. It's weird DX12 support.
Prague is really impressive, other locations are pretty good too. The amount of details they used and all that fancy lighting and shadows is amazing. Night Prague is on a whole new level.
Music is fine.
Most side quests are interesting and good too.
Now the main story is not as good as it could be. While Versalife, Illuminati, Page and the other vital parts of Deus Ex world were mentioned, they are not really connected to the Mankind Divided game. You are not getting in touch with any of them and the story feels like an in-between filler. Adam himself is not really that motivated and well written in Mankind Divided, he's not trying to save his waifu, there is no Panchaea-tier final, antagonists are not really that remarkable as well.
Oh and don't freak out because of "micro transactions". I only noticed it myself in a main menu after reading a bunch of comments and discussions about the game. It's completely irrelevant and does nothing to you if you want to play fair and explore everything by yourself. The game is not even that hard to be honest, you will find lots of medkits, ammo, hacking programs and exp to lvl up.

I'm surprised by all the negative reviews. I guess if you didn't really explore the levels, you could probably finish the game sooner.
But there were so many hidden nooks, lots of things to hack, many opportunities to utilize your augmentations. My playtime of Human Revolutions was around 70 hours. My playtime of Mankind Divided was more like 54-55 (+the Janson story, which took probably another hour to finish). The levels were varied, and full of places to discover.
And the game lacks the flaws of Human Revolutions (which had a terrible opening level and while the final level of Mankind Divided wasn't 'great', it was certainly better than the 'zombie level' of Human Revolutions. And I'm certainly not knocking HR, overall, as the middle is great, especially with the missing link restored to it. But it started off bad and ended bad. Mankind Divided was just fun as a Deus Ex game, and ends abruptly, but at the same time, the main story thread it was telling was completed.
Certainly, some tweaks could help near the end. And I'm not fond of them replacing David Sarif's voice (though it suffices) Overall, I loved it. I rarely buy full priced games, but this year I bought Fallout 4 and Mankind Divided, and will probably buy Dishonored 2, since it is basically Deus Ex set in a steampunk like world. and I absolutely loved the first game (and that was another one that was rather short, but the game and story and all just worked so well, and the levels allowed many opportunities to use your abilities, so I was ok with it).
And being a big Deus Ex fan, I love all the new additions. They refined the Aug system from HR, and the new Augs are fun, especially remote hacking. I liked that I could play the game lethal or nonlethal, and there were lots of ways through levels. The basic gameplay is everything I could want from a Deus Ex game. More so than HR, because MD hits the ground running.
I see complaints about the story... and I don't get it. HR never really went the distance as far as Conspiracy theories go, not like the original Deus Ex. But you see little building blocks here and there, in HR and MD, leading to the foundations of what became Deus Ex. Would I lke more Conspiracy Theories in this mix? More secret societies? And what not? Of course, but neither game really does enough with it. But the story is entertaining enough, certainly as much as HR, though it never builds to a ridiculous anticlimax (just an abrupt climax), and the core gameplay and the levels allowing a player to flex out their aug muscles seems much more solid in MD.
I'm not fond of the microtransactions, they suck. But they aren't in your face about it in this game and they certainly aren't needed. Same with the DLC that came with preordering. I never felt like I was grinding to go up levels. I leveled up, getting praxis kits, at fairly regular intervals. So yeah, the fact that microtransactions are there, baaad. But you can easily ignore them and never think about them while playing the game, so it's not as big a deal as some are making it out to be.
So really, not sure what people were expecting. I will say the DLC offerings for the season pass seem weak as hell and not worth picking up. The Fallout 4 Season Pass was definitely more than worth it, as I will be jumping back into that next now that I have finished MD, and now the nuka cola theme park has been added and I've been hearing great things about it.
Bottom line, love MD and will play it again at some point. And if you are a Deus Ex fan, and like to explore levels (not just stick to main story points), and don't mind a game that is a bit shorter than HR, I recommend it. I enjoyed it overall more than HR.

Just like Diablo II to Diablo I, Torchlight II is a serious step-up compared to Torchlight I. Big open spaces, various locations and a nice facelift for the already great game mechanics improved the hack'n'slash action-RPG game nicely. The insanely awesome game music score was composed by Matt Uelmen who also created the music of Diablo I and II (and Torchlight I, to be exact) so you'll get into the same way awesome atmosphere while listening to the pinnacle of game music tracks, ever, period. The GFX are, just like in Torchlight I, cheery, cartoony and cute that is a slight mismatch to the super heavy dark music but that doesn't make this great game any way lesser. It is fun, agile and stabile, one of the most solid games you can get now'days. It is not about a highly elevated background story or refined characters as these aspect are kind of flat (Diablo II dominated that round far) but the game itself has a somewhat easier heart so heavy content would fit here like a classical music middle part to an AC DC song if you know what I mean.
So, if you haven't had it yet, it is about time to get it during the goddamn holiday game sale, right?

"What happens when DLC goes to far?
Basic features are now DLC! Animation? DLC! Pausing the game? DLC! Moving to the left? Well, tha'ts included. No, it's not! DLC!"- DLC Quest trailer
DLC Quest is an open-world side-scrolling DLC-em-up.
Upon starting the game, you can only move right. Nothing else. You collect coins as you move, and eventually bump into a shopkeeper. From him, you can buy the ability to move left. Then, later, you can buy: jumping, weapons, pause menus, and more!
DLC Quest is much less an actual game than it is a hilarious satire.
For anyone and everyone who thinks that fifteen-dollar map packs and four-dollar weapon skins in modern video games are ridiculous, play DLC Quest, and laugh with me. It's not very long, but then again: It's only three dollars.
$3/1.9 hours = $1.58/hour.
As a game: 6.5/10
As a satire: 9.75/10
Final Score: 8.13/10
Letter Grade: B-
Money/Playtime: $1.58/hour

Shadow Bug is a generally fast-paced platformer where it's more of clicking onto enemies to teleport/launch to them versus typical platforming. Each level is timed and you gather score throughout the level, with the goal of reaching the end in under a certain amount of time with a certain amount of points. I had fun looking at the ways I could potentially shave time off of my runs and then practicing those strategies, sort of like mini-speedrunning.
Levels are increasingly difficult and incorporate new mechanics as you progress that are quite cool and satisfying to master.
A lot of your time spent playing would likely be redoing levels over and over, trying to improve your times, similar to Dustforce, although mechanically easier because it's mainly clicking with your mouse cursor.
The visuals are pretty nice (reminds me a bit of Ori) and the music is pretty solid, doesn't get irritating to listen to over and over and definitely helps the mood of the game as you're going through levels.
I'd definitely recommend checking out Shadow Bug if you like games similar to Dustforce in which it's basically mini-speedruns of levels. (especially for $5)

A tiny insect is watching his forest decay and be destroyed as it is invaded by machines and flooded with pollution. Setting out on an epic journey, he must discover the source and defeat these giant enemies. It's actually quite a moving tale when you think of it - especially when the environment is such a hot topic right now. It's also a great setting, with the juxtaposition between the light and airy forest and the machines that invade it. We journey through the forest, down the sewers and into the factory to find the source.
* Beautiful artwork.
* Fluid movement and keyboard/mouse controls.
* Unique gameplay.
* Excellent level design with formulated progression.
* Good range of enemies with different abilities.
* Fairly short game, completable in 3-4 hours (or hypothetically under 30 minutes for a full speedrun if you're God-tier)
* Limited replayability (once you have all stars per level, there's nothing else to do).
* Not good for controllers, ups the difficulty level by 6 billion.
* The final two levels are extremely difficult compared to the rest of the game.
The gameplay took me a little getting used to but is very unique. It's a platformer that has no jumping ability (and trust me, I instinct-spammed space a LOT in the beginning, it won't help). Instead, your ninja bug can zip from enemy to enemy, moving and killing them in one stroke. You can walk back and forth using A and D, but the majority of the movement is made by targetting an enemy. You can then move in any direction at great speed, and control the direction of your descent. You end up bouncing from enemy to enemy in fluid, smooth motions.
It's both a precision and a speed game. You have to be exact or you're going to be devoured by creepy creatures, impaled on thorns, sliced by spinning blades or trampled by machinery. At the end of each level you have a score. One star for completing it successfully, two for completing it under an allotted time, and three for collecting enough power ups. Sometimes it's simply not possible to both speed run and power run so it adds that extra challenge and replayability, with some levels having secrets to be found. A speedrunner will enjoy the challenge immensely.
There is a decent range of enemies, many of whom have unique abilities, such as plants that spit venom at you, or the birds who pick up spiked seeds and drop them in inconvenient places, such as on your head.  As the levels progress, minor new mechanics are added that give a little bit of extra depth and complexity each time. From swinging spikes and levers, to keys and unlockable doors, to moveable boxes to... well, I'll let you discover for the rest. You're drip-fed the changes so as each new things is introduced you have time to naturally learn how to respond until you're dealing with everything at once like a pro. Well, that's the idea anyway. My execution was a little bit off to say the least (400th death inc...)
On a difficulty level I found the game fairly easy until the final two levels. Although I did die a LOT, the game has short levels and very frequent checkpoints, meaning it's easy to have a stab at the same section multiple times very quickly until you get the hang of it. I'd say it's challenging enough to keep you interested, tax your fingers and get those brain cells whirring... until you get to the last two levels. The difficulty ramps up to insane and I did find the final two levels frustratingly challenging. It took me 2 hours to complete levels 1 through 34 and then 2 hours to complete levels 35 and 36 - levels that should be able to be speedrun in a few MINUTES apparently. Well then, screw lasers, seriously.

Men of Rohan! Lend me your ear!
Okay, so this is a fantastic game. It's a MMP, for starters. The communities are nice, there's awesome gameplay, and it's LOTR! What else could one ask for? The map is massive and stretches from Ered Luin to Central Gondor and the Dead Marshes. You can pick from 5 races (the Beorning class must be unlocked, but the Man, Elf, Hobbit, or Dwarf races are free) and from I believe 9 classes. Whether you're an Elven archer, gallavanting along in Ered Luin or a Hobbit burgular, sitting in the Prancing Pony in Bree, adventure is sure to happen in this game.
Now, you start off with the prologue. Elves and dwarves start in Ered Luin, men start off in Breeland. I have had a character for each race and would personally suggest starting off as a man. In the Man prologue, you spawn in Archet, just north of Bree. You've just been broken out of jail by Strider. Unfortunately, one of Strider's ranger friends is stabbed by a Morgul blade during the prison break, which in turn means he's eventually going to become a wraith. The town of Archet is attacked by local brigands (or rebels), who are ultimately under the leadership of Angmar--the Terror of the North. The country of Angmar is growing again, building up armies that are destined to destroy Middle Earth. Can you stop them?
The storyline takes place at just about the beginning of the Fellowship of the Ring. Although not part of the Fellowship, you will meet iconic characters along the way who are part of the Fellowship. For example, in the Hobbit prologue, you encounter Merry, Samwise, Frodo, and Pippin. In the Man prologue, you obviously encounter Strider.
One thing I like about the game is it's content of iconic LOTR places. Unlike the movies, the game contains place such as the Barrow-Downs and the Old Forest (including Tom Bombadil). Midgewater Marshes is always a fun place to play for lower-level players. Bree is the hub of action in the game for other online players [unless there is a festival or special session going on].
Another thing I love about the game is the Fellowship mode. You can invite ANY player [who is on your server] to be in a Fellowship with you, which means you can help each complete missions and such. They can help you if you need help defeating Wargs in the Lonelands. It's a VERY fun mode, and is probably my favorite part of the game.
Almost congruent with the Fellowship mode is the Kinship mode. Your fellowship ends when you turn off your game, although it can very easily be started again. A kinship, however, is more of a long term deal. You're always in a kinship [unless you decide to leave or just don't join a kin in the first place]. Kins are nice for obtaining knowledge from higher-level players or just getting to know others. It is a wise decision for lower-level players to join kins, just to get a feel for the game.
You can unlock Monster mode after you hit level 10 in normal mode. The only bad thing about Monster mode is that there aren't very many people on it at the same time, which makes it hard for Fellowships.
Although the game is free, one of the cons is that there are in-game purchases. BUT, THEY ARE NOT REQUIRED. In fact, you can gain Turbine Points by completing certain deeds. For example, a deed may be "Kill 60 Wargs". After killing the 60 wargs, you would be rewared with 10 Turbine Points. As I said the purchases aren't required, but they can certainly help speed the process. Players are entitled to 2 characters AT THE SAME TIME (not including monster mode) on an account, which means you can do the same deeds for 2 different characters, but all the Turbine Points will go to the same account. So there is a way to "beat the system". You can access the store directly on the game and see how many points you have.
Overall, this game is one of my favorites! It's a very fun MMP and will be enjoyable for anyone who likes LOTR. This review has been written from the stand-point of a player on the Imladris Server. Happy gaming!

I played beta and launch of this game... there was a lot of potential and it was very pretty at the time of launch- especially considering it was competing with the very cartoony look of WoW. There were some really interesting, unique features to the game as well as beautiful environments that were neat to explore as part of LotR lore...
I popped back into the game, just to check out the f2p spin and see how things have evolved. On the upside, the game doesn't suck and all of my characters were still there. The down-sides, however, unfortunately, make me not recommend it. From my perspecitve, the game hasn't evolved (possibly de-volved), is a bit dated, continues to be a bit clunky, and is still not quite intuitive (coming from a veteran MMO player: EQ, SWG, WoW, Vanguard, Eve, AoC, CoH/V, DC Universe, D&DO, ESO, Entropia, SWTOR, blah blah blah).
Most importantly, it seems barren now... so, if I want a LotR fix I'll just play one of the quality single player titles to get the same jolt... or maybe Skyrim. If I want a solid MMO (with actual players to interact with) to swing a sword around in, I'd spend my time and money on ESO or WoW. But, for other people, I guess if you really hate on WoW or ESO for whatever reason and really need an MMO fix in a similar genre or are REALLY into LotR and are willing to pay to play, it might be worth it.
All of that said, it really is free to play at the start- so trying it and not liking it will only cost you the time to download, the space on your hard drive (temporarily), and however much time you put in. If you have time to burn and enjoy spending it trying new things, it probably won't be a waste.

The Sims 3 is an incredible game. It makes life seem just about the same, easy at first, harder as you continue, or just depending on what kind of life your sim lives. The base game itself without any DLCs or CC installed, is very small, but still quite entertaining. You do indeed have to play it for quite some time to get your Sim somewhere great in their simlife. With DLCs and CC installed, it's even better. CC can be made completely by you or found on the internet and made by someone else, but it gives you capability to fully customize your game, and the fact that the developers let the players create and install CC is grand. the DLCs make it possible to live in the city, or with pets, etc. Without it, if you were to let's say install a pet, it wouldn't work out. The DLCs and CC make the game much more than the base game is. As well as the many other versions of the game that you can buy, it puts so much more variety into the game and makes it so much fun to play. It's definitely worth the money in my opinion, just make sure that if you go all out, you have enough storage for it. For those of us looking for a Wipeout fix, this is a decent purchase. It leans too much to the arcade side of things, though this could be solved with a difficulty option. I don't expect Kerbal Space Program physics but it would be nice to have a Need For Speed mix of realism and arcade. Right now we have Ridge Racer / Mario Kart with some Trackmania thrown in. For example: rolling gives you a speed penalty but due to the nature of the tracks it becomes an advantage in tight curves. That makes yaw less useful than it could be because there isn't that much inertia. While I buy into the game's premise of maglev technology (this is a game after all) it breaks the immersion having such responsive and physics-defying controls. The game is still in early access so it can still change for the better (and I am an eternal optimist). Here's hoping for a game that's more serious about competition.

This is probably the best RTS and I played most of them from Dune 2 to Starcraft 2. If you could not stand your armies being obliterated in 2 seconds like in Starcraft 2 you might try this game. Battles take time and you can have fun even if you loose. The resources comes from points that you need to control so there is no turtling and there is constant action all around.
++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
The pluses:

+ Best RTS gameplay

+ Nice campaigns with cool, good quality videos (worth to get all expansions for all campaigns)

+ Graphics are good even today and the art style is fantastic

+ Cool animations when you get special kills. Throwing, cutting slices, blood split around...

+ Awesome voice acting and great sound affects

+ Good music

+ 9 distinctive races in multiplayer - (you must get all expansions to get them all to play against humans, but in skirmish against AI all are present and available) Some with different resource mechanics.
# Orcs - green skin brute killers that like axes and bigga guns "Orkz Orkz"
# Space marines - genetically modified humans with awesome mechs and tanks "For the Emperor"
# Chaos - tainted space marines with Demons on their side "Do you hear the voices too?"
# Eldar - Elf-like aliens with sophisticated technology
# Imperial Guard - Imperial Army that rely on spamming large masses of soldiers and tanks
# Tau - advanced race fighting "For the Greater Good"
# Necrons - living metal organisms
# Sisters of Battle - female order dedicated to worship of the Emperor "To the Emperor, my life; to Him, my death."
# Dark Eldar - Eldars tainted by Chaos that harvest Soul Essence from fallen opponents

+ Many game modes for (1v1, 2v2, 3v3, 4v4, Free Fall All) and settings (control and hold 50% of points, 66%, Annihilate etc.)

+ Pretty fast to find a game in lobby (even for 8 players)

+ Still living community
+ Lots of mods (some add new factions and many new units)
------------------------------------------------------
The minuses:
- code for servers is bugged (sometimes players drop at beginning because out of sync)

- 1v1 Automatch sometimes take some time to find opponent (but instead you can create game in lobby and someone will get in pretty fast)

- Automatching for bigger number of players (more than 1v1) might take A LOT of time (but like I sad before, games in lobby are filled fast)

- Stats displayed for players are bugged
======================================

TLDR: An interesting concept, but the execution is too buggy for me to enjoy.
I would really like to give this game a good review; it's a neat concept that, to begin with at least, seems quite well executed.  Unfortunately, the more I played, the more I began to suspect that it's actually riddled with bugs.  The gameplay is simple, you teather to the circles in your path by holding space, and then orbit around them, de-teathering by releasing space.  The problem is, the game dosen't seem to think that it's all that important which circle you teather to when you press space.  At first it seemed that the teather attached to which ever circle was closest, but the more I played, the more times I noticed that apparent rule being broken, and the more it started to annoy me when I died because of it.  One More Line bills itself as a "skill timing game" but the most important aspect in any game of skill is consistancy in its mechanics, and One More Line lacks that consistancy.  Perhaps there's some qualifier to the rule of "attach to closest" that would explain the apparently random cases where the teather attaches to the seemingly "wrong" circle, but the tutorial video is bugged out and won't play, so any explanation it might have contained is lost.
This is a great buy when it is on sale for $1. I wouldnt pay much more for this game.

This is a descent squeal, but I am not convinced at the augmented vs natural storyline. In the last game the augmented went nuts and started killing people, but that wasn't their fault. And I feel that dividing society up into two was very disingenuous as the story doesn't cover people who gave up their augmentations to try and re-integrate into natural society or make any distinction between those who became augmented through accident (maybe they lost a limb while at work or through a medical condition) or those who became augmented to become super people. It also doesn't consider augmented individuals who might try to hide their augmentations. The augmented here are down trodden victims who need to be cared for by corporations, governments and aid groups, rather than capable individuals. I found the stance that the naturals take in fearing augmented individuals and considering them all to be bad, to be horrifically over simplified.
Other than the story, this was an ok squeal. The hub areas are nice to explore and like the previous game there is some really nice architecture. The big new addition is a few new augmented powers that Jenson gets, their appearance is never properly explained despite Jenson doing a few small quests to discover their origin as this has been left open to another sequel. The ending leaves a lot to be desired.

Being enamoured by the 2-level Deus Ex demo that came with a magazine disc back in 2000, there was no way I wasn't going to pre-order Deus Ex Manking Divided. However, I didn't imagine that it would be this long since the preview till I came up with the review, but such are the vagaries of life. Having said that, Steam puts the play time for my first playthrough at a little over 60 hours  at the 'Give me Deus Ex' level with the 'Desperate Measures' DLC (not including the Breach Mode). This length is simply a reflection of my playing style which involves a stealth only approach and exploration of the complete map the first time I enter it, including hacking all doors/computers and finding alternate paths. I must add that this style of playing might only be for fans of the franchise since it really tends to get tedious after a while. It has exceeded the time I spent on Human Revolution only on account of the larger, free-roaming maps. For those playing through the main story alone, I can't imagine the game length even extending 15 hours.
So what's the verdict on this one? On the plus side, the gameplay has certainly been improved if you consider the changes to the cover system, hacking, health and bioelectric energy systems. The game stays true to the Deus Ex template of having alternate quests, conversation choices and alternate pathways. However, this is not necessarily good as it feels really stale in its implementation and seems to be there just for the sake of it. Also, the decisions made in conversations, especially concerning high profile characters like Miller seem to have little effect on the overall story as against the situations with Paul and Jock in the first game of the series. The developers have tried to bring in some degree of freshness through experimental augmentations but I didn't need or want to use any of them apart from Remote Hacking. I have a particular gripe with the way the side missions are handled which are more of a "go there and do this" kind of a thing. An open-ended approach (as in the original game) wherein you discover and choose your path without worrying about a checklist would have certainly been more engaging. To me, it seems that the developers have put too much focus on unessential aspects at the expense of a good story which has always been Deus Ex's strong point.
The game's marketing did a great job of hyping up the game's premise through the live action trailers but the game fails miserably to deliver on that front. The game stands a notch below Human Revolution and quite some way away from the original game in terms of its story. The previous game epynomously focused on the idea of human evolution through augmentation. Even then, Purity First depicted the fracture in the society as not all conceived augmentation to be an evolution of humanity. Mankind Divided, on the face of it, takes this concept to the next level where the society is already deeply divided with the "evolved" beings being on the side of repression after the Panchaea incident. One can draw analogies to the current state of society which is divided on race and caste rather than augmentation. However, this tension is never really felt through the game. It tries to enforce the feeling through police checks throughout and poverty at Golem city but none of them really strike an emotional cord. In fact, the variety across the locations is sorely lacking, especially when the original Deus Ex managed to convey much better ambiance through its rudimentary graphics but awesome soundtrack. There is just one antagonist who appears at the end and even then I inadvertently defeated him in seconds with weapon misfire that brought him right next to me. What's worse is that the game has been left open for a sequel without a proper ending. The Marvel-like in-credit cutscene makes it even more unbearable since the game could have definitely used a conspiracy story arc and if it was thought of, it should have been part of the main game rather than DLCs or sequels. I am not too enticed at this moment about playing as Adam Jensen once again only to have the story tie up somehow with the original game and JC Denton. This is pretty much evident by the desperate attempts being made to put in to play all the main characters from the original game.
Moving on to other extraneous aspects of the game, the pre-order consumables turned out to be absolutely unnecessary since the game is benevolent with XP if you engage in exploration. Also, the micro-transactions are thankfully unneeded. Stealth gameplay does not require any ammunition, so you are left with a lot of cash as well. As far as augmentations go, hacking and invisibility are the only ones I ever needed to explore the entire map at a decent pace.The Breach mode also deserves a mention here since I am least enamoured by it having experience it partly during the main game. This makes it  pretty evident that there is hardly any depth to this game and as I mentioned previously, the developers are blindly following the Deus Ex template without proper thinking and integration. I almost forgot to mention DX12 which was unusably buggy till recent patches and just as it has finally reached a level of polish, it is essentially useless since the game doesn't offer much replayability and I am not inclined to spend on DLCs unless there is a bargain-basement sale. A post-game check revealed that I missed just one side mission - " 01011000" and hence I am satisfied with my gameplay. Also, there is only one "either or" mission selection scenario in the game and a properly timed save allows one to try out both, even though you have to eventually select one of the options.
To conclude, on its own, this would be a "just above average" game. Being part of the Deus Ex universe only makes it even worse and is more or less a slap on the face of long term fans.  For the sake of the franchise, I hope they abandon the protagonist and somehow complete the story arc  (even if through DLCs) before the next iteration so that we can have a Deus Ex game that doesn't have to follow the shadow of the original game and fail miserably while doing so.

Pro:

Con:
However Some years ago some changes were made that will doom this game before Barad Gularan is shattered to dust:
After Turbine locked out Codemasters, all servers were converged to the US. Eversince, the quality for EU players is diminished. This goes especially for riding War Mounts, which is required to be responsive but a sad joke in reality. Despite several updates, rubberbanding and 5ish second delays are still common.
Along with this change, they seem to have let go all engine related workforce. After quickly introducing a DX11 render path at the time, they simply stop to develop graphics any further. The game looks and feels more and more ancient; textures, animations and immersion feel exactly as old as the game is.
The only people that seem to still work for Turbine are creative artists. The Battle for Helms Deep also introduced instances to play the Siege of Helms Deep which corresponding to their technical possibilities (see above) was realised okay. However 12 months later bugs and inconsistencies in these instances are still unfixed.
All in all:
If someone would invest into Lotro to update its ancient engine and do something else than publish new outfits and mount textures, it could provide a great experience and it would be a blast to see Sauron take his final glimpse, but in today's state, I feel the lidless eye will still shine at the time they have to pull the plugs. I would love to recommed this game with all my heart, but I cannot suggest to get into this game that presents crippled graphics, is PayToWin and charges you generously for features that should be free.

I am not writing this to buck the trend of Postive Reviews, nor am I writing this to troll. It's simply my opinion.
Brothers is a game that is... disappointing. Really disappointing. Sure it's fun to play and some of the setpieces are amazing, but as Yahtzee said in his review of this (and Papers Please), it's just too short. It takes about 2 hours to pass, and that's it. Unlke Limbo, which is also a very short game, there is nothing particularly memorable about this one. Pretty much everything that happened in the story is easily predicted, and when SPOILER WARNING! SPOILER WARNING! HOOT HOOT, PUT IT ON MUTE! your girl companion kisses the older brother whilst the younger brother is jealous, it's so painfully obvious that she's about to stab you in the back, which she predictably does right after the cutscene.
The soundtrack also starts to really grate on me after a while: I don't hate a capella, but this just sounds like Throat Singing to me. It's hard to take the drama seriously when there's a bunch of people going "EEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEH OOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOH EHHHHHHHHHHHHH" in the background at a ridiculously loud volume.
The two main brothers are also pretty boring stereotypes: the younger one is "shy and nervous" because he accidentally offed his Mum when he was yonnger, and the older one is "cool and cocky." The older one is actually bearable though at least he doesn't constantly whine about his Mum.
I paid/downloaded this game because I wanted to see for myself if Yahtzee was being a bit too unkind to it, and also because the reviews suggested that perhaps he was wrong. So I came into the game with a pretty neutral bias. However, I beliee Yahtzee is right on the money with his review on this game. It's good but not memorable, and it's just too short. My individual complaints are about the bad story, the soundtrack and how that last plot twist was so stupid and unnecessary and-SERIOUSLY, WHY DID YOU HAVE TO KILL HER? SHE WAS SO NICE AND COOL!
Anyway, I doubt this will show up on the review page anyway but if it does, make sure that if you do decide to buy it, take the game with a pinch of salt.
P.S. I don't care what you say, the Spider battle at the end is almost a complete rip off of Limbo's Spider battle.

Formula Fusion has bought back happy memories of time spent ploughing through the WipEout games in a way no other game has been able to yet.
The game is in Early Access but what is included so far portrays the direction of the game well. The three tracks are varied in theme, layout and challenge. Niagara GP is a good intro track, Manna Hatta offers a good challenge.
The Camera is unusual but once you have adapted to it, it feels better than Wipeout cameras. Showing me more of what I want to see as opposed to being tied to the craft as it was in previous AG racers.
I am happy with the state the game is in, well worth it for the cost and I am excited to play each new build and see a little more of where the game is progressing!

Everything in this is great, the graphical quality is amazing and the artstyle is a modern reboot of the older WipeOut.
Obviously this game is in early access, so there are SOME quirks such as the handling which is always being improved as updates continue to be released. There is SOME frame drops in some of the much larger circuits in normal races against opponents, though this can easily be fixed with LoD models of the crafts.
One thing that mainly annoys me is the particle effects emitting from the craft when going over boost pads. The speed in which they travel backwards makes the craft look like its moving slow, not faster, and the rockets not having better particles. But again, can easily be fixed later on.
In lower graphical qualities, the settings appear to be rendered at a lower resolution and then scaled up, which is something I personally don't find very appealing to the eyes.
The crafts' sounds are very basic, and could do with something new to make them sound a bit more powerful. Maybe something similar to craft sounds from WO2048. Maybe something different with every craft speed class to make it all sound "fast", rather than a low-pitched hum.
Other than the "issues" listed above, I find this in-progress game very fun. Keyboard controls could do with a little tweaking, though!
TL;DR: negative reviews are mainly existing because this is an Early Access title. Don't let that be the deciding factor for you, This game has serious potential. You won't regret it.

BugZy\'s Review: One More Line - A great little arcade game
The following is my opinion.
One More Line is a great little arcade/party game where you swing around circles on a randomly generated course in an attempt to beat your high score or your friends, colouring the track with the constantly growing trail of your semicircle character.
You must hold the “space” key (“A” if you wish to play using an Xbox controller and “X” for PlayStation controllers) in a skillfully timed manner to navigate through the course, trying not to crash on the edges of the map or the circles that you swing around. Be careful though, because one mistake and you’re gone.
The game features 2-4 player local co-op so you can race against your mates in a bunch of different gamemodes such as Chaos, Destruction, Time Attack and Survival, or if you don’t have any friends you can play by yourself and try to beat your own high score.
As you play and accumulate mileage you automatically unlock new hats and trails to customise your icon, to show off to your friends how hardcore you are.
The game is small, but for $3, I believe anyone looking for something to play with mates should have it.
I rate One More Line 8/10 boomerangs.

I think this is a great game, and it has been a blast to play.  But I think it all depends on your play style.  I have always enjoyed taking the stealthy, non-lethal approach in games like this.  I also love to explore and find all the hidden areas.  So far, I have spent almost 62 hours and I am in the final area.  I'm sure this game could be completed far quicker using a run and gun style, which I might try on the next play through just for a different experience.  But the greatest amount of satisfaction comes in making it through an area without being seen while still picking up all the good stuff.  Also, the side quests are essential to making this game longer and more fun.  Some can only be found through exploration, so be sure to look around!
Pros:
* Great stealth game
* Lots of fun augmentations to play with
* Very few bugs in my playthrough and almost no crashes
* Good pacing and stat progression throughout the game. You feel powerful, but never overpowered.
* Extremely detailed areas
Cons:
* After the first few hours, there isn't much to spend money on and you end up with a lot of it
* Before leaving an area, it is sometimes necessary to consult a wiki to make sure you aren't missing any side quests since those are the meat of the game.
* Some augs are hard to use with the default keyboard mappings. A good mouse with lots of buttons is critical so you can remap the aug abilities.
Overall, I didn't feel the game was too short.  But again, that was due to my play style.  If you are only looking for a good FPS, look elsewhere.  If you like a good RPG/FPS/Stealth hybrid with nice emergent gameplay, this is your game.  You won't be disappointed.

Well looks like I'm the only one who likes this game? I think the game is great, not as great as Human Revolution or Deus Ex 1. but great enough to be classified  as a deus ex game. (Deus Ex Invisible War was a bad game.)  The game fails to be memorable as the other 2 games because ever since Deus Ex 1 set the bar for the deus ex game with the best storytelling. Mankind Divided feels like a story primarily focusing on Adam Jensen's life... instead of focusing on the real problems such as the Illuminati and the augment segregation. Instead we spend our time hunting terrorists and rarely (like 3 missions.) you go after the Illuminati. And this isn't a horrible thing... it is just it breaks away from the traditional Deus Ex storytelling. The story tells it's tale really well. But you're going to have to get used to the fact that it's a different experience than usual. But the side missions were hell of a lot better than HR.... the side missions are kinda like little nostalgic trips to those who have played the first Deus Ex game.
Gameplay and the level design is where the game truly shines. You have so many ways to play the game it's usually crazy, with the combinations of the augments, weapons and other items which can make your build work whether it's stealth, loud, lethal or non lethal and it's not like you are stuck with a certain combination is limited to one style. You can combine many augments to approach different ways to complete a mission. And speaking of missions, the level design is absolutely prefect. Probably the best I've ever seen (And I'm talking about the single map missions such as GARM, Golem City, Dubai and London are excellent and well done. Hidden routes scattered everywhere which gives the explorers a chance to fully appreciate the work Eidos Monteral has done.
As for the microtranactions, breach and the season's pass (which the worst part about this game in general.) I'm surprised the season pass was lower than usual for a season's pass (regarding seasons passes are always a 60 dollar offer when a AAA game is released.) I feel like a season pass is unnecessary, (unless you really wanna play that "Bomb threat" DLC. The DLC that came out so far are actually really good but not worth a season pass. Also single use microtransactions are a "lolwut" moment for me. Seeing how Enix had the balls to do this doesn't surprise me seeing what they've done with Hitman last year. And also if you really want praxis point/credits... there are trainers that are easily accessible and defeats the entire purpose of the Microtransaction. And if you don't want a trainer, there is enough praxis points from farming/grinding a bit to nab a praxis point. trust me praxis points isn't hard to earn. And as for breach, breach sucks... they could have used the time to make breach toward the main game to fix the ending.
So the main game (Not breach, dlc and extra content.) deserves a 8/10. The story is fresh, there is a lot of content to go on in fact I haven't finished the game yet and I'm still at 72.2 hours. (but I've seen the ending before keep that in mind for a comment I'm going to make.)  The game isn't short as people make out to be, it's a matter of rushing through the game and taking your time to fully enjoy what the deus ex universe has to offer. This game can be a 10 hour game to some while others it can be a 50+ hours game.
As for the ending, it's rushed and I don't like it... but hey I'm not too upset because of 2 things.
1.) Mass Effect 3 ending was worse and had more impact on me which actually soured the mood, Deus Ex Mankind Divided did not.
2.) There is about 29 more years of Deus Ex lore still remaining to release a final game or 2 to catch up with the Denton Era... So I'm not surpirsed about the ending but slightly disappointed. Some closure would have been nice but even the Human Revolution endings weren't really special to begin with.

This is a must have in your library if you're into fighters, as a long time Mortal Kombat fan since the 90s while it is a fun game but it is not in top list of favorite MK Games but it is still enjoyable.
Firstly, you're gonna need a somewhat beefy PC to run this or else you're going to have problems, this game runs 60fps but the cut scenes are locked at 30.
The graphics are amazing, sometimes while playing single player i just like to look at how well designed some arenas are, like The Pit for example, animation is pretty good and character detail is near perfect.
The character roster to me is abysmal, not really a fan of the new characters that were introduced, and the stages are too limited and not memorable along with the music, the UI however is pretty good and design.
The online....i won't say it's dead but there are still a few players online but if that's an issue you can always hit up the forums and find some players, the netcode is absolute garbage but when it works it works.
There is a lot to do in the single player aspect and a nice reward system and unlockables as well as you progress in the game.
Fighting mechanics are pretty damn good, combos are kind of hard if you're new to the game but easy to master with a bit of practice.
The gore and violence is all there, Mr. Ed Boon and Co. Did not hold back at all, fatalities and brutalilties are top notch.
Conclusion, i would not pay full retail price for this, get it on sale.  I recommend playing Mortal Kombat Komplete Edition before this though if you haven't.

This was recommended to me by a good friend with a similar taste in games as me, this was a game I had heard of but never bothered looking into, I hadn’t watched the trailer or anything. I took a gander and it looked amusing so I thought I would give it a go and I was actually pleasantly surprised with what I found.
DLC quest is very simplistic. It hasn’t got a massively complex mind-twisting plot line, it isn’t overly hard gameplay wise, and it actually isn’t even that long of a game… but one thing for me was certain, despite all those things, it was very satisfying. It plays on the mechanics and features of classic adventure games well, and in a tasteful way. There’s so many references and fun things to find along the way that makes you chuckle to yourself and say “I see what they did there…” and I really think that the humour in this game is what makes it great even though it’s so simplistic.
The game also has this OCD “collect it all” thing going on as well, which I can never get enough of, especially if it’s somewhat easy to do. I spent around 2 hours on this game and left it 100% done, all “awardments”, all coins, everything. And it’s a great feeling being able to do that. It didn’t take long, sure. But I think it was just the right length, and didn't feel like it was all for nothing.
All in all, this game is great. And better yet, CHEAP. It has nice music, a wonderful humour to it, a somewhat interesting and random storyline, good controls and everything on that technical side and a great feel to it atmospheric wise.
Buy it!

After playing (and absolutely LOVING the first Trine), I went into this game with pretty high expectations... And let me tell you, it didn't meet them... It smacked them over the horizon with a giant hammer and set whole new levels of amazing!
The original Trine was one of my favourite games of all time, and still is, but now along comes Trine 2 and takes it many steps further!
It feels much bigger than the first game. The levels are even more beautiful and varied, the puzzles and area designs even more genius and fun to figure out, and just as in the first game, there are always multiple ways to overcome obstacles!
Example: Got a lake of lava to cross? Make stepping stones across it with levitation, or use the grappling hook to swing over it, or jump across some tricky timed platforms that will try to drop you in!
The platforming is solid, each character has a nice variety of abilities for you to learn and improve, and there plenty of new beasties for you to defeat (yes, it's not just skeletons over and over this time!)
Not only that, but there's also the added Goblin Menace DLC, which adds a great amount of new content! New enemies, new storyline, new music, and of course, new levels, each one with its own unique design and theme!
I really cannot give this game enough praise. The visuals are beautiful, colourful, and magical. The music is all fitting and wonderful to listen to. The game is just so much fun to play.
So if you enjoyed the first game, or even if you just enjoy platformers, with some light puzzling that won't destroy your brain, this gets my highest recommendations. It is unlike any other platformer I have ever experienced (other than the first Trine, of course, but even then it's still on a whole other level!)

I really want to recommend this game. It's a lot better than reviewers gave it credit for-- to be fair, it's nothing particularly special, but it's also a competent (if unspectacular) rail shooter that reminds me a lot of the ones I used to play back when I was a kid. Would I sooner play something like Time Crisis? Sure, but this scratches my arcade light gun shooter itch well enough.
Unfortunately, the PC port is all sorts of screwed up. It runs horribly on the highest settings (despite being a game that looks like it came out of the early 2000's), is incredibly prone to crashes (I went back to do the first level in order to complete a Challenge, and it crashed three times in a row at the end, costing me my progress), and the mouse controls have a certain level of sluggishness that really hurts a game like this.
What a shame. Like I said, this game is not the garbage fire that most reviewers claimed it was (which is to say, it's not a particularly good game, but it's far from awful), and I'm willing to overlook a lot of the issues (horrible sound quality, graphics that are about 15 years out of date, occasionally questionable level design) in the spirit of it pushing the right arcade nostlagia buttons for me, but these types of technical issues are simply inexcusable for a rail shooter. And while, to the developer's credit, they released some free DLC long after most devs would have left their game to rot, there's little hope that these issues will ever be fixed. Too bad.

I really liked this game, but I may understand it's not for everyone. Firstly this game is on-rail shooter, and as such this game is about dexterity and fast action, this goes more towards arcade then the fps. Secondly this game is about discovery. At first one may find this game too hard, but after choosing lower difficulties and leveling-up Rambo and acquiring new guns, things become much more enjoyable and addicting. I don't care about voice acting or graphic (some people complained about those), and in fact those aspects ware ok for me. There is a bit of nostalgia here as well, as the Rambo series was shown then I ware a child. The climate is here, and with each re-play of the maps one is discovering new elements and bonuses. Maps can be played with different styles, using different combos, different perks. Still this game is hard to master, I only managed to get three stars on second map (by the way I'm playing in offline mode, check achievements for proof). Since we are at 2nd map, yes there are some quick time events in this game, but there is also "no qte fails" perk which can be picked up, for 2nd map it's almost a must.
It is sad this game is no longer available at Steam store, however since it wasn't completely removed it seems it can come back in future, maybe there ware some copyright issues or something.

After recently watching  Stallone (again) in First Blood , I remembered this game got released in 2014, but at the time gave it a miss because of the negative reception it received, Fast forward to 2017 I decided to buy a physical copy as it was no longer available on the Steam Store (Amazon £9.99) , At first glance I thought this game looked ok for a last gen console port and as a Fan of Rail shooters I thought what the heck let's give it a playthrough , To my surprise the game very quickly captured the Rambo in me and before long I was hooked.
GFX are absolutely fine and the game runs at a solid 60fps, The Gameplay is easily the best part of the game, challenging but fair, the progression system keeps you interested with the promise of Rambo becoming stronger faster and better as you yourself learn how to combine the skill tree unlocks and weapon upgrades.
For anyone who likes fast paced action games which require an instinctive gameplay style (twitch reactions) this game is a must have and deserved much more praise than it got at the time of release.
I pretty much own every rail shooter worth having on PC, but Rambo The Video Game............. for me is easily the best, No gimmicks,  just plain old school gaming, in fact the only thing missing from Rambo is the ability to use a light gun, however KB/M controls I found to be excellent, with no aim assit or mouse acceleration, the game does reward those who are skilled in the art of aiming.. This game (or review) is not aimed at your typical CoD or Battlefield player, This is a Rail Shooter of the highest quality and IMHO requires  more skill than most recent AAA FPS games.
I have since purchased a Steam key from the Publisher on eBay as the retail disc does not include the Baler Team DLC.
Lessons to be learned ? Always trust your own instincts..  :d: Does not feel like a console port either.
Rambo unlike most Rail shooters (auto aim assited) requires some skill.
Verdict: Top marks easily the best Rail shooter on PC 10/10.

Stupid Rubbish Game

First...
What is a video game ?
Why do I play a video game ?
A Game is basically an entertaining activity, some are more stimulating than others, and some stimulate reactions over concentration. If you get this logic right; you can discover a whole world of possibilities through video games. Someone could just decide to create a "goat Simulator" for fun (and you would pretend to be a goat), or create a Massive Multiplayer Game where everybody interacts with each other to accomplish goals in the game.
There is a myriad of games out there today and some will tickle you to play, based on your interests of course.
About Lord of the Rings Online :
1st. Interests:
Yes I am interested in the Lord of the Rings lore. I like the Medieval style, the powerful evil, the hobbits, the elves, the faith, the glory, the flowers, name it. I read the complete story years ago, way before the movies. Am I a complete sold out and corrupt Lord of the rings fan ?  Nope, not at all. I just like the writing style and the human-side, possibly believable logic-reality-fantasy, story of it all.
2nd. The Genre:
MMO. I am not a MMO FAN, in fact, I hate MMO's. They are a repeatable-similar-cut-and-paste infinite same thing said differently, lather repeat. This type of game is kinda of free-roaming-reading do the same thing. The story is vaguely known, the sense of it is tasteless.  Just roam, talk to someone and pretend it is fun. Now that's my point. (Lord of the GATHErings I called it back in my debut)
3rd. Entertainment:
Is Lotro entertaining? Well... I must say that something was entertaining, and still is... after playing this type of game for so long now... and still playing it !
What happened to my anti-MMO player side ?  It got impressed !!
The cutscenes were a nice feature that propels you directly into the current conflict (linked to the departure of the fellowship...and following right down in their footsteps is totally great. The feeling of being part of the LOTRO world was achieved greatly with all those characters and storyline. The sense of my character being known to this fake-world was cool.  There is also an outrageous number of QUESTS ! From main quests, side quests, skill quests, deeds quests, trait quests to crafting quests, I am probably forgeting some.. there is so much.
Yes, the graphics are now outdated even with full DirectX11. But it doesn’t get you out of the story that much. If you like the Lore, you will probably find it cartoony acceptable.
What was the most entertaining to me, was the fact that I can take out the time I want in the LOTRO world to do whatever I wish. Roleplay with some stangers, do quests, craft, manage my house and garden decorations, look up the price of some useless item that some people desire. (Of course, in other MMO's you can also lose your time the way you want) But the most appreciable assets in those moments; The sounds !
Everytime I hooked up my headphones.. I was submerged in the wild environment, the ambiance and the tension felt everywhere in the wilderness.
LOTRO convinced me where no other MMO could. The sound ! Especially in Moria... this is where it all began down the hill for me... I became a LOTRO FAN :) in Moria.
Before that, It was Lord of the Gatherings !
I hopped in from time to time with a friend or two... running beside them and trying to follow up their leveling. Which was a pain ! Since they were so much into it and were leveling Fast in VIP mode.
OK Now we get to VIP and the Free to Play thing.
YES, before... believe it or not. IT was not FREE. You had to pay the game, and subscribe for the experience. I was not playing at that time.
It then became f2p. Which is a matter of attracting new players to try the game and hopefully, make them pay to achieve their pleasure.
It is FREE totally up to lvl 20... then you get the point, that if you want to continue and level up... or have some fun in this world, you will have to grind a lot of time to achieve some goals and earn some turbine points (In game store currency) to buy some useful needed quests pack or stuff. Yup, it’s a business world, where programmers need to eat, and infrastructure guys needs funds to host the game on Technical Horsepower, If you want a free computer, free energy, free internet, free games... well... Then you better get out and change this world to accept FREE as a currency.
In the meantime, you won’t have any time left to play your favorite game, you will probably be outside growing your food and waiting the harvest to exchange some for... lets say... a computer! :)
Is this game entertaining? YES, to me it is! And it is well worth some money. I bought some Turbine points with real money when there was a double bonus points event... and then waited for the 30-50% rebate on quests pack that comes along once or twice a year... It was well worth the ride. (More than VIP)
4th factor: Replayability:
Yes you can replay over and over again. Let’s say with another character.  There is so much quests... that you can probably live a lot of adventures in a completely different manner.
The rest will be similar, in traits, deeds, skills and all with a slight new flavor. It's the same Game.
5th factor. Price over time spent:
If you pay 60$ per year for the new call of duty and you only play the campaign like me... well it is a shame. The game is much more satisfying online versus people. You can frag for a full year ! 60$ for 300 hours of game play.
But for me... Since 3d Shooters is not my Main Genre, I play the campaign for 15 hours, do some LAN party with friends... and then put it on the shelf. 60$ for 40 hours ! Not the most satisfying purchase.
In LOTRO, I spent about 70$ and got... if one level is 3-4 hours roughly...  320 hours since 2010 and I am not done at all with my purchases !  (Played with independent Client)
It is well worth the run.
If you are a Lord of the Rings enthusiast, you will probably like it even more. Besides that, it is well balanced in simplicity and complexity and its pace follows comfortably your period of learning the game.
It's a MMO, you may be charmed by the genre or you may hate it. But from an adventurous point of view, even with my hate of MMO, I still have fun in this game.
Conclusion, LOTRO is good, and for myself, my adventures continue mainly because of the subject world; Lord of the Rings, and its outstanding engineering sounds that keeps me coming back into the woods.

As it stands, this is pretty lame. It lacks what I thought really made the WipEout games fun: The atmosphere. It really felt like you were in a near future, deadly racing competition with high stakes. All the cool looking ships, the high tech dangerous weapons, and the smooth, fast steering of the ships. The OST added hugely to the experience, and add it althogether, you had an incredible, atmospheric, futuristic, intense racing game.
I don't know what the road map is for this game, but as it stands, it has none of that. There are long stretches of road where you have no music. Just the quiet noise of the engine. When you grind against the wall, it doesn't feel like there's any impact, you just slow down a bit. Additionally, it sounds like dragging a cinder block across concrete. Not very inspiring. While the steer stays within the ballpark of the previous WipEout games, it doesn't feel as good. It doesn't feel like there's much impact, and the, as it stands, calm enivironment of the game takes away from the intensity of the games that this claims to be the spiritual successor of.
As it stands, I can't recommend this. Slap it on your wishlist, and wait. I've been told by a reddit user that the game will likely have a full release in Q3 2016, because, as he said "That's when the budget should run out." So, hold off. Wait for the (hopefully) better experience.

I was curious about this game after I played FAST Racing NEO for Wii U, for which I was a bit disappointed from the big amount of glitches present in the game, so I decided to buy it to try something similiar, but different at the same time.
Let's start from the game's positive aspects.
- Tracks desing is great, each one of them has got an unique setting and a different kind of driving design that makes them easily recognizeable from each other.
Mannahatta is absolutely astonishing, with it's rain effect and under costruction/hi-tech scenario in which tha track is installed.
Atlas Torres concept is almost never treated in actual racing video games, so I suggest you to check some pics of the track to make you understand what I mean.
Niagara GP track design is good, but it's a little bit naked of elements surrounding the track. An update is planned the next month for Niagara GP, and I hope for a good revamp of the track.
- Ships are separated in classes, which is a good thing for racing and time trial competitions. This choice prevents a single ship to prevail on the other ones, and gives the opportunity to try different competition settings. F4000 is the main ship they're working on actually, and it feels really good to drive. The ship sliding feels natural and fun to play. F3000 is a lot faster than F4000, but it has similiar physics to the last I mentioned, so it feels a little uncomfortable to drive for who has never tried it. Just make some practice, and you'll find out it doesn't feel that bad to drive.
- Game's graphics looks amazing for this alpha stage; details for the two available ships and for the tracks themselves are truly curate. Graphic effects are still a bit strange, but for this alpha stage they're pretty good. I couldn't imagine how the game would look in it's complete release.
- The actual OST of the game is good to enjoy, I would like to hear something more like this in the future releases. More Drum 'n' Bass, please!
- Practice Mode is good for those that don't understand well the physics of the game, making you avoid to touch walls with antigravitational waves that pull you at the center of the track. Give it a try if you just bought the game and you want to get into the game a little.
Let's now talk about the game negative aspects.
- As of now, there are only two items available, and you could set just one of them available for a race. They still feel weird to use, as they don't slow you down when you get hit by them; you just lose shield. I hope they will add more of them in a Mario Kart way, and that they will be revisited with the full release.
- A single boost pad sometimes could give you a double boost out of nothing. A glitch that needs to be fixed soon.
- Passing between two near boost pads with the ship could cause you to get a doubled boost. This compromises/randomizes a little time trial competitions, and could be extremely clutch on races when you don't except to get a double boost.
- Opponent's AI is still a bit easy to beat. Also, the frame rate drops and then fluctuates between 25-45 fps on tracks like Niagara GP and Atlas Torres when AI is moving. An issue that needs to be fixed soon.
I also want to talk about neutral aspects of the game.
- The ship's handling feel ok by now, but it's still a bit woody, especially when you're trying to countersteer. But R8 Games is actually working on it, releasing with every patch a refreshed and refined handling system.
Even if there are a lot of things to fix for this game, it's still in early access, and to see an huge work like that drives me to think at what the game could look once it's finished, and to tell you to buy the game if you like racing games.
Also, there are a lot of features that are coming to the game in the future, like online multiplayer races, endurances, more items and a lot of stuff like that, so the game will have a lot to offer.
If you like Antigravity racing games or the Wipeout series, give Formula Fusion a chance, you won't be disappointed once the game will be released.

I'm a big big Wipeout fan. From the first one on a PS one, then to 2097 on my PC with my Voodoo2 card and then on my PS2. So i backed this up...
CONTROLS:
@ the devs. Seriously. Do you have magnets on your walls?! I found out today why i really REALLY dislike this one so far.
It's not that it doesn't have the aesthetics of the franchise it aspires to be (even though it has the same people that did them what they are... still eartly access. Character could come further down the line.)
It's that the craft slides left and right even if you are not touching the controls. It's not a flight sim! Yes they are hovering vehicles, but the core gameplay is racing. I'm expecting that if i don't hold the stick, then it'll go forward, not forward and carry momentum sideways. I ended up trying to correct the flight path only to hit like a ping pong ball left and right.
CAMERA:
When i hit on a wall, the camera jumps left and right to simulate the hit. Understood. But it does that in so few frames that is almost instant and alienating/jarring to watch. Put a couple more frames in it, or just don't shake it as much. Put some spark particles on the side of the wing that touches the barrier and put a "sssshshhrhrhrhrhhsshsh" sound.
And why is my gamepad controlling a mouse pointer in the menu? I'm not playing a PlayStation 1 point and click adventure game. I was going left and right with the stick waiting to see options being highlighted only to realise that i was moving a circle.

The graphics are great, the tracks are ok so far, but ship handling and physics are still terrible which are IMO the most important aspects of any racing game. Even more in an AG racing game. R8 is making progress, but I think the effort is not in the right place.

tl;dr
At first it was a bad early access (at least if you expected same level of gameplay as in Wipeout series) but since last 2 releases it seems to be much, much better. Keep an eye on this one if you like AG racers.

One More Line is a hypnotic game of survive.  The concept is crazy simple; don't hit any objects or veer off the course.  The problem is you can't simply steer where you want to go.  Your only means of changing direction is to grapple hook onto the direct objects that clutter the track.  Once attached to these objects you'll start to spin around them and will continue doing so until you release.
The speed of your ship is what makes this such a challenging game.  You only have split seconds to decide if you should attach yourself to an object.  The farther away from the object the better as you'll have more time to think and examine any immediate threats.  This is a huge problem as one of the easiest ways to fail is to swing smack into a near by object while rotating.  Also, if you're too close when you hook on your ship rotates so quickly its basically impossible to tell which direction you'll be heading once you release.
As you continue playing though the game you'll unlock different options to customize your experience.  You can choose different outfits for your character and different tracks for the contrails of your ship.  These choices aren't very thrilling but they at least provide an excuse to continue playing.  Then if the challenge of beating your high-score isn't enough to keep you entertained there is an option for local multiplayer which can go up to four players.  A series of different game modes offer quite a bit of variety for multiplayer.  This is a very fast paced and unpredictable game the would be perfect for parties or a good laugh at a competitive get to together.
The sound design is where this game really shines.  The music is thrilling, it keeps you pumped up and ready to face the crazy trials this game will put you through.  Death is so quick and is written off almost instantly.  Simply click the retry button and you thrown straight back into the world.  Meanwhile the game cheers you on in its rhythmic robot voice singing out "retry" or "one more line".  This feels kind of reminiscent of Minecraft's "just one more block" mentality.
There is no doubt that this is a super light game.  That being said One More Line is quite fun and very addicting.  Most rounds won't even last half a minute.  I almost wish the ships speed would have started out slower and got faster as you progressed upwards.  My main complaint is there is little to no time to react and stop yourself from swinging right into another object.  Also there are times when I'm certain I press the grapple button a fair distance away to find myself slamming right into the object.  Its not perfect by any means but its an inexpensive game with a amusingly simple mechanic.

I've tried many times to write a decent review of Mankind Divided, but I failed because it all comes down to preference. Do you like the setting? Do you feel that microtransactions are not invading your gaming experience? Is the storyline enough to keep you entertained for more than 10 hours? Then this may be for you. However, although I recommend the game to a veteran Deus Ex player, I cannot recommend it to new players. The storyline is bland, excessively diluted, and requires multiple media to be enjoyed fully. If you dont buy the prequel - the novel Black Light, which bridges the gap between Human Revolution and this game - and Children's Crusade, you miss many points of interest that would have let you experience the story in the correct way. This is not acceptable in my opinion. And it is not acceptable that a new patch causes more troubles, or even opens more bugs - for example last patch saw a main characfter spawn two times and be alive and dead at the same time -.
That being said, this is probably the closest "positive"  review to a "negative" that I would give. I dont want Adam's adventures to end, but the developers need to do at least three things in the next installment:
1 - hire a better writer
2 - find another publisher or fight off the bad influence of corporate businessmen that just want to fiddle with the game to gain more money
3 - focus on what Human Revolution offered and return to it's glory as close as possible
I have enjoyed the game mechanics very much, but everything else needs a major return to HR's pacing, art style and characters.

I'm on board with others who say it's about a 6-7/10. But if I have two options, "Recommended" or "Not Recommended", it's hard for me to assign most of that scale to "Not Recommended" and say that it needs to be an 8.0-8.5 before I'll recommend it. I love the DX series, the original blew me away, and HR was a proper prequel. But MD strayed not in just one direction, but several that made it more of an action stealth game rather than a stealth action game.
Some Pros:
- Interesting new augs, though some of them seem borrowed from other games (i.e. Blink from Dishonored)
- Rich city, Prague, with detailed background
- Cleaner, more interesting HUD than HR
Some Cons:
- Politics have influenced this game heavily. I could swear there was an altercation where someone said "hands up! Don't shoot!" to the police. I mean...really?
- That rich city? That's where you really do most of the action. The developers used the subway system to break the city up into zones, thinking this will be enough to be different, like ME was with Hengsha, Detroit, RBS, Montreal, Singapore and of course Panchaea. In MK, you have Prague, Golem City, the GARM facility, and London. And there isn't a whole lot going on in the GARM facility, and London is MK's Panchaea.
- The augs are stupid overpowered. Yes, you are hamstrung for a bit, but that doesn't last long, and then you get a happy loot crate of PRAXIS kits to get you to super soldier status. Like others, I played not using them much, and even added a rule - no knock-outs - just to keep it challenging. It still wasn't, even on the highest difficulty.
- I spent far more time in side quests than I should have, but it wasn't for the abundance of them - it was because the designers thought it would be awesome that a few fetch quests should cross loading screens not once, not twice, but FIVE TIMES. I think Adam Jensen was just as bored walking down the subway tunnel as I was.
- The plot. Well...the plot was something out of Splinter Cell, or 24. Big bad is a mercenary group that wants to have someone else take credit? Okay. Where's the intrigue and suspense? The original DX was chalk full of it, and you became involved continuously on plot points involving the core elements of DX - Illuminaiti, MJ12, the all-seeing eye, etc. Here, you are chasing down a pro-aug group in a run down city that practically telegraphs "Hey! These are the fall guys!" and the musclebound Hulk Hogan you just happen to meet in the back alley for no reason other than to advance the plot? Of COURSE he's the big bad. He's eloquent. With lots of guns and muscles. Why the hell was he hanging out right there if he was supposed to allow the pro-aug group to be the fall guy? Has he NOT read the rules of being an evil guy? You don't hang around for the hero to see you and make a connection that maybe you're the real bad guy!
Yes, more cons than pros, but I've loved the series and put up with IW right from the start. The game has beautiful graphics, an intuitive (somewhat) interface, some interesting sideplots, but I'm not sure this is the DX game we wanted. It might be the Splinter Cell game we never asked for, but it's not formulaic of DX.
