Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is the epitome of the phrase, one step forward, two steps back. I hate comparing it to Human Revolution as it was something special, but Mankind Divided feels like an underwhelming, repackaged experience. That’s not to say it’s a bad game as there’s a decently sized city to explore and the Breach mode is highly entertaining, but it’s a step down from a five-year-old game. Most of the supporting cast of characters never fully become developed, and it doesn’t help that there’s no stakes throughout the eight to twenty hour long campaign. No one is truly put in a situation of peril.
Worst yet, the scenario layout for the main missions is easily described as uninspired, lazily slapping shortcuts all over the place. Granted, there are various ways to approach each area, but every single scenario is broken down in the exact same way where there’s far too many open grates to hide in and easily accessible security terminals to gain access to. Even the fantastic conversation system is less impressive due to it being underutilized this time around. Thankfully, the core stealth component is as exceptional as ever and even the gunplay is more of a viable option. This is aided with the additional abilities to Jensen’s already capable arsenal. Despite being a successor to Human Revolution, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided somehow ends up feeling more like a predecessor. I still recommend to buy it and play it though, but not for the full price.

You don't sit down and play for an hour (after the first hour, anyway).  You just check in for a few minutes every few hours or so as progress continues even when the game is shut down.  It scratches that management itch pretty well.  And yes.  That rainbow-haired girl in blue
pure brony bait.  Unashamed, at that, which is actually rather nice.  No worries, non-bronies -- if you don't know anything about the fandom then you likely won't even notice the references.
Noteworthy is the bonus/reset feature.  At any time you can reset the game.  It's a sort of new game+ feature in that resetting applies a permanent, stackable muliplier to your progress that affects time-based content.  The more you've done, the higher the multiplier.  The higher the multiplier, the faster things move.  As you retain in-game achievements and certain stats, it's actually tempting to utilize.
Finally, there's a special currency earned by achieving certain milestones.  This currency can be used to purchase a variety of bonuses including -X- hours worth of progress, increases to the multiplier, additional time blocks (the stat that determines how much you can do at once), bonuses to stat gain rates and more.
Also: a bouquet of flowers is going to cost you more than a private island.  One of the girls wants two of them.  Another wants just over 15 million dollars worth of tequila, which amounts to all of 25 small glasses.  Apparenlty inflation skyrockets like nothing we've ever seen before in the next few years.

The game has 4 missions based on the first movie, 7 missions for Rambo II and 5 missions from Rambo III. There's also free DLC that has 3 missions that are quite enjoyable but the last one had unexplainable bad fps for me.
I'll recommend a playthrough of this game if you want something simple to blast through.

Ok lets start off with this gem. You are Sergeant Rex Power Colt and basically you dont give any f***s. Rex Colt is on a mission to stop a mad man from arming nuclear warheads and blowing up the already destoryed world! This game is similar in fasion to Far Cry 3, but it fully embraces its silly 80's Sci-fi action. This is what makes the game fully enjoyable as an expansion. The main story line is tons of cheesy one liners and typical 80's plot twists, but still tells a convincing of enough story for you to want to play. If you were to pick up this game for the story alone, you are looking at the wrong game.
The character cast is limited to about 3-4 main characters and numerous minor characters. I will not spoil each group of MC's, but each feels completely at home in this sci-fi world Ubisoft has created. Some of the characters are your typical one dimensional 80's cheese, but that's what you WANT to expect. This game is all the cliches of the past made just for today.The characters flow into the story quiet well and it makes the game into an amazingly stupid action title. Cutscences in the game are presentated as "arcade style 32 Bit" interactions and add to the atmosphere of the working sci-fi title.
The levels that you interact with are great. It terms of size relative to Far Cry 3, it is just alittle smaller than the first island you start one. There are not alot pacing breaks.Entering buildings and having a pause to say go into a dungeon are a thing of the past. Most of the world is on the map and never take away from the game itselves. It's completely open world and thats great and bad. It's great to because you are a cyborg bad♥♥♥♥♥and can do whatever you want. The downside is that it lacks the depth of exploring and uncovering mysterys. They still have hidden files and items, but that alone has something lacking that Far Cry 3 had going for it. The hidden items reveal backstory on characters and thoghts. What it has that Far Cry 3 does not have are tons and tons of hidden easter eggs. I won't ruin them but when you find them you will chuckle at each and every one of them. This expansion is a single player expericence only, unlike Far Cry 3 which has some multiplayer elements.
Gameplay wise it is identical to Far Cry 3 minus a few things. Since you are a bad♥♥♥♥♥mofo cyborg you can run infinitly and you no longer take any fall damage. This is because you are a cyborg....do i really need to explain the science behind it? Moving on you get about one of each item and upgrade it with the "money" you get in the game. These futuristic guns are not only badass but become better with upgrades. Just like Far Cry 3, you will find that one or so gun that will be your bread and butter (for me it was the pistol and machine gun). The hunting is not as in depth as it was in Far Cry 3. It exists but usually as a means to upgrade your weapons or complete achievements.
In terms of replayability it is moderate to high depending on what you want to get out of it. Since this goes through UPLAY and not steam the achievements are fun to get but dont count outside of UPLAY. This count be a damper to some people, me on the other hand did not mind and still 100 percent this game. After trying to get all the achievements it is great to just run around and kill stuff or explore the island and find all the items and easter eggs. You could restart the campaign, but most people will not and be satisified with the game.
The achievements are fun and enjoyable for anyone who is a completionist. As i stated before, they count towards UPLAY achievements and not STEAM. Some could be time consuming to level up or upgrade weapons, but if you are an expericenced gamer you can get 95 percent on the first playthrough. My ranking on difficulty for getting all the achievements ranges from easy to average.
The video, audio and control layout is basically all the same as Far Cry 3. The graphics are great just like Far Cry 3, but it is a darker game with lazers and light beams lighting up the screen. This is the majority of the "light" in the game. It is suppose to be a destroyed wasteland from a nuclear war so dont expect lush bright sun effects. the audio is superb with the soundtrack taking the cake. It is one of the most memoriable soundtracks of any video game in recent history. With typical 80's sci fi movie sound and power anthems it will make your experience in this world that much more enjoyable. The layout for controls is the same but the tutorials are fun and make it easy to get back into a FPS if you have forgotten (i know you havent).
My final thoughts on Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon. This game brings back fun into a game without sacrificing too much core gameplay. it is a fun game from beginning to end without too big of hiccups of run here and do that. It is just long enough and just short enough to never feel like it stays too long in one place. The sad part is when you finally complete the game it will leave you wanting more. Many gamers will find it hard to find fault in this game and enjoy this expansion.
My overall rating for this review will be 4.5 out of 5.

By now I think most people know how GTA plays, so I won't go into that too much. What I will say is the online and offline play offers vastly different but excellent gameplay opportunities.
The online multiplayer is one of the better sandboxes on the market that you can enjoy with friends. Freeroam around the entirety of the map and get up to all sorts of shenanigans with dozens of players. You also have the option of playing matchmade game modes like standard DM, TDM, races, and a whole slew of special game modes. Some of my favourites: Stunt races where you're basically on hot wheels tracks, and hunting pack where you have one player playing as the driver of a car that'll explode if it goes too slowly, and others trying to either stop them or get them to their destination.
The single player campaign still remains one of my favourite stories in a while, because it really makes you feel the fantasy of planning and pulling off major heists. Some scenes feel straight out of the Italian Job or Ocean's 11. The characters are memorable, and not always for good reasons. You'll figure that out yourself pretty early. These are not nice people.
There's a reason why this game has sold so many copies. Give it a try the next time it's on sale or you're drunk and want to spend money. You'll be glad you did.

Having written a fairly negative review in March, here are my impressions as of May 2016 :
I'm still not sure whether to recommend this or not. The game still severely lacks content, with only two crafts (only one being usable in races) and three tracks. Considering that there is a greyed-out "garage" section on the main menu, I suppose that more content is coming.
Since the last version however, many of the problems related to the physics have been addressed. The game now feels way more consistent.
The crafts still handle a bit counter-intuitively, but it now feels like it's by design, and that I just need to "git gud" in order to win some races. I still tend to finish most of the races dead last, unless I go for "practice mode", which seems to make things easier. There should be some way to control the difficulty level.
As far as graphics go, the game looks nice and shiny. The tracks look really nice, with fairly high resolution textures on the materials, detailed reflections and really convincing (physically-based?) lighting. However, this comes at the price of performance. The game is very taxing on hardware, especially on the Mannahatta track. I get 40~50 FPS on that track at 1080p, Epic details (i5 3750k @ 4 GHz,  16 Gb RAM, GTX 980).
Sound effects are a bit lacking, and the music is kind of bland for the most part.
It is still early days for that game. It does however show some potential. Hold your purchase if you want to have a ton of fun right now, or bite the bullet if you want to help the developers deliver what could be a decent spiritual successor to Wipeout.
Original review :

The handling is pretty good, though it takes a bit of getting used to. Really, really nice graphically, especially the Niagara GP circuit. You can notice the different teams handling differently (personal fave so far is the team "OK") so there's nice variation. You also get the same sense of adrenaline rush and reward after practice that you get in Wipeout, which I love.
Downsides: As mentioned, the controls take a bit of getting used to. At first it's very easy to over-steer, making it feel like drunk driving, but once you get the hang of it, it's not so bad. Could do with being a /little/ less sensitive though IMO. The game also seems to have mixed performance. I can run it smoothly on highest settings, but it seems like every so often the game ♥♥♥♥s itself for a few seconds and lags really hard, and then goes back to normal. Optimisation problems maybe? Turning the graphics/resolution down has not fixed this. Also, the rockets seem really overpowered as a weapon. If you get hit by one when your shields are at 3/4 full or less, it seems like you just die instantly, it's ridiculous. Unless I'm just really unlucky.
Problems aside though this has serious potential and I'd really love to see it succeed. It's nice how the devs listen to feedback from the fans too (if you're reading this, hi, R8!). Might be a bit pricey for the average gamer due to its Early Access status, but if you're a racing game or especially a Wipeout aficionado, it;s well worth the buy.

Single Player:
If you intend to buy this game solely for the single player, don't bother. Although the single player story is decent, with some pretty funny missions and moments, R* has decided to abandon single player expansions in place for GTA Online content for making more money. If you wish to buy this game for the single player, get it when it's like £10 or £15, NO MORE!
GTA Online (World):
The Online world multiplayer of this game revolves around using in-game currency, which can either be grinded or bought using Shark Cards, to buy stuff you want. From cars, weapons, garages and apartments, everything that you want, you will need earn cash to buy. The only problem is, the payouts for doing missions ansd heists (the best ways you make money) are constantly being nerfed and / or patched by R* to get you pay your real life hard-earned money on Shark Cards. There are many different kind of shark cards from Red Shark ($100,00 for £2) to Great White Shark ($8,000,000 for £60), this is how R* want you to get the in game cash to buy your stuff. The Great White Shark's $8,000,000 may sound like a lot, you may be thinking you can buy a lot of stuff in the game with that... wrong! The way the pricing works in the game will make you burn through a lot of that cash on maybe a few super cars and maybe a high end apartment... FOR £60!
This price gouging becomes increasingly more obvious with each DLC released. New vehicles are "drip-fed", with one vehicle sometimes every week (sometimes longer) in an attempt to try and prolong the life of the game and also encourage people to buy shark cards. And if you wanted to try a vehicle out in the single player in order to maybe avoid wasting your multiplayer cash on it, guess what? YOU CANNOT! It was decided to make these vehicles multiplayer only so people have no way of testing them in singleplayer prior to purchase to see if they want them.
If you do not wish to play in the online open world, then you can always do some online modes from racing, team deathmatch, heists, missions and more. However, the match making system used in this game is one of the most appalling system I have ever scene in gaming. If you want to find, for example, a random race, you will start searching. If a race is not found, you then have a decision to find a DIFFERENT type of mode job (adversary or TDM) or host your own race, there is no "try again" option, no "return to open world" option. And here's the reall kicker! If you choose to look for a job in a different mode and fail to find one, it then asks "do you want to join a race in progress?". I mean what the hell! That should be the first damn option you get, not to look for a different type of job! Trying to find a job of the type you want to join can take up to 20 mins, and then when you get in, you have the risk of disconnecting, being kicked or a game bug getting you stuck on a loading screen (can be quite frequent). This combined with an excessive quantity of modes (most of which nobody plays) and low payouts can make finding and playing jobs truly frustrating.
It is clear R* and its parent company Take-Two Interactive have no interest in fixing current problems in the multiplayer scene, they only have an interest in shutting down money making glitches and loop holes which make heists easier all for the sake of milking as much money as they can from you.
If you do ever intend to buy GTA 5 for its multiplayer, WAIT FOR IT GO ON SALE and do NOT buy shark cards! You are better off farming your own cash or running into a hacker who can gift you cash (not condoning it). Also be aware that the points I have noted are the main points I choose not to recommend this game. There are still many other problems with it...

First off it's a rail shooter. If you don't like rail shooters, this is not for you.
Second, it's a 2014 game, so the graphics are not up to today's standard, and it shows.
And third, Enemies do look a lot alike. Might be because they are in uniforms with hats. So I could see why they might resemble each other.
Now having said all that, let's call this game what it really is... A guilty pleasure.
You play as... You guessed it, Rambo. And yes, they use Sly's voice as well as the colonel's voice as well.
You play through the first 3 movies, but first you start off back in Vietnam, and must free yourself from capture.
For a 2014 game, I personally found the gameplay pretty solid, and the graphics and audio are quite impressive.
It's a simple game where you shoot people, and blow things up.
The game is just like Rabo himself.
It's not the prettiest or the most liked, but it gets the job done in the end.
Don't take my word for it, and check out my video by clicking on the link.

Rambo the video game is a rail shooter with cover system (i.e. time crisis) with a few extra features, and you do get to play John Rambo and use all his signature weapons, as well as relive recreations of some of the most memorable moments of the first three movies, including in-game engine recreation of a lot of the famous scenes in the movie. However, the game itself is lame enough that you may not want to try.
Extra combat features added includes grenades, and a "reload" mechanic that gives you extra ammo if you reload with right timing on the buttons, as well as a perk and skill system that give you minor bumps in damage, life, etc. Kills also charge your rage meter for rage mode which is basically bullet time. Frankly, adding all these extra mechanisms into a cover shooter makes the game frivolous that I rarely if ever use them (and I admit, I'm not a very coordinated person). The game is also notoriously hard, even on easy (at least for me). Frankly, a game on easy should be passable even for neophytes after a couple tries. If that's not the case, perhaps easy is not easy enough.  The game is also fond of QT events (i.e. press a key at the right time) for a lot of the stealth parts.
The graphics, for 2014, is still lame. It's bad enough they had to release a DLC called Baker Team to justify the price, i.e. a lot of "hypothetical" missions that Rambo had gone on in Vietnam. With a pretty high end machine for them the cutscene stutters, even when playing at 720p. And some of the sound effects are just... bad.
All in all, if you paid more than $5 you got ripped off. It's here for nostalgia, nothing more.

I was specifically looking for a coop game to play with my wife.  I like grinding/action/fighting type games, she generally likes the more puzzle types.  So, finding a game that met in the middle is quite hard to do, especially while working together at the same time.
This game satisfies all of the above.  Lots of puzzles, a bit of kill things, coop, platforming, can play on the same device, or over the network, it looks great, it is fantastic.
In the game, you play a fighter, a wizard, or as the archer/thief.  You can switch among them to manuever through each stage, or with multiplayer, each player can pick their character -- or, even better, you can have the option for any player to be any character, even the same as the other players.
One psuedo-drawback due to this character/power diversity, especially playing multi-player, many puzzles can be defeated quite easily, but the game keeps it pretty fresh throughout the campaign, though things stayed interesting throughout our little adventure, keeping us up late at night, wanting to play more.
If you're familiar with other games, like Little Big Planet, or Smash Brothers (adventure mode), this game is more or less like those things combined, with its own flavor and twists.
I play few "indie" games, and of all the ones I've seen, this one easily takes the top ranking spot as a "best of the best".
Ok, that's the general idea, now on to more specific things:
The game camera follows all players on the same, local device, but in network play, you each get your own camera.  This is my preferred camera style, so they nailed it here.
The puzzles in the game can be easy, or hard, based on the choice of character.  For instance, the wizard can leviate himself, through stacking blocks, or levitate other players to, more or less, defeat many platforming problems relatively easily.  The warrior or the archer/thief?  Not so much, but at least the thief has the neat grappling hook to swing around with.
This isn't to say one character is useless.  Honestly speaking, I switched to the warrior when a small horde of enemies would show up, or when something needed to be smashed in the environment.
Experience points are awarded by getting these magic bubble things with gears in them or potions, instead of grinding and killing everything that moves.  The game rewards exploration by stashing these things in discoverable locations, and spawning a couple when you defeat monsters, heavily favoring puzzle solving and mobility for powering up your characters.
See a strange barricade at the end of that pit you're stuck in?  Smash it with your (warrior's) sledgehammer, or shoot it with flaming arrows (one of the archer's upgrades).  It might break, leading to a secret stash of potions.
All in all, this game is very rewarding and visually pleasing.  The only downside, I can see, is the higher graphics settings can be quite taxing on moderately powerful gear.  Good price, great multiplayer, if this goes on sale, buy it... if you can't wait, buy it, you probably won't regret it, especially if you're looking for "that game" you can play with your friends and family that like puzzles and action.

I remember, with a warm nostalgic glow, when I first came across the gem that was Wipeout XL a very long time ago. It was in a box of games my brother sent me, hand-me-downs that he didn't play anymore or never grew a fondness of. I remember how roughly the racers handled on the tracks, they required real control, it was more like flying than racing, and the frictionless environment would almost let you go faster than you had any business to. There was something about the game too, the environments, to me they seemed realistic but surreal, like something from both the future and the past, and the lights, it was like someone dropped a disco bomb on Tokyo.
At the time Wipeout XL came out, graphics accelerator cards were fairly new, and I was always excited to try a game that made use of the new hardware. I couldn't believe the night and day difference between the pixellated oldies and the smooth high res new hotness. It felt like game designers could communicate more to the player through their graphics than they could before, that they could present the world they wanted to present as they wanted to present it. Everything felt very futuristic and authentic and this went a long way towards immersing the player.
It's been a long time since I played a wipeout game, I have wipeout pure for the PSP which was okay, but not a modern title that utilized my hardware and just didn't quite ring with me like Wipeout XL, and then I came across Formula Fusion. I was hesitant at first, I've been burned with early access titles, but I saw that they just released a new update and strong was my jones, so I figured I'd pick it up, try it out for a little bit and if I didn't like it, I'd just return it.
I installed the game, loaded up the first race, the music hit, the damp uneven track of New York raceway spread out before me, a familiar grin began to spread across my face. This was it, the Wipeout XL of the modern era.

Original review.
Formula Fusion is a futuristic racing game made by R8 Games partnering with Designers Republic. The game at launched in Kickstarter and Steam with the equivalent buzz of Yooka Laylee. Billed in many gaming journalism websites as a “spiritual successor made by former Studio Liverpool developers”, sleek looking graphics, the intent to ride on the E-Sports bandwagon and delivering high speed antigravity racing game akin to the “agile, complex and nimble” WipEout and not the “straight speed, no turning required” F-Zero.
They say in Kickstarter that the initial £35,000 KS target was to allow them to create the
They actually doubled the goal to £79,656 and in 3 Aug, 2015, they launched this game to Steam.
Like any alpha, there are lots of bugs that has yet to be solved and content that is lacking at launch. You can wall ride your craft without care about the hull integrity without getting penalised by slowing the craft down. The UI is minimalistic; the bad kind of minimalism which you need to squint down the screen (not up!) to see the important information like the amount of weapons tokens to deploy your weapon, the time of your lap as well as the energy level that you’re in.
The replay value are also lacking. There are currently three tracks to choose from, all of which are reverse or reskins of one another. The 3 additional “QA tracks” exclusive to “Test Pilots” were textured in bare bones grey. One of the tracks struck me as amateurish and so basic that I personally doubt it's been made from some AAA developers like Studio Liverpool. The craft design were nice but currently all the teams selection are cosmetic and doesn’t affect the stats of the craft.
The weapons selection? Two. Just two different selections of weapons. One is a hold-space-for-three-seconds-to-fire rocket and the other is the fire and forget “force wall” in WipEout 3.
This would have been ok if the game is updated in a consistent time with a solid roadmap. Maybe monthly? Bi-monthly perhaps?
Nope! The last update of this game was in 25th August 2015. Even when they secured new investment on the 5th of November, there’s no update from the time this review was posted. There are no guaranteed dates for the next update.
All of this while some of the development staff and 2 community managers (one of which I will vouch on being extremely supportive) were laid off as their contract ended.
Formula Fusion itself is nice, shiny and cool to show off your friends your GTX 980’s capabilities but from the content, the update schedule and stability as a company, it’s plainly not worth your $20.

+Decent Platforming for the most part, some of the later levels had jumps that where a tad annoying (A ceiling above you that would cause you to easily mess up a jump and fall to your death)
+Rather easy combat, some enemies can be more challenging but most die in 1 to 2 hits with the normal sword.
+I enjoyed the art style.
+I quite enjoyed the soundtrack.
Neutral
~Has a few upgrades, the health one seems like the best value as it adds 2 health.
~You get a double jump but only if you jumped yourself, you only get one jump if you fall off a ledge.
~Short game (This is in the neutral category because it's a very cheap game.)
Cons
-Boss's seemd very easy.
-Some very precise jumps
-Terrible use of waypoints. Best example being one level was extremely easy start then you hit the waypoint and its just a gauntlent of hard jumps and enemies places in spots to specifically cause you to lose health.
-Inconsistent terrain damage. My favourite here is the rolling rocks, no matter where you touch them they where an instant death (even if you jumped and landed on top). Various spikes would be instant deaths or a tick of health. I did notice that it was more wall/ceiling spikes where instant death and ground where just ticks of health, regarldess was a bit frustrating.
-The volume options didn't work in game.
Overall I feel like this game was enjoyable and would reccomend giving it a go.

This little gem fell into my lap while I was browsing my suggested queue.  I am a huge fan of anything rogue like, and have quite the collection of games like this.  I picked this one up for less than 5 dollars and after a couple of hours of playing, I have to say I would have payed twice as much for this game.  You start with one of four classes (I know there are 16 but I have not made it far enough yet to unlock anything else) and you are dropped into a random dungeon filled with all the loot, stat boosts and monsters you would expect from a game like this.  The graphics harken back to top down RPG's of yesteryear such as Gauntlet and the like, and this is a very good thing.  You will encounter a range of monsters with various attacks and speeds, and you have to not only be light on your feet, but fast thinking to balance attacks, skills, and your potions and scrolls.  The music is enjoyable, and fits the tone well (I have not passed level 4 yet, but do hope there is other music than the one track I have heard so far, or the music might get a bit old after a while)
There is a few hiccups that I have seen as far as the AI getting caught on corners, and a bit of a hard time making shots on the edges of doors, but nothing game breaking at all, although I do hope the developers make some fixes on future updates.
All in all this was money well spent, and I was enjoying my self so much I had a hard time pulling away to write this review and the one more indepth one on my review blog
I will be doing some more indepth play through on my Four Feathers Gaming channel on youtube soon and am looking forward to the future updates that the devs have instore for us.

The amount of effort that went into QA (balance, bug fixes, netcode, server management, etc) is close to nil. DC's, exploits, poor server connections, netcode bugs that result in crashes, getting stuck in black or white screens during load and having to force restart the game, hackers, glitch exploiters, expensive weapons and vehicles that exist only to grief other players to frustrate people into buying Shark Cards, terrible transaction logic (when you purchase A for your car, and then purchase B, you have to rebuy A to equip it and no discount/refund is given for the transactions), I can honestly go on and on and on about how poorly GTAO was designed and implemented. When the game was designed to prioritize micro-transactions over everything else, you will not have fun with it. I am writing this as I quit trying to play GTAO after 10+ "Program has stopped responding" crashes, "Lost connection to servers, kicking to GTA 5" error messages, and game loading to white/black and nothing else while trying to play with my girlfriend. For the 3 or 4 hours I played, I think 1 hour of that was actual game time. If I were to ignore all these issues, would I recommend the game? Yes. But they happen in every single gaming session (today being especially worse), that there are absolutely no excuses for the devs.
tl;dr: if you can deal with terrible quality for a finished product, go ahead and buy it. By no means is it an unfun game, just very frustrating when the devs can give less♥♥♥♥♥♥about common QA issues, and would rather make "features" that promote Shark Card sales.

Virtual Basement is just another game-development company to look out for in the future. Their first release, 'The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare' absolutely shows alot of potential, and makes me hungry for more. Powered by the fantastic Unreal Engine, they have created a game that combines warfare with elements that takes us back to our childhood. The characters in the game reminds me of the soldiers from the 'Toy Story' franchise, which was my favourite back in the early days. There is one common opinion I have heard from other people that have played this game: that it gives us a nostalgic flashback from either a game or movie from our childhood.
The online gamemodes are fun and innovative. Melting down a wall of ice before the other team, pushing down a cup from the table before the other team, playing football and many other innovative gamemodes you never thought could fit into a competetive shooter. My favourite one is where both teams spawns on each of their side of a bathtub, where the object is to capture a flag located on a floating boat toy in the enemy's territory and bring it back to the spawn. A challenging capture-the-flag with a twist. There is also a CTF map under water! Besides from the modes that may be confusing when playing first time, they have also included traditional modes such as TDM, FFA & domination.
The gameplay mechanics are also great. You spawn with all weapons, which are made for different kinds of situations. A traditional AK for spraying down your enemys, shotgun for close combats, an RPG that is overpowered, a sniper for long-range attacks and a flamethrower that works great for melting down ice, but not killing. These are all pretty well-balanced. Key for this is the cooldown you get after using an RPG, which would make the game broken if you could use it  at all times. The game does not have that many players (yet), so if you have friends to play it with, it would make the game more enjoyable if you don't want to spend some extra time to find a good server.
The game is constantly being updated, and the developers are active when it comes to interacting and reviewing feedback from the community. This seems to be the start of something good, so I look forward to see what more Virtual Basement may be cooking up for us in the future!

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is the epitome of the phrase, one step forward, two steps back. I hate comparing it to Human Revolution as it was something special, but Mankind Divided feels like an underwhelming, repackaged experience. That’s not to say it’s a bad game as there’s a decently sized city to explore and the Breach mode is highly entertaining, but it’s a step down from a five-year-old game. Most of the supporting cast of characters never fully become developed, and it doesn’t help that there’s no stakes throughout the eight to twenty hour long campaign. No one is truly put in a situation of peril.
Worst yet, the scenario layout for the main missions is easily described as uninspired, lazily slapping shortcuts all over the place. Granted, there are various ways to approach each area, but every single scenario is broken down in the exact same way where there’s far too many open grates to hide in and easily accessible security terminals to gain access to. Even the fantastic conversation system is less impressive due to it being underutilized this time around. Thankfully, the core stealth component is as exceptional as ever and even the gunplay is more of a viable option. This is aided with the additional abilities to Jensen’s already capable arsenal. Despite being a successor to Human Revolution, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided somehow ends up feeling more like a predecessor. I still recommend to buy it and play it though, but not for the full price.

I actually absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing loved the game until the last 5 minutes. I already mentally placed it in my top 3 favourite games ever somewhere halfway through.
I approved the brave decision to place the action in eastern Europe a lot, instead of US or China or whatever big marked the devs probably should be aiming to please. I loved the claustrophobic, decaying atmosphere of Prague in the future, so strange and alien yet still bringing the familiar vibes of the city I know. I loved how the aftermath of the Incident played out, how it had an actual impact on the world, on the whole cross section of the society. I loved how the game didn't stray from showing the whole spectrum of human reactions to the unknown and to the tragedy, how it mirrored both the history and present events in Europe. How there were bad and good people on both sides of the barricade. I loved the disturbing imagery of the aug holocaust and the repressions even if it left me felt empty inside at points (because it felt so real).
I loved the music, electo tracks with classical vibes. I loved the art style, color scheme, the character design and level design, extrapolating from the previous instance of the franchise, mixing the contemporary, futuristic and baroque style flawlessly. I loved the voiceover, mixing and matching different languages (both in visual and speaking form). I loved the weather effects and how they reflected the changing tone of the game.
I loved all the new animations. I loved the new gameplay mechanics and how they balanced different playstyles, making them all viable and fun and how them made the world feel more real, fuller. It also felt good not to have the prolonged boss fights anymore.
I loved how we were finally given the protagonist with personality. Jensen's character in HR felt surprisingly onesided, here, there was so much more done in that matter (getting over the whole "I didn't ask for this" stuff definitely helped and gave us the feeling of progression, too). MD's Jensen is a really likeable dude (who - as it turns out - has a sense of humour, which came as a huge surprise), while I never considered him anything else than a vessel for player character in the previous game. It made me actually care about what happens to him at the end, not just aim for the solution that felt best, plot-wise (it's usually a lot of people dying as I kinda like downer or bitter-sweet endings).
I loved how the game didn't force any love interest into the plot despite having all the set-up ready to do so. I loved all the little easter eggs and nods and little jokes hidden around.
I liked how the game ran well on my potato (despite some rare issues like desynced sound or screen tearing in cut scenes).
All those things were probably not objectively as good as I paint them, but the game just hit a spot for me as the 80s eastern European kid, keen on dystopian themes.
But the ending destroyed most of that and felt like a ♥♥♥♥♥ slap right to my face. You want answers? ♥♥♥♥ you. You want some conclusion or explanation? ♥♥♥♥ you. Go and buy the next game. In five years. Or whatever. Or some DLC, more likely.
edit:
This review was written immediately (think "just as the credits stopped rolling" immediately) after finishing the game and originaly beared "not recommended" mark. But as I took some time to actualy think things through and I can't leave it like that.
Sure, it felt disappointing not to get closure, not to get all the answers I wanted to get. The ending still feels rushed, like stuff was cut out, either to sell it later as a DLC or because devs ran out of time or they lacked the ideas (I want to believe it's not the case) or wanted a cliffhanger for the sequel or some other reason I can't think of now.
But the game still offers hours upon hours of an entertaining gameplay and most of it's pros can't be invalidated by the ending.
Ending which kind of fits the tone of the storytelling, actually, even if it feels abrupt and unfulfilling. The stuff you have to deal with through the storyline is more than a single person can handle, no matter how effective you are at punching folks in the face. Hoping that one man's actions can change the world is unrealistically optimistic in this setting.

Updated Review:
Now that the game is out of Early Access I've played through most it and raced on all speed classes with most of the crafts.
Visually the game is quite stunning with it's textures, materials and crafts. Most of the visual effects though are just stock Unreal engine effects so it can look a bit like a tech demo at times.
Sounds are good, not at all bad but nothing really gave me a rush of excitement when hearing it.
Music is a nice mix of a few different flavors. Didn't dislike any of them but my top pick for soundtracks still goes to WipEout 3, which I'm aware isn't the most popular one among most.
This being made by what I'm aware as most of the same team that has worked on WipEout before a lot of my nitpicking comes from someone who has been playing the WipEout series from back in 1995 on the PlayStation 1 to every single release following that. This was a series that thrilled me to no end as normal wheel vehicle racing games didn't do it for me.
With that said the actual racing is lack luster, there are very few mechanics to utilize other than the boost, airbrakes and simply letting go of the thrust. The act of air braking a corner smoothly feels mushy and most of the time even on a entry level speed class with good timing it's just better to let go of the thrust... that just feels terrible to do every time. There are no gut dropping heights to boost from or even split choice tracks to make a last second choice of left or right.
What I feel is missing most from this game is that "thing" to pull off to feel super awesome about yourself, early WipEout games it was to boost off of a high ramp then curve in the air and land exactly in the middle of the track. With wore modern versions it was to barrel roll with the smallest of jumps to get a boost at the cost of some shield.
There is a garage section to customize your craft and pick what power ups and what weapons to race with. Being loaded out with the same 2 weapons every race removed that element of excitement and split second choices that had to be made at top speeds. Most of the time I didn't feel challanged, just kept the shield on the whole time and spammed a rocket or two.
As a die hard fan of AG racing that bought a PSP and a PSVita on launch day just for wipeout. Still has 30.83 towards the Beat Zico trophy. Walked 3 miles in knee deep snow at 15 years old to buy from the only video game store near me for WipEout 3.
I might of raised my expectations a little high for a modern Windows version. But this is how feel about it; What I was looking for isn't here.

This game gets a full recommendation from myself, and it belongs in your collection if you enjoyed the Far Cry franchise, 80s action movies, or just an excellent open world first-person experience.
As an aside, I'm not a huge fan of Ubisoft's UPLAY, and I'm not sure if it prevents Steam from tracking play time (I did get 1 of my trading cards). By NO means does it render this adventure unplayable.

Game looks OK and controls alright, but difficulty is wildly variant.  The enemies tend to be trivial, but the game has awkward jumping sections where you get to contend with fiddly hit-boxes, jerky platform motion, and instakill spikey bits.  The game doesn't follow normal platform game conventions for visuals - so while the elements are all plain-old platformer things, you're often surprised by how things behave.  That was a disappearing platform?  Really?  I've played tons of platformers, and most follow visual conventions to tell things to players while still keeping a unique style.  Eg. I just played "You have to win", and while it's a tough game, it quickly communicated to me what I needed to know to play.
And it's not just visual, it's "gameplay contract" stuff.  Sometimes you have to blind jump.  Sometimes blind jumps kill you.  The enemies move erratically, like the frogs don't finish their jumps they just kind of come down when they want.  Sometimes something is a functional graphic, sometimes it's just background (ie. you won't know what "spikey stuff" will kill you until it kills you).
Most frustrating is that it has a "lives" mechanic - so you can restart from a level checkpoint until you're out of lives.  I understand this is how games used to work, but there's a reason games don't work this way anymore - it's frustrating and boring.  It's not like the game is trying to get my quarters or something;  all this does is encourage the player to kill themselves until "game over" if they're at the start of the level with men down - because you don't want to work your way to a checkpoint if you've only got one guy left.  Suiciding is boring.
Also, the power ups are lame (and, again, feel irrelevant since the challenges in the game seem to be mostly environment).  Like, the ice projectile thing freezes an enemy, but you can't go hit it while it's frozen.  That's lame.  There's no joy to the combat.  You don't feel like you're chopping at dark demon monsters, you're just kind of waving your sword hitbox around and dealing damage.
Anyway, enough complaints.  The game seems to basically work, and I'm sure most players will get their $1 worth of entertainment here.  But I thought I'd give some feedback that's hopefully helpful either to the developer or potential players.

Sometimes, you don't need a new mechanic.
Sometimes, you only need a truly good level design.
I won't lie, this is the first puzzle game I played, back to the era of (glorious) 256 colors. That wasn't a time to have fancy graphics, and by fancy I mean you didn't had much space to represent your stuff. So you needed to be kind of generic to be understantable.
Chip's Challange is a survivor of that era. It's simple and square, to the point that is able to make it's tutorial a series of simple levels (as in the original Super Mario Bros) and you won't notice (ok... you will notice because of the level name XD)
There isn't tricky movements or restrictions. You move, push, press, pick and avoid. But from such simple blocks comes great combinations to all kinds of level design: Not all levels are puzzles, some are action, some are about timing, others rushing, others memorized movements, others about adventure itself, or troll levels, or pure endurance, or even levels you can be a smartass and skip... We even have levels about
,

Because of this HUGE variety designs present in this game we have not a simple action-puzzle game,
. it's not more a style present in the games of today and it's because of this that Chip's Challange holds it's ground even today.
I can guarantee, that you will like at least one level.
And that level will be really special. (or frustrating... MUuuahhahahahhahah)
It's a must to any decent wannabe game developer.

This is definitely one of the best RTS games out there, have been playing it for 8 years now (not all the time) but I have not found any RTS that matches this. here are a few reasons why.
1. The huge range of units and races:
Ok so most RTS games will default to 3 or 4 factions, this one however (as long as you have all the other expansions and core game) gives you up to 9 playable races. and its not like their all similar either, each race is completely unique and different.
2. no rule restrictions:
So some RTS games I have recently had a look at will limit rules, for instance you cannot set your own teams, map position etc. This has a wide range of rules you can change to your way of playing.
3. The huge ammount of maps:
I have looked at some of the new RTS games, and one thing that turns me off is the map selection. They will have about 10-20 maps, usually with 1 map being an 8 player (if they even have 8 players allowed) this game however has over 100 maps! With both even maps for competitive matches or more unfair maps for free for alls, 2v2v2's 2v2v2v2's etc.
4. The game play is both fun to watch, and very competitive (suits any style of play)
Even after 4+ years of playing this game, I still learn new things, tactics, this game is very balanced, and there is no issue of players spamming mass of units to win.
If you do get this game and enjoy it, I strongly reccomend you download the supermod 'Ultimate Apocalypse mod' The latest version is 'The Hunt Begins'

I've played through the PS4 version twice.
It's such a shame that with this engine and the stealth gameplay mechanics that they couldn't provide a richer experience that lives up to the Deus Ex name. Instead we get a game that spends 90% of it's time in a 5 square block radius of Prague. Instead of traversing the globe in search of answers, you're going from local shop to local shop. What's there isn't bad, it just feels like a fraction of what the game could've been.
Your augs are far too powerful and take away virtually all potentially fun and challenging scenarios by basically giving you cheats, to put it bluntly. I was able to extract my own intense moments from the game by severealy handicapping myself and forcing myself NOT to use the augs the devs so wanted me to use. By limiting myself to using no augs (yes, that defeats the idea of the game), I was able to have some truly intense and edge-of-my-seat experiences with stealth.
IMO, when you start the game, you should choose what style of gameplay you want to have. Based on that style, you should have a totally unique set of augs to choose from that would SLOWLY make you a badass (which, by the time you reach that level of badassery, so too would your enemies, making it vital to upgrade yourself).
Instead, you have a very broad range of augs dealing with every kind of gameplay mechanic. So while the developers idea of "player freedom" holds true in that you can choose your own path, the problem is that you can choose... all of the paths at once, basically. Player freedom is great, but it's crucial that games challenge the player to have make choices and to sometimes FORCE certain restrictions to keep the game fun and challenging.
What we get here is basically Crysis. They want you to feel like a cycber badass and even talk about this in interviews, etc. But that's not what Deus Ex is about to me. And it's clear they want the player to 'have fun kicking♥♥♥♥♥ rather than get lost in a world of intrigue and being forced to find your way.
The worst part? There's clearly a direct sequel coming that will likely stray even farther from what Deus Ex is. I feel we're a good 10 years away from a proper reboot that will hopefully bring this franchise back to its true roots.

If you love Rambo and incredible ’80s action, then Rambo: The Video Game is exactly the game you’re looking for.
As soon as Rambo: The Video Game was announced, I was ecstatic. The trailer made the game seem like nothing but balls-to-the-walls action, recreating all the kick♥♥♥♥♥Rambo♥♥♥♥♥♥that Rambo did in the Rambo movies. It was seemingly going to be everything I had ever wanted a Rambo game to be, going all the way back to 1988 when I spied the cover of the Rambo NES game and imagined what treasures the game might hold. That game did not live up to my internal hype, but Teyon’s Rambo: The Video Game didn’t just live up to my huge, unrealistic expectations, it shot an explosive arrow directly into their heart and machine-gunned them as they begged for mercy.
This is not Call of Duty. This is not Bioshock. This is not Mass Effect. This is mother♥♥♥♥in’ RAMBO, one of the great action heroes of the ’80s. Teyon takes each film's unique feel and runs with it, crafting levels that are as intense and furious as Rambo himself. What other game has enough balls to throw “ONE CHANCE – YOU OR THE CHOPPER” up on the screen, right after you watch Rambo screw an explosive head on to an arrow shaft? If you don’t scream a big ♥♥♥♥ YEAH after you see that, you might consider a career in something other than playing kick♥♥♥♥♥action games.
At times, though, the game does get frustrating, but I can easily explain this away with two key points. First: Rambo: The Video Game is old school in its approach, just like an old arcade game. This is a score-based video game, where skill and quick reflexes separate the Rambos from the Trautmans. Certain sequences are initially difficult, or play on the old “There’s no possible way I could have done anything about that until I died from it once” frustration, but remember the great arcade shooters of old, specifically the shmup sub-genre. If you want to do good and score high, you memorize patterns. Rambo: The Video Game is no different. And like those arcade games of old, Rambo: The Video Game doesn’t care if you make it to the next level. You only move on when you’re badass enough to do so.
And secondly, there are the light RPG elements. You begin the game as a “stock” Rambo and as you play and level up, you are given skill points to invest in passive traits, as well as up to three perks that will help you succeed. We begin the game as Rambo escapes from a POW camp in a hail of bullets, the voice-over telling us that something in Rambo changed that day. This is when the man, John Rambo, was traumatized to the point of becoming the relentless killing machine we know today. Over the course of the game we are leveling up Rambo… and ourselves. What may be challenging at first is never out of reach with practice, perseverance and more power. If you keep dying, you’re just not Rambo enough yet.
So yeah, you might be frustrated at first, but get up and try again. Rambo wasn’t built in a day. He was trained and molded and traumatized into the man we know, so think of your first time through the game’s levels as your training in becoming Rambo. When I started the game, I was in no way prepared for the final mission that literally ends with almost non-stop explosions coming from a series of rockets, tanks and helicopters. It’s a harrowing, exhilarating experience — perhaps the most action-packed, intense level I have ever played — but it’s one that I needed to train for.
I love this game wholeheartedly, but if I had to critize something it would be the way the QTEs are implemented. Shenmue, the game that introduced QTEs, is my favorite game of all time, so I LOVE QTEs. The way they work in Rambo: The Video Game is hard to get used to, though. The button presses aren’t always intuitive, so I failed them many times over. And this isn’t Shenmue or Heavy Rain... Rambo: The Video Game does not script out conditional events based on your pass/fail of the previous QTE. If you fail, you fail. End of life. It makes sense in Rambo’s death-dealing world, but even I found my patience tested at times. The developers foresaw this and included a “No Fail QTE” perk to fix this problem, but I refused to use it. If you wanna be Rambo, you gotta take the hits and get the button pushes right! There’s nothing half♥♥♥♥♥about Rambo, so I felt like using the perk would somehow tarnish his image and make my completion of the game fraudulent.
This game in an incredible tribute to the legacy of Rambo, and now features an original, extra campaign (which is also BADASS). If you LOVE Rambo, this is a must buy!

Rambo: The Video Game is a mediocre rail shooter that delivers you a few adrenaline-fueled hours like Operation Wolf did 30 years ago. The best video game based on a movie series. Hyperbole aside, the Rambo video game does what most other movie-based video games fail to do; make a game centered on the theme of the material. The choice of making it a rail shooter was often rediculed when this game was first announced and after playing it, I understood the genius behind that decision. Making it a survival RPG like Farcry 3 would have been cool, but would have such slow moments in the story, the emotional impact to Rambo would have been lost. By automating the movement of what the player (and character) was trying to accomplish, the momentum was maintained of being a bad-mother-trucker conflicted with the reality of war. There were several times in the middle of the gameplay where I'd think, "This is messed up." as I took in the carnage I was doing during some missions. Not even games labeled as horror give me such a sensation. To keep the first paragraph as short as I can, if you love the movies and want a faithful adaptation, get this game.
Since I did my best to glow about how amazing the game is, I'm going to list the negatives now.
- Not every scene is exactly what happened in the movies. For purists, it might be a deal breaker but it doesn't really change much of the story.
- The quick time events don't do a great job to help players gauge the timing of button presses. I still can't tell if the game difficulty changes the speed and by how much. Almost requires using the auto-succeed perk
- 3 out of the 16 default missions are painful to play through. 2 of the missions from memory involve avoiding the cops and not trying to kill them. Problem is that there are so many coming at once to shoot Rambo, they often get shot again as they start to fall down and get killed. The last mission almost requires level grinding with how tough those guys are.
- The challenge missions to unlock weapons aren't fun. They unlock in sequence and you can't unlock weapons next in line if you didn't unlock the previous, wasting time for most players. Even worse is the final mission has you using one weapon only, so you can't even use your hard earned rewards where it could help.
- The video cutscenes tend to lag. The game plays the highest quality settings for the cutscenes regardless of your own settings, so they will be choppy if your graphics card can't handle it. A real shame
- Not stable of a game. Tends to crash every now and then. Thankfully it has crashed at the start of a mission or at the end of one with my data saved in game when I beat the mission.
3 out of those 6 complaints are minor, with the cutscene and quick time events being a big enough problem to lower the overall score. The crashes are annoying, but I haven't had the crashes affect the game or my computer and won't dock it for that. If the crash happened mid-level, I'd be furious with how hard some of the missions are.
Overall score: 9/10

Remember the old coin-op, low-res hack-and-slash games of yesteryear? So does the dev of Mahluk: Dark Demon! Remember the charmingly bare-bones mechanics, the simple-yet-enjoyable gameplay, the relentless side-scrolling from left to right, with just a wee bit of up and down? Yep, he fondly remembers all that too!
Remember the way that you only had so many "lives", and if you died, you went all the way back to the beginning of a level? Remember the punishing difficulty, from practically the word "go", where you have that one tricky jump which takes two minutes to get back to, even if you're starting to speed-run the ♥♥♥♥ing level and ignore all the juicy collectables along the way, just so you can get back and try/die in that one spot yet, yet, yet again?! Yup. The developer of Mahluk: Dark Demon remembers that like it was only yesterday. Shame he had to be such an unforgiving♥♥♥♥♥♥and follow that old-school formula to the absolute ♥♥♥♥ing letter.
Since the advent of semi-frequent checkpoints and permanent saves, I really don't need games to be this unforgiving any more. If I want unforgiving, I can get a job, or receive marks back from my university lecturers. I still want games to be a teeny, tiny bit of FUN, goshdarnit. And doing the same few minutes of a level over and over and over again is no longer my idea of fun. It ain't the 80s any more.
Trust me, there's a lot of recent gaming trends which I dislike as much as anyone - hell, seemingly more than just about EVERYONE - like "open world" games where you grind for eighty hours and buy houses to put "wives" into and pick up and buy and sell stuff 'til the friggin' cows come home. And I don't mind the odd bit of primitive graphics, sound and gameplay as a bit of an antidote to the mega-uber production values we're all so accustomed to these days. But the "spirit" of old-school gaming doesn't need to mean implementing every single limitation of those old games which I thought we'd gratefully left behind DECADES ago. Give me a sword-and-sorcery version of Limbo any day.
I'm certainly not going to give this game a thumbs-down, as it has a nice sense of "style" and certainly does what it sets out to achieve. And what it sets out to achieve is admirable enough, it's just sadly not quite my "thing". Maybe it'll be YOUR thing?
I think I've told you all you need to know. Suffice it to say, only stubbornly stone-age era (aka "hardcore") gamers need apply. Wusses like yours truly should probably just stick to games which - while they don't necessarily "hold our hands" - at least give us a leg-up every once in a while.
Serkan Bakar, you are one truly ruthless mother-♥♥♥♥er. Congrats on the game, one way or another.
Verdict: 6.5/10.

There's a lot of original stuff in that game, the new gravity gun is pretty fun and the level design is reminiscent of HL1 mixed with the physics puzzles of HL2. If you're a fan of the Half-Life series, then you'll no doubt enjoy this short romp bludgeoning zombies with your crowbar and wreaking havoc on Combine soldiers.
The atmopshere is excellent: dark, moody, and a tinge scary at times with some visual humor scattered throughout. The story is basic and told through visual elements (living quarters, death scenes), journals, and QR codes you can decrypt (which give you some useful gameplay tips as well).
The music added cohesion to all of the above, bringing it together in a way that was engaging. It wouldn't be out of place in an official Half-Life game, including the way it queues you to changes in the environment like right before a firefight.
Honestly, Transmissions: Element 120 is very faithful to the elements that made Half-Life 2 such a huge success, while adding new elements and slight twists on the original gameplay, such as "gravity jumping."
My favorite moment? Crushing Striders with shipping containers! Don't wait; download and play this game!!

I never played Chip's Challenge until now. Though, I have played a series of games in the vein of it. So I thought "Eh, I have some loose change on me, perhaps I'll give this a shot"
I'm aware this is quite a nostalgic puzzle/action game, with classic-style graphics and a midi soundtrack. In the game, you have to gather chips before reaching the exit of each level, all while overcoming obstacles all around the map, requiring the reflexes and brains to do so.
At first, I thought this game was cool, however, I came to the point where I asked for a refund because it's not what I was expected in terms of level design (It was on sale when I purchased it). It's one of those games where it jumps you right into it; no start screen or anything. And the levels, even in the early ones, are tricky that it hurts for me. Another major issue too is people were complaining that the game requires internet connection, unlike all the other Steam games that can be played offline.
This is just my opinion of the game. I'm not saying it's a bad game in general, I just don't like the taste in level design. Everything else is okay, but the levels were built to get on my nerves. I didn't get far enough into the game (Almost reached Level 20), and I had to give up on the "Castle Moat" level. Other levels were ridiculous also, requiring many rounds of trial and error to do so.
Long story short, Nice concept, bad level design IMO, online only, 3/10

The user interface does require a bit of work. At first I found myself clicking on a UI element which didn't display anything due to the fact that I didn't click on the previous one, and it wasn't obvious at first glance. However once I had it figured out, it did the job well enough.
The gameplay was pretty good! The turning took a little getting used to but once mastered, it became an easy task to pull off. The speed pad boosts are much more rewarding than you'd find in the Wipeout games. The in-game HUD could have been a bit better. Most of the information regarding the ship (such as armour, speed, etc.) is shown right behind the ship, which is constantly moving and turning. At times I was unable to tell how much armour my ship had left, and when I attempted to check I was often thrown off course. Though that may just me me, other people may tell you otherwise.
As it stands, this game is on a good path and has tons and tons of potential, and I can't wait to see what becomes of it in the future.
Good luck, R8 games!

The game is much improved in many areas, but the story is short, lacklustre, too heavy handed (YES, WE GET IT, RACISM EXISTS), and the game ends abruptly and way too early. If I had to describe Deus Ex: Mankind Divided in 3 words, they would be "Is that it?".
Wait for a sale.

Oh, what the successor of Deus Ex - Human Revolution could have offered: A new protagonist, a new story taking place between the mid-2030s and the mid-2040s, closing the gap between Human Revolution and the original masterpiece.
But no, Deus Ex - Mankind Divided happens to be the only game within the series, that offers the same protagonist as one of the previous titles. Sometime before the release I read a preview which stated that this was a pure marketing-made decision, since Adam Jensen was so popular among the fanbase. And after my first playthrough I do believe that statement.
Please don’t get me wrong - many aspects are astonishingly great: The art design is still extremely impressive and the same goes for the music. The atmosphere, consisting of scenario, characters and just the world itself, unfolds after the first steps and completely sucks one into this fascinating universe.
But Deus Ex - Mankind Divided lacks one thing that makes the storylines of Deus Ex and Deus Ex – Human Revolution so outstandingly great: Credibility.
Beware, dear reader, a mild spoiler ahead: After his first mission Adam returns to Prague and just in the moment of his arrival, someone is committing a terrorist attack at the very same railway station. The game starts on the next day and Adam is ordered to take the subway to travel to the headquarter of the organisation he is currently working at. The streets are crowded and barely anyone is even talking about the catastrophe which took place the day before right at the very next vicinity. I always thought such a thing would be the theme of all themes...
The story misses to catch the player since it slowly starts drifting away from its own essence.
And a point I strongly dislike is the cashgrab-mentality behind this new instalment: The game starts with a gap between its beginning and the end of its predecessor. You want to know the story behind Adams transfer to the TF29? Buy the book! And the microtransactions of course - in a full priced singleplayer-game. This alone could be an instant downvote.
I was pondering a long time about giving Deus Ex - Mankind Divided thumps up or down. It feels wrong to disapprove this game for what it is. As a game for itself, Deux Ex - Mankind Divided is great and would definitely deserve a thumps up - but it disappoints as a Deus Ex and as the successor of Deus Ex - Human Revolution.

=====
=====
In summary:  buy the base game but avoid the tacked on DLC which ignores your hard investment into character progression.
I quote Jensen "I never asked for this". I hate it and love it at the same time. If you are looking for a complete satisfactory story, move on. If not, this game is good but not great

is an atmospheric, adventure, platformer indie game with heart, emotional content, and great sound. We set out on a journey towards uncovering a cure for a man who fell ill. Unfortunately, during this time period that the game takes place in, medieval it looks like most, doctors were not present and medicine was meager; the technology advancements we have in present-day was never present. What is his specific indisposition? We are not clued in towards the specific illness; possibly one could assume hay fever since his deportment facsimiles it as such. Two brothers bond to solve puzzles together, move obstacles, objects in securing the long journey that is brought forth ahead through fantastical enemies, real-life ones, and a secular cult ready to kill us.
A rare cabochon in the indie market and scene comes
predominantly marketed toward drama, tear-jerker, and adventure audiences. It takes the core rudiments from excellent drama movies incorporated in the exemplums of today that relate to real-life quagmires. The main plot centers around a castle and a populace that two brothers burgeoned in all speaking one language. We bring the old man to someone who can help him.
However, he assigns us our extended peregrinate towards finding the only cure. The cure is healing water present in an oasis that is supposed to revive any of all afflictions when drunken. That is after the water has been collected from a flask. We must work together, taking turns with our brother as well as working simultaneously. The little brother has an advantage, such as the ability to slide through small spaces, while his brother is good at swimming, pushing obstacles, and hitting switches.

The presentation is opaque; no one word nor sentence can describe the immersive landscape. The graphics are beautiful; rivers with waterfalls flowing into them, bridges, ledges, logs; log branches to walk beyond, and a castle. The snowy environment is found later in the game, while in the beginning, it must be summer because the sun is bright, no waterfall nor rain exist. This is part of the reason we are led to gather this healing water from the oasis because, in our town, it looks like there has been a massive water drought. The environment is heavily inspired by adventure based films tied in with drama. These days, I never watch movies. As a result, I cannot compare it to any specific motion picture.

This game requires a controller all the way through because keyboard controls will, simply not be effective. It is a puzzle based adventure game with platform elements. The platforms, later on, borrows characteristics from
such as wall running, rock climbing, strafing across ledges, and in scaling walls. All puzzles are easy to figure out, mostly levers, pushing objects, turning objects.


Graphics are well done, compared to any adventure, drama movies that have come out within the past half decade. There are two seasons in the game, summer, and winter. The characteristics of this are glaciers, ice peaks, waterfalls, torrential rains, a couple of underground tunnels, and grassland. Subtitles were supposed to be present, at least, to my knowledge. However, I never found an option in the menu to display it which would have been nice to include English subtitles as well as other languages so people can understand the dialogue. I am uncertain of the specific language spoken throughout the whole game. Nonetheless, the non-verbal cues we are given incorporated through the dialogue makes every cutscene and conversation in the game understandable. They focused more on emotion in the non-verbal cues to be understood better than the whole story rather fully told verbatim.
Gameplay fits well using the fundamentals of the platforming across high ledges but adds one new feature; the ability to control both brothers at the same time, working together while strafing buildings. One example of this is near the end of the game when you use the rope to tie yourself together with your brother which functions as a harness. You have to coordinate your movements together with your brother. When you are rock climbing, jumping upwards, you swing one of the brothers through the rope with the proper layout of controls meant only for a controller in mind. You swing until you hit the next small rock, actually more like a little circle of something similar to a pillar, but too insignificant to be considered one.
It follows the length of a conventional drama, however, extends it by double the time spent in this game rather than watching a movie in the same blend of genres. This is appropriate for an adventure game, the emotions of happiness, joy, sorrow, grief, fear, and dread. The story of
is around three hours through the main story. The story flows in chronological order, including the ability to interact with the dead ( i.e. ghosts of those in the community who have died) while you are sleeping, hearing them call your voice, trying to guide and comfort you within the spiritual realm. It is touching, emotional and a loving repositum to the heart's core.
Controls are responsive most times but can become a little awkward in the more difficult sections. Interactions which are sometimes comedic in nature, doing behaviors that are auto scripted, are controlled by the left and right triggers on the controller. In contrast, the movement of both brothers is controlled separately; right movement stick for the young sibling, the left for the older brother.

Reto (developers) used to have an active productive community that designed maps, layed out roadmaps, proposed balances to weapons and vehicles and weighed in on how people would have loved to see this game progress, Reto however went in the opposite direction... the "silent majority" direction (also known as the easy money grab direction).
After 3 years the same old bugs still remain unfixed, player options are limited (squad 2.0), the grind has been made infinite unless you buy gold, broken tank system, constant inbalance of weapons (buff / nerfs of weapons after every patch),RTS is broken, etc..
and with their most recent update they broke their own sound system.. i kid you not, RETO have implemented a feature called sound occlusion which is a fancy word for directional sound effected by enviroment...and its a sad joke... you cant tell where people are shooting from or even hear someone when someone is firing a MG42 right next to you...
for me this was "one feature to far"... the feature that broke the camels back if you will.
So my advice to potential H&G players would be... try it out ! its free to play after all !
However dont sink any money into this game... save that RL money for games that are actually finished by people who know what they are dooing.
Yours Truly,

Chip's Challenge 1 is a remaster of the original Chip's Challenge game 90s and early 00s pc game. If you tried to get the original running on your newest and latest pc and failed...well I've got good news! This classic game is remastered and now on Steam!
Graphics:
The graphics are more fluid and smooth in terms of movement. I remember the time I had Chip's Challenge on Windows 98. On my version, the movements were snapping from cell to cell with no change on the sprites, not the current one where they flow and show moving animations. As of the art, it went from MS paint quality to today's bright pixel art. I have to say I love it!
I know there are people who are nostalgic and don't want to see the new graphics, but want to go back to the old one. It is possible with some modifications to your game folder. You can check my guide for more information on that. However, it's only for the Windows 95/98 version so far.
Music:
Remember back in the day where Midis was a thing? Well...it's a thing here basically. The music throughout the levels is piano ragtime, where it's upbeat piano music, which I enjoy. Again, there is a way to modify the sound, which is covered in my guide.
Story:
Chip wants to join the Bit Buster's computer club and wants to hang out with his crush, Melinda the Marvel. In order to do that, however, he has to go through 144 (yes 144) puzzling levels that involve collecting chips. And...well that's it.
Gameplay:
The goal of each level is to collect the required amount of chips and enter the chip socket. However, there are some levels where you don't need to collect any. There are levels where you need to collect colored keys to open colored doors, and hit switches in order to open or close things. There are obstacles such as monsters that have specific movements. For example, Teeth will come straight after you, and spiders follow a set path. There are also obstacles that affect movement, such as hyper fields that force you to move to an area, or an ice path where you can only cross. There are also obstacles that can kill you, such as fire and water if you don't have the right boots collected.
Each level is unique and presents challenges. Some are easy. Some are next to impossible. On the original Chip's Challenge, you had a password system. Now you can go back to any previous level manually. The only problem, however, is you can only go to a level if you can unlock the previous one. You can also modify the game to have a snap movement, rather than a smooth movement.
Overall:
Chip's Challenge is back and remastered for old and new pc gamers for newer systems. The gameplay is the same as before, the levels are the same, the graphics are smooth and stay true to the nostalgia, and the music brings us back to the glory (or annoying) midi days. This is a game that anyone can enjoy, even if it's someone who plays solitaire or minesweeper on the computer. Chip's Challenge was a lost gem when we had to upgrade our systems, and had to find a way to get it again. Now, the gem is back with the glory it deserves, now on Steam.
Pros:
-Updated graphics, which can be changed.
-Fluid movement, which can be changed.
-Running on newer computers (duh)
???:
-Midi-style piano music. (can also be changed)
Cons:
-TEETH. (lulz. actually no cons here XD )
