Genre: Action FPS, Stealth, RPG
Year of Release: 2016
Developer: Eidos Montreal
The game’s story takes place in the year 2029, two years after the events of the last game where, steep into a technologically advanced era where robotic augmentations are used at mass to enhance human life, an augmented citizen catastrophe kills thousands of lives and created a massive upheaval towards augmented citizens. You play once again as Adam Jensen, an augmented cop for hire who now works for a global anti-terrorist organization called Task Force 29. In almost no time at all, Jensen is on the heels of a secret organization manipulating global events, and the conspiracy-heavy narrative typical of Deus Ex games kicks into high gear.
Though the game has an outstanding introduction and immersive atmosphere, the story never adds up to anything all that substantial or meaningful by the end. The game definitely has a lot to say in its social commentary, but it never really seems to know how to say it, especially considering one of the focal points in the game’s advertising campaign (the divide between humans and augmented citizens) is rarely touched upon in the main story. The game world definitely reflects those themes, but it never leads to any great conclusion or idea like Deus Ex and Human Revolution both have. In short, it's a huge disapointment, and poses what will probably be a much more interesting sequel to come.
Thankfully, Mankind Divided truly shines in its gameplay. Just about every mission in the game can be approached in a multitude of ways. For instance, if you have enough skill points, you can probably hack this elevator to the roof of a building. Or if you’re perceptive and stealthy enough, you can find an air-vent to sneak through and climb the elevator shaft manually. Maybe if you have armor-piercing ammo, you can shoot your way through a guarded area and retrieve the keycode for that elevator. There are so many more ways depending on the scenario. And without the amazingly robust level design and versatile upgrade system that this game has, a lot of that wouldn’t be possible.
It only further helps that the game has what may just be some of the best controls in any game I’ve ever played. Nearly every minor little inconvenience I have ever had in a stealth or shooter is addressed here, and that’s a big deal. The cover system is very tight and allows you to navigate exactly where you want to go. The AI is fairly smart and difficult (depending on difficulty of course), the game is filled with a variety of individually customizable weapons, and some of the new abilities compliment aggressive as well as stealthy playthroughs pretty nicely. The only negative worth mentioning is that stealth players will be able to level up much quicker than players with an aggressive playstyle due to the XP difference.
As a PC port, it'll be somewhat difficult to hit the settings you might be used to hitting with your hardware. I played with a GTX 970 and an AMD 8350 with 12 GB Ram, and I was only able to hit Medium-High settings. This isn't that dissapointing though considering the game looks phenomenal on almost all settings and how detailed the environemnts are.
The game also has a secondary mode called 'Breach' which is intended as a competitive multiplayer. You run through a polygraphic maze of hackable obstacles and robots and retrieve data points, and then escape. It's a fun time waster, but nothing more, and no where near as fun as the campaign.
In conclusion, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is probably more disappointing than what I was personally expecting as a sequel to Human Revolution, especially given the opporunity to build off the intelligent themes from the prior game. In spite of this, Mankind Divided should not be discounted as just another game; it’s gameplay, level design, and controls are easily the best of 2016, and considerably the king within its own genre.
Worth it if bought slightly discounted (but play Human Revolution first)

Microtransaction for, let's say this straight: CHEATS!

Is it the extensive background you can read?

Is it the way the game keeps fading to black after pretty much all interactions?

Is it the gun fight system?
Is it the cover system?
Yes and no...

The devs have reappeared a little and added a new patch. However, I feel the last few patches have been taking steps in the wrong direction and a lot of the decisions being made on all aspects seem to tarnish the gameplay. Motion blur is a mess, speed on slopes completely contradict half the tracks designs, the weightless feel of the handling and the overemphasis on hitting speedpads whilst they're in poor positions. It feels like they are playing tug of war in designing this game and I hope it ends up being pulled into the right direction.
I would also like to mention the UI and I/O errors that persist throughout the game. There is still the issue of the mouse appearing on graphical settings change, the blurry UI fonts and quads are a pain to work out and that hasn't changed either. Another issue is that no settings are ever written into memory correctly it seems; start a new race and your graphics settings will have changed. Go back from your current race settings and they will be reverted to their original state and plenty of other adverse behaviour. Personal Background: First Kickstarter project I've funded, and I am not disappointed. I'm just as amazed by how soon I got to play the spiritual successor to Wip3out as I am the scope and vision of the project.
Like you've probably already read, YES this is extremely spartan and early access. The controls screen is a low resolution mockup. The menu (while simple and elegant) does indeed have problems with spacing, and even though controller support works in-game, don't expect to be able to map inputs or even use it in the menu. That's nothing to say of the buginess of the actual game. Audio glitches are regular, player ship falls through the track, the hud needs work, and optimization needs a looooot of work (consistent low fps across all setting levels).
All of this goes without saying. Do not buy this as a game. The only reason to buy this is if you didn't kickstart it beforehand and/or really want to track the progress of a game very deep in development. Not much point to unless you're a Wip3out/AG racing game fan. Then, it's actually really fun. Very simple, but very fun.
However, what I can say of where I see this game going, this is gonna be amazing. I can already feel the smoothness (barring bugs) worked out, the controls feel natural to me, and the graphics are fantastic for such an early build. I'm actually very impressed. These devs KNOW what they're doing. They have a vision, and thankfully, they know how to craft it. I'll be keeping a close watch on this. At the moment the bugs and general glitchiness leave this barely a playable demo, but it is playable, and (will be) very awesome.

(Review based on v0.0.4)
First of all, some background. I've been playing the WipEout games since I discovered the third and went back to play 2097 and 64 and Wip3out Special Edition. I played a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of Pure and HD/Fury. A bit of Pulse. I have Fusion but didn't liked it too much. Haven't played 2048 much since I don't have a Vita. So, moving on...
The content is minimal (one ship, one track, two weapons, two music tracks, prototyped menus) so don't be buying this expecting anything near a complete, satisfactory experience, not even in the user interface. Buy this in order to support the developers so they can add content and fulfill their vision.
What you get though, is a pretty promising skeleton of a game. The sole ship is beautifully rendered and the track looks nice (although I hope the floor gets higher resolution textures later on). The handling is based off 2097's. I'm not so sure about that since I liked the "floaty" handling of 3, Pure, Pulse and HD/Fury, it was nice to have some altitude control. This doesn't apply here, ship's altitude is fixed at the same height always. Not a bad feature, mind you, I guess I liked it when it felt a bit like an airplane and not a hovercraft ala F-Zero. The handling has a learning curve, specially if you're used to Wipeout HD, but it becomes second nature.
I liked the boost of the speed pad. The camera struggles to keep up with the ship for a fraction of a second when you get a boost, which enhances the feeling of speed greately. I hope that in future versions they make the camera feel more like a real floating object so this motion becomes more natural.
NO MORE RANDOM WEAPONS, my God, how am I glad of this and I hope it's not just a placeholder feature. This was what was holding Wipeout back. Didn't you hate when you were last place and you got the goddamned mines? Or when you got the quake while at the head of the pack? Sure, 2048 lets you distinguish between offensive and defensive pickups, but these subsets were still random. No more random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t here, it seems. If you want to see how much this impacts this kind of combat racing games, go play Blur on hard (an awesome and underrated game, by the way). That one opened my eyes. Leave the random nonsense ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to Mario Kart.
TL;DR: I didn't even cared to look at the feature list at this stage of development, I'm a WipEout fan and I'm glad to throw these developers some money so they keep WipEout's spirit alive. But If you're not a diehard, consider waiting a bit more until more features have been implemented (or buy it and leave it in your play-it-later list). What's here, shows promise.

Trine 2 is a pretty fantastic 2D puzzle-side scroling/platformer. Don't judge me by my playtime, since I already  play the first one for a decent amount of time, and I must say that Trine 2, stays true to the original while improving every aspect from the first one.  Beautiful graphic and clever , well thought mechanic is the strong point of Trine 2 (also 1).
Story (9/10)
Since I just play a small amount of time on this game and haven't got at least a quarter of the journey yet, I leave this one mostly at 'pending'. You probably ask why I give it a 9, its solely because of the excellent, bedtime-fairy tale story narrative, the narrator is just plain amazing. And I really look forward for the rest of the story, so far it has an excellent main pot, setting, and pace.
Graphic (11/10)
For a 2D side scrolling, Trine and Trine 2 offer a very distinct art style and stunning background, lifelike, and capture the fantasy setting perfectly. The graphic is the first thing that caught my attenttion to this game. I'm not  a fan of 2D platformer with 3D background, hell.. I find most of the background-character combination is just bland and dull, I'd rather play a full 2D platformer. But Trine manages to do it flawlessly. No or really rare platformer treat your eyes  like this. The set pieces are also varied, atleast until now, but I can see the creativity in there, I bet I'll see many more gorgeous places as I go through. It's purely beyond amazing.
Gameplay (10/10)
Balanced, well thought, unique, diverse, and clever. I like on how you solve the puzzle, its not 'linear', with 3 characters available, you can choose a variety of ways to solve the puzzles. The map layout is one of the best layout I've ever seen in a platformer-puzzle game. Also, this game make an intellegent use of its physic. Overall its fun and of course challenging without being unreasonable / over the top. What I meant with "over the top" is in many puzzle game (not only platformer), the puzzle is like..complicated, complicated in a way that its breaking the fourth wall, I mean..when I solve the puzzle, I was like..uhh..really? Trine didn't fal lto that category, the solutions are logical. If I can name other game, it'd be Portal 2, the same unique concept with 'ordinary but creative' problem solving method.
Music (9/10)
Another game which has an amazing soundtrack, when I can say a game OST is amazing? Its when the soundtrack is well placed and help to set out of the mood.
Conclusion (9/10)

I had no expectations for this game or the series, and I hadn't played the first one either. This game floored me with how complete it felt. It was challenging, accommadated my playstyle, and was deep in scope and theme.

Bullet-point rundown (spoiler free):
* Fantastic Deus Ex experience with great dialog, political intrigue, action, stealth and world building. If you enjoyed any of that from previous Deus Ex games you'll enjoy this game.
* The ending actually gets me pumped for the next game and isn't as bad as people make it out. I actually find it much better than HR's ending where it was 3 buttons that all lead to a monologue over some video, questioned the outcome of Adam Jensen, and the finalised the ending with some speech set to a black screen. It's just popular to hate on this game so the ending get's trashed.
* The level design of this game is AMAZING. The craftsmanship and intricacy of it all amazes me.
* Prague is quite large and has different weather and times depending on where you are at in the story.
* Several missions lead to massive levels.
* Both combat and stealth have more options available from new augmentations that really layer on the strategy for either gameplay.
* Lore heavy game like all other Deus Ex games. If you are into this like I am be prepared for a lot of reading.
* Both Breach mode and microtransactions can be completely avoided and do not affect the main game in any way. Neither are pushed onto you at any time.
* Runs very well on PC and has plenty of options and a benchmark built in.
* Exploration is rewarded. You can discover several stealth ways of getting through an issue or bypassing one altogether. There are hidden pocket secretaries, loot locations, etc.
* Clocked in at just under 50 hours. This included a single play through where I got pacifist. I read most everything (but not nearly 100% of it) and did not do everything (only got 2 bank vaults for instance). Anyone with less hours did one or all of the following: did not play all missions, did not stealth everything or did not read/explore. Consider their play style and yours when reading their opinions.
* Related to the length. If you check howlongtobeat (the website) you'll see Human Revolution averages 21.5 hours for main quests, and averages at 43.25 hours for completionists. People who throw out larger numbers must be comparing to some other game.
* In trying to figure out why this game is currently sitting with mixed reviews I can only assume that either it's bandwagon game hatred which runs rampant in the industry these days or some idolization of Human Revolution (an amazing game) much like Final Fantasy VII which leads everything else to fall short. I, for one, highly recommend this game.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a perfect, bite-sized serving of of gaming goodness. It plays like a condensed version of a typical Far Cry game, but with a heaping helping of insane humor and crazy weaponry. The main campaign doesn't last long, only clocking in at about 5 hours, but the content it contains is perfectly tuned to be a fun and polished as possible. The humorous writing is spot-on and each level gives you something unique and fun to do. Outside of the main levels, Blood Dragon gives itself some replay value with side quests and collectables for you to tackle, which is satisfying and adds another 6-ish hours to the game. This game is a good value for its price point and is sure to please.

This game is amazing.

A standalone mod, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a retro-futuristic FPS action-adventure game based on an island where you play as a cyborg. The game does an amazing job of putting over the 80's, retro, "robots are going to take over the world" theme. A fairly medium sized story mode will entertain you as you stop the bad guys, kill the evil robots and save the world. After you've done all that, there is a number of unlockables and side-missions to keep you busy after you've saved the day.
One issue that people might find a bit annoying is that you need to download and install and then register your game with Uplay in order to play Blood Dragon. I didn't have any problems on my end, but it seems to be a different case with some other players. Overall, there shouldn't be much of a problem with Uplay and this game is worth it you enjoy these types of games.

Where do i even start here? Maybe with the first thing you'll see: Rambo is dead, that's how the game starts. He died in 1988....wait, what?
As a big fan of all 80's action movies and liking Rambo a lot the first thing you see is a low blow to all fans. Rambo died in this game seemingly after his third adventure, leaving out the fourth movie that came out a couple years before this abomination got released. So the developers got their hands on the Rambo franchise and seemingly ignored it.
Not a good start.
The game is a Rail-Shooter, meaning you're movements are pre-programmed and all you do is moving a cursor over the screen, shooting enemies, occassionaly throwing a grenade with some Quick Time Events thrown in. If the game came out in 1995 in the Arcades, it would've been a hit because it offers more than then contemporary Light Gun Shooters like Virtua Cop offered. But we're not in 1995, we're in the year 2016 and Rail-Shooters are dead, mostly for a good reason, there aren't even that many light guns around anymore.  And Light Gun Shooters on PC don't work. With the mouse you can quicker and easier react to where to shoot and what to do and this game is on the same level as Star Wars - Rebel Assault from 1993 which had literally no gameplay, was easy as ♥♥♥♥ and only sold because of the license. Again, over 20 years ago.
Anyway, let's go to the game and the next low blow (after declaring Rambo dead and mixing up his birth year with 1946 instead of the correct 1947) to all fans is the fact that nobody looks like their counterparts of the movie. I know it's hard to get the rights to display actors but considering they have a scanned picture of Trautman showing up it boggles my mind that the Trautman in the game itself looks nothing like Richard Crenna and so doesn't Rambo, it looks more like a cosplayer than Stallone. Everybody else looks absolutely nothing like their movie counterparts. Teasle isn't recognizable at all, so i Galt or Zaysen from the third movie.
The movies are also quite condensed and changed. First Blood starts as a QTE-heavy battle in the police station, then you kill a ton of cops in the forest, then you're suddenly in the city causing carnage, again the last part doesn't happen in the movie or in the book and several parts that could've been interesting are skipped. Like the cave scene where Rambo fiths against Rats (or bats in the book), that is just skipped.
The Movies are cut into several levels after which you get an evaluation of your skills and gain XP which you can use for skills that make your life even more easier (bonus stuff like "get 5% health per headshot") and upgrading your weapons to contain more ammo or deal more damage. Though the guns actually don't really feel that different. AK47 and M16 are interchangable and blasting away with an Mac-10 isn't different to firing an AK.
First Blood Part 2 follows the same path of replaying scenes from the movie, while deleting some and getting entirely new stuff in. In the movie Rambos boat doesn't get attacked by torpedoes, here you're tasked to shoot them down...with an Ingram. How a Mac-10 found it's way to Vietnam, i don't know, the weapon never even shows up in the movie but here you are shooting down torpedoes with it. Silly. Julia Nickson-Soul was a good looking woman in the movie playing Co-Bao, in the game her name is "Coo" and she looks horrendous. Again, it hurts.
I stopped playing there to be honest. It wasn't fun at all. I do like Light Gun Shooters, i do like Rail Shooters if they're done good. Rambo III on the Master System is still fun and way better than this abomination here.
I also have to mention the sound. Ripping out voice lines from the movies is not a bad idea but mixing them with new lines spoken by other people doesn't work. Even worse in this game the volume is changing, the new dialogue is way louder than the stuff taken from the movies, so i constantly had to work the volume knob on my mixer.
Graphically, i already said that nobody resembles the actors in the movies and everything else is extremely outdated. While i don't follow the "it looks like a PS2 game" claims because that's wrong, i'd say it's very first generation Xbox 360 graphics and also a bad audio experience.
Honestly avoid this game, even if you like Rambo and the movies. Get a Mega Drive and Rambo 3 or a Master System with Rambo - First Blood Part 2 and a Light Phaser and Rambo 3, those are better experiences than this abomination of a game right here.

While the game itself is relatively new in terms of EA, and content starved for the moment (1 track , 1 craft with skin variations, 2 game modes), many of the core features that exist in the game are done quite nicely. Mechanics seen in the Wipeout series, such as Air-braking might feel strange at first because of the lack of drift, but after a few sessions you become accustomed to it. Collisions can also be unforgiving  (similar to those in wip3out) where one bump into a wall can cause a massive slowdown, emphasizing the need to remember where speed pads are placed and to optimize your racing line accordingly. Weapons are also included in the game, allowing you to pick from either the offensive missile to lock on and attack opponents in front of you, or a barrier that can be placed down to slow those behind you. Keep in mind that these are weapons you choose to take before the start of a session, so you appear to be limited to a single weapon type during a race.
Overall i wasnt expecting too much at the start of EA, so i was a bit pleased to see the game functioning rather nicely (aside from the occasional crash between sessions). If you do decide to jump in and buy the game now, beware of the songs that are currently added. You'll probably go insane hearing them loop endlessly. :D
Alot of work to be done. But this is going to be good.

The Early Access release of Formula Fusion on Steam gives us beautiful demo to play, and a sneak peek into the future of an amazing looking game. The visual refinements are already in place, the sense of speed, manueverability, and rich environments are there along with a refined and unobtrusive interface.
The Challenge:
Make no mistake, this is a "demo" based on an "Alpha build"--its incomplete, its a mere snapshot, there are bugs, and not a lot of features. Most of the people already playing it bought it thru the Kickstarter and the Test Pilot Program.
The Benefits:
You already know if Forumula Fusion is "your thing." You can buy Early Access now, and participate in the game's development, along with all its bugs and glitches, or you can buy at release, when the game is clean, refined, and bug-free.
I bought into the original Test Pilot Program and the Kickstarter, because I want to play a version of the anti-gravity reacing games I love on the platform of my choice, and not be locked into a console development cycle.

Having logged 6 hours of gameplay so far, I can tell you this game is well worth your time despite being a little bare for the moment. The developers are working long and hard to bring us the next-gen anti-gravity racer we fans have been itching for and Formula Fusion does not disappoint. Be aware that as of the release date, there is only one track available. However, the level of refinement of both graphics and gameplay both indicate to me that FF is sure to be the new gold standard in AG racing games. Handling is new and unique (possibly subject to change). AI skill level varies realistically and definitely presents a challenge as you move up through the ranks. AG racing is back!

The following is a 1080 Review of Legends of the Universe: StarCore.
:
Legends of the Universe: StarCore is a basic Metroidvania that is isolated on a giant space ship, where your task is to retrieve the object known as the StarCore, a power source that is powering a planet killer.  If you are familiar with the concept of the Death Star, then you can get the general picture as to the scale of the ship in question.  The map is approximately 15 areas large, with each area connected to each other by way of teleporters.  In my playthrough of the game, you can easily reach most, if not all of the areas with a little backtracking and exploring, which is good in a Metroidvania.  You can gain upgrades by entering into blue cubes, which again, you can find most of them with a little backtracking and exploring.
Unfortunately, this is where my praises of the game will have to come to an end.  The plot of the game seems to be a bit poorly written.  Not that I didn't take away anything good from the story, mind you, just that most of the explanations that they gave for taking away the player's abilities appears to be a bit cliche at best, and the fact that the final boss (referring to the ship's captain) isn't exactly final appears to be ripped right from Metroid.  That isn't to say that taking inspiration isn't entirely bad, it just that it is presented in bad taste, in my opinion.
+ The game is the perfect length for retention.
+ Most areas of the game are completly accessable with a little backtracking and effort.
+ Most of the power ups are accessible with trial and error.
- The RPG-like stats are completely unnecessary for a game this size.
- The writing is severly wanting, though not too terrible compared to what I normally see from AAA publishers.
I am proud to give this game a solid 6/10, and I recommend it.

I've played this game for ages (since 2009). Thousands of hours more than Steam will show. It has been a long running favorite with huge amounts of space to explore and a skirmish system that other MMOs need to pay attention to.
The downside is the game is starting to show its age a bit more than WoW does. The art in the game manages to land square in the uncanny valley and the player animation is sloppy. Anyone with a speed buff comically trots in place when starting or stopping. No ability to unsheath weapons, and everyone in your party will be synchronized when entering or exting combat. These things are minor, but jarring. Hunter's port system has become a chore, and travel from point to point to point is now confusing and tedious. Travel needs to be revamped to just a drop down of where you want to go at this point. Also, a lot of this game is simply NIH going extra lengths to not be WoW even when WoW-like was the right thing to do.
The upside is the game continuously expands and improves. New gameplay mechanics, often new innovations, are introduced with each year. The lore is immersive (as it should be), and elaboration happens with consent and approval from the Tolkien estate. The cosmetic outfit system is an example of a place where WoW (and every other MMO) specifically needs to take notice. Content is often truely difficult rather than outright unfair, even when playing retro-content several levels under you.
Warsteeds were a fizzle addition to the game, largely because they amplified the slop in the controls by an intentionally sloppy and unweidly system. PvMP (because WoW calls it PvP) is amazing, but often unbalanced as stats start in favor of monsters and end in favor of Hobbits by the end of an xpac cycle. Legendary weapons are not cosmetically customizable and obsoleted every xpac. This flys in the face of the intent of the original intent of the system, and is a very tedious grind. The legendary system is also confusing and dependant on huge amounts of randomness. Keep these as your forwarning as they will be the biggest sore points.
Despite the complaints here, I still love this game. I still recommend this game. I hope that they will approach fixing the sloppy controls and simplify the legendary system as these are the only things causing me to drift towards other games.

Having enjoyed Deus Ex previously, I'm actually quite used to disappointment. The series, and I say this as a fan, has really only produced two great games: the original and Human Revolution. Brilliant games, mind you, but of the 5 or 6 series entries if you count mobile titles, it's not really a stellar track record.
What I never expect from a Deus Ex game, however, is close-to-greatness. The series historically has either hit hard or dropped the bat. Mankind Divided is therefore, if you'll excuse the pun, in a league of its own.
The game doesn't start particularly strong. The opening mission, which I played at this point a few months ago, was long, rather dull, and highlighted a few of the game's glaring flaws all too readily. First and foremost, Square Enix and Eidos really could stand to drop some of the series' cinematic pretense. This will sound like a nitpick perhaps, but I do not need the game to cut to a cutscene every time I knock a guard unconscious. It just isn't needed.
In addition, I found the map design this time around rather... safe. It's not really bad, mind you, but it's expected. I stumbled into the location of security panels (aka, the stealthy player's coup de grace) almost always without fault as the first room I'd happen upon. This occurred far too often for me to call it luck.
In general, in fact, the game feels half-complete. The story in particular, which will make or break any Deus Ex title, is rather lazily thought-out. Desperate to encompass a metaphor for racism, Eidos tries to equate its augmented civilians with sufferers of real-life racism. This could have been interesting, but the metaphor rapidly falls apart in-universe. If, in the events of Human Revolution, all augmented citizens went crazy at once, how is fear towards them NOT justified? It doesn't mirror real-life racism, in which a handful of extremists result in unfair projections onto a race.
The core gameplay, I actually quite liked. The game's systems are a vast improvement over any previous Deus Ex title. The cover systems are natural to the point where I can't imagine them working any other way, and the combat is as fast-paced as you'd expect.
Unfortunately, none of the above can justify the game's most glaring flaw. Despite looking at best "okay" for a 2016 game, Mankind Divided struggles to maintain a constant 60fps at 1080p on ultra for all but systems with the literally-best GPU currently available: the Nvidia GTX Titan X Pascal. I do not believe the developers' minimum specs, given that my old GTX 770 had trouble maintaining 30fps at all on ANY resolution, at ANY setting.
If you have a beastly PC and don't mind the story being rather questionable, the core game here is about 30-40 hours of fun. I didn't get the same sense others did that it ends abruptly either, for whatever that's worth.
However, given that the store page doesn't exactly tell the truth about system requirements, I can't help but not-recommend to the average consumer.

- Intense shooter experience - if you choose to play it as a "shooter", not as a "cover in the airduct like a ♥♥♥♥♥" simulator
The bad:
- I tried, for about 3 hours, but I can't beat the tutorial mission with my Steam Controller. Zero aim assist. This is actually a good thing in part, because I rediscovered how much I love playing with a mouse and keyboard.
- Minor technical problems. That means the game crashed once. Also it has some quirks. I have the Steam Overlay w/ keyboard on shift + tab, and after activating the overlay it kept reopening the inventory, until I pressed tab again.
- Feels short compared to Deus Ex, Deus Ex: Invisible War, and Deus Ex: Human Revolution
- Not enough side missions
- Limited to only one city - which might be bigger but still
Overall, I'd recommend it, because it is a good game, but it was kind of short. Best enjoyed after a playthrough of Human Revolution - I'm not citing the older games, as those are set in the future relative to these two games, and don't have much, or anything to do with the story here. Let's hope we'll get a sequel in less than 5 years.

.
Like some of the other reviews on here, I can agree the game is "rough around the edges" so to speak, but it is far from a deterrent to the core gameplay, which is this game's star.
Powerups/upgrades come at a steady pace which really helps keep the flow of the game moving forward. It has yet to feel stagnant as I've explored and re-explored areas with new abilities. The level design is varried and evolves as you progress and never feels overly designed to extend/pad play time. Like a good platformer it rewards exploration.
It does have it's quirks like the weapon firing on release and not press of the button or the ability to walk off a ledge then jump midair - but you quickly adapt and accept. If anything it actually gives the game its own unique feel.

The most violent fun I've had in ages, and now one of my favorite games. There's lots of content old fans of the series will love, and new fans might be surprised by how interesting the story can be. Mortal Kombat brings more to the table than Street Fighter or any other 1v1 fighting game, IMO.
The good: The gore is more realistic and satisfying than ever, though I miss the visible damage fighters suffered in MK9. Combat is fun and the weak links in the roster are few. The sexualization of the female characters in MK9 didn't bother me, but I can't complain that NRS wants to take their franchise in a more mature direction with the more realistic redesigns in MKX. The characters themselves also seem to have grown up.
Old characters are missed but the new ones have grown on me, and even the horror movie DLC characters don't feel like as much of a slap in the face as they did on launch. The Tarkatan Xenomorph is pretty cool. That being said, if NRS decides to release more DLC, which is unlikely, I hope they'll remember the original characters we miss.
The bad: Online gameplay is frustrating at times (but not as bad as it was on launch), especially for international players. I'm in Australia; the online servers for PC are a ghost town. Fortunately, I don't play with others much, so that doesn't bother me. Mastering more than one character is hard, but the ability to post combos on the screen is greatly appreciated and is something MK9 really lacked, IMO.
Despite playing for 200+ hours I've never been able to advance beyond what I call "educated button mashing", but maybe that's just how these games are. I've played with both a keyboard and Xbox controller on PC and prefer the keyboard, as I've discovered special moves are easier to pull off that way. I look forward to seeing if gameplay improves on the Xbox or PS4, but I've played worse ports.
I admit my interest in the game dropped sharply after I finished the story (which seemed shorter than MK9's) and I unlocked everything in the Krypt, but somehow I keep coming back to it. 200+ hours of gameplay can't be wrong. As far as I'm concerned, this is the best MK game yet.

I beat it fully in about 5 hours, and I enjoy to take my time with such games. Rather, it's a game based around story. To that end, I would say that the story is quite strong most of the way, with the smaller stories you observe being much more powerful than the main one. In particular, the (spoiler free) tale that stands out to me is the one related to the burnt house. It's not really related to the main story, but it's still a powerful example of how good non-verbal stories can be.
All in all, I would recommend buying this game to play in one sitting, possibly two if you're an achievement hunter. While difficult to swallow at the full price point, I enthusiastically recommend it on sale. It is well worth what you spend on it.
Pros:

First things first: Yes there is a free version of this game on mobile. The problem with that version, is that every 3 runs or so, you are bombarded with advertisements. In a game where you can make mistakes that will kill you in an instant, those 3 runs sometimes will go by so fast, you get interrupted by an ad quite often. Not a truly gamebreaking thing, but an extremely annoying thing none the less.
So why get the Steam version if mobile is free? Well, I for one prefer the feeling of pressing a key over tapping a screen. Sometimes touch screens are wonky, and will register your touch, even if you aren't actually touching the screen. This can lead to frustrating deaths in this game. By pressing a key (Which is the Q key by the way) that random element is eliminated.
If you are bad at games like I am, you will also appreciate being able to play uninterupted by advertisements every time you make a misake. I've had great runs, and I have spurts of really really bad runs. It's nice not having to look at yet another Walmart Special when I'm goofing up.
And let's be honest, this game costs less than a Big-Mac burger. Well worth the $3 pricetag.

TL,DR: If you have an Android phone, play it on there for free (apparently, that version has ads). If you're curious, search the name and play it for free on-line (that version DOES NOT have ads, as far as I can tell). If after that, you want to pay $3 for it, do so to support the dev. If you're a card addict, wait for the game to go on sale.
And, if you want to read the dev telling me things I already know about this game (because I paid money for it and played it) and how to spend my money. . .and trying to tell me why certain features are worth my money (SPOILER ALERT: it's because they are fun), then check the comments for my review. This feature comes free of charge, but is technically an ad. Which is weird, because I paid for an ad free version.
-------------------------------------------------------------
I wish there was a neutral rating for games like this. It's fine. It does what it does and it's okay. It's nothing great, but it's not a bad game.
One More Line is a simple game. You're a little "D"-looking thing and you being propelled upward. There are obstacles in your way. If you smash into them, you die. If you smash into the wall, you die. If you click with the mouse, you'll be pulled into the orbit of of the obstacles. If you click again, you'll be released. The score goes up as long as you're not orbiting an obstacles and the goal is to get as high a score as possible.
And it's fine. The name is true, you'll want to give it another go. The (I think) one music track is funky. It requires some skill, there's challenge. It's fine.
Here's the thing though: it's a mobile port. Not only is it a mobile port, but it's mobile port that is free on android phone. Don't have an Android phone? You can play it on-line for free. Now, this isn't necessarily bad. Enchanted Cave 2 is also free on-line and that game is great. However, it has a lot more depth. There's more to do. One More Line, is the perfect mobile game. It's simple, it's quick, it's best when played in short bursts. There is not a lot to it.
Also, it's a lazy mobile port. It tells you to "touch" and the little tutorial screen that pops up the first time you play does not seem to want to go away by clicking with the mouse.
Granted, there are features not in other versions. Apparently, the multi-player is exclusive to Steam. However, I, personally, am never going to make use of that. There's cards, there's achievements.
$3 isn't a lot, but it feels a bit too much for this. This is a perfectly fine game to get on sale for $0.99 if you like achievements and cards.

One More Line is a very fun "how far can you go before you run into something" game that stands out in a market flooded with them. it has good music and visuals that keep your attention. It's name is perfect for it, since you'll constantly want to give it one more try to get further than you did before.
they fixed my only complaint about the game, so kudos to the developers for listening to their players.

I've played this game for ages (since 2009). Thousands of hours more than Steam will show. It has been a long running favorite with huge amounts of space to explore and a skirmish system that other MMOs need to pay attention to.
The downside is the game is starting to show its age a bit more than WoW does. The art in the game manages to land square in the uncanny valley and the player animation is sloppy. Anyone with a speed buff comically trots in place when starting or stopping. No ability to unsheath weapons, and everyone in your party will be synchronized when entering or exting combat. These things are minor, but jarring. Hunter's port system has become a chore, and travel from point to point to point is now confusing and tedious. Travel needs to be revamped to just a drop down of where you want to go at this point. Also, a lot of this game is simply NIH going extra lengths to not be WoW even when WoW-like was the right thing to do.
The upside is the game continuously expands and improves. New gameplay mechanics, often new innovations, are introduced with each year. The lore is immersive (as it should be), and elaboration happens with consent and approval from the Tolkien estate. The cosmetic outfit system is an example of a place where WoW (and every other MMO) specifically needs to take notice. Content is often truely difficult rather than outright unfair, even when playing retro-content several levels under you.
Warsteeds were a fizzle addition to the game, largely because they amplified the slop in the controls by an intentionally sloppy and unweidly system. I've played tons of Clicker games, and Crush Crush is definitely beating them all and is my favorite, here's why:
In all of these other games, all you do is click, click, click... And buy upgrades. And then eventually the whole game plays itself for you, and all you have to do is buy upgrades and reset the game for the prestige bonus. They're all the same.
Now, here's why I like Crush Crush: This game actually has a personality to it. All the girls in the game have a different personality, they make funny jokes, and they're cute as well, without needing to go the way the Sakura games go, this game is adorable, and family friendly for everyone.
Now let me explain how this game works; You date the girls, and you go further in your relationship by doing various requirements in the Affection Metter, such as going with them on dates to certain places, buying them specific gifts, being better in a hobby/ job and also the clicker part: Affection Hearts. Affection Hearts will always be a requirement to the next level in a relationship, and you can get these in a few ways: Clicking on the girl, buying the girl a gift, or going on a date with the girl. Gifts and dates each give a different amount of Affection Hearts, the more expensive the gift/date is, the more hearts you get. So if you don't like clicking, you can not do that at all, and just buy things instead (the game could not be considered a clicker game because of that as well).
You earn money by doing jobs, and you unlock new jobs by becoming better in a hobby. Both of these require Time Blocks. Time Blocks are basically your "time" For example, you have 6 time blocks, and working at the restaurant costs 3 Time blocks, and improving your hobby in dancing also costs 3. You can spend them on both, and be left without time blocks, but time blocks are infinite use, so if you need more time blocks, you can just stop one of your jobs or stop one of your hobbies, and your time blocks will be free to use again. Pretty great system in my opinion, as well as allows you to focus on what you want. You get more of them by going higher in a relationship with a girl, as well as for getting 4 achievements each time.
The game is completely free to play, it has however microtransactions for gems which can be used to speed up your game progress, or get more time blocks, HOWEVER, you can do all of that completely normally by playing the game, as well as there being a reset system in the game, which allows you to speed up your game progress too. In other words, gems are completely unnecessary, and you can do everything by just playing the game normally. (You do get gems by just playing the game as well, so you can collect them up and buy something from the store if you want for free).
That's pretty much it. The game is cute, family friendly, free, has mechanics which make it a lot more interesting than other "clicker" games, and in general is pretty well done. I might as well mention that the developer is really nice, and they're listening to feedback and improving the game constantly.
I recomment it completely, it's a lot of fun.

Crush Crush is an idle game themed around dating random girls you accidentally "meet" in unique catastrophic ways.
The aim of the game is to fill up each girl's affection meter to the "Lovers" stage. To reach the next stage, you have to meet certain requirements and objectives, such as reaching a certain job title in a certain job, reaching a high-enough level in a certain job, buying them certwain gifts and clicking them enough times.
Jobs and hobbies take up Time-Slots, which you only have a small supply of, so you can only work at so many jobs and hobbies simultaneously. You can unlock more time slots by reaching the next affection meter stage for a girl and getting achievements.
Jobs give you money each time they are completed after a certain amount of real-life time. Your hard-earned cash can be used to spend on gifts and dates for your girls.
Hobbies take up real-life time and Time-Slots, just like Jobs, to level up specific Traits, like Surfing
levels up your Buff trait.
I love the backgroung soundtrack and the character design, both in art style and personality. However, I am not keen on how hard and slowly you have to grind to fill up each girl's affection meter (then again, I am pretty impatient and don't like waiting to level up in (m)any videogame(s), so maybe the idle game genre just isn't for me) and how rare diamond drops are.
Speaking of diamonds, Diamonds are the premium currency of this f2p game. They can be used to skip levels in your hobbies and to buy what you normally would with your usual money.
If you like idle games like Cookie Clickers and AdVenture Capitalist, you may also like this game.

I really enjoyed Deus Ex Mankind Divided even though I was expecting disappointment given all the negative stigma about the game on steam, though I believe it was the typical result of poor pc optimisation on launch, but im glad that wasnt true. Allow me to sum up the game in Pros and Cons,
Pros
Refined Deus Ex HR gameplay with great new augments
Excellent graphics for the most part
Excellent Lore (not the main story by this i mean information found in the game world)
Great soundtrack and voice acting
Interesting and varied side missions
Exceptional Level Design
A good city hub (but it is limited to just this one which is sad)
Cons
Choppy framerates and crashes within the first few weeks though the game mostly runs fine now
A Story that sadly falls flat towards the end of the game leaving many questions unanswered
A sequel bait ending
Lack of a second city hub (despite Prague being large and interesting a second city hub wouldve been much better)
Overall i'd say its a worthy buy for Deus Ex fans but sadly the game lacks the charm and gripping story that Deus Ex and Deus Ex Human Revolution had.

Interesting little tactical shooter, focused on Co-op play. People who are fans of the previous game or older games like "Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30," will likely enjoy this game.
Pros:
-Authentic USMC conduct and squad commands, and there is a good amount of customization for your soldiers loadout.
-The campaign is at least 10 hours of varied types of combat across Tajikistan.
-The co-op mode "Fire Team Engagements" are intense and each represent specific types of objectives found in the Campaign, such as escorting a convoy or rescuing helicopter pilots trapped behind enemy lines.
-Hardcore mode strips HUD assists like mini-map, making engagements with enemies much more dangerous
Cons:
-The graphics were a little dated even for 2011,
-There isn't much content available out of the box for the Fire Team Engagements (made worse that you cannot buy the Valley of Death DLC since Games for Windows Live Marketplace is down)
-Everyone dislikes GFWL
-Some poor placement of checkpoints if playing on Normal or Experienced Difficulty
-Some missions could use more freedom, such as being able to flank from another side or steal enemy vehicles.

I never thought Brawlhalla’s intense four-player multiplayer battles needed more fighters, but eight-player brawls have become one of my favorite modes in custom games. Eight-player battles are online-only,  which is an unfortunate limitation, but if you get a group of friends together you’ll fill these big, vibrantly colorful arenas with sheer madness happening in every corner. Each character displays fantastic personality in combat, drawing on a rich history from dozens of different beloved games. As I strike, dodge, block, and weave through seven other fighters, a match builds up to a climax that’s genuinely fun, each and every time. That represents Brawlhalla as a whole: it’s bigger than ever, but remains laser-focused on the finely balanced action that makes this a legendary fighting game series.
The attention to detail in every part of Brawlhalla is fantastic, and all of it is delivered at a speedy and smooth 60 frames per second. With so many tiny details and references to observe, it’ll take lots of hours to see everything Brawlhalla has to offer. Excellent moment-to-moment combat is the real jewel of this game, and the many ways it can be played, from the keyboards to classic  controllers, make it a gift that keeps on giving. The action scales incredibly well: two-player duels are tense, while eight players all trying to smash each other out of the ring is complete chaos. Turning items off removes the random element, turning it into more of a test of skill. But that’s just the beginning.
The constant variety of the multiple modes keeps me playing. Brawl of the Week, for instance, makes learning new characters’ moves easy by putting them in playful solo or co-op adventures. Brawlhalla’s online modes offer lots of match types to play with, from tense 1-on-1 showdowns without items, to 2v2 faceoffs in Ranked 2v2, with up to two fighters playing from the same computer. Just like in Mario Kart 8, getting friends together can be a little bit of a hassle involving Steam messages because Brawlhalla’s system doesn’t allow for messaging. But once you’re all set up, you can launch private matches with friends and unleash characters with customized movesets, or watch other players’ strategies through handy replay and spectator modes. Sadly, eight-player Brawls doesn’t make the cut in matchmaking, but four players is more than enough for a good brawl.
Nearly every aspect of Brawlhalla seems fine-tuned not only to appeal to the nostalgia of long-time Super Smash Bros. fans, but also to be accessible to new players. Once they’re hooked, it draws them in deeper with a set of great modes and tempting rewards. There’s just so much here, and I’ve rarely seen a game with so many enjoyable and replayable ideas in a single package. Playing eight-player matches and classic two-player brawls are only the beginning, and I don’t see a reason to stop playing Brawlhalla for a long time.
So far most addictive game I have on steam.

I never thought Brawlhalla’s intense four-player multiplayer battles needed more fighters, but eight-player brawls have become one of my favorite modes in custom games. Eight-player battles are online-only,  which is an unfortunate limitation, but if you get a group of friends together you’ll fill these big, vibrantly colorful arenas with sheer madness happening in every corner. Each character displays fantastic personality in combat, drawing on a rich history from dozens of different beloved games. As I strike, dodge, block, and weave through seven other fighters, a match builds up to a climax that’s genuinely fun, each and every time. That represents Brawlhalla as a whole: it’s bigger than ever, but remains laser-focused on the finely balanced action that makes this a legendary fighting game series.
The attention to detail in every part of Brawlhalla is fantastic, and all of it is delivered at a speedy and smooth 60 frames per second. With so many tiny details and references to observe, it’ll take lots of hours to see everything Brawlhalla has to offer. Excellent moment-to-moment combat is the real jewel of this game, and the many ways it can be played, from the keyboards to classic  controllers, make it a gift that keeps on giving. The action scales incredibly well: two-player duels are tense, while eight players all trying to smash each other out of the ring is complete chaos. Turning items off removes the random element, turning it into more of a test of skill. But that’s just the beginning.
The constant variety of the multiple modes keeps me playing. Brawl of the Week, for instance, makes learning new characters’ moves easy by putting them in playful solo or co-op adventures. Brawlhalla’s online modes offer lots of match types to play with, from tense 1-on-1 showdowns without items, to 2v2 faceoffs in Ranked 2v2, with up to two fighters playing from the same computer. Just like in Mario Kart 8, getting friends together can be a little bit of a hassle involving Steam messages because Brawlhalla’s system doesn’t allow for messaging. But once you’re all set up, you can launch private matches with friends and unleash characters with customized movesets, or watch other players’ strategies through handy replay and spectator modes. Sadly, eight-player Brawls doesn’t make the cut in matchmaking, but four players is more than enough for a good brawl.
Nearly every aspect of Brawlhalla seems fine-tuned not only to appeal to the nostalgia of long-time Super Smash Bros. fans, but also to be accessible to new players. Once they’re hooked, it draws them in deeper with a set of great modes and tempting rewards. There’s just so much here, and I’ve rarely seen a game with so many enjoyable and replayable ideas in a single package. Playing eight-player matches and classic two-player brawls are only the beginning, and I don’t see a reason to stop playing Brawlhalla for a long time.

The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare is a by-the-book, pure multiplayer third person shooter by developer Virtual Basement. The players assume the role of plastic toy soldiers as they try to clear different objectives across different maps taking place in different rooms of the same house (like the kitchen or the bathroom).
Each of the ten maps the game is shipped with host a dedicate game mode that requires the two team to pursue a single objective while they try to kill each other: while some are derived from your typical multiplayer shooters, like capture the flag or control point capture, others are more unique and are about manipulating the level's assets in a certain way to achieve victory.
The Mean Greens could however really use a loadout/inventory feature for the players: as it stands, each soldier comes into play with the same five weapons (an assault rifle, a bazooka, a sniper rifle, a shotgun and a flamethrower). On top of not allowing the player to personalize his/her arsenal to fit his/her own playstyle, the stock loadout basically forces everyone to stick with the most powerful weapon for that specific patch cycle and pretty much nothing else.
Another issue that plagues this game as this review's writing is the extremely low number of players worldwide: while finding a match isn't impossible per se, having a series of maps with one team (or both) missing some players is something that happens fairly often.
The strongest suit of The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare remains its presentation: the design of the single maps is always very inspired and plesant to look at and explore as you maul other players, and the soundtrack, on top of fitting the general mood of the game well, is remarkably good for an indie game. If all of the above is worth a purchase is honestly up to you

Coming from somebody that did play Diablo 2 back in the day (and wasn't as fond of it as other people), this game takes the typical frustrating aspects of that game and throws them out the window. While it's possible that Diablo 3 does some of these things as well, I'm afraid I haven't played that game yet.
First, you can load up your pet with unwanted loot and send it back to town while in the middle of a dungeon to sell for you. Generally returning after two minutes. You can even have it purchase stuff in town for you, like potions or scrolls. It's so nice to not have to constantly port back to town to empty out my inventory.
You also don't have to click on gold to pick it up. You just have to walk over it. I may never play Diablo 2 again after getting used to such a nice feature.
You get a hotbar for skills. You don't even need to have potions take up space on it because pressing Z or X automatically uses your best healing or mana potion. So I can press 1 for a firestorm, press 2 for fire pillars, press 3 to summon a ghost, etc. It kinda feels like playing an MMO.
You can find ambiguous spells on any character that you can have four of equiped at any time, offering some variety into your gameplay. Like a spell that summons a horde of zombies, or a simple fireball, or a passive buff to your EXP and gold earned. The really cool part is that your pet also gets four spell slots and will use any spells automatically when you get into a fight and they're off cooldown. I have my pet set to summon two hordes of zombies AND some skeleton archers, with a passive spell that increases his damage and shortens the time it takes for him to get back from town.
There's so much this game does right that it makes me kinda disappointed that the devs have moved on to other projects and don't plan to update Torchlight 2 anymore. But still, the game has easy intigration built in for the modding community. Totally recommended.

Heroes&Generals, it is RPG like but it still keeps its properties as a FPS. It has its diificulties, like trying to level up and getting aesthetics. Matchmaking is quite balanced, don't expect a person to stay the same squad as you for more than two matches that is if you are at a lower rank, in other words don't expect to make friends if you're still a noob. The maps can sometimes be huge (depending on what type of battle you're playing) which makes you really feel immersed in the game itself. With the addition of 'med kits' to the game, I say it feels very 'Call of Duty like'. The med kits also can help newbies who are new to the first person genre.
Overall, Heroes&Generals is the best replacement to Call of Duty on Steam. You'd need time with leveling up, but that can be over come with a veteran membership. Gaining aesthetics needs a lot of skill and I coldn't argue with that. The matchmaking is pretty well balanced and the Generals aspect of it really sets this game at it's own genre of the FPS genre. Even if you are new to the FPS genre The med kit really helps you get through a match without dying every single time you spot an enemy, the maps are huge but you will always find your own role in the battlefield. I would reccomend this game to anyone new or old to the FPS Genre. Thanks to it's RPG like weapon upgrading system it can really be appealing to MOBA players as well. I definately reccomend this game especially if you enjoy the old Call of Duty games.

It seems like I'm the only person that actually read the press release and knew this game was an on rail shooter. Even the description on Steam stresses the fact its a rail shooter on three occasions. Of course people just look at the pretty pictures and assumed it was another first person shooter. I personally love rail shooters and it's such a shame it's becoming a dead genre. So I was really pinning my hopes on Rambo The Video Game, unfortunately the combination of bad game design and lazy production values hold it back from being a fun arcade shooter.
Rambo the Video Game recreates the events of the first three films in the franchise. You play as John Rambo, a Vietnam War veteran unable to readjust to normal society and learns the battlefield is the only place he can call home.  The developers have managed to replicate all the key sequences from the movies, while adding a few of their own. The voices for Rambo and Colonel Trautman were taken directly from the movies and were spliced among newly recorded voice overs (comprised mostly of UK actors using a poor excuse for an American accent). The end result is an inconsistent audio mix that comes across as cheap and lazy.
The game play is an on rail shooter with a cover system similar to Time Crisis. Unfortunately this so called "cover" doesn’t protect you from certain enemies and can easily be destroyed by enemy gunfire. To make matters worst, half of the game is spent standing out in the open with zero protection. A huge problem when reloading your gun turns the player into a sitting duck. This has to be the most frustrating on rail shooter I’ve ever played, in fact the difficulty on the last level spiked so hard, the only way I could finish this bloody game was by adjusting the difficulty to the lowest setting.
The developers tried to mix in a couple of ideas from other genres, but they don’t exactly work in the simple on rail shooter. Does every game need to have stealth these days? As well as those bloody quick time events, in fact one whole mission is nothing but quick time events. A testament to the game's lazy design.
Now to be fair there are some interesting ideas, including the RPG style upgrade and perk system. You can also disarm enemies by shooting the gun out of their hands and a wrath system where Rambo does his trademark screaming, which allows to gain back some health with every enemy he kills. So that's how he survived the fights in the original films.
It took me 3 hours and 6 minutes to finish the story mode and this includes all my failed attempts and watching every cut-scenes. You can play through the missions again to unlock all the weapons and perks. There’s online leader boards and two player co-op. But it still doesn’t hide the fact it’s a really short game.
The issues with Rambo The Video Game stem from it trying to do too much with a simple genre. Plus the low production values, terrible quality control and bad graphics are really glaring for a game in 2014 from a non-indie developer. If you’re looking for a good Rambo video game, keep an eye out for the Sega arcade machine from 2008 and leave this one to rot in the hole it deserves to be in.

I just have finished Deus Ex: Mankind Divided and I need to say that I am disappointed. It is not bad game, but is it very mediocre at best. There is nothing extraordinary, nothing really involving, nothing worthy remembering. I hoped for much more.
It seems to me that this game does not know what it really want to be. It is a RPG, but with very few choices and even if there are some interesting quests where you could expect some cool solutions and a little bit of freedom they are limited to cosmetics, fake decision making. Story telling was rough. Most characters were introduced in a way that I did not care/trust them at all. The order of events had often no sense. There was almost no motivation for my character to do what he was meant to do. Many times I knew more that my character was allowed to know and I was not able to use that knowledge.
It is a shooter, but some mechanics are really off, there is no that much variety in terms of weaponry, enemies are rather boring on their own. AI is not up to the task most of the time with some spectacular fails in rare occasions.
It is a sandbox game as well, but world is divided into small regions and most missions take place in separate levels where you can access only one in the storyline. There is also not that much to do in this sandbox, all your options and activities are very limited. And it feels artificial. NPCs are not doing anything special, they just stand or walk most of the time, there are no interesting interactions with them.
Visuals are also mediocre. They are fine most of the time, but you can feel repetition all the time, there is a lot of low quality assets, and from time to time you can spot some glitches. Even level design is so "in your face" that it is impossible to immerse yourself into the world. Each time I needed a cover to sneak around I found it, even it had no sense to place it there. Each time I needed a ventilation shaft I knew where to find it, even it was stupid to build it in that place. Each time I needed some breakable wall, some heavy container, elevation, or anything I needed to progress in matter I wanted - it was there and it made no sense in terms of "veracity of the world".
It feels like something bad happened during the production, that they had to rush it, that they had to make some serious changes when there was not time to do it right.
It is not a bad game, but it could be so much more. I really couldn't stop playing previous Deus Ex, but this time I needed to force myself to keep going.

I really would have liked to give this a positive Review, but on my Journey so far I really can't, some may argue that it's still EA or that my experience with this Game should stay soly based on the Steam Version, but well here goes:
I first came across this Game around Valentines Day, when it was on Kongregate, and it sure was a nice Game, only 6 Girls, much Humour and Potential, it build up over the Weeks, with slowly but still thoughtful Updates, till V 0.20, which was the most balanced Version in my Opinion, and it introduced the best Girl as a topping :P
But after that it went south, as soon as the Cashshop hit, the Timer of Hobbies got secretly increase by a large margin.
Following the Cashshop release they've gave an optional Gem refund, but if you had the 10 Gems from Valentines Day, you wouldn't get those back, which wasn't that negative, but pretty much Neutral since it was Optional...
Then they've release another Girl as April Fools, which was quite liked by the People, so they decided to keep her around, but the twisted part of that decision was, that they to decided giving her Diamond Rewards.
While I would have been totally fine with her having no Diamonds even after staying, was that when you were already on a later Relationstate with her, there was no way to get the Diamonds for the earlier Stages since the Diamonds are bound to the Achievments you already had at this point.
So while it was possible before, the Dev decided not to give another Free Refund, instead said: "If you want those Gems, do a Hard Reset!"
And in the last Update (0.31~2), they reduced the total amount of free Gems by 15%, with the reasoning of Balancing, since they've added a new mechanic which allows you to gain more than 13.75x prestige Multiplier (still capped, 64x), but in the same Move they have Quadrupled the purchasable Multiplier from x256 > x1024.
So you have more to buy but less for free, making the Gap between F2P and P2W even wider, how is that balancing?
As well that the latest Girl takes 2 Gems at a certain point, which wouldn't be so bad, if this Girl would not have an as of this Version Endgameperk, to get her to Lover you need 2 Hobbies at Lvl.60 which is current Max. So while you could still gain +9 Gems from her, this only applies if you can finish her the very first Time you go past that point. To make matters worse, she has 2 of the 2 Gems required to advance States, where she does not take the 2 Gems the first Time, so you can't even be sure if she is not kidding again, if you don't already know that she will take them.
And the thing that you stilll need 10 Gems on Hand for her Lover State, which she also does not take, but having 10 Gems leftover at this point as F2P is kinda unlikly, especially since even when you have the current Maximum Multiplier for Hobbies, x64 Prestige x1024 Cashshop x16 Gilding, it would take ~7 Days to go from 59>60 alone.
Anyway that's my 50cent for now, will keep an Eye out, but at this point, I don't think the Game will recover that much, again sadly, it really had great potential.

The Sims is a series of accelerated modern life simulators that are ideal for people who want a fast break from their real lives. The experience of starting a new game and gradually accumulating money, friends, lovers, kids, and material possessions is fulfilling in an almost RPG-like way. If that concept sounds interesting to you, try this game instead of the rather regressive newer entry in the series, Sims 4. You can often get the main game along with a few expansions in a Steam sale.
A couple of warnings: this is a rather old game, and there are sometimes some technical problems. Some of the larger towns such as Isla Paradiso and Lunar Lakes have so many simultaneous NPCs doing stuff in the background that it can cause the game to hang up and freeze for several seconds at a time--sometimes forcing you to use console commands to get everything unstuck. This is unfortunate since those maps are fun to explore. Avoiding exploration in a game because you're worried that it's going to freeze up tends to kill the fun of the experience. This problem even happens on a modern, overclocked 4.3 ghz, 8-core CPU. The game was made before processors like that existed, which is probably part of the problem. The fact that the game has over half a dozen expansions piled on top of it doesn't help, either.
Also, there is (or was, perhaps) a bug in which the launcher would not update properly. This got in the way of the game recognizing your EA account, and therefore you couldn't have access to optional items and towns you've purchased in the Sims store. It seems to be working fine now, though.
Again, as my hours played probably indicates, this game is a fulfilling time sink if it's something you can get into.

That being said - the game is a RAIL SHOOTER not a 1st person shooter and you can see the graphics in the gameplay videos and screenshots on the store page. So complaining about the graphics and how it is a rail shooter is really silly.
Regardless, the game is actually pretty fun and short since it's a really straightforward arcade style rail shooter that recreates the major scenes from the first three Rambo films. It makes my inner nine year old oh so happy.
I tried playing the game with a wireless Xbox 360 controller and with keyboard/mouse. It is immensely easier with a mouse and I do not recommend trying to play this game with a controller. Aiming with a joystick on a controller is really sluggish, especially with the 'aim assisting' feature. Just remember to crank up the sensitivity regardless of which control mechanism you use.
I enjoy this game but I can only recommend it to players who like rail shooters and/or are big fans of the Rambo films. I bought this game on sale and as much as I like the game, I don't think it is worth spending more than $10 on it. The base price of $40 is ridiculous.
Final Thoughts - This game is stupid fun despite all of its flaws, but don't pay full price for it.

TL;DR - It's fun and it looks and plays pretty much exactly like you would expect a light gun rail-shooter in the arcade to.  Story runs about three hours.  Replayable if you really like rail-shooters. (plus it has some challenges you can go back and complete)  Look at some gameplay footage if you're not sure. A delightful arcade rail-shooter!
All but one review that I read for this game prior to buying it were negative.  Of all those negative reviews, about half were people saying "IT SUCKS DON'T BUY IT," or simply shouting profanities at the developer, which is less than helpful.  The other half was mostly long winded ways of saying "I am angry because this game is exactly what it says it is and not what I want it to be," that is an arcade rail-shooter that plays like an arcade rail-shooter and not like a normal PC/console FPS.  The other few reviews were people complaining about technical issues which will vary from machine to machine.  The one positive review that I read started as negative until the guy played it a bit more and realised, "Hey, this isn't half bad.  Heck it's actually fun!"
While not perfect, Rambo The Video Game is far from bad.  It provides a good challenge with fun gameplay for about three hours or so.  You get to use a nice variety of weapons that all differ in their own way slightly and you can unlock them all to use in any mission by completing challenges you unlock by progressing through the game.  There's an active reload system similar to Gears of War only much faster, and if you jam your gun at the wrong time you're as good as dead unless you quickly switch to your secondary weapon.  The cover system works pretty well and the game is smart enough to not let you sit there all day by either making your cover destroyable or having a grenadier throw grenades at you.  Managing your rage meter and when to unleash it to restore your health isn't terribly hard to figure out as long as you keep an eye on your health.  The vehicle segments and stealth segments with the bow are lots of fun and the explosive arrows are about as fun as you'd hope they would be.
Overall I'd probably give the game at least 7/10.  I didn't experience any bugs or technical issues.  I had a lot of fun with the single player and I plan on trying out coop with my friend this weekend.  If I remember to then I'll add on to my review for coop and using a controller to play instead of the mouse.  My only real complaint about the game is that the quick time events are really hard to judge (which isn't really an issue because you can get a perk that prevets you from dying if you fail one).
I would reccomend buying the game on sale, as it isn't really worth $40.  I got it for $10 myself and I'm happy with what I got for that.  If you intend on buying this game, make sure that you're expecting an arcade rail-shooter and not a Triple A FPS.  The game has about the same production value as the actual Rambo arcade light gun game (which is also really fun).  The graphics LOOK like an arcade rail-shooter.  If you're not sure then watch some gameplay footage.
EDIT: I tried out playing with an XBox 360 controller.  It's certainly playable, albeit a bit awkward at first.  When playing with the controller there's a bit of autoaim to help you out, which doesn't feel intrusive and is actually helpful.  Mouse and keyboard is probably the better option for most people, but in the end it comes down to preference.
DOUBLE EDIT: Tried out local coop.  Plays just like single player only you have TWO guns shooting at once!  You share health and rage which works just fine.  If you play local coop I reccomend going into the display settings and turning off display weapons to make it a bit less cluttered and confusing.
TRIPLE EDIT: The Baker Team DLC is pretty fun too.  Voice acting is as corny as ever.  Adds a few more challenges and weapons.  The levels provide a decent challenge and if you like the rest of the game (which you should) then you'll enjoy the three new Baker Team levels as well.  Plus it was free, so that's always awesome.  On the subject of price.  I would say the game is worth the new $13 price tag.

I have to say I love this game, already placed it on my top 5 of all time. Note of the top 5, 3 are Deus Ex games, The orginal, Human Revolution and now Mankind Divided. I just love the series.
What makes this one stand out is the atmosphere, they really aced the future feel of Prague. The futuristic movie posters, the future looking building in the background, the clothing, yet all build in an old town area which was 2x the size of either city in Human Revolution. Also the side missions were done excellent, one mission I spent 3hrs just on that one! They were very well done and even those they didn't enhance the main plot, were very interesting. For those who blew through the main plot and missed the side missions, they missed half the game.
Some of the negative review completed about only being one main city, I did not have a problem with this as this city was much more detailed then any in Human Revolution, 2x as big and had 3 cycles, day, night and curfew which all had different lighting and atmosphere. There were also several other locations to visit through the game, one of them being a pretty huge area but this wasn't a city and was mostly linear. The other smaller missions outside of Prague were linear as well.
If you enjoyed Human Revolution pick this up. If you enjoy games like System Shock or first person RPG with story, pick this up. 10/10 in my book. Can't wait for the next one. Note I even enjoyed the free add-on mission, I got 90min of gameplay from it. I spend 32hrs on Human Revolution and 8hrs in Missing Link, Mankind Divided playthrough took me 43hrs, though I did all the side missions and explored and enjoyed ever moment of it.

The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare would probably have been my dream game when I was a kid. There were Army Men, but unfortunately I never got my hands on that game. This game makes me feel like a kid again and it's a damn good feeling. I absolutely recommend this game and here's why:
There are 10 maps and each map has it's own gamemode. There will be more maps and gamemodes coming soon according to the developers. Each map design is astonishing and the detail put into them is amazing. Sometimes you just want to look at your surroundings and appreciate the thought put into those maps. There are 6 weapons you can use which are the classic assault rifle, shotgun, rocket launcher, sniper rifle, flamethrower and a grenade. As of right now, flamethower is mostly used for objective maps rather than as a weapon, since in recent update it was nerfed pretty badly, however, shotgun is a VERY powerful weapon in close range. The game doesn't really have a big learning curve and gameplay is very simple. You just hop in a game and have a good time. If you have a friend to play with, I highly recommend it, because I find the game much more enjoyable when you play it with a friend. Soundtrack is very catchy and probably one of the best I've heard in years. Developers are very active in Community Hub and they are always there to assist you with your problem.
While I highly recommend this game, there are also things that need to be fixed. Firstly, I think that shotgun should have a nerf, since it's mostly a one shot kill from a close distance. In smaller maps people mostly use only shotgun, because there's no reason not to. Secondly, I've noticed that the flamethrower does not register its hits as much as it should. There's no use in using it as a weapon as of right now. And last thing should be progression. I like games where it's simple, but there should be something that keeps players coming back. It doesn't have to be something fancy, but at least badges or levels for your accomplishments would be a great start. Sometimes it just feels to repetitive and you don't feel satisfaction in winning a game. It does feel amazing to make a plan with your friend and succeed in it with or without a reward, though.
Overall, this is one of my favorite games and I can't wait for new content!
