If you've read my
review, you'll know by now how much this game meant so much to me in my childhood. As such, I'll skip explaining it all over again and just quickly say a few things:
Chip's Challenge, released in 1989, is a puzzle game with Sokoban elements. I LOVED the complexity and variety in this game. I still do. The old feelings of frustration when you make a button press mistake when you're so close to finishing the level...as well as the old feelings of jubilation when you complete a fiendishly tricky level, are what, in my opinion, makes this game a stone cold classic and get a perfect rating of 10/10.
NOW: onto the remake itself.
This appears to feel mostly based on the Lynx version of the game (with moving animations and stuff) as opposed to the old MS version (where you have static moving images). It looks flashy and all but I grew up playing the MS version so I'm VERY used to those sprites. Thankfully, you can mod them (as well as the old songs) into the game and play it that way (check out the guides in the Community Hub).
Speaking of songs, while I initially planned to mod in the MS version music, I was pleasantly surprised and thrilled that the music was comprised of Scott Joplin piano rags. (They're public domain in case anyone's worried - i.e. perfectly free from copyright and can be used anywhere.) Ragtime has personally been one of my most favourite classical music genres, and while the renditions here are at times a bit too flat (ah well. You don't have a lot of room to put feeling into synthesized beats, I suppose.) and in the case of a few, a bit too fast, I find them still catchy and fun to listen to.
As far as I have observed, the old glitches and bugs from the MS version have been fixed, meaning some of the old exploits used to speedrun the game are no longer possible. This is part of the reasons where I feel the game loses some of its charm - the bugs were what used to make speedrunning more fun, and in some cases levels much less difficult and impossible. On the other side of the coin, some of the levels can now be played how they were originally intended to, which is a blessing I guess.
Definitely, for me the most negative aspects are the options menu and the sound effects. Selecting window size as 1x, 2x, 3x, 4x...not very helpful, in my opinion. Not just that but it also requires a program restart. I'd rather work with normal resolution option choices. I didn't quite like the new sound effects, and as another reviewer commented, they overpower the music when left on default settings. Of course, you can change the sound effect volumes, but I'd rather not have done that in the first place.
But still. This game gets a glowing recommendation from me, almost purely for the nostalgic value you'll get out of it if you've played the old one. Go forth and experience the joys and frustrations of my youth.

This is one of the best games in the 3D Realms Anthology.
I've played this many times over the years, and while yes this recommendation has a fair bit of nostalgia behind it, I would not recommend many of the other Anthology games the same way I recommend Mystic Towers.
You're an old wizard and your goal is to destroy the monster generators in 12 towers, along with all the monsters. BUT you have a piddly amount of health. AND you have to eat and drink to survive. AND if you want to kill monsters within the next century, you have to conserve your consumable spells. This game is tough. It was tough for 10 year old me when I bought it and it's just as tough now.
You move in an isometric grid, the game is real time and has you moving through rooms of a tower. The levels are not randomzied which thankfully allows some strategy when approaching each one. Monsters roam throughout the rooms however, making it a bit more complex. There are a variety of spells, most of them are damage spells, there's a healing spell, a teleport spell (only between set teleport points), a levitation spell, a reveal spell, and a bomb spell (used to destroy monster generators). The meat of the game is finding the best ways to kill monsters from across the room without them eating you. Because monsters are moving constantly, the worst feeling in this game is using your last lightning bolt only to have the monster move to the side. Wizarding ain't easy.
You can control it with a mouse if you really want to lose quickly, or use a keyboard. Best option is a gravis gamepad but if you own one you have probably played this before.
What sets this game apart isn't the obtuse controls or (personally) insane difficulty. It's things like the sound and music. The noises enemies make as they attack you are ingrained in my mind forever. They're indescribable grinding screams. There is no tutorial level. As opposed to say, Commander Keen 4 where the first level is an upbeat village toon, the second you step foot in a tower an ominous tone plays and you realize you have no idea what's going on.
The monster design is another huge part. Sure you have your basic spider, you have a dragon, you have a floating goat head with spinning knives, you have your three legged earthworm, your classic steam powered single-wheeled lizard robot. But there's also fun monsters like ghosts and other things I can't even describe without sounding even weirder.
You can get drunk in this game and fart and spin around and make happy noises in the middle of a dungeon.
This game is great. Even if you turn it on for only ten minutes and die to a snake wearing its hood as a dress, you'll have a good time doing it.

here is a small review for those who do not know this game:
back in 1990s we had games which might take ages to be finished and there was no season pass + DLC or microtransactions inside, every game had a "freeware"(aka DEMO) version which was giving you full access to the fisrt episode of the game without any charge, the Freeware was long enough that you could not even believe it was actually a DEMO because it would take maybe a week to even finish that DEMO.
Mystic Towers is a survival exploration game and somehow it is "Amnesia of 1990s" because for its time and for our age on that time this game was actually really scary, you need to Eat + Drink + Fight monsters and explore the area to find keys to open doors to next level, the monster AI is designed very well, once they are low HP they run away from you and avoid you at all costs.
There is no microtransactions, you can buy and upgrade your weapons with the coins you earn during gameplay ;)

This game is worth the price tag,  and if you have the reflexes and brains to get to the last tower,  I will personally mail you a delicious loaf of stale, pixelated tower bread.  Stay retro my friends.

I'll start this off by saying that I spent much more time playing this before it was out on Steam, and I'm writing the review now, because it is still a memorable experience.
While some people will insult the game for its largely p2p-based system, Turbine points (premium currency) can be obtained by completing little feats of strength, such as killing 30 wolves, or completing a dungeon set for the first time. While, yes, it is kind of a hastle to get 800 of them for the Warden or Runekeeper classes, I certainly had fun doing so, and what makes the game really fun is that on some servers, there are so few people that you and your friends can co-op with very little competition for kills. There are also some very strange happenings that occur with players (I.E. someone skydiving from atop Weathertop on their horse and supersliding (dead) to a very distant place, a prospector in a level zone 10 levels above his somehow making it work without help, mad dashes through Orc-infested ruins with legions of enemies following) too.
All in all, if you're looking for a F2P game that can keep you occupied while you wait for the next best thing, here's one I wouldn't hesitate to recommend with an 8/10, because mounts are also a P2W system (F2P mounts are slower), and also, like almost all MMOs, it gets repetitive, but that's a signature of the genre at this point.

I don't like giving bad reviews. I really don't but this game was not what I expected it to be.
It would have been a really great and fun game had it been a free movement 1st or 3rd Person Shooter. This game would have been a blast! I could have seen myself actually having a lot of fun with this. But sadly, the WHOLE game is a rail shooter. All you can do is duck out of the way, aim and shoot.
And stay away from using a 360 or any other game controller to play this. The accuracy is a mess even with aim assist. It's almost unplayable with a controller. You have a much better chance playing with a mouse and keyboard for better accuracy. And speaking of aim assist... just turn it off, believe me you will hate it.
What also gets me is the audio. The background music is great! It's Rambo music and it's crisp and clear... until you hear the voices which sound like they were ripped from a VHS tape version of the movies with a low sample rate.
I'm thinking the devs wanted to make the players feel like they were getting an Arcade experience like Operation Wolf or something but with this game, it just doesn't cut it. I mean the idea was great to make a game being Rambo and it would have been a TON of fun had there been free movement like other 1st or 3rd Person Shooter games.
For the price they are asking, I can not recommend this game. Maybe if it was $14.99 USD, then yea.
But, if you are really into Rail Shooter games, then you might like this game. I also like Rail Shooter games. But just couldn't get into this one. :/

Love the game.
I've played through the first couple of missions so far, and I'm happy with my purchase.
The levels seem to be a mixture of rail-shooter and QTE sequences, with ample cut scenes
recreating important moments from the films. The game an arcade style game where your
main objective throughout the missions will be to gain the highest score possible.
The graphics are not the greatest, but the graphics and game itself are not half as bad as
most of the negative reviewers claim. Fans of the Rambo films will no doubt get a kick out
of this game. The voice acting are actual clips from the movies, which can be good or bad
depending on your opinion. The sound effects average, and the controls take some getting
used to. I find the game to be fairly difficult even on the easiest setting, but it get's easier
once you get the hang of the controls and understand how to best you "wrath mode".
"Wrath mode" is a special state you can enhance Rambo with once you have earned it.
Killing enemies during "wrath mode" is the only way for Rambo to regain health during
missions. You can also unlock various perks, attributes, and weapons as you progress.

There are many great qualities about this game; it's difficult to pick an area with which to begin.
Both the artstyle and the graphics are great. The worlds through which the player travels are awe inspiring. The developer crafted a vibrant world that acted perfectly in concert with the overarching story. Everything was in proportion to the characters at their starting point, but as they ventured farther and farther from home, the scale of their world dwarfed them. This mechanic worked well to make the characters appear small and somewhat insignificant, but as the player guides them through, there is a feeling of accomplishment, or perseverance that is rewarded.
The basic premise of the story is nothing remarkable, but it does serve as sufficient to motivate the journey; two brothers need to obtain medicine to save their ailing father. A simple idea, but something that resounds within all of us. The brothers do what they must to continue upon their journey to save their father. I do not want to tell much more about the story, as there are smaller stories encountered through the world, and the ending was very moving for me.
The controls work well for the most part. Personally, I usually find myself having difficulty for the first thirty minutes or so. One thumbstick and the corresponding trigger control each brother, and there are times where I had difficulty in controlling both at the same time. However, I do believe that this is something that will vary from player to player. The mechanics are sound, it's a matter of training the brain to use controls in a different manner than to which it is accustomed.
Overall, this is a very easy decision to make. I whole-heartedly recommend this game.

Imagine if the first 100 hours of Battlefield were just walking around a "field" without any "battle," This is just one example.

There is nothing more annoying that a swarm of enemy tanks(or even just one or two good ones) that can just shut down any attempt from a team to even leave their spawn. The main gameplay of this game isrunning across fields and through forests, either hoping nobody sees you or, if you have a rifle, hoping they don't get a headshot so you get a chance to return fire. On some of the small objectives, or objectives with clear choke points, they can just kill anybody that tries to enter the area, and there is nothing you can do. What's even more annoying is when you can sneak up on a tank and have literally nothing to do to it except sit there, hoping it doesn't see you or run you over, and wait for the driver to peak his head out. You should at least be able to sabatage the tracks or something. And the MGs need to be nerfed into oblivion.
Also, there are automatic assult rifles with sniper scopes. Even Battlefield 1 wasn't that absurd.

Never been too heavy on the fighting game genre, but I've always been a fan of the Mortal Kombat series. I had the first one  on the SNES, but only sparingly played the ones released afterwords until Deadly Alliance. After the the MK vs DC returned the game to 2D fighting, I thought the reboot of the series was amazing and easily the best done reboot for a video game franchise I've experienced yet. It's sequel was not a dissapointed, and a fine addition to the series, and easily my favorite one to date.
Gameplay: Like I said, I don't play too many fighting games, so I can't really compare it to anything except the other entries to the series. With that said, I find it to be the most polished and fluid Mortal Kombat game to date. Solid roster of fighters as well.
Single-Player: The story mode is fun. I personally very much enjoy the MK lore, and this was a good addition to the storyline. Along with the classic tower mode, the living towers add refreshing replayable to the game. The Krypt is neat, but not much else. I suppose it's the best Krypt in the series, but that's not saying much.
Multiplayer: Solid for the most part. My Internet is pretty meh, so I don't play online so much. Usually get brutally punished as well.
Graphics: Very solid. Looks really good. Frame-rate jumps from 60 to 30 when you go into anything that isn't just regular combat (fatalities, x-ray moves, cinamatics). Can be a bit jarring. But completely fine for the most part.

Trine 2 represents a 2-D jump & run adventure game with impressive artwork, beautiful design and sophisticated puzzles. As already introduced in the original Trine you can switch on the fly between three different characters, a knight, thief and wizard (still no fireballs). It is also the basis for the great puzzle system this game offers, and the multitude of possibilities to solve each one of them.
The balance between combat and puzzle sections leave no room for boredom. And the adjustable level of difficulty gives newcomers and veterans a fair chance to prove their abilities. Furthermore the multiplayer adds some extra life to the game, as the experience is genuinely different.
The DLC in form of Goblin Menace adds a couple new levels, a new story, and several new skills which will also be available in the original game.
Overall Trine 2 feels more refined than its predecessor and the beautiful artwork in combination with the creative puzzle sections are very persuasive and entertaining. In addition it offers enough content to justify itself as a worthy sequel to Trine.

Singleplayer achievements: 97

Every Sims title to date that I've played manages to make me feel the same way. I just end up being enthralled by it. And while I always felt that The Sims 3 didn't have a lot when it came to base content, it does offer a lot of worthwhile stuff in the expansions – things that I don't really remember being in any of the Sims titles before it.
For one, I think even though the learning curve is steeper when it comes to building houses, there are more advanced options and it just feels more complete than it did in The Sims 2 for instance.
And I also feel somewhat the same about towns. There's somewhat less freedom when it comes to creating towns from scratch, but you are just given a lot more customisation over that town and it feels more alive. In fact I think customisation is the key word when it comes to The Sims 3 and it applies to more than just the town or colour of the walls. You can customise pretty much anything, from furniture to the clothes your sims wear. And if that's not enough, you can download things from the community that other people have made themselves, or buy other stuff made available on the store.
Some might cringe at this sort of thing, but I think in the end its one of the reasons why this game is still played to this day, and I think it has had the longest lifecycle of any Sims title, and why this one in particular is on Steam. Because there was certainly a demand for it. I mean, the fact that I would rather buy this and most of the expansions here than play Sims 2 which Origin offered for free at one stage is a testament to just how good it really is.
True, it is buggy, not very stable, and it still leaves something to be desired in terms of graphics, but if you're willing to put up with all of that, I think you'll find it more than a little rewarding, and it will take you ages to get through all of what it has to offer.

DLC Quest is a short game whose raison-d'etre is to satirize all the DLC practices you love to hate, along with a variety of other negative aspects of today's gaming world. The game features two main quests - the original DLC Quest, and a "sequel" titled "Live Freemium or Die". Each quest clocks in at around 1 hour or so (assuming you complete them at or near 100%). Gameplay is typical 2D platformer style. All you do is run around, jumping and collecting coins, which are then used to purchase "DLC" (missing game features that, when reinstated, allow you to continue progressing). You basically just repeat that cycle for an hour and you're done. The game itself is really easy, so this isn't really something you'll want to play for a challenge. Rather, it's all about the humor and satire. So how is it in those terms? Pretty decent, actually. Some of the writing is a tad heavy-handed, especially near the beginning, but overall I found it to be pretty well done, and even laugh-out-loud funny at times (well, maybe more like 'chuckle-out loud')... anyways, I guess my point is that the game got right what it needed to get right. It's hardly a challenge as a game, but the 2 hours spent playing does provide some interesting moments that you probably won't find anywhere else. If you're up for an experimental experience, and don't mind taking a chance at the low price tag, I say go for it. Just don't buy it expecting anything more than an interactive satire/spoof.

While incredibly short it was well worth the price. The comedic references throughout provide a good laugh. The satirical portion of the comedy accurately portrays most methods that have been implemented in recent years. Resulting in a laugh or two then transitioning into a dark realization of the present circumstances. The gameplay is limited but decent...until you encounter spikes, then it quickly loses it's appeal becoming stale and repetitive. Give it a try.

It's Trine 1 gameplay. Not too much is different. Few tweaks here and there, but all you're really getting is a new story. Pick it up if you enjoyed Trine 1. Pass if you didn't like the mechanics or the story.

I finished the "Complete Story" version of Trine2, which is an extended version of the regular Trine2. The extra content ("Gobling Menace DLC") is almost of the same size as the original, and it's equally nice, maybe even prettier! It took me about 13hrs to beat the whole game, and it wasn't particularly difficult, especially when you get the hang of it.
It's essentially a puzzle platform game, with a bit of action (battles) at some points. You have three characters (fighter, mage & rogue archetypes) that you switch to any time during play; each character has unique abilities that will help you get through the various puzzles you come across. Each level of the game (there are about 20 levels for the "Complete Story") has about 10-15 puzzles to complete, with save/checkpoints every one or two. Most puzzles are typically "get to the right of the screen" type, over chasms or mechanisms or beating foes, and can usually be solved in a multitude of different ways. The puzzles weren't too challenging, and some of them might be a little repetitive, i.e. you could easily go through them using "standard" techniques. There's also hints to get you going, if you're stuck on a puzzle for too long. I played with WASD keys + mouse, and there are also some more keyboard shortcuts; controls were quite simple to learn & master and I encountered no problem. No glitches or weird bugs fell to my attention, and the physics engine of the game was quite robust.
The story is all set in a fairy-tale world, which some might find a bit "underaged" (as if it's meant for children, i.e. far from "mature"), but I didn't mind that so much. The graphics are ASTOUNDING, computer-made but beautiful, and fleshed in 3D even if the game is essentially 2D. Lighting and other visual effects are particularly well done and there's some pretty animations at the end of each level. There's a great variety of "worlds" you're going to have to go through: from dark dungeons to ice-caverns, to jungles, to deserts, to floating-islands, even to the belly of a giant beast! Each is rendered in a very pretty and unique style. The three heroes (along with the narrator and some other characters) are very well voiced, all along the story and at each level. The music is nice too, although I can't state anything special about it.
Recommended, if you like puzzle-platform games that aren't too difficulty. The graphics are also a BIG plus to this game. You might wanna pass this, if you don't like fairy-tale settings or puzzles :)

“Ingredients:
•4 russet potatoes, peeled
•1 lb ground beef
•1/2 tsp cayenne
•1 tsp paprika
•1 tsp cumin powder
•Oil for frying
•Salt & pepper
•1 cup shredded cheddar or Mexican cheese mix
•1 tomato, seeded and chopped
•Sour cream
Quick Guacamole
•1 avocado, pitted and peel removed
•Juice of 1 lime
•1 tsp fresh cilantro, chopped + more for garnish
•1/8 cup red onion, chopped
•1/2 jalapeno, seeded and chopped
Directions:
Report this ad
1.Cut potatoes into French fry lengths (a mandoline comes in handy here). Add to a large bowl and fill with enough cold water to cover the fries. Refrigerate for about 30 minutes to 1 hour.
2.While the potatoes are soaking, cook the ground beef. Warm a medium skillet over medium-high heat. When the pan is hot, add the ground beef along with the cayenne, paprika, cumin, ¼ tsp salt and ¼ black pepper. Cook, breaking up the meat so it doesn’t form large clumps, until browned and cooked through. Keep warm and set aside.
3.To make the quick guacamole, smash the avocado in a small bowl with the back of your form until smooth. Stir in jalapeno, red onion, cilantro, salt, pepper and lime juice. Cover and set aside.
4.Pour oil into a dutch oven or heavy bottomed pot until it is 3" deep. Heat over medium heat until the temperature reaches 375 degrees. Drain potatoes and dry completely with paper towels. Fry the potatoes, working in small batches, until crisp and golden. Remove to a paper towel lined plate to drain. Season immediately with salt.
5.Add the French fries to a cast iron skillet. Top with the cooked ground beef and shredded cheese. Turn on oven broiler to high and broil until the cheese is melted and bubbling, approximately 2 to 3 minutes. Remove from oven, top with chopped tomato, guacamole, and sour cream. Sprinkle with extra fresh cilantro and serve immediately.

It's a ton of fun, and since it's not tied to the Peter Jackson LOTR, you get to see a different style of Middle Earth. The fact that you get to be any race in Middle Earth, and that they all have unique backstories for your character is pretty cool. The music and atmosphere is great, and the combat mechanic, while fairly unimaginative, works very well. THe community is big and most people are nice, helpful, and have an appreciation for the source material.
That being said, the fact that you have to pay to play for pretty much anything not related to the main story line past level 20 means that you will either have to fork over tons of cash, or just grind for hours and hours.
Overall, I have and will again recommend this game, but with a few warnings.

I can't believe that this game is getting scores like 30%. It's an 'on-the-rails' shooter, like Time Crisis and the age-old 'Operation wolf' (remember that), and doesn't pretend to be more. The graphics are nice, not mind-blowing but very decent, and the game has a silky smooth framerate. If you're expecting an openworld FPS then you're going to be disappointed, but if, like me, you are a fan of those ever-diminishing light-gun games, this is a worthy addition. My only real complaint is that it would clearly be better suited to using a light gun, and the pc version doesn't appear to have that option. Other than that it's good fun, and a good way of getting in some target-practice in preperation for any other FPS multiplayer games. Just know that you are buying a no-brainer rollercoaster of a game, not a shooter which requires to much of the old grey matter. It's just a bit of arcade-shooter fun!

Edit:
After  a few more hours of game play, and  ignoring my original disappointment, I actually started to really enjoy this game, so have  changed my thumbs down to a thumbs up.  I still recommend waiting till this is on sale before buying it.  Once you've got it, take it for what it is, a  budget  title  following the story of Rambo in his first three movies.  I'd l actually like to see a  sequel released covering the  fourth and final film (though it is rumoured that Stallone may do a fifth film - even tohugh he's approaching  70 he's still looking amazing).
Original review with  some changes in the first day of release:
Hmmm!  I was really looking forwards to playing this game ever since I saw it was coming to Steam several weeks ago.  The intro movie in the Steam shop window gives you the impression that it's an open world game, or at least with some freedom of movement; but,  in reality you don't even get to move Rambo yourself, basically, this is a rail shooter.  All you do is shoot and occasionally duck behind cover. (later in the game   you have to select from   the usual WASD keys to activate actions such as knifing   one of the police officers that were searching for you in First Blood part 1.  If you get the timing spot on, you'll just disable them and get good points  that  help you to level up and unlock  perks.  If you  press the key too early   you kill the officer and get fewer points, if you press the key too late you get shot in the head and have to restart from a checkpoint.    Your movements are controlled automatically; and, after watching the German videos by KeysJore on you tube, it looks like   all of the game is like this.   You can see the first intro’ game
.
There's no health packs and the only way to gain health is to go into wrath mode and kill enemies.  The more you kill in wrath mode, the more health you regain.  Trouble is (as far as I can see so far in the game), wrath mode initially only lasts for seconds, so, unless you are lightning fast, it's hard to get a kill  during this time, even though the enemy are firing at you in slow-mo.  Thankfully, as you earn perks you can  increase the length of time wrath mode  remains.    There are loads of  perks such as   no QTE fails, earn 5% health for every head shot, reloading behind cover gives you 20% more  ammo, kills during wrath mode earn 25% more health, moving in and out of cover 50% faster,  reloading faster, deal more damage, as well as  loads more  and some of which are upgradeable. and for achievement hunters there's a generous number of achievements to be earned.
Whenever you level up (by scoring points) you earn skill points.  these can be spent on various skills such as Toughness (harder to kill0, improvements in  different types of  weapons  for example, light and heavy weapons a swell a sspecial equipment  and of course wrath.  there are  five upgrades for each skill.  with respect to wrath, each upgrade adds   a new  wrath bar to  your HUD.  The first upgrade effectively doubles your wrath bar.
On my first try I didn't even get past the first stage, but, once I'd realized how to gain a 200% mag fill  it made it easier to avoid getting shot as often, and once I'd earned my first perk, I spent it on the wrath perk, which  enables you to recharge your health  when you make a kill in wrath mode.
As Rambo is one of my old favourites, I'll probably continue with the game, but I am very disappointed in this offering.  It reminds me of my disappointment with one of the Medal of Honor games I got for free when I bought the Wii several years ago for family gatherings.  It plays very similar with respect to no movement control.  It's like someone else has played the game through and recorded all the movements necessary.
My advice is wait till it’s on sale before you spend your hard earned cash.
Edit:
With respect to  recovering health, I think the trick (after studying the videos a little more), is to concentrate on killing  one enemy at a time; for each kill you get about 20% of your health back, so you can afford to lose a little health from other enemy fire  while   aiming at one of them.   As you progress you unlock perks that can extend the wrath mode, which then becomes   a little easier and more useful to use.  Wrath mode is activated by filling a kill bar.
The game covers the first three  films in the franchise i.e. Rambo First Blood (1982), Rambo First Blood II (1985) and Rambo III (1988), pity they didn't add the latest movie released back in 2008 20 years after the last one.
second edit:
Thanks to Bridget Fisher, I finally read the instructions (instead of jumping in blindly the first time around)  and found I actually enjoyed the game   more than previously despite it being  a rail shooter.  I'd ignored the instructions for getting   a 200% mag fill, which  in this game makes a big difference  with respect to losing health. I do think  it's a little too expensive, especially here in the UK.  If you get a friend in the US to gift it to you, you can save a further £5.
Overall I've changed my opinion of this game after   playing it for  three hours.  Now I give it  a thumbs up.  :)

Just finished my first playthrough. In the 80 hours it took I searched every nook and cranny and dark space, read every bit of side story, got in some fun fights, used some really fun abilities, and beat the game with 5 Praxis I had absolutely no use for.
The End... (of this chapter, anyway)
Yes, the ending was abrupt and left more questions than answers, but I paid $60 and had 80 hours of fun. Just put that into perspective and compare that value with other games. These negative reviews are only complaining about the ending, but they have 30-50 hours played, and they're saying they didn't get a value. B.S.
Gameplay.
Furthermore, the mission structure and level design is more complex than previous games. Veteran Deus Ex players are all too familiar with attempting to breach and area and finding the 3 basic ways for entry: hack the electronic door, crawl through the vent, or break the wall. Infiltrating in this game is far more complex than that in a great number of circumstances, which is the most welcome change at all. We forgive that basic gameplay format because we love the story, but that's not necessary this time around. The level design is the best it's ever been, so naturally infiltrating areas is the most fun its ever been.
Boss Fights.
Oh, about those boss fights. I seem to recall players complaining in Human Revolution about being forced into boss fights with no passive alternative. Well now they put only one in the game and made others optional. You just can't be pleased, can you?
Black Market Augmentations.
One of the coolest parts of the original Deus Ex. You literally found augmentations hidden around the game and added them to yourself at the cost of other abilities. I get that Jensen didn't choose his augments, but this is something they seriously need to bring back - powerful augments that are hard to obtain, incredibly powerful, but come at some other great cost. Heck, we've even got a doctor now that can put them on!
Deus Ex Machina.
I thought the point of Deus Ex was to literally become the god of the machine at the very end. This is how it used to work, but hey, Adam Jensen's story isn't over yet.

As a surprise fan of Human Revolution (I've never been overly big on stealth games dripping with philosophy) I awaited Mankind Divided with interest. Sure, I wasn't desperate for it, but it was definitely on my 'to get' list.
I had a fondness for the borderline monosyllabic Adam Jenson and his chums at Sarif, and HR was a game which certainly fleshes out its plot and characters, maybe overly saturating the dialogue at times.
Mankind Divided was released to the usual mixed reviews on Steam - the main negativity on the forums was the technical side - the game was miles off fully baked, and still is, in truth, and complaints were aplenty about the abrupt and unsatisfying ending too. I haven't got to it yet, but I have to say the quality of the game so far, technical quibbles aside, is quite exceptional.
It is safe to say Mankind Divided is a truly brilliant game, one fans of the series will adore if they accept its shortcomings, and one which could win a few new ones too.
Once again you're Jenson, relocated to Prague at the base of your new employer Task Force 29. Once again before long you're embroiled in conspiracy, plot, decisions, and tragedy, and the more the story unfolds, the more questions you'll have. It's a complex diatribe, as the Deus Ex universe generally is, and understanding everything going on takes a lot of going - but the game leaves itself open for those who don't want to pay too much attention to the story by making the game technically a real delight.
Sure, there are framerate, DX12, SLI, and graphic problems throughout, with one or two borderline disturbing glitches, but DEMD is a game which is plain fun to play - it is a real blast of a game, looks gorgeous, and the mechanics of the game engine are extremely tactile.
The hacking system is still a pain, if not as much a pain asa it was before, and the augmentations are predictably enhanced with a new overclocking option, but really this is HR enhanced - it is the same philosophy as HR was, the same gameplay style, but it is done even more enjoyably than that was, and is far better fleshed out in the right ways.
There are plenty of missions, and plenty of choices - there is no lack of content here, and while for all I know I'm right at the end, the content thus far has been good enough to justify the cost.
Once this is fully baked and polished (especially for multiGPU) it will only be even better, but even as it is it's remarkable.
Unfortunately one drawback, from a technical aspect, is the quite diabolical loading times. A 2 minute wait is not uncommon here and it's something Nixxes really needs to work on for the next update.
I have also heard complaints about micro transactions, and that the Frank Pritchard expansion is a con - it's probably true, Eidos' sales model is probably not the best, but it you overlook that for the sheer quality of the game? You won't be disappointed.
But it's probably best you know the ending is abrupt and disatisying in advance, like I do.
EDIT 19/10/16
I have to significantly edit this review. Since writing this piece, the game's quality, environment, and, thanks to bad updates, stability, have all gone south and thoroughly soured my experience of what was growing into a truly excellent game.
Updated notes:
-The first 'act' in Prague is the best part of the game by miles - the daytime setting is a lot of fun, and involving, looks beautiful and keeps your attention. The second act in night time Prague is still good, but not as good and a lot of the charm has gone. The third act, which is further night time Prague is just not fun at all with a challenge thrown in that doesn't even seem that necessary. Hence the enjoyment factor just keeps deteriorating until the final FINAL section which, frankly, is unimaginative piffle and generic beyond words.
-On my rig, it is impossible to run this game in SLI in DX12. 980SLI and I am forced to run in DX11 and its reduced performance due to a DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG crash in DX12 SLI which support just refuse to address - this complete lack of interest in assisting my issue is leaving a sour taste in the mouth. Meanwhile DX11 performance has deteriorated with every update. Great.
-Loading times HAVE been significantly improved, with loads following deaths massively reduced.
-The story, frankly is a bit of a mess.
-I saw a review which points out the choices in this game always suck. And it's true - you're constantly given bad choices - sure, life isn't black and white, but then, that's why we play video games. And whenever you're given options, neither outcome is 'the right one' or good.
-The micro stuttering whatever mode you play in remains an issue. For those unsure, this is when your framerate is perfectly solid but you still see a visual stutter.
Technically this game is a mixed bag, and the content sadly goes downhill the further into it you go - I would still recommend it, but I'd wait till it's fully baked (if it ever gets that far) before committing.
Further update: 25/11/16:
I stand by everything I said already, but now that Nvidia MGPU is fully supported in DX12 I can say from a technical point of view the game is now completely baked - it runs great, looks great, and there are few glitches. I'm going through it again on New Game+ mode and it gives a much better way for me to savour it properly. Now that the game is completely polished I can't really fault it - the latter two sections are the weaker ones but the game, as a whole, is the best Deus Ex I've played by some distance, and now that it's all finalised and the technical quibbles have been resolved, I can't recommend this game highly enough.

Bear in mind that negative reviews for this game often concern issues surrounding the dlc and bad optimisation. I'm not here to be an apologist for SE and their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ business practices, I just want to focus on the game itself.
Though it is by no means perfect, this is a nuanced and fairly polished semi-open world action RPG. A lot of care has gone into the design on both a pratical and aesthetic level. The story is muddled but certainly not bad. The gameplay is excellent. There are very few games out there that will provide you with anything close to the same blend of cyberpunk/dystopia with open-ended gameplay and exploration. I feel inclined to support projects such as this due the large amount of effort that was involved and the relative sparsity of games of this genre when most developers are either making derivative multiplayer games or empty open-world sandboxes.

Trine 2 takes a bold step and turns into a more puzzle-oriented game with a reworked and upgraded balance and ability system. Completed with larger, more detailed and even more charming levels, the game is superior to the predecessor in almost every way. Too bad the DLC couldn’t hold this level of quality.
Like all sequels, Trine 2 tries to give you more of the things that made the first installment good while trying to re-balance or redo all the parts where it lacked.
This of course means that the game looks even better than Trine. The levels offer more variety, they are more detailed than ever, and they are also are more challenging, forcing you to use all three characters for real this time.
This also takes us to the more criticised part: whereas Trine was a traditional platformer, Trine 2 is more of a puzzle game with platforming elements. There are several parts on every level where you may need to stop and try to figure out how to proceed, and it usually involves the abilities of at least two characters. On one hand, it’s a major improvement, but on the other hand it does feel like a setback compared to the first game’s fluidity.
Whereas Trine used the simplest of stories, Trine 2 tries to give you a little more complex narrative on why are you visiting the various levels. Don’t expect anything groundbreaking, though. The three main heroes also receive a makeover, giving them truly unique character traits and personalities, and their banter has improved a lot too.
Sadly the game is not without faults, and these faults even have a name: the Goblin Menace DLC. Even though it gives you even more levels, all of them rely on one new gimmick: the anti-gravity arrow. If you like puzzles, you'll love this game.
Chip's Challenge is the same straight-forward yet entirely maddening puzzle game you remember from the Best of Entertainment pack on Windows 95. This version looks slightly different from that, and the movement is a little bit different as well but not frustratingly so. You adapt very quickly.
I haven't gotten far enough to see if the bonus levels are included in this one or not, but it's everything my mother, brother and I loved about CC when I was a kid, but now in a package that doesn't require an emulator set up to play.
What I really love about CC is that you can sit down and work on a puzzle for a whole afternoon, or you can try a few times and keep coming back to it until you get it figured out, and then come back to it a few more times until you're able to execute the solution without burning, drowning, sliding, forcing, monstering or time-outing into oblivion.
You may find graph paper and coloured pencils helpful, although there are also an abundance of level maps and walkthroughs available online if you're not the sort to draw out your own solutions.
The one downfall CC has is that most of the puzzles, once solved, do not have a ton of replay value; however the sheer number of levels in the game does IMO make up for this shortcoming.

Some people say that the game is unbalanced because of certain characters being simply 'better' in terms of stats than others, or the weapons they have. And while that is true, with most players believing that any character with a spear is a 'good' character, it doesn't mean you'll always lose when playing against those characters. In fact, when most of the players use 'good' characters like Hattori (Spear and Sword user), you can surprise them with somebody people don't usually play with, like Thatch (Sword and Blaster user) or Scarlet (Hammer and Rocket Lance user) because those players will only look for strategies to beat 'good' characters.
Once you get to higher ranks and tournaments, however, you will start to see that the 'less played' characters begin to simply lose against popular ones. This is something that will be present in every game you play (generally). But if you put in the time and effort into using your favourite character, learning moves and techniques, you can still top the tournaments.
Note: I'm not an expert at this game, however I'm giving people a rough idea of what to expect, and to ignore reviews of people who don't recommend the game because of the fact that it's unbalanced.

Some people say that the game is unbalanced because of certain characters being simply 'better' in terms of stats than others, or the weapons they have. And while that is true, with most players believing that any character with a spear is a 'good' character, it doesn't mean you'll always lose when playing against those characters. In fact, when most of the players use 'good' characters like Hattori (Spear and Sword user), you can surprise them with somebody people don't usually play with, like Thatch (Sword and Blaster user) or Scarlet (Hammer and Rocket Lance user) because those players will only look for strategies to beat 'good' characters.
Once you get to higher ranks and tournaments, however, you will start to see that the 'less played' characters begin to simply lose against popular ones. This is something that will be present in every game you play (generally). But if you put in the time and effort into using your favourite character, learning moves and techniques, you can still top the tournaments.
Note: I'm not an expert at this game, however I'm giving people a rough idea of what to expect, and to ignore reviews of people who don't recommend the game because of the fact that it's unbalanced.

Okay, I'll get right into the grit of it. Brawlhalla is not Melee. I personally love Melee, there is an active melee community and even a community for people who like to play melee without owning a gamecube or leaving their desks and it still has a live competitive scene and yada yada yada - we get it!
If you'd like a melee, either play melee (Anther's Ladder or something) or consider Rivals of Aether.
Brawlhalla is a fighter that is somewhere in between analog fighters and digital fighters. It utilizes full stick motion for movement and focuses on ones ability to time their attacks and move around the map using them, like an analog fighter.
But it also feels a lot more restrictive, or rather, the skill ceiling is lowered HEAPS (like a digital fighter, shots fired).
To sum up quickly to any smash familiar player, brawlhalla is a smash game in which slow time is permanently enabled as well as lighter weight. In which instead of completely unique characters, you have an array of character with different stats (as well as costimized stats like sm4sh), who uses a common weapon, unhanded, until you pick up a frequently spawning item which gives you one of your two weapons that are determined by the character you chose. The weapons are each visually unique, but some are generic and have similar attacks to others of the same type.
Its... a lot simpler when you just play it.
Gibbing is very uncommon unless you spike an enemy, the ability to recover is very high for most characters, with two jumps and an air dodge that can be aimed up, combined with the low weight, leading to that.
Not all characters are unlocked by default. there's a rotation of free characters like many F2P games, and a not-too-shabby income of in-game currency to unlock characters you love in particular, or at least, not too shabby for the current number of characters. I'd hope that as the character pool increases, the devs can up the income slightly to compensate. (But past has shown that F2P devs never do)
Worth a shot, overall, even as a smash player.

Hmm, a game to a genre I like, in a setting I like, with gameplay that I mostly like. With some issues though.
Performance: Pretty demanding. I really recommend like R9 290 / GTX 970 or a better card even for just 1080p. I completed it on 1100Mhz R9 280X, i5-3570k @ 4.5Ghz, 8GB 2000Mhz DDR3. Settings: like medium, with tessalation and contact shadows off. The performance was generally like 50-60 FPS, with some dips to 40's in the most populated areas and over 60 FPS in the easier to run areas. I don't think I had technical difficulties, except with the DX12 version which seems to be unstable maybe?
Writing: Generally okay, but the story didn't really touch me. Just felt rather generic and still overly twisty/complicated. I guess bonus points would for having to make some choices during the game, but not sure those were really that big of a deal.
Setting: Praque 2029. Augmented people like you are bad, mkkay, so nobody wants to really trust you and cops hate you too. I thought the areas were all beautifully crafted with a lot of exploration possible, maybe the strongest point for the game.
Gameplay: Well, I'm not sure the terminator approach is doable...I didn't try the bulletsoaking augs, but without them you die preeetty fast. So in the end you pretty much want to sneak as much as you can. AI is quite dumb, like sure there are areas where you get killed almost instantly when seen, but often you can just abuse the pathing and covers so easily. Even if they see you, they might not make an alarm instantly, felt quite forgiving.
Shooting guns was okay, hacking got pretty boring, augs were barely needed.
Level design was pretty cool, but if you use the vision aug it can really kill off the fun of exploration. I think almost all combat might be skipable and there's certainly many chances to hack the security or use some other diversion tactics.
Graphics: I guess it looks okay, but seems to lose out to Witcher 3 and Rise of the Tomb Raider for example. Could have been better optimized I feel.
Overall rather disappointing ending and it's hard to recommend this game over Witcher 3 GOTY for example. Still a game worth playing if you like the series or genre and can get it at -50% or something.

I loved the original Deus Ex. I played it for the first time over a decade after it came out, but I could still appreciate what it had done for gaming as an industry and as an artform. It's possibly the best written game of all time. It introduced alternative paths and ways of doing things like stealth vs action vs hacking in a first person perspective like never before. We're still feeling its influence.
Human Revolution was a solid attempt at modernizing the formula. The writing didn't wow me to the same extent, but it did ask some interesting questions and tell a compelling, personal story.
Mankind Divided is a lackluster, emotionless continuation.
Oftentimes if a game is good, I'll say to myself, "All I want is more." Mankind Divided delivers that, but sadly it turned out not to be enough. Everything is too similar to its immediate predecessor. The augmentations, the gameplay, the weapons. It's like they started development on this one by copying and pasting the resources from the first, and then barely made any modifications.
Things that they
change are often worse. Take, for example, the idea of your experimental augs overloading so you have to permanently disable some. It's an annoying idea to begin with because it encourages you to simply avoid all the new experimental augs.
Ugh.
I really enjoyed the first few hours I spent exploring Prague. The change of location was welcome. And it's always fun to stumble across a random side quest without meaning to. The problem is that the quests and exploration were front-loaded: when I returned to Prague after new missions there was rarely anything waiting for me that I didn't expect. If a developer relies on only a single hub city, then they need to make it come alive, not feel like a static set piece.
The ultimate problem was with the story. It was not suprising in any of the usual mind-blowing Deus Ex ways. Nor was it an impactful, intimate journey like in Human Revolution. We were given something cold that concerned itself primarily with the physical existence of the characters. It wasn't epic or adventurous. It did not move me in any way. It's worth quoting Faulkner's Nobel Prize acceptance speech here because it exactly describes Mankind Divided's story:
Finally, all the extra bonus features like a permanent death mode and the arcade Breach mode are things nobody wanted, nobody asked for. An RPG should be about experiementation and exploration, but an ironman you-only-live-once difficulty is totally contrarian to those ideals. The experience suffers for it. And Deus Ex without a story driving it, like in Breach, is devoid of any life or meaning. The resources that went into developing those parts would've been better spent simply improving the campaign.
Mankind Divided isn't a bad game. The fundamental idea is executed well. The problem is that it wasn't a very good idea to begin with. Just like a summer blockbuster, the problem is not in the production value, but in the writing. This script needed to a lot better while it was still on the drawing board. So instead of a true sequel we got something that feels like a large expansion. If there is a third installment, I'm willing to bet the events of this second game will easily and quickly be glossed over without losing much. That makes me sad, which is more than I felt at any point while actually playing.

- Some parts of the game feel repetitive

Despite the bad, I'd recommend this game if you enjoy RPG/Shooters with a strong plot.  It's improved over Human Revolution in gameplay aspects, but falls short just a bit in story telling.

Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon is one of those rare cases were the spin-off game is actually better than the main game in my opinion. It takes much of what Far Cry 3 does, condenses it into a smaller environment, makes everything much faster and easier to get to, makes you crazy powerful from the start, injects a crapload of style and 80's/90's referential humour into it, and offers a shorter and much easier to get into experience while giving you just enough stuff to do outside of the main story to easily justify the standalone price. Everything from the visual style to the cheesy neon environment and cyber-esque enemy designs just makes the short time spent in this game a joy. Throw in an amazing 80's style new wave/techno soundtrack from the guys at "Powerglove" and you have one of the more unique looking and sounding games of the last few years.
An easy recommendation.

From a player that's played this game since release back in 2007, playing across 3 servers, founder account, over 15,000 hours logged over the years. I can tell you that my feelings for this game are very genuine and it's taken me a good two months to write this review after leaving the game.
I'll be honest, the game truly has fallen from what it used to be, it's become, let's say, easy from what I remember years ago. Angmar content is probably on par with what vanilla WoW was for me, The massive amount of meticulousness that had to go into every single character that you had. From the start of character creation, you were in danger of getting absolutely smacked by landscape mobs if you were a certain class and pulled mobs badly (I'm looking at you hunter). The way you had to play a class was very different from launch than it is now, and I'm not saying that's a bad thing at all, things change, just me reminiscing over times long past. This is just the tip of the iceberg so to say.
Now, on to the content. The developing team behind LOTRO has put out content consistently that appealed to the audiences up to Rise of Isengard, which in my opinion, was one of the best expansions I've ever played in any MMO. The content before and including Isengard (Angmar, Mines of Moria, Seige of Mirkwood) are incredible, everything from the instances, zones, questing, down to the ambient sounds, it was amazing. Now this basically talking about the expansions as a whole, (I consider Angmar an expansion in this list, but it was vanilla content more or less) but the zones in between the major content areas were amazing as well, North Downs, Lothlorien, Evendim, Enedwraith, If you have never experienced the night in Forochel, you are missing on one of the most amazing game sceneries ever. Great instance designs in all of this content, from forging into Carn Dum with your friends and overcoming the managerie of bosses and Mordirith, to conquering places like Barad Guldur and the Tower of Isen along with toppling Saruman in an incredible battle atop the tower itself. Many many memories will never be forgotten that pertain to such events that took place in the game.
Alas, many new players will never get to experience this content simply because the game has progressed far beyond all of this. Most of the players that I met during my final year and a half or so were players that were there to rush to level cap and do "end-game", that's the joke kids, there is no end-game. All it is at level cap is a daily grind for your daily reputation factions for that "highest tier raiding set" that you will never put to serious use because most of the players that play the game now will NOT run content that will challenge them. It's that simple, I led pug tier 2 challenge runs on my main server of Windfola for years for players not in raiding guilds, and people would rather run Sambrog 6 man spams for crap rewards than spending a little more time in a bigger, more challenging instance for big reward. It pained me to see that the game populace had declined to such a lazy group of "give it to me without the challenge" group of people, because let's be honest, anyone that played in vanilla LOTRO can tell you how bloody hard it was, JUST to get your resistances right to actually stand a chance in Carn Dum, let alone actually fighting the bosses. But don't be let down, there are groups of players on many servers on both EU and NA that play around the level of that old content when it was released so they can specifically run that content and have it challenge them, they are great people and they organize themselves in server world chats and forums still.
Now on to the "current" content. After Isengard, the game started to decline, Rohan was a let down for most players, the introduction of mounted combat looked fun on paper, it was ok, but it was buggy, and it never really fit in with most players. The landscape was pretty for a bit, but you got used to the rolling plains. The instances were sadly a joke in terms of difficulty, aside from the raids in that cluster for the expansion, the three raids that were introduced were pretty fun and challenging at the highest difficulty of tier 2 challenge, Fires of Smaug and Battle for Erebor were great fun, but the third, Flight to the Lonely Mountain was pretty much impossible at release because it was buggy, it got fixed, but far to late for such a simple problem. Then you had the the most outrageous rep grind in the form of Hytbold reconstruction, something that would take around a solid month to complete if you were very diligent about your dailies, something that had to be done to aquire your level 85 class set pieces. It wasn't the worst thing ever, but the real knife in the back really came with the area expansion of Wildemore with the atrocious rep grind at the end of finishing every quest in the zone, it was terrible, an everyone that I knew hated it, and it was all for a shiny epic accessory piece that didn't mean a whole lot.
After this Helms Deep released, Big Battles came with it, I won't go into detail about it, but it was something to see, especially as a player from the beginning. All the classes were redone, traits were completely overhauled into tree progression, basically the game was stripped and redone in most aspects. No new instances were included, no raids, nothing except the battles that most hated, I did my progression through them, did A LOT of bug report testing for them over the months, some say to this day that they are still buggy. When they released update 14 I called it quits, said my goodbyes to many, and uninstalled.
As for players that really enjoy playing PvP, I STRONGLY recommend you watch videos and visit the official LOTRO forums and read through the PvMP threads. Personally, I think the community for PvP is toxic and players are simply looking for who has the bigger E-Peen at any given time. On any server you will find flavor of the month players that jump from class to class every update so they can destroy you with minimal effort, it's just terrible habits that a fair amount of them have and it's nasty, one of the main reasons that led to me leaving the game, considering there really is no PvE endgame anymore.
Now, don't get me wrong I will recommend this game to anyone that every asks me about it, it's very good looking, classes play pretty well, questing isn't a total bore, crafting can be ok, there is amazing RP opportunity. Just remember that this game has been around for a good while and is going through it's decline because of recent content release, but there are still servers with 200+ player login, people still play this game, I leave it up to you to decide whether to drop subscription money to do a large amount of things that this game has to offer in terms of content. I've made many dear friends because of this game, maybe you will as well.
As for the players that have never progressed anywhere near the end of a character's leveling path and experienced a large amount of this game, they truly have no opinion of the game. They haven't gone through anything that would give them any right to judge the game in any way shape or form, it hurts greatly when I read a review from someone that hasn't even logged an hour and down votes this game.

I enjoyed the style and story of this game. The atmosphere of the world of the future is extremely engaging, palpable. You listen to Picus news and they sound like it's actually happening right now. It is quite entrancing.
But the game itself simply hasn't evolved enough since Human Revolution. I could go on for a long time explaining it, but here's the basic deal. The game actively encourages stealth by giving you more exp and making NPCs think better of you if you don't kill. But if you play it as a stealthy pacifist, you get the following results:
* Practically all weapons become useless. Even stun pistol isn't necessary, because you can sneak to anybody and take them down.
* Half of augmentations become useless and thus experience becomes useless about half into the game or earlier.
* Difficulty levels become useless because they don't affect anything outside shootouts.
* Complex stealthy routes are practically useless, because you can easily turn off cameras and sneak through the front door almost anywhere.
* 90% of ingame items like ammo, painkillers and energy batteries become useless.
* Money become almost useless because there's nothing a stealthy pacifist player can buy except a couple of Praxis kits.
Plus a number of questions arises:
* Why are there lethal takedowns? They provide zero benefit over non-lethal ones.
* Why the thugs say to each other things like "I'll go check that noise" but if you take them down, nobody goes to check what happened to them?
* Why stunned people never wake up by themselves?
* Why stunned people can be woken up by NPCs but Jensen has no way of waking them up?
* Why throwing stunned people off a balcony or dragging them headfirst up the stairs doesn't kill them?
* Why cameras have huge indicators of their field of view only visible to Jensen?
* Why is every building and even CYBERSPACE full of gigantic vents that an adult man can get through?
* Why is there only one type of hacking in a CYBERPUNK game? (not counting magical remote hacking)
* Why is menu and inventory navigation more cluttered than before?
I expected more. While the world of Deus Ex has evolved, the game is simply extremely outdated.
Recommended for hardcore Deus Ex or cyberpunk fans only.

Mankind Divided is a welcome return for Adam Jensen and his pointy beard and humourless personality. This is a dark and gloomy future for humanity, where so-called terrorists appear to be controlled by the illuminati for their nefarious agenda. The story is difficult to follow, I'll admit, but there's plenty of parallels to the modern world - PICUS = CNN? Augmented people = muslims or blacks? If the message that we're supposed to absorb, is that nothing is as it seems, and that the powers that be are hiding something, or secretly working for some dark agency with an occult agenda, and that mankind is basically screwed, then yep - it worked. Level-design was great, soundtrack spot-on, and environments were suitably depressing. Did I enjoy this more than HR? The only disappointment was that there's wasn't more of the game, more places to visit, and perhaps a few more missions. It ends kind of abruptly. Still, I got about 25 hours out of this, and would definitely recommend to fans and newbies, but I'm not sure there's much replay value here. 8 /10.

As a fan of the Deus Ex series, I was skeptical that Mankind Divided was going to be a great successor to Human Revolution; especially after the bad taste I was left with after Metal Gear Solid V not delivering my expectations last year; I still did preorder (because I am stupid and thought the 20% discount was worth maybe getting a bad game) and was optimistic.

The first segment of the game brings us to a smaller building, mainly used a segue to teach us the mechanics of the game and about certain things, thankfully it doesn't make us walk for 5 minutes just showing us this building (looking at you
) and it gives us an option to skip the tutorial segments as the building still is a functioning part of the story and gives us a secluded playground to test out the augmentations from Human Revolution and also testing out your weapons. None of the new augmentations that were added to the game.
The game done something that Metal Gear Solid V didn't do whatsoever right, it gave us an interesting world that was designed so well, there were so many times in the game where I went into a place through a dumber route because I wasn't looking for another route and brute forced through and then find another way into the same place that would have saved me a few minutes and a lot of Biocells and effort, then when I replayed that same segment, I'd find another two methods to get into that same place; the GARM facility experienced a little bit later in the game is a good sign of this.
This game's story was quite predictable as it's a Deus Ex game, you know you're going to work for a corrupt force; the real question is "When will they turn on you?", this is the only question I was surprised at the answer of, SPOILER ALERT:
. But most questions you'll ask in this story will be answered in the most predictable way; and the questions you don't get answered are set up for the next game; the main place where the story and writing often shine are in the Side-Missions, which.. sadly; often brings you to the same places regardless of actions taken in the quest, but at the same time your actions can reveal a clearer picture of the situation.
The soundtrack in this game is almost as good as Human Revolution, I don't think it was; but I'm not saying it's bad.. I really liked all of the tracks in this game, it's just that I prefer Human Revolution, not much else I can say other than it fits the vibe that the game goes for.
I played the System Rift DLC, beat it in about 3.5 hours (got the DLC one night, the internet went down in my home, played the DLC and turned off the PC, found out I was still eligible for a refund and I took that) and even though the System Rift DLC was well done, I felt that the DLC was too short for the money it was asking for.
The Jensen Story that you get as a Pre-Order, Desperate Measures, disgusted me. The content was great and was very well done but what sickened me is the fact that you can tell exactly where in the game it was cut from the main game and that you can tell that Square Enix was the one who pushed for the removal of this Side-Mission and introduction as a DLC.

The game is quite.. short, it took me roughly about 24 hours for a Foxiest of the Hounds run, which was my second run, merely because my first one had an issue where it would crash when returning after a certain side quest (this issue has now been fixed, but game me a lot of time to replay the game with a more desirable outcome for certain choices I've made) and both runs took me a total of 35 hours altogether.. that's not to say that the game will be finished definitely at 17 hours, on my second run I spent 5 hours in just the first time in Prague, and I STILL felt like I hadn't found everything in the area and I felt like I was rushing to the finish even though I took my time.
The pricing of the game; which is 50 euros at the time of writing is a slight bit steep for the length of the game, I would extremely recommend this as a pickup at the price range of 20-30 euros.
Mankind Divided included a lot of nods and stayed true to the timeline presented in Deus Ex and it's showing Manderley before his time at UNATCO,
Eidos took really delicate care to what they are doing with Deus Ex and try not to retcon anything except a certain something that hasn't been explained ;). It's really nice to see them not try to wreck the series and try hard to stay faithful to the original.

A lot of other reviews already state the pros and cons of this game, so I'll be little bit in depth from another angle: from the PoV of someone who loved the previous game of the franchise (Deus Ex: Human Revolution), I would like to discuss the story/plot of Mankind Divided.
First thing first: what other reviews are claiming that the story of this game being incomplete, is completely true.  However, whether and how much it affects the “fun” of the entire game is up to each individual.  Also, I hope you played Human Revolution.  That game is a classic and is universally agreed to be much better than Mankind Divided as both games currently stand.  So, if you haven’t played the prequel, stop reading any further and go play it instead (also because spoilers!).
On another thought, if Eidos did not make the sequel a direct continuation of Human Revolution’s plot, and maybe if we’ve gotten another protagonist and his/her story might not feel so incomplete.  Anyway, Mankind Divided requires the player knowing the story’s background to fully understand and enjoy.
Let’s remember that DXHR tells a complete story of a conspiracy, with branching endings that makes sense and was satisfying.  There is only a segment of a DLC story that was separate, but later on was integrated to the main campaign (if memory serves me right).  Mankind Divided, however, has a♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of loose ends—even apart from the main conspiracy that feels like suddenly closing the book half way through.
Also worth mentioning is that there is no canon ending to DXHR, which in my opinion, severely limits how the setup of Mankind Divided’s plot.  By that I mean not only the action of players who choose one of the three endings in DXHR has zero impact to this game’s plot, Mankind Divided’s plot setup must conform to *all* of the three endings.  This is also the reason why there is no reference to the pilot lady from DXHR at all in Mankind Divided; because she could be either alive or dead, and evidently it’s much harder to make a sequel story regarding her than the three endings of DXHR.
Back to the topic of Mankind Divided’s plot being incomplete… It is now obvious the loose ends are intended for selling DLC.  Desperate Measures, a DLC comes with the game’s release, is so separate that MAIN GAME PROGRESS (AUGS/ITEMS) DOES NOT CARRY OVER!  Looks like the next DLC (System Rift) has the same issue.  Just what the f___ is Eidos thinking??
I don’t know about you, but even though I loved DXHR, I’m not a sucker that Eidos hope me to be who would constantly throw money to them just to get a complete story.  It is totally unacceptable, and the greed really kills any further motivation of me buying the next game of this franchise.
Take my advice.  Don’t buy this game now.  Wait until Eidos stops milking money, integrate all the DLC into the main game and releases a “director cut” version like they did with DXHR.

All of the characters simply have two weapons (which aren not even unique to the character) with varying (but pretty similar) speed, range and power.
By not having any special mobility moves the game lacks huge impact moments typical of Smash Bros. Fighting to avoid falling off, by using skills and precise timing, while the other players try to prevent it from happen, created in Smash bros memorable moments.
Punching people in this game is devoid of any depth or satisfaction, it's just a matter of spamming attacks on top of a chaotic platform, dodging and jumping in between.

As a stand-alone title, Blood Dragon is a fantastic first-person shooter. It uses the same game engine and mechanics as Far Cry 3, but does away with the skill tree and inventory management. You can still upgrade weapons and level up, but given that the game is much shorter, everything is scaled accordingly. The weapons are awesome, they all feel great and look nice. It's still open-world with plenty of firefights going on and garrisons to take over with side quests and collectibles for weapon upgrades. What amazes me is how they've managed to deliver the full Far Cry experience in such a short game. To do EVERYTHING - i.e. take over all bases, complete story, random exploration, hunting all animals, getting all collectibles, all side quests etc. takes around 8 hours, and even on Hard the game isn't much of a challenge. Despite the short length, it is perhaps one of the most action-packed, no-fillers shooters ever. The level of comedy, references, quotes are better than any other shooter I've come across. I'd go as far as saying that if you have never played a Far Cry game before, this is the best one to play! It still retains the essence of Far Cry - it's all about survival, still has that Rambo bad♥♥♥♥♥feel to it and rewards stealth. In some respects it's more similar to the original game because of the dragons, which can be compared to the mutants but only much cooler. In summary, Blood Dragon is a great shooter. Although its length can be criticised, one must remember that the game was not sold as a full title. Personally I think it could easily be a $35 game given the quality and entertainment value. If you've yet to play a Far Cry game and you're a fan of shooters and cyberpunk themes, Blood Dragon is a must-play.

In Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons you follow two siblings Ayi and Nayi on a quest to find a rare plant to save their dying father. The game features an interesting way to control both brothers: left joystick and the left shoulder button control the older brother, and right joystick and the right shoulder button control the younger brother, which are both controlled simultaneously to navigate through the game world and solve puzzles. Without any (understandable) words mentioned to the player, the game signals quest items through clever camera movement and interactions between the brothers. The game takes a comfortable 3-4 hours to complete and is very enjoyable for winding-down after playing a more stressful game.
Overall, the game is very enjoyable and worth its price. The art is beautiful, the music is amazing, the sound effects are well-done and the story is easy to follow.
TIP: If you regularly mix up both character controls, try to keep the older brother (Nayi) on the left of the younger brother (Ayi), since Nayi is controller with the left hand and Ayi is controlled with the right hand.

PRE-REVIEW NOTES
===============
MK X had a bit of a rough launch on the PC, even being denied the 2nd Kombat pack for the longest time, but now that that has all been included (finally) along with the updated GGPO netkode, here are my final thought on it.
I've played this game on both PC and PS4, my hours indicate mostly my time is spent on console, but the the two different versions of the game are practically the same now. With thast out of the way, how is the actual game?
================
TL;DR is at the bottom.
=========
Story Mode
=========
Mortal Kombat X is easily the best MK game in the entire series in terms of gameplay mechanics, how combos function, and overall feels truly like the next evolution of the MK fighting game franchise. The story mode (while one can argue seems to be a bit lacking) provides a new story to embark on, now following outside of the tournament format. However it does kind of feel like everyone's power level is off. I won't spoil anything but once you play it you'll see what I mean. On top of that certain areas just don't feel fully fleshed out like they should have been. The 2nd chapter of the game (while one of the most interesting parts in the plot) simply feels unfinished or completely rushed. I would've like if NRS had included more chapters in the story mode to spend more time on areas where more time is sorely needed. However for the most part, what we are given in the story mode is still enjoyable minus the obviously skewed power levels.
========
Gameplay
========
Gameplay is easily the tightest that it has ever been in the series. Kombo strings feel fluid and responsive, aswell as with each string and even each individual button having it's frame data right beside the input in the move list. It's great for those who want to really get good at the game, but it's not required if you simply want to know what you need to press in order to execute a string. These strings can then either be cancelled into a special move, or depending on the string, can launch your opponent for an oppurtunity to juggle and do even more damage. Each character's strings feel like they belong to their respective characters, and while FGC purists may not enjoy that the game has switched to a more kind of 50/50 meta, most combo strings that start or end with a 50/50 usually end that player's turn for pressure, if not completely punishable into a full kombo. It feels like a perfect blend of casual and and fighting game enthusiasts type of gameplay on top of the characters each having 3 different variations that can instantly change how a character's playstyle works and feels. The fighting itself feels polished and has hardly anything that really feels rushed or glossed over.
=====
Online
=====
Thanks to the last balance patch that finally included the GGPO netkode into the PC version of the game, the online is superb. Never has the series felt so close to emulating an offline match, but in an online environment. You have Ranked Matches, Player Matches, Private Matches, 100-man Player rooms (which can be made by anyone at anytime) 3v3 or 5v5 team battles, Tower battles, Online practice, Test your luck, it all just adds to the complete package that is already here. But the thing you will appreciate the most is just how the online works now. GGPO has saved this game online. I hope more fighting games take notice of how the online functions here. (Just don't ask about how it was before GGPO, it was awful, let's forget pre-GGPO even existed)
=================
TL'DR / Final Conclusion
=================
Mortal Kombat X feels like the next evolution of the MK franchise. While it still has it's downsides, I feel like the pros definitely outweigh the cons here and I can't wait for what the next MK game will look like. Hopefully they take what works here, and fix what didn't. Then we will have a real contender for the Fighting Game Genre.
