Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is an awesome Deus Ex game that bring all the elements we love about the Deus Ex universe with the exception of the perfect story driven experience its predecessor had brought us.
Does this make it a worthy sequel?
Have you ever had TV show you were a long time enthusiast of it and at some point came a season that made plot progress very slow?
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided was for me the filler season of the 'new' Deus Ex story line (considering Deus Ex: Human Revolution as a way to reboot the franchise).
It really is so awesome in so many ways, but leaves you without the satisfaction of witnessing a complete story unfolded in front of you.
Now before you jump into conclusions let me say the story we get to see in this game is interesting enough, it gives insight on what is going on in the Deus Ex universe.
It's not a bad story, but it's more like the developers wanted us to be prepared to something that is about to come,
something that needs time and effort in order to be brought to life and needs some feedback from the players over ideas and elements and pieces of plot that are going to be used.
Thus in combination with the never ending need for income from a publisher, comes this title.
What we get from Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a combination with every single thing we loved from the gameplay, the graphics, the physics and the skills we were introduced in Deus Ex: Human Revolution, all buffed up and evolved.
In terms of gameplay the developers did not choose to do any dangerous experimentations with any extreme new elements.
The whole system is a balance of what we had with extra details, an better AI, a nice variety of enemies to face, a few new skills on your augmentation-skills-tree and a very well thought off architecture of ways the player can choose to complete any objective without having any one of them being any less rewarding than the other. From being stealthy to go guns blazing loud. From using mainstream paths to exploring every corner and finding alternative routs to get to your objective. Whatever the type of your favorite gameplay is, you will enjoy it to the max.
The melee knock-out and kill animations are enjoyable, in fact, I got so many enjoyable moments in my first 2 runs that I felt fully motivated to be stealthy, to explore alternative paths, to chose whether I wanted to be deadly of spare my enemies as I progressed through building on the set of morals I wanted to set and support my role playing experience.
Also worth mentioning is that among the collectibles in the game, you get to find items that are some sort of barcodes, that you can scan with your phone and unlock developer material regarding the game such as interviews and demonstrations. I found that to be really cool!
The graphics of this game are neat. But ultra specs can be pretty heavy if your hardware is not up to it.
Turning of MSAA and lowering the shadow detail option seem to bring you a very nice experience with smooth FPS and satisfying details. The environments are very well designed and the face expressions seemed so nice. I actually enjoyed 99% of all interactions with NPCs in my first run without skipping dialogues.
Physics seem to be at very nice levels in the game with pretty well done ragdoll physics on bodies and I met absolutely no collision issues throughout my play time.
The only bug I can think of meeting in the game was a couple of times where I engaged into convos with NPCs and their guns textures were not loaded and they ended up looking like holding invisible weapons.
Other than that everything looks great!
Mindblowing, immersive and full of character with a few Blade Runner retrospective elements such as color themes combined with neon lights that gave me doses of nostalgia.
The world of the Deus Ex universe is a gloomy vast world with neverending details no matter if it's daylight or nighttime.
The environments are awesome no matter under what circumstances you find them in. NPCs feel alive, engaging in dialogues, maybe not as generic as in other open world masterpieces we have seen so far like The Witcher 3, but still enough to make you belive that the world designed is alive enough. With details varying from the NPCs clothes and suits to buildings, to the whole outstandingly detailed level design of the Golem City (inspired by the Kowloon Walled City in Hong Kong).
The game's OST is no more than simply outstanding. Nothing less was expected after having gotten a taste of what Deus Ex can offer us from the Human Revolution.
I mean seriously. Just listen to the ending credits song!!!!

Elias Toufexis voicing Adam Jensen is as badass as ever. All main and secondary characters and NPCs are so well voiced and designed, bringing life in the game's world. I would stop and interact with as many NPCs I could on my first run hearing their generic lines curious to see how each NPC fits the world is set it and how it's influenced by the way the story unfolds around them.
On a sidenote, I want more from Duncan MacReady. I find Peter Serafinowicz to be a badass and I wish to hear more from him in the future!
The game includes a New Game Plus mode which allows you to reply the game by keeping the skills and inventory items you had at the end of your first playthrough. Offering you easy access to achievement hunting and alternative choices in quests when replying it.
There's also a game mode called Breach where you get yourself into sets of trials, unlocking info about some small storylines that are interesting but it gets repetitive very fast.
And then there's a choice in "Jensen's Stories" where you get to play a side quest of the main story - though all your skills and items are reset. But it's interesting and enjoyable nevertheless
We do not see much more than a piece of the city of Prague and a couple of interesting locations (GARM and Golem City).
Everything in the game seems to be leading you somewhere and right when you have yourself fully immersed in the plot, THE GAME JUST ENDS.
It left me with a completely WTF feeling and it took me some time to digest what happened and why it happened.
The game offers you a very tasty list of things to think about regarding the world of Deus Ex. It explains quite a few interesting stuff. But it ends up being something like a giant side mission to a plot that is yet to come.
Everything with the campaign seemed perfect until you realize that you end up experiencing a filler.
Some people might get disappointed to this, however when I look at the whole of the picture, I am not going to say that this is a bad game at all. It's just that after what we got in DE:HR we are expecting something more than what we got.
What the heck is with day one DLC? And how ridiculously stupid is it to offer skill point packs in a SINGLE PLAYER GAME?
I mean, ok, DLC weapons? I'm ok with that. But praxis kits? This is absolutely hilarious. Why would they even do that? The game is not even that hard even at the hardest setting.
You get plenty of praxis kits during your game run, you unlock even more by doing the other game modes, and you can even unlock even more if you play the mobile phone game DeusEx:Go.
I really don't understand in what way they thought that this idea would be cool on release. Because of that move, they got an unfair amount on negative reviews on Steam on day one of the game release. Was it really worth it? Come on Eidos.
This game for me is a 8/10.
Could had been even higher if the main plot was fulfilling. The day one DLC is setting a bad example which I hope is not followed.
The game is awesome. It's not just above average. But it's not perfect. For its price.
Recommended

Wow....Transmissions: Element 120...just wow. This game really surprised me. I honestly thought it would be.....eh. But the game was really good. It had three key elements; graphics, gameplay, story. It made you wonder who you were, what you were there for. Something that was good, but also a tad bad. I think it was a good game, very fun and quick.
The beginning was good, made it feel a bit like a horror game, which is cool to
with Half Life 2 (no pun intended). Then the opening on the small train felt really tense and great. Opening the doors and seeing the stunning graphics was a nice little surprise, and very nice. Definately mastered the graphics for the game, it was great, the effects they added, the lighting wasn't over the top or too little. It just all fit in really well together. Nicely complemented each other. Which is a good thing for a game.
The combat was nice, and felt really smooth. There was plenty of ammo and health, which never got you worried you'd die soon. The stealth in the game was cool, I found that really useful and fun. Really nice touch. And the striders at the end were a nice little challenge.
The gravity gun itself...ahh...what a nice weapon. It was useful, helpful and easy to use...but too damn OP. The cool down for the aux power was ok, but I think it needed to recharge slower, it made the game a bit easy at the rate it charged up and how you could just kill enemies insantly. Either that or just...more enemies? But still, a nice weapon none the less.
The trophies were great! Nice and easy if you knew what you were doing and a great feature. I found the gnome one great, just sitting him next to you whilst you crawl through sewage or a vent. Really funny to see and really great.
The cutscenes were ok to me, although I got some people telling me they took control away from you. Personally, they were just right, and fit in nicely. Since they were short, it didn't really matter to me but everyone has their own thoughts.
The story itself was ok, but I think it was confusing in some places. I know you were meant to question what it was about, but it never really explained. Where you Gordon Freeman? Were you Shepard? Were you a citizen or a Rebel? It could potentially be confusing at some bits, but it was ok sometimes.
Overall, a really nice game and definately worth getting...especially if you like Half Life and cause it's free! So enjoy and be sure to play in the dark, since it's much more spooky then. Have fun and we'll see about that....

Well, this game is a lot of fun. I don't necessarily consider it a game, though. I consider it a simulator. Something to improve your actual skill. If you are not into RC cars in real life, then this really isn't for you. It can be fun for people who aren't interested in RC cars, but I think there are better games for pure entertainment value.
If you are a very serious RC enthusiast, specifically a 1/8 buggy person, then you have to have this simulator. So, that is the perspective that I am going to abide by, someone who is very much enmeshed into the 1/8 buggy off road racing. There is a lot of on road stuff in this game that is very good, but I have paid it no attention.
Firstly, you absolutely HAVE TO purchase the adapter for about $19.99. without that usb adapter there is no one you can take it seriously. Secondly, I recommend using or buying the a spare receiver strictly for this game. It is very wise to use the same transmitter that you race with in real life and then adding another model for the sim. Getting or using a second recover is strictly for convince. If you are dong going to play on a laptop or you know that you are willing to take out your existing receiver every time you want to play, then that is fine.
Secondly, I highly recommend that you buy the most expensive versions of the game. The ‘lifetime’ or ‘ultimate’ version. No matter what you do, you have to purchase the basic actual game for around $20. Then, you can buy DLC and expansion packs. I recommend buying the lifetime version, because the dutch guy that owns the company is actually working constantly to update, upgrade, and add content. It is very much worth it, in my opinion. All the tracks and buggy packs, ect will work out to more expensive after a few years. This simulator has been around a very long time and it is constantly getting better.
Now, for the actual review. The physics are very good. It is not a very demanding game to run at the same time. The tune-ability is extraordinary. My only criticism for nitro is that they engine sounds become for discriminatory. The engine tuning is actually a factor at the most competitive levels. For electric, I would appreciate more variety of hardware to choose from, but then again the fact that they are all essentially equal is a good thing. Like the chassis, they are essentially all the same at the competitive kit level, which is a good thing. Another criticism would be that on the setup sheet they offer you a more clear visitation of what and where you are chaining things.
It comes down to your tune, setup, and above all driving skill. Which is great. The competitive levels available are outstanding and I can honestly say there are some guys in this game that are beyond pro drivers from all over the world. I really appreciate the completion.
To summarize, invest some money into this simulator and it will turn your real life investments into another realm. If you are running a buggy that, at one point, was worth around a thousand dollars, then spending the total of a new brushless motor combo or a low level nitro engine is more than worth it. What this game offers has honestly improved my driving significantly that would equal probably dozens and dozens of full days worth of driving. I love this simulator and it is such a great thing to exist for the RC hobby.
My final tips: Have a dedicated receiver for the adapter. YOU HAVE TO BUY THE ADAPTER. Download and research other peoples set ups. You can download files and then move them over to a file inside the game through your computers file management, then when you open the game they are there. Add all the ‘groups’ and ‘clubs’ that you can, because they host races. If you just race the official races then there is less content, but the official races are the most competitive.

Hidden object games have come a long way from their iSpy/Highlights inspired roots, branching off from simply searching for random objects in a scene of junk into something more akin to a casual adventure game. Angelica Weaver is an exceptional example of this, blending traditional adventure and HOG gameplay into an enjoyably ridiculous murder mystery, all held together with impressively high production values.
Catch Me When You Can follows Chicago detective Angelica Weaver, on the case for a serial killer that seems to be copying a series of murders that occurred a hundred years ago. For reasons never quite explained, Weaver can revisit scenes from the past, and in doing so begins to piece together both the murders from the past and how they tie in with the present. It's predictably convoluted and ultimately leads to a rather silly and anticlimactic ending, but on the whole it's just compelling enough to keep you entertained.
A bit more frustrating is its often confusing puzzle logic and consistent inability to properly communicate where you need to go. I'd often find myself clicking randomly around the screen hoping to trigger something I'd missed before, only to find I needed to travel several screens back and use a random object to obtain another random object which somehow let me progress past where I was. It's not so awful as to make me quit the game, but it's annoying to have to rely on the hint system so often when it should be a last resort used for particularly challenging puzzles.
Although perhaps not a showcase of the absolute best HOGs have to offer, Angelica Weaver is on the whole a rather enjoyable (if occasionally overly self indulgent in both its story and illogical logic) casual adventure that is almost completely satisfying once you look past some of its more persistent issues. Though I doubt we will ever see a direct sequel, I wouldn't object if Mumbo Jumbo continued with this style and quality of HOGs, which are if nothing else miles ahead of most games of the genre.

The only thing that annoys me about this game is the title. "Catch Me When You Can"? When I can what? Be bothered? Find the time? It doesn't sound like much of a challenge! However, the game itself is better than its title.
Angelica Weaver is a psychic cop. Wait, it gets better! Actually, it really doesn't, but when it comes to fruity storylines these hidden object games usually take the biscuit anyway. Honestly this one is better than most, and it provides as good a hook as any to find all those hidden objects. I also appreciated some half-decent voice acting for once, at least with the main character, who fortunately is who you'll be hearing most of the time anyway. I do like the fact that hidden object games have such strong female characters; some other games could learn a thing or two.
The game itself is a pretty good point and click adventure game for the most part, collecting objects in your inventory to apply them in other locations. It's not quite Monkey Island, but it's a good time. There are quite a few puzzles throughout the game, although you've probably seen their ilk before, and they're mostly easy. Stress free, you might say. You'll also find quite a few hidden object scenes, and really that's what we're here for right? Fortunately these are very good, some nice artwork and objects that help to push the story forwards, often prompting brief pieces of dialog from the main character. Even better, you can replay all of these from the main menu later to try and find every last object in the scene, rated by your speed. You'll only do this once after which you'll have memorized where most things are, but it's nice to see.
The game will last you at least 5-6 hours if you do the bonus content as well (which acts as a suitable epilogue to the main story), and another hour on top of that to do the infinite hidden object scenes, so it should keep you busy for a while. You can also unsettle your friends and family with Angela Weaver specific wallpapers and screen savers [not tested].

Verdict: Simple and pleasant fun.
If you're looking for a fun little time killer that doesn't involve much of a time or mental investment than this game is well worth the price. In OESE you are the only vessel that escaped an exploding planet and it's up to you to find a new home by traveling through space filled with strange creatures, starships and more than a few things that would happily make you explode in to thousands of tiny pieces.
The game is a side scroller of sorts where you are given three options for every encounter as to how to handle a situation. While a little tricky at first it doesn't take long at all to figure out how to survive. Essentially you need to collect new crewmen via trading with other races which in turn are used as resources of a sort to level up your ship. All the while trying to improve your standings with three out of four factions in order to get an X, Y and Z coordinate to a suitable planet. From there you simply research a warp drive and high tail it to victory.
My only real complaint is the frequency of 'NOX' vessels. These pop up every 5-10 encounters and often force you to make a large sacrifice in order to continue. From giving up a few hundred crew to losing all power or shields and even damaging your relations with factions. It can get frustrating but certainly isn't game breaking. All in all it's a solid little game that's sure to provide more little laughs than any kind of grunts of anger. A solid buy for that quality alone.

The puzzles and HO scenes are good and just like the first game. The HO scenes are more of a collective puzzle scene as each object you find can be used to unlock further items. The puzzles are not too hard and I was able to solve each one without using hints or a guide.
Fast travel is still present and a great help.
Graphics and art style are very good and maintain sharp details even at 1440p. Voice overs are hovering around average to below average.
A few basic collectibles are here as well. One of which builds a machine that unlocks 20 bonus puzzles in the Extras menu. This sounds cool, but the 20 puzzles are the same but with different layouts.
I played the game on the hardest difficulty which isn’t too bad. The map still shows you what part of the world has actions available if you get stuck. It doesn’t show you which screen, just which area has one, so you’ll still have to search a bit.
Only 1 minor interface issue this time. The map button is still too close to the hint button. You could accidentally press it trying to look at the map.

OK. It's a year later and I have a kick-*rse machine now. Where was I.... Blood Dragon. Oh yeh! Blood Dragon....What can I say? Blood Dragon is friggin awesome!!! A pastiche of 80's sci-fi and video arcade tropes, you play Michael Biehn (Terminator, Aliens blah) playing Max Colt Power, an elite cyber-soldier unit from the future that is 2007. Given that Blood Dragon was released in 2013, references to the future-past of classics like Escape From New York give an indication of the trope-savvy hilarity this game promised in the trailer. Jumping The Shark? - check. Crapsack World? - check. Say No To Drugs? - check, check and double check! This game ticks all the boxes, without being annoying hipster fan-boy crap.
Visually, it is a red neon vision of an 'apocalypse that's had an apocalypse' as you race around the island dispensing 'democracy' from an exotic variety of weapons. It is Far Cry 3, but this time as a futuristic cyborg sandbox adventure. The same enjoyable handling of the character as before, all the same elements are there, only this time around you are virtually unstoppable.
That being said, Blood Dragon is NOT an epic like it's predecessor Far Cry 3. I completed the missions very quickly, with nothing left to do but clean up the island with a ridiculously powerful wrist-mounted super-weapon. Killing things and blowing shXt up while searching for VHS tapes was immensely satisfying. I knocked it over in less than 20 hours.
Daffy, violent, hilarious good clean fun, I thoroughly enjoyed this stupid non-epic popcorn fare. I'd like to see more games like this.

Funny as all hell. Don't take it seriously, it's a parody of 80's action films. Play This game! A+

Blood Dragon, for those who do not know, is a homage to 1980s and early-1990s American action movies. As a child, I watched many of these movies like Predator, Commando, Cobra, etc. This game does a fantastic job of bringing together the best elements of those movies; absurd plot, bad guys trying to take over the world, horrible dialogue, non-stop action, and a complete disregard for reality. The graphics suited the setting well enough with an absurd amount of neon lights. The soundtrack was fantastic, capturing the feel of those 80s-synth-heavy soundtracks and the obligatory montage sequence.
The game has a few flaws of course. It is rather short, especially if you don't liberate all the enemy garrisons. Also the enemy AI seemed to hiccup more than a few times, leaving enemies glitching in place when they should be leaning into cover. These were all minor issues though as the game played smoothly for me.
To anyone that likes first-person shooters and loves mindless 80s action movies, check this game out.

Everything about this game screams 80s campy action in all the best ways. It is incredibly self aware and pulls off the humor wonderfully. It isn't very long, but that helps the humor not drag on or become over done. Over the top is definitely something that this game does everywhere else though to great success.
The biggest fault I have with it is honestly having to use UPlay to run it. This means achievements are there and not on steam and you have this extra program running (which is what counts towards gameplay time, not actually being in the game). UPlay gave me no problems, but it was still annoying to have to deal with.
The game combines stealth elements and outright gun battles quite well where failing at the one can easily be made up for by the other. If you have patience, stealth will make many sections rather easy (especially after you unlock the "Heave Beat Down" skill). The pace is right though so even if not always challenging, you want to see more. And checkpoints happen enough that challenges aren't going to set you back too far.
For technical frustration, exact edges of cover are a bit vague. This results frequently in arrows bouncing off of open air because the polygon was actually a bit bigger. But you get used to it.
But at no point was the game not supremely fun. And unlike many others, it ends on a quite high note.
If you enjoy FPS especially with some open world to it and are happy with campy humor, this is a must-play

I really enjoyed this game. You play through as cop named Angelica Weaver, who can receive visions from the dead, which she uses to solve crimes.
The gameplay is broken up into three different kinds of play. Most of the game will be spent in a sort of point and click adventure mode where you'll collect tools and other objects to help you progress through the game. I was actually suprised how much of like a classic point and click this felt like.
Every now and again you'll search a location more in depth with a more traditional hidden object screen with a list of objects to find. This was fairly well designed and only one or maybe two times was I asked to find an item that I wasn't sure what it would look like.
And thirdly, occasionally you will reach a puzzle or minigame to mix things up. I really liked the puzzles, I never really felt all that challenged by them? But, I have played a lot of puzzle games in my time so, I might have had a lot of prior experience on my side. However, I don't believe the puzzles were meant to be all that difficult, instead just rewarding and fun to play with. I was quite happy with the puzzles.
If I had anything bad to say, the writing of Catch Me When You Can is a little clunky at times but has a good payoff. And, the voice acting was a little flat, kinda under acted at times. But, these were minor hiccups and I was able to take them with a grain of salt.
This edition also features some extra content which was pretty decent too. After you finish the game, you can go back and play any hidden object screen in an infinite object mode, where you find every possible object in the screen. Also, there's an extra chapter which surprisingly added a lot more to the story than I was expecting.
I wouldn't just recommend this to fans of the genre, I'd recommend this to fans of adventure games with an open mind. Hidden Object games have come a long way and arguably have more room to grow, but this was a great bit of fun.

I paid a little over 30€ for it.
I played a little over 30 hours of it.
And I'd give it a little over 30/100 fun points.

The gameplay isn't really bad but essentially just a rerun of Human Revolution. It adds experimental augs for which you'll have to "trade in" regular augs. However there's only a handful of those experimental augs and just like Human Revolution you'll only need like 5 (of the "old"!) augs to explore the whole gameworld or to fight even the tougher enemies. Everything else is really just pizzazz.
Also just like Human Revolution the gameplay basically trips over itsself regularly by throwing an e-book or a hacking terminal at you (meaning: reading / minigames) while you're exploring or doing sneaky snek stuff.
The hacking can be a decent element of suspense when you're trying not to be spotted but reading an e-book, pocket secretary or some freshly hacked e-mails for a blip of what is essentially a fart in word form isn't exactly great design.
Takes you out of the moment to reward you with an access code you'll likely not use because hacking the lock gives you EXP or some hogwash about the Illuminerdy (or similar) .
Which brings me to the "story".
I haven't finished the game so maybe there's some extremely redeeming storytelling towards the end of the game (really doubt it).
The main characters are dull and uninviting (pretty much like Human Revolution). Jensen's still the ultimate edgelord looking and acting his absolute coolest at every turn. I'm sure I'd be impressed if I were 12 or if all those edgelord tropes hadn't been turned into 3 Matrix movies already.
Side characters are introduced as quickly and heartlessly as they are killed off or just disappear again.
The dialogue and actual plot I've seen so far couldn't be more vague and boring.
In a nutshell: "Augs are bad now, hmk?" and "Something something Illuminatoes...".
If you like Dan Brown's nonsense your nipples will probably pop right off and fly towards the heavens.
If not then you'll be bored out of your mind forcing yourself to the next big revelation of bla-bla for a few times before eventually never wanting to play again.
3ish/10, wouldn't buy or play again. If you feel like you really want to, for the love of god don't pay the full price for it.
EDIT:
One important thing to mention: This fully priced, AAA, million billion dollar production value blockbuster of a game featured microtransactions from day 1.
Those give you access to pretty much everything including the, compared to Human Revolution, now rather elusive Praxis kits. Nice one Eidos / Square.

As a huge fan of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, I was deeply disappointed in this sequel. Starting with quite extreme performance issues, leading me to perform a GPU underclock in order to fix graphics crashes every several minutes (sic!) and be still left with unbearable performance. I can't quite understand such a need for resources that this game has, providing that there is no real upgrade from the previous game, the graphics and resources demanding details are concentrated only in certain points of interest, the rest of the world is quite blunt, but credit where it's due to, when there is a spot of detail concentration, it looks very good and tells you that someone has spent an awful lot of time to get it done.
Nevertheless I cannot justify the storyline, even with completion of pretty much all the side quests that I've stumbled upon, I still feel like it's not enough, and the constant travel between the districts was quite a pain in the butt. Especially with the times required to wait for the level to load up.
Upon the final boss fight, in retrospect I felt like fighting Jaron in Human Revolution, and when I beat the boss, I was like "oh cool, now I get to finally chase after the illuminati!", and then the game ended. Nothing more. Just ended. I just sat there and was like "what the heck?" - the storyline felt like I was in the bloody middle of it! 3/4 of it at the very last! It was a great disappointment, especially combined with how the game performed and all the issues I had with it.
I feel like the developers had a strict timeline and couldn't lead the story any further, polishing what they had up and releasing it as is, like some alpha state preorder game. I don't feel like I got what I paid for. I feel very disappointed especially with all the hype surrounding this game.

If you're the type who likes to take all the side questst you find and experiment with different playstyles, this game is definitely worth it for you.
The game is amazingly well designed, especially the level design just blew my mind (there are so many ways to deal with every encounter that I sometimes had to stop for a minute and think about what approach I'd like to take... then sometimes things didn't go quite as planned and I ended up needing to go guns-blazing through it. This game by the way does not make it too easy to go all gung ho on your enemy because you die pretty fast if you're getting shot at. E.g. you need to shoot them before they shoot you. I also like the moral choice you always have to either kill everything that moves, knock them out, or just sneak past them so they never even know you were there.
This game wildly exceeded all my expectations, in my opinion it is much better than human revolution. But it does have a few downsides.
1. Square Enix has been becoming increasingly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as a publisher lately, and surprisingly enough in this game DRM doesn't seem to have been much of an issue... But the DLC is completely bonkers. If you buy the DLC packs which give you weapons and♥♥♥♥♥♥ you only get them for one save and you can never use it again. There's a way around this issue though (start the game, get to your player home, grab all the DLC weapons and put them in the storage lockers then save and you can always start the game with all the DLC guns on hand, sadly I didn't realize this till too late though) so this is what I think is the biggest issue that people are complaining about. It's nonsensical.
2. The story, while quite good (imo better than in human revolution), is pretty short and just ends with a very offputting cliffhanger (you feel like you're only halfway through it when it's over) but despite this lack of main story, if you are taking all the side quests and fully enjoying all the game has to offer, you'll easily be able to squeeze 20+ hours out of one playthrough (many people have gone over 40 hours, for me it was 26 hours) and that is a clear statement for the value of the game.
This game is fun, very fun, it's main selling point is the gameplay and it does deliver that in spades.
I'm not some die-hard deus ex fan at all (I didn't even like invisible war, and human revolution only kept me reasonably amused, it didn't majorly impress me at all) I just like good games, and this is a great game.
I gotta tip my hat to the level designers again though, I have never seen a first person shooter with such amazing level design before, it's truly marvellous. Even if you're normally fighting in closed corridors and interiors and relatively narrow spaces, the game almost feels like it's an open world because there are just so many ways to get from point A to point B (even if we're just talking about getting from one room to the next one, there's always bound to be an alternate route!)
There are a few lesser downsides I found in the game's design though.
1. Battery system, while it can be argued to be fairly realistic, it is extremely annoying that no matter how many battery upgrades you get, unless you use battery cells to recharge your battery you will only have a very small battery pool to use with your augs. Now the good thing is that you can always use "one" augmentation move whenever the need hits because of this minimum battery charge, but at the same time, if you want to use more, or if you want to create some sort of combo it's gonna cost you a battery cell, battery cells are fairly rare so you can't just be using them all the time every time or you'll run out pretty fast. I think this system was poorly designed as all it did was limit the player's freedom. There should have been a battery upgrade that could mitigate this problem.
2. While the game has a sexy sniper rifle available, I was hard pressed to find a use for it. Unlike many of the games weapons it was incompatible with the silencer mod, and because most of the game happens in very tight quarters there was practically no occasion where I thought "oh how handy it would be to have a sniper rifle with me right now" because 90% of all encounters were close or mid range (perfect for an assault rifle or pistol, or even melee moves!) I just don't see how a sniper rifle fits in such a situation. What's more is that even if you do find an interesting vantage point, the loading distance is limited anyways (uGridsToLoad=5 much?)
But well, that's about it for things that annoyed me.
I loved everything else about the game to pieces, people have been focusing quite a bit on the few negatives they've been able to find about this game, but the positives massively outweigh them. You probably won't regret this purchase unless your expectations are simply too high.

OESE is a simple game to pick up but gets harder and harder to walk away from. The retro styling looks really nice and the ambient tune is strangely relaxing. This game challenges you to survive as long as possible and I am determined to keep beating my previous record, that is what this game is about. Brilliant fun and would definitely recommend this game.

Review Excerpt:
"And this is OESE. OESE is a space survival game which relies on resource management mechanics in which your ship flies along trying to survive long enough to find a new home. Along the way you are joined by a tiny and somewhat fun little robot and encounter any number of around a dozen different races along with multiple different planets and space phenomenon. Your objective is to survive to the point where you can establish a new colony…. Aand it’s actually more difficult than you might think. I’m not even sure there IS an end to this game but it offers some decent diversity and is very simple, but seems to do what it intends rather well.
OESE focuses on turn-based resource management where you have crew, shields, and power along with your three primary stats: Military, Diplomacy, and ship. Each stat determines how well received your ship is by those you encounter as well as how much shields you can garner and trust me, you will need quite a bit. In addition, to all of this you have a giant cube vessel called the Nox that will come along periodically and will require you sacrifice quite a bit…. Aaand I have to say that this game does throw in more than a few Star Trek references.. including  a creature that you encounter that is obviously a hat-tip to the chrystalline entity."
All in all an entertaining little game. For $5 I have no problem recommending this to others.

A friend bought me Dawn of War Soulstorm, so I now have all the original Dawn of War games. Soulstorm keeps up the Dawn of War greatness just like all the other Dawn of War games, and I am happy to have it. I recommend it to any RTS fan!

The squad system revolutionized RTS. Nothing has been quite the same since.
The addition of two races in the final expansion of what I daresay is the RTS of the decade was not surprising, but maybe raised a few eyebrows. To some, updating this game with more content seemed a waste - why bother spending time on adding things to a game whose graphics could easily be dismissed as much too old for the current era?
And yet, Dawn of War remains timeless, and so does this expansion. A sprawling campaign, active online community (even now, in a time of "superior" graphics and smoother gameplay), and a well thought-out set of mechanics that ensured every race had their advantages and disadvantages, some canceling each other out, others complementing each other, to create a blend of nine staggeringly complex races.
The learning curve of some races is high, and low for some others. There's something in this game for anyone who's even thought about playing an RTS. Mastering a race is, in itself, a reward. And a set of over a hundred maps, ranging from tiny two-person maps to sprawling eight-person arenas, will only add to the experience of doing so.
Overall, 10/10. Solid soundtrack as always, decent enough graphics (they were ahead for their time when the first game was released) without taking too much of a toll on your system, eye-opening variation in mechanics for all nine races.

There's 2 ways to look at the game
The gameplay, and the devs.
Let's be honest, the devs don't listen to the players much, and often add ninja nerfs. There's a bit of Russian bias, but if you're good you can probably overcome that. I find the gameplay fun, there's a bit of a grind, but it's there to give you something to play for. You can unlock plenty of things, for 3 different factions and I think that if you're bored with having everything for one faction (Somehow) you can move onto another faction. Money isn't everything seeing as you also need to progress through ribbons to get a lot of things, so this game isn't that much pay-to-win seeing as people have to donate plenty of money.
It's like a WW2 battlefield, but you have to buy things, and to get those things you need to go through ribbons. IE, to get the first pistol, you have to buy it, and then go through a pistol ribbon to unlock the second pistol, and it's like this for plenty of other things. It's costly, so people don't usually spend real money on boosting these ribbons.
Over all, I like the gameplay, I like grinding for the things, and destroying OP Russian SMGs gives a great feeling. I like the idea of war, and how people actually have to manage resources and send them to different battles. I would recommend people to try and play this game until they become rank 4 or 5 and then judge.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is the standalone expanion for Far Cry 3, which was originally about survival and a bunch of pirates that have been ordered to hunt you down and kill you. Blood Dragon is completely different in the sense that the survival element has been completely removed from this standalone expansion.
Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is basically a gigantic spoof of 80's movies and filled with 80's references in a comedic sense and cyber-punk manner. I didn't grow up in the 80's so I don't really get the jokes, but to anyone who has. This is the game for you! Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is in my top 3 best games list of 2013, it's cool, it's funny and down-right stupid. Unlike Far Cry 3, which was based on the harshness of the jungle, the enviroment and the enemies, this game is NOT a frightful survival game, which I meantioned at the start.
THE STORY: You play as Rex "Power" Colt, a cyborg military man who is rebuilt to be better, stronger and faster. You start out in a machine gun turret inside a helicopter (Yeah, best beginning ever) and descend to take a tutorial (which shows a comedic part of the game) When Rex Colt takes the tutorial, he is frustrated and angry and wants to shoot things, while the tutorial lady is speaking. (Quite a funny scene) It is chock-full of bright lights, with a cyberpunk feel to it making it graphically impressive.
THE PORT: Excellent port, has and FOV slider, full world detail changes and nice options to do with textures. Why did I list the FOV slider as a key feature? Becuase this one can go anywhere from 55-110, varies quite well when you really have a look at it.
RELEVANCE: This standalone expansion is quite similar to the base game, only cybered-up and takes off more 80's movies.
PROS
+Nice options menu and graphics customisation
+Funny plot and comedic "hints"
+Isn't another ♥♥♥♥ing MMS (Modern Military Shooter)
+Nice change from a jungle-theme to a cyber-punk theme
+You run faster than you drive
CONS
-Short story
-Low replayability
-Everything is red
-Smaller map
-Useless side quests
-Small amount of weapons (Some credit to the creators anyway, most of the weapons are spoofed)
-Requires a Uplay account.
9/10, would definitely recommend picking it up on a sale.

Building on the successes of their award-winning Midnight Mysteries adventure series, MumboJumbo has created an all-new adventure franchise. Boasting interactive backgrounds, story-driven puzzles, an animated main character, voice acting and a rich narrative filled with twists and turns, Angelica Weaver: Catch Me When You Can is action-packed and sure to be another hit!
Angelica Weaver, a detective on Chicago’s Special Task Force, must use her renowned deductive skills to stop a present day killer. The only way for her to get ahead of this killer is to first identify a murderer who escaped justice over a hundred years ago. Angelica has the ability to connect with the dead. Through supersensory visions she is able to jump back and forth between crime scenes on the streets of historic London and present-day Chicago where the victims reveal to her their final moments. Work with Angelica as she puzzles her way through the past and uses her insights to stop the pattern in the future in this hidden object puzzle adventure.
Angelica actively participates as you explore detailed environments and sift through hidden-object scenes for clues. Using Angelica’s journal and a highly developed hint system, close the case in the present and in the past, by piecing together game-changing information for an unexpected twist.
Angelica Weaver’s intriguing story is complemented with stunning visuals and sound effects that captivate and surprise. This compelling adventure, full of challenges and dozens of unique puzzles, delivers yet another thrilling experience from MumboJumbo.
Be the detective! Angelica Weaver and the city of Chicago enlist your help.

Angelica Weaver is an adventure/hidden object game that has you chasing a serial murdered in the present, while trying to solve a related, unsolved case in the past. The main character has psychic powers that are used for a few things, including seeing the crime scene of the past yourself.
This game is pretty stupid on all levels. Most of the gameplay involves either clicking everything on the screen or trying all of your inventory items on every you can interact with. This game has plenty of adventure game logic too... there are several times where you're given multiple items that all have the same purpose, but you can still only use one specific item in each place. There are no interesting characters, and the story is just awful. This is meant to be a mystery, but it fails in that regard too, because you don't meet the killer at all until the end.
The game has only two positive points. The first is that the art is nice. The second is that there are some actual puzzles, though they're so easy that this almost doesn't count.
I wouldn't recommend this to anyone at any price above free. Even if it was free, I don't think this game will even be worth the time spent for most people, though if you're a fan of adventure games, your time may not be entirely wasted.

Torchlight 2 is a really well made ARPG. It improves everything from the first game (You should still check out the first game. Its great.) and adds a few new features.
Torchlight 2 continues the story from Torchlight and the three original player classes returns as NPC's. The vanquisher and destroyer gives you an few quests. The alchemist got corrupted and serves as the main antagonist. The story isn't that good or gets in the way. It's mostly there to give you a reason to keep on killing monsters. And the killing is vey fun. There are 4 classes this time around. These include the outlander (long ranged guns and traps) , the berserker (fast melee attacker) , the engineer (heavy character and summoner) and embermage (magic user) so there is something that will fit everyone ps play style. Each class has diversified skill trees so two playthroughs with the same class can be totally different. You can splay as a outlander who uses traps and bows or a outlander that uses shotguns and pistol, each one complimented by the skill tree.
The graphics are still cartoony and colorful. They have been improved and there are a lot of new environments to explore. Speaking of the environments, Torchlight 2 is set across four acts over huge areas instead of being confined to a single dungeon. The monster variety and count is higher than Torchlight 2, which give the player a continuous supply of XP and things to kill. Torchlight 2 also have multiplayer with instanced loot. It's great fun but I only tried it once.
If you love ARPG's try Torchlight 2.

This game should have been titled: 'Deus Ex: No Resolution', because that more accurately describes the state of this game, after Square Enix allegedly carved it to bits with their irresponsible corporate meandering.
How, you ask?
Well, As was implied by the beginning of this review, I have read ruminations from a multitude of sources that S.E. Told Eidos that they were to split this game into multiples to appease their corporate masters. Guess what? The game's writing reeks of being stuck in development hell, in a state that reflects this problem perfectly.
Still, the plot is good on multiple levels. I got about 36 hours of game play. It was worth full price, to an extent, even though I didn't pay $60 for it. However, the writing is awful. As soon as you begin to gain traction in the main storyline, things just drop into the abyss and leave you out to dry. There are no answered questions in the end, and you're only left with more, where you're expected to draw your own conclusion. Except, they didn't pull it off in a satisfactory manner. Instead, it just leaves a bitter taste on the tongue once you reach the end.
This game was more about the side quests than it was the main storyline. They were all fun, except literally all of them unfolded downtown at the central hub of Prague, and it turns into nothing more than a continuous loop of running back and forth between the different pedantic sections of the city. If you're interested in sideline storytelling that glimpses into the individual lives of people living in the Deus Ex universe, than this game isn't bad. You mostly spend your time as a detective than you do a secret agent uncovering mass conspiracies. There are a few interesting twists and turns as the plot unfolds, but unfortunately they all end up at dead ends because there is no resolution on any of these themes.
What else is wrong about it, you ask? As everyone else has complained, the microtransactions. They are not intrusive in the game in any way, but the problem with them is that it takes time away from the developers to focus on essential aspects of the game, like polishing bugs and performance issues. What's worse is that the microtransaction system was apparently demanded to be implemented, by corporate, at the last minute; and I suspect that is why the game ended up getting delayed from its original release date.
There's also the DRM they crammed into this game. Apparently, you MUST be online in order to play it. And, allegedly, they use the online connection to track metadata on your gameplay the entire time. A little bit ironic, isn't it, since the Deus Ex franchise has always had a tendency to focus on corporatist greed and corruption? It's no wonder they implemented Denuvo, though, because Corporate seemed to just *know* that no one would actually want to pay for this game, once they found out what a poor job they did on writing the plot.
I wanted to like this game. I tried really hard to like it.
I did, in a way, because I got a close glimpse at the trials and tribulations of individual random citizens in Prague. Aside from that, though, there was no real plot structure. I can't imagine how short the game would have been if I had only focused on the main storyline.
I don't even know how they managed to hack this game into what it is. It feels as though Eidos was doing their best to write a worthy successor to Human Revolution, but then got attacked after they were about 1/4 of the way in their plot development writing. I can just tell Square Enix ruined this for Eidos, or maybe Eidos just doesn't care anymore. I don't believe that, though, given the things I've read about some 'anonymous' developers coming clean about how they were forced into corners they didn't want to be in by corporate.
Unfortunately, this game is following the modern trend most games are being subject to, where avarice prevails past actually writing a good ♥♥♥♥ing story. This seems to be the prevailing theme for almost every single game I've played in the past five years, maybe more. The corporatization of the gaming industry is poisoning everything it touches. I was foolish to believe that, just maybe, Deus Ex would be enlightened enough to rise above this effect. I was wrong, unfortunately, and was left disappointed and estranged by one of my favorite game series, AGAIN. Time after time... woe to anyone who wants a fair and balanced game with superb writing in the modern state of the game industry.
Shame on Sqaure Enix for doing this, like so many other games they botched. Too bad the ruined another good piece of art that could have been profound if not for avarice.

////Great, but way too short.////
Transmission: Element 120 is a great concept, but I feel like the final product didn't fully realize what it aimed for. Introducing darkness az a puzzle element is a grand idea, but there is only one room (from the very limited amount of rooms) where it plays an important role, and this room's only purpose was to introduce you to the mechanic, only to forget it for the rest of the game. Other great addition is the re-purposed Gravity Gun. Now, instead of grabbing heavy objects, it creates a ball of kinetic energy which you can use to reach higher ledges and platforms. You can shoot this ball underneath yourself to boost your way forward, pretty much like you rocket jump in Quake games. This device can also be used to tear down obstacles in your path, or propel objects in the game world. I pretty much enjoyed this version of the good old Gravity Gun.
The game is surprisingly short. When the end credits rolled, for a second I thought this is the beginning, but soon I found out, that it's over. Maybe, that way my fault, I did not read the description that it is a short single player experience.
It also features Steam Achievements, a few of them, they might keep you interested in a second or third playthrough, but that's it. The replayability is not strong.
Other things I should mention is the perfomance. I had poor perfomance, considering the age of the engine and the raw power of my hardware. (i7 + GTX 1070) I had huge drops in my FPS due the Multicore Rendering option in the settings kept going to 'Disabled'. I had to manually set it back to 'Enabled' after every load. But even then, I had poor perfomance and my fps kept going between 50 and 165 (my max refresh rate). G-Sync in my monitor worked hard to adjust the adaptive refreshrate.
The sum it all up,  I had a good hour of enjoyment despite the flaws, I would recommend you to check it out. One of the best short-single player Half-Life mods out there!

This is a really fantastic game!
The level designs are incredibly creative. There are multiple gameplay modes that span classic CTF and death match, and many modes that are just unique to this game (at least for me). In one mode you have to melt your team's dinasaur in a freezer. Sounds simple but the other team's dinosaur is within shooting range so you'll find yourself watching your back constantly. There's another mode where your team defends a birthday cake while the other team is trying to light all the candles within a time limit. When the time limit is over, the teams switch roles and you have to beat the other team's time.
You don't have to pick your role. Everyone gets the same weapons layout which means you get every weapon in the game. Assult rifle, sniper rifle, shotgun, bazooka, and flame thrower (and one gernade). There's no ammo or extra gernades; what you get when you spawn is what you'll have. The gameplay is so fast that it doesn't matter. One thing that I didn't like is how long it takes to switch weapons. But that also might be what makes things actually work in terms of balancing the game.
It's very fun multiplayer. I highly recommend this game.

So for the 3 hours I played this game is was pretty fun. Just a PC version of Super Smash Brothers (so expect all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t maneuvers from that game just repeated here). I like the characters that are available for selection as a new player they were fun and weren't too hard to get the hang of. Controls are responsive even in the online mode which was nice as I wasn't lagging 3 seconds behind my commands like most online fighters.
Controller play is by far the easiest way to play the game, but if you don't have one, the mouse and keyboard is just as good with the only downside being that your mouse will occasionaly be way off to the side or the corner where the "leave match" button is causing you to either stop attacking or leaving the match, or being interrupted. Pretty big annoyance really.
The biggest downside to this is the marketplace. I don't have a problem with it really, just that, I enjoy these games as single player and not so much as multi-player even though that is what they are intended for. I don't like that I have to grind away hours and hours and hours a day against players who have a clear skill and experience advantage over me, just so I can earn a few of the in game currency to purchase a different character from the roster.
The marketplace is also very expensive. It's almost $6.00 for 140 of their in game currency and that buys you maybe one or two things...maybe. The gold you earn from your fights is so pathetically low that you'll be grinding away in the multi-player fights trying to get enough to unlock a guy you like.
The game is highly repeatative like Smash Brothers but moreso since all of the characters play the same. There are no unique moves between each of the characters and instead they use different flourishes for the direction you press...so there's no real variety between them other than the animations. It's not like Smash Brothers where you can choose a character and they have a completely different playstyle from one another and while Brawlhalla possesses some pretty decent art and design, the characters are all fundamentally the same and don't have much difference in the way of mechanics.
Personally I would like to see these games have a single player option that allows single player mode to unlock characters for play only in that mode so if I wanted to just play this game solo and never go online then I could have that option. Instead it is forced multi-player if you want to play more than just the basic characters or you have to spend money. I suppose if it had a good sale this would be a half decent investment if you're really into these games but even then probably not as there just isn't a lot to it. The marketplace is pretty much exclusively skins and vanity items (which is good) and that is pretty much the entirety of the content.
The game is still early access so it's got that going for it, but like a few people have said, it looks as if the micro-transactions are the big focus at the moment rather than polishing the game. It's good, it just needs some fine tuning to make it great.

So for the 3 hours I played this game is was pretty fun. Just a PC version of Super Smash Brothers (so expect all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t maneuvers from that game just repeated here). I like the characters that are available for selection as a new player they were fun and weren't too hard to get the hang of. Controls are responsive even in the online mode which was nice as I wasn't lagging 3 seconds behind my commands like most online fighters.
Controller play is by far the easiest way to play the game, but if you don't have one, the mouse and keyboard is just as good with the only downside being that your mouse will occasionaly be way off to the side or the corner where the "leave match" button is causing you to either stop attacking or leaving the match, or being interrupted. Pretty big annoyance really.
The biggest downside to this is the marketplace. I don't have a problem with it really, just that, I enjoy these games as single player and not so much as multi-player even though that is what they are intended for. I don't like that I have to grind away hours and hours and hours a day against players who have a clear skill and experience advantage over me, just so I can earn a few of the in game currency to purchase a different character from the roster.
The marketplace is also very expensive. It's almost $6.00 for 140 of their in game currency and that buys you maybe one or two things...maybe. The gold you earn from your fights is so pathetically low that you'll be grinding away in the multi-player fights trying to get enough to unlock a guy you like.
The game is highly repeatative like Smash Brothers but moreso since all of the characters play the same. There are no unique moves between each of the characters and instead they use different flourishes for the direction you press...so there's no real variety between them other than the animations. It's not like Smash Brothers where you can choose a character and they have a completely different playstyle from one another and while Brawlhalla possesses some pretty decent art and design, the characters are all fundamentally the same and don't have much difference in the way of mechanics.
Personally I would like to see these games have a single player option that allows single player mode to unlock characters for play only in that mode so if I wanted to just play this game solo and never go online then I could have that option. Instead it is forced multi-player if you want to play more than just the basic characters or you have to spend money. I suppose if it had a good sale this would be a half decent investment if you're really into these games but even then probably not as there just isn't a lot to it. The marketplace is pretty much exclusively skins and vanity items (which is good) and that is pretty much the entirety of the content.
The game is still early access so it's got that going for it, but like a few people have said, it looks as if the micro-transactions are the big focus at the moment rather than polishing the game. It's good, it just needs some fine tuning to make it great.

This little gem is, of my experience, one of the most fair free to play games I've ever encountered. The store is jam-packed with cosmetics and such, but the legends (characters) you can unlock with gold earned from matches, quests, and daily login rewards. All together, it's not really that hard to get up to the price points of even the more expensive legends, as long as you enjoy the game enough to play it. The gameplay is fast, furious, and surprisingly tactical - there are genuine combos, and a well thought out approach will win over button mashing 11 times out of 10, but both thought and speed are richly rewarded.
There are balance quibbles I could make, but that's true of any fighting game, and I feel that things are pretty well handled here in general, with nothing toxic enough to actually corrode the fun of the game. The only serious criticism I would level, as things currently stand, is that it seems the netcode still leaves something to be desired. "Teleporting", suddenly finding your character in a completely different place than you thought they were, is relatively normal. I just tend to recover quickly and move on, but some people have worse issues or worse luck than that. All in all though, I'm very fond of Brawlhalla and think it's developer is a great example of game development and the free to play model being handled the right way. I very much look forward to the netcode being improved, and the promised Linux port as well!

Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ guys, I think this is the best hidden object game I've ever played. I'm praising it so highly for one specific reason: The hidden object areas have PURPOSE. I love all The Sims games, but Sims 3 always stands out to me as my personal favorite. I've spent countless hours in this game before I even had it on Steam to keep track of play time (I can't really begin to fathom the hours spent in it outside of Steam.) I got my fun from creating all my favorite characters from video games, anime, movies, tv shows, etc, and watching them all live in the same town like some sorta huge messed up fanfiction. If things ever got stale, I would just change up my current household, make new sims, or even change neighborhoods for a new start. With all DLC (not gonna talk about the prices) it adds a lot of new features to explore in your Sims game from seasons to pets and supernaturals and even time travel! Also this game being open-world compared to TS2 and TS4 really make it unique to the other Sims games. Though being open-world created a lot of routing issues and lag, the trade-off is worth it in my opinion. It really made the whole world feel alive when the sims in your game are always constantly doing something.
Only con I can say about the game is to be wary if playing it on a stronger PC without using an FPS limiter because the game will burn up your GPU (and possibly destroy it altogether) due to outdated optimization for newer GPUs.

So it would be hard to recommend this game. One has to question "Why do we play games?" for this to be reviewed properly.
For me, I play games to have fun. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided tests this quite a lot. Stealth can be a fun idea - hide from all your enemies and get rewarded in the end. Deus Ex has this, but you get really no reward other than an extra 10 experience points. There's no penalty for absolutely wasting everyone you see, either. Deus Ex can't make up its mind on whether it wants to be a stealth game or a game where you go guns blazing. Personally, I like being a machine God of death.
Which brings me to the leveling system
Just like the last game, the hacking system makes it easy to become a machine God of death. F5 to quicksave before hacking a terminal, hack terminal, receive xp. Failed on the hack? F9 to quick load. I gained several levels through this alone, and investing in skill trees that make hacking easier is a waste of time. All I did was dump praxis points into the capture software at the very beginning and hacked everything.
But the problem is, this game makes it hard to become a God of death and use all your powers effectively. You really don't need any of your powers to clean a room - just a good gun. Upgrade the shotgun to the max and equip a silencer (A silencer on a shotgun? How in the...) and there are no foes that will escape you. The alternate ammo types have very, very limited use.
Also, the money system is near useless. I think I was at 100k credits at the end of last playthrough. At first I needed credits for praxis kits, so I'd knock out police, take their gun, and sell it. I did this to all of prague. You'd think police would get wise. Then, since it didn't matter, I started straight up murdering police. No real challenging enemies to speak of.
Overall 5/10. I wanted to like this. Human Revolution had a cooler feel to it and a better storyline. This storyline was tinfoil hat-esque. This should have been DLC for HR, not a brand new game.

To properly appreciate this game, you need to invest a fair amount of time into. I would say the game itself is a fairly standard RPG, perhaps above average for a free to play and it doesn't bog you down in restricted VIP only areas. However, a big selling point for me was the fact it was LOTR and I got to explore all the places I wanted to visit from the films. This was FRIGGIN AWESOME. I admit, I spent the majority of this game playing with friends, so I cannot vouch for the solo experience but questing together was the most fun I had on an MMORPG.
Throughout the game, you may be able to save up enough currency to never need to invest actual money into it, however I bought the mithril starter pack which gave me enough points to progress as far as I wanted. The first purchase you need to save for is buying a horse to actually be able to get around. This is relatively painless and involves completing a fair few early tasks to get the points. Apart from that advice, take your sword, your bow and your axe and go out and explore the world of MiddleEarth!

Torchlight II is a competent ARPG with flashes of brilliance that is let down a little by a story that doesn't know when to quit and long stretches of sameness in skills, equipment and environments. As any good entry to the genre does, it brings some innovations to the table and has a tight set of core mechanics, and multiplayer helps prop up the corners when they start to sag. It tries a little too hard to tick some items off the standard checklist though (SO MUCH NOISE AND FURY YOU'LL LOSE YOUR CURSOR ALL THE TIME!), which can make it a little tiring to play for long stretches. Still, it's a worthy purchase and you'll get your money's worth solo or with friends.

The most important question is: is DE:MD worth paying the full price, or should you wait until the Steam sale? If you're a veteran DE player (like myself) then you'll experience something similar to DE:HR with enough changes to make the game interesting. It might seem a little easy, but don't forget that you already know how to play a DE game (and there are ways to deliberately make the game more challenging). There are some surprises, but it's mainly a current-gen presentation of the DE:HR formula. The story is good, but not quite as tight as HR; however, this doesn't take anything away from the experience.
If, on the other hand, you're new to DE games, you'll experience a game with a fair learning curve (not immediately straightforward, but not ridiculously complex either). The game looks wonderful, has an intuitive control setup and rewards patience as much as risk-taking.
Be aware of the bugs and possible crashes; however, Square Enix are constantly updating the game based on our feedback and the only problematic crash is easily fixed by lowering certain settings in the graphics options (this has almost no effect on the in-game visuals themselves - check the forums for more information).
Summary: if you enjoyed Human Revolution, you'll probably enjoy this. If you never played Human Revolution, buy that, play it and then buy Mankind Divided.

I enjoyed playing Mankind Divided but it never quite reached the same level as Human Revolution. There are less locations to explore (Though Prague is huge!) and I never really felt the same sense of uncovering a huge conspiracy that I did in HR (and the original Deus Ex!).
The same frustrating battery limited augmentation system returns from HR which is a disappointment. The new augmentations are great fun to use and feel suitably powerful, I just didn't use them that much because of the restrictive battery system.
Most of the new characters in the story are pretty dull and I can barely remember any of their names. Contrast that to HR where I can remember many character names and it paints a pretty poor picture. It was always a highlight when old characters appeared in the new game but I always wanted them to stick around longer than they did.
It also ends very abruptly. I seriously thought there was another story arc that would start after the final mission but nope, credit roll.
I think if you enjoyed Human Revolution you will enjoy this as well, it just doesn't hit the same peaks as the game before it did.

I was really looking forward to this after Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising, which I found to be a great and awesome military tactical shooter, but after a single mission, I uninstalled and wrote this review. Do not buy this game, it is not worth your money. Go buy Dragon Rising instead, and if you've already played it, just skip this one, because:
1. Poorly done console port. Whereas Dragon Rising had keyboard controls which made sense, this one was purely made for consoles, and the keyboard controls are a simulation of the keyboard controls. Not only that, but some controls are missing, such as the squad member selection controls. (mapped to f1-f4, and cannot be remapped)
2. Horrible AI. In the single mission I did, the AI squad mates were constantly getting stuck and failed to navigate to where I told them to move. I had to resort to having them follow me around as I navigated the map. Adding on to the control issues above, it's hard to issue commands to 2 of your squadmates, you have to do them separately.
3. Bad/unrealistic gunplay. The guns feel horrible. There does not appear to be bullet drop (what with all the CQC, it's hard to tell as well), and bullets seem to be instakill or miss, at least for the beginning sniper I was using.
4. Chunky movement, long unskippable car-ride scenes. Movement feel very odd and chunky, random walls can and cannot be jumped over, and AIs from both sides have horrible animations. You're constantly on a car moving from location to location. You can do nothing while this is happening, the rides are frankly too long, and all of it is unskippable.
Overall, the game just does not feel good, and it's a constant fight with the controls on the keyboard and mouse.

Bought it on a sale a while ago. All though the game is a couple of years old, it didn't feel that way.
I did come across some annoyances when playing through the campaign, which could be worth poiting out. For ex:
* Waypoints sometimes updates (moves forward with you) even if you find your own path towards your objective. Sometimes however, they don't, which forces you to run back and step right on them in order for them to update. This can be quite annoying if your in a stressed situation.
* Ofthen when you have the team following you and stop in cover, for instance behind a building, when enemys are encountered, your team tries to find good firing positions themselves. Often this activity involves the AI team members to run out of cover, sometimes to the other side of the building - ending up on the enemy side of the building with no cover = canon fodder. So, instead of being able of focusing on the enemy - you are also focused on giving life support to your stupid AI team members.
* There is an unresolved bug on mission 8. You are tasked to clear a small village of enemy troops, main objective being a tower in the village which you must reach and clear. However, even if you achieve the objective the game doesn't recognise it. Forcing you to load last checkpoint and do it all over again, and simply hope the bug does not appear again.
The above negatives are directly gameplay affective. However I found one last annoyance which doesn't affect the gameplay, but rather the feel of the game. And that is the voice over for the intro of every mission, it sounded silly and didn't seem to fit in with the rest of the game.
Despite of the list above. I still found this game to absolutely be worth the time I spent with it.
It's real fun gaming, good challenges in the game. I like the feel of the game, even if it changed a little from the previous Operation Flashpoint.
Overall a very good game and now that I've tried it I wish Codemaster would reconsider and produce more games like it. If you like military shooters I think you should try it out.

The execution was done really well, the weapons, levelling up and choosing the right guns for the right mission was fantastic. The enemy can have seriously good accuracy and you don't just cop 20 rounds to the chest and regenerate like you're Wolverine. I would say that this game was an experience that was rare to find in this day and age. Great shooter, great gameplay, sound quality was solid and the voice acting was very good!

"The Mean Greens" is a multiplayer third person shooter from the perspective of toy army men (like those old 3DO games). This is a setting I was very excited to see again. It allows for creative maps including the inside of a fishtank, a foosball table, and a birthday cake. Each map has its own unique game mode, which means most maps are very well tuned to their mode. Unfortunately, this also means that the game may become stale; if you like deathmatch, you only have the Toybox map for team deathmatch or the Art Table for free-for-all. That said, I got plenty of value because I do enjoy objective modes.
Gameplay is rather simplistic, I believe by the developers' intentions. The movement and shooting mechanics are fairly standard, reminding me a great deal of Battlefront 2. Every player has access to the entire arsenal at any time (no classes or customization) meaning each soldier is able to handle every situation. Personally, I find this refreshing; there is no need to worry about unlocks or classes, and the game is easy to pick up and understand. However, progression systems are pervasive for a reason, and players may find themselves bored as a result of this omission.
Connectivity is the biggest issue facing this game right now, but even then I feel the problem is overstated in many reviews. The option to have the game place you in a session was problematic and is currently disabled for reworking. I've personally had few issues with the server browser and can get into a game in less than a couple minutes at most. If this issue is holding you back, I'd recommend hitting the follow button and waiting a month or so. Patches have been frequent and I expect a few more in the next month or so.
