Updated Review, Thumbs Up (28 Aug 15):
In short, I used to take issue with the long-standing fact that not all content was available to owners of the Steam release of VRC-Pro, and that the various platforms were not at parity with one another.  That issue has now been largely resolved, in the form of an all-inclusive DLC which unlocks everything for the life of the product.  The full package doesn't come cheap, but I feel the asking price isn't unreasonable considering the niche market, licensed content, and comparitive pricing of other simulation dlc (e.g. DCS World, The Pinball Arcade, etc.)  In every other regard, I continue to feel that VRC-Pro achieves its aim of providing a realistic simulation of and training tool for rc motorsports.  So the devs have delivered, and fair is fair - I would now recommend VRC-Pro to all rc enthusiasts, including those who prefer Steam as their gaming platform of choice.
Original Review, Thumbs Down (18 June 2015):
I would like to rate VRC Pro positively - I really would.  But I can't at this moment in time, and I'll elaborate as to why, with the hope that I can change this rating in the future.  Do you see the 15th of June (2015) update posted here on Steam with a video of offroad track "Psycho Nitro Blast 6"?  You can't race that track if you own VRC Pro on Steam rather than the Freemium/Subscription version.  Or many, many others.  Also, you can't access a number of performance parts that top race winners are using.  Even if you buy all the Steam DLC, there is a heap of content that is not offered to you.  It's been this way for awhile now.  You can have fun, as well as high-performing RC cars, with what is on offer in Steam VRC version... BUT... there's a glass ceiling built into this version, which means it is just not-at-all on a par with the Freemium version.
I find it really grating to be left behind after I've shelled out ~£30 plus the cost of a real RC controller and usb adaptor.  Some users will point out how inexpensive this is compared to a real RC car and track time...surely I should be thankful that I *only* paid £30 for a handful of cars and tracks? By that logic, racing a Ferrari around the Nordschliefe in Assetto Corsa or flying an A-10 Warthog in DCS World should me cost thousands of pounds for the experience!  After all, I *would* probably be a better IRL A-10 pilot if I mastered the DCS version, no? In the virtual, PC software world, however, £30 is the price of a quality full-release title, sim or otherwise, and I'm not pleased that the Steam release of this title is a second-rate citizen.  And yes, I will pay for good DLC - but the developer has to actually offer it up for sale first!
How is VRC Pro as a an RC simulator, then?  Well, credit-where-it's-due, it's pretty impressive.  The physics are realistic, as far as I can tell, and it does feel quite a lot like I remember of driving my high-performance nitro RC vehicles some 10+ years ago.  The graphics are good enough to suit the purpose, though the camera can take some fiddling around with to make it feel right.  I play it stretched across 3 monitors, and find that to be a really nice option if you have such a setup.  Overall, I could easily feel more positive about VRC Pro if all existing versions of it were at parity with each other.  If you think you can be happy having a decent collection of cars to bash around a decent collection of tracks, and aren't necessarily wanting to access more than is bundled here, whilst being teased with new-release videos of the sweet new tracks accessible only to the Freemium version players, then, by all means, give this one a go.  Otherwise, perhaps it's just best to skip this version and decide if you'd be better served by just going straight to the Freemium version.

Good hidden object game.
The Four Horsemen doesn't really have have those big hidden object scenes, the ones it has work more like an adventure, but basically, it's a collection of casual puzzles strung together by inventory puzzles: you find some item and have to remember that the puzzle you need it for is halfway across the map, unless you don't play on hard, in which case the map shows you where to go. It's done fairly well, and it does have 2 bonus objects hidden in every big scene. Just don't expect much of a story or explanations why there are so many puzzles and why the parts are all over the place (i.e. don't expect a point&click adventure).
Gameplay-wise, if you are going for all of the achievements in one go (which means hard mode), it's a lot of pixel hunting and searching and some casual puzzling.

Sadly, not as good as Dark Overlord. They share some common features (which is why I recommend it), but Four Horsemen has far more unintuitive gameplay. You'll probably end up using the in-game Strategy Guide way more than expected.
I was really hoping Four Horsemen would live up to its predecessor, Dark Overlord. They're in the same universe with the same protagonist and by the same developers, so what could go wrong, right? Apparently enough to make it a disappointing followup.
The backgrounds and drawn versions of the characters are just as nice as the previous title. A few scenes have some strange or confusing angles to them, but I'll chalk that up to "artistic freedom". The character design is definitely better.
3D cutscenes are also just as clunky where movement is concerned, but I'd still say it's an improvement overall.
The positives fell apart for me here. While Dark Overlord was more-or-less simple to figure out where you needed to go next, Four Horsemen dropped the ball. I often found myself wandering back and forth between locations trying to figure out my next course of action. If you're playing on Easy or Normal and not bothering with achievements, you may not have an issue, since the map and hints directly indicate what you should do next. But playing on Hard mode with the achievement requirement of no Hint use whatsoever (even outside of games/puzzles), it was frustrating enough that I resorted to the in-game Strategy Guide a lot. I try to avoid doing that whenever possible, but some actions were simply too obtuse or unintuitive, like needing to click on a thin, easily-overlooked chain hanging from the ceiling not once, but twice in order to continue. Unless you're pixel-hunting, that chain just looks like a generic fore/background element. And that's only one example. I could write up a whole list.
I did like that they kept the multi-use tool aspect, and the knife and hammer remain at your disposal until the end of the game.
There's one point where an annoying app-style "rate us" window pops up, clearly identifying the game as a (lazy) mobile port. I don't know why nobody bothered to just take that screen out, or change the word "touch" in the achievements to "click".
The bonus chapter was okay (minus the "wtf do I do now" moments), but somehow felt lacking compared to the first game's bonus chapter.
The puzzles were good and varied, with the difficulty bumped up a tad from the previous game.
If you're going for the "Lord of Animals" and "Artist" achievements, you're going to need the Steam guide (not the in-game one) and some quick visual thinking, respectively. However if you missed either achievement during gameplay, you can exit and try again via the Extras menu instead of starting a whole new game. I really appreciated that.
The HOGs on the other hand, were kind of disappointing. It seemed like most of them were the "find then use" silhouette type, but with actions or hiding places that were more of a chore than necessary.
Four Horsemen also continues the "beyond objects" trend, but it seems like the devs got a bit overzealous about it. They doubled (or even tripled) the hunt with a set of parts you need to find for some kind of machine, which means there's 1 morphing object and 1 machine part at every location, plus 20 lorebook pages scattered about. The number of parts and pages you find are accessible via the toolbar and journal, but afaik there's no way to check how many of the morphing objects you found, other than catching the number that pops up when you actually find one. Your best bet is to not leave a location until you find both the object and part. The pages stick out against the backgrounds, so they weren't a problem.
Pretty solid, though kinda forced at points. You don't have to play Dark Overlord to follow or enjoy this one, but it helps. Suzanne's defeat of the Dark Overlord made her a legendary figure in the Lost Lands (which apparently operates on something akin to "Narnia Standard Time" - a few months for us = centuries for them).
a wizard named Maaron knew of Suzanne and summoned her (what is she, a genie?) to help with their Four Horsemen crisis. Of course nobody thinks to call ahead to find out when's a good time, so Suzanne effectively gets kidnapped in the middle of a shopping trip. The tie-in to the existing Lost Lands universe and previous game did a lot to help the plot, seeing as there's no explanation of why everyone thinks Suzanne is some kind of messiah until you find the last lorebook page, which makes a direct reference to the ending of the first game.
And not that it matters for gameplay, but some of the basic facts are a bit inconsistent, at least where Maaron is concerned. In the bonus chapter he talks about summoning Suzanne because he knew of her prior deeds, but in the beginning of the main game he seems utterly surprised that she's a "fragile female" (really?) and not some buff and mighty hero.
You're introduced to some of the lore of
the Lost Lands through the pages you find while you're exploring, which is a nice touch if you like reading, but they're really not much more than another collectible (achievement included).
Unfortunately the grammar and spelling suffer in this game. I don't know who slacked off at Five-BN, but it led to a lot of oddly-constructed sentences. To be fair, most of them were in the written parts (only two or three in VOs). Nothing immersion-breaking, but enough to notice.
Voiceovers were as high quality as Dark Overlord, with the exception of the mermaid, who was only a few notches less annoying than the protagonist of
. Thankfully you don't have to talk to her much. Maaron and Folnur (
the dwarf) were excellent. There was only one inconsistency I noticed in the bonus chapter, when you speak to Tectonica. At some point the text says "but you may cut it with a diamond thread", while the actress says "but you may smash it with a hammer". Those would yield wildly different results. :P
The music was hit and miss. Most times it suited the context well, but there were several moments that felt out of place. SFX were fine.
If I was to rate Four Horsemen as a standalone game, I'd probably give it something slightly higher than "meh, it's decent". But as a sequel in an existing universe with the same protagonist, it has a little more charm. Unlike Dark Overlord however, I don't see myself going out of my way to replay it in the future.
Play Dark Overlord first for a more cohesive experience.

This game is quite noice. As far as my knowledge of 2d platformers go, this is very well done.
The graphic style, which is something I value highly, is very "unique". There might be others like this but I have never seen them. It seems very chalky or sketched or coloured, and the cutscenes show this off very nicely.
The music is also something I really enjoy in a game. Although the music fits very well with the game, I am not a very big fan of it, It seems a bit bland. But as I said, gets you in the mood.
As for the actual platforming it feels very slick, but it is unfortunate that there is no controller support as this would make jumping and moving much easier. You use wasd with lmb for attack and rmb or shift for character special moves.
The boss battles in this game are executed very nicely. They have a small range of attacks but each are extremely different to one another and are very difficult to avoid the first time you fight them. The health is a decent amount, not too much but enough to seem a challenge.
The different weapons in the game are a nice touch and each are good for different things in different stages. Some feel very nice to play with but some seem a bit hard to master
as they are a bit slow.
The storyline is very simple but it doesn't really matter as the game is more focused on completing the stages quickly. The characters you unlock throughout are really nice and include a bit more "oomph" to the game and each include a nice challenge.
Overall, I would give this a 4/5, great for what it is worth, a few dollars (or pounds for me) and is extremely entertaining. However, it is not for everyone. :)

It's a few hours of solid action platforming delivered in bite-sized tactical chunks that play out perfectly for what they're meant to be. At its price point, Eldritch Hunter one of the more engaging and slickly put together games I've played in a while.

Sometimes i write a review to praise a game i liked very much.
Sometimes i write a review to bash a game i hated very much.

Then im wondering whats the point of writing a review on Steam anymore? Everybody can buy the game, try it and refund if they dont like, so whats the point of a player review? None whatsoever...but i like doing things for no reason, especially when i wake up at 3am and cant sleep anymore :P
Eldritch Hunter is a hectic puzzle action/platformer based on pattern learning with a very unforgiving difficulty curve.
Bought the game because i liked the art style and because i like platformers, but this is not a platformer at all.
Basically all levels i played were 1-2 screens large (so nowhere to roam and nothing to explore)  and required some platforming skills, coordination, reflexes and....drums rolling....thinking....because at the heart of this game is solving difficult situations, therefore solving puzzles of different kinds, timing puzzles, control puzzles, platforming puzzles, shooting puzzles, positional puzzles...you name it.
For people looking for an action-platformer with original graphics (like this game seems to be)....look elsewhere, this is not what you get here.
This game is for people looking for a challenge, solving reflex-based puzzles in a quest for the best time.
There is very good quality stuff on offer here, its one of the best puzzle/pattern-learning/difficulty-based games ive seen.
Personally i hate this kind of games, but despite this fact, i cant help but recommend this game because there is no denying it does exceptionally well what it sets out to do, and thats a quality very few games have.

A clever little action-puzzle platformer about a little girl shooting at tenacles and slimy things with dungeon punk style guns. I've been really looking forward to this one, and I was thankfully not let down.
Add this one to my cute but devious category, This game has a cute, cupcakey hand-painted character look, but has some very tricky gameplay segments that test your tactical planning as much as your reflexes.
In this game, you go room by room, level by level, clearing out enemies and making your way to shoot the evil priest, which is the target of every stage. However, this game is not a Contra-esque action shooter, but more of an action puzzle. Many enemies are traps that leave behind obstacles or fire hard to avoid missiles when killed, and if you go in guns blazing you can end up boxing yourself in. The game also makes copious use of pest-spawning flesh creatures that make being accurate and choosing good footing to advance with important to not getting bowled over by an endless steam of worms.
This is one of the areas where the game does alright. The different weapons all have their uses, while still being adaptable enough to allow the player something of a favorite playstile. For example, the basic crossbow has enough damage and fire rate to swiftly mow down a swarm of pests, but it is a bit more deliberate against larger enemies or spawner nests. A shotgun blast can scatter groups of small creatures and punish big ones, but it's not the best for driving off an advancing swarm with its slow rate of fire. The fire bow can lock down a spawner or enemy bottleneck, wreathing anything that comes at you in flames, but it is less effective for attacking or hitting moving targets.
It's all pretty cleverly done, and the game never runs out of tricks. There are only about ten unique enemies or so, but it's paced out that even in the later stages you'll encounter new threats and still see previous enemies being used in sinister new ways, as well as getting new weapons and finding new ways to purge.
I don't entirely agree with the scoring system though; especially for a game as short as this. You are rated on time and time only, so the faster you stake the priest, the more medals and weapons you unlock, which can make getting better times on harder levels easier. I feel like the game shines most when you are playing to completion though, taking on each enemy as it's own obstacle and enjoying the challenge of clearing the board as opposed to rushing.
The game is short, but sweet. It can be cleared in under two hours if you are quick. Still, it's got pretty solid core design and I don't think I was cheated for only four dollars.
Overall: It's a nice little adventure with a cute protagonist and some fairly serious challenges. Recommended for classic hardcore arcade fans. If you find yourself longing for some challenging 2D action or are a fan of the old lovecraftian setting, this one is a nice little nut for you to crack.

Pros:
-Bloody incredible graphics, both background and foreground.  It's actually the only game a have that i've actually wanted to take screenshots of.
-Great music, infact, if the pack i bought didn't come with the seperate soundtrack, i'm getting that too.  Kind of a mix between Pirates of the Carribean and Harry Potter.
-Decent story so far, though i've only gotten through 5-6 levels.  They're long levels......
-Upgradable characters.
-Switch your characters as oftern as you want or pick a favorite and own it.  Each of the t3 characters have a point, purpose and tactic to use.  I've tried building up them all at the same time and they're all pretty good.  But if you just lvl up one character a lot, there will be ups and downs to that too.
-Collectable artwork and peoms in game as well as the Steam acheivements.
Cons:
-Controls are a little laggy and they dont respond well to what i'm wanting but i think that's just cause i'm not quite use to the physics of the game yet.
-Big-as-hell bosses but they're EASY.... I was like... "What?... That's all i had to do???".  This is offset the the difficulty of the level itself, which can be quite challenging, leading to the next con....
-Each lvl is made up of several problems in seperate areas (sometimes no fighting at all, or a little, or then it's time to get out the warhammer and and brace yourself), but some of these prblems are pretty tough... i got stuck on one for at least 15 minutes.  And certain problems require you to have certain character upgrades.  This is offset by the fact that the narrator gives you hints as to how to solve the problem.
All this said:
Worth the buy while on sale.  Bought Trine 1 & 2 for $4.99 for the pair while on sale.  Money well spent, and i'm hoping for a 3rd.
Update:
Just checked to see if the 4.99 comes with the soundtrack and artwork.  It does.  Artbook looks great, litening to the music now and loving it.  Worth getting for .99 even if you dont get the game IMO.

You acctually mimic the movement of the characters by the means of your controller and sometimes you must figure out what to do with you controller to solve an in-game puzzle. Weird how people are not recommending the game mostly based on the lackluster story and abrupt ending. I mean, yeah, more bossfights would have been nice, but considering how they were crap in HR and it still didn't affect the overall enjoyability of that game, why would not having bossfights be a deal breaker here?
However, the gameplay is really good (it's essentially the same as in HR, but more polished), the world/level design is AMAZING (there are many different ways of getting from one point to another, it's a great treat for people who are into exploration), the side missions are pretty damn good (they happen to be better written than the main storyline) and the world itself is really immersive despite dumping the♥♥♥♥♥♥filter and therefore losing a bit of artistic identity.
Gameplay is king, guys. You still get 20-25 hours of FPS/RPG/stealth goodness here. So far it's my second favorite game of the year, just below Dark Souls III.

Unfun and broken experience overall.
I've played this game for a long time, so I feel that this review is most accurate. I've found myself at a brick wall. Over 200 hours in this game, and I'm stil stuck on the gold rank because this game's matchmaking (and fighting in general) is terrible.  Ranked matchmaking is terrible unbalanced. I don't understand how me being a gold rank should pit me against diamonds and platinums, the highest levels in the game. It makes zero sense whatsoever. Worst part is most plats/diamonds have some annoying gimmick to their playstyle because this game reinforces gimmicks, dodge abuse, and spam.
The fighting is fun at first, until you get to the higher level, where no actual fighting is happening. Just pointless spamming and dodge "tactics". All you have to do to win is to just spam dodge with a high speed and/or high dex legend.   There's no actual strategy involved, and the meta itself is broken. There is no reason to play a high strength or high defense legend because
1. The majority of legends are high speed high dex
2. They can spam their sigs and dominate slower characters
Also majority of weapons are broken, especially the lance and the spear. With these weapons (and just about any other weapon) no skill is required since the weapons have high speed and range making them impossible to dodge and making the victim subject to spam more than they already are.
Also every single match is plagued with lag Lag LAG. Up until 2 months ago the servers were at least serviceable. Now not so much. Half of the time what you see isn't what's really going on. It's really annoying when my screen shows me hitting a combo but the server says ♥♥♥♥ you and you find yourself falling off the map.
Another detriment is the game doesn't have any type of followable logic whatsoever, there is zero consistency with the legends, the weapons or the attacks. I don't know how to put it into words, but its one of the things you see after you lay over 200 hours of the game. I've always ending up yelling "THAT'S ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T" at the screen out of sheer frustration.
Also the devs have lost all interest in balancing legends. Back when Kor was introduced, the devs took time to listen to complaints and balance out the legend, now they pump countless new legends out their asses for the sake of selling a few more skins
Last but not least is the cesspool of a community this game has, nothing but♥♥♥♥♥♥talkers and players with no respect for the game or other players. People who go their farthest to either♥♥♥♥♥♥you off or make you feel inadequate. Of all the terrible qualities this game has, this is by far the worst.
I've come to this conclusion after a very long time playing this game, I usually never write reviews this long but I felt the need to get these gripes off my chest. There are other free games you can put more time into without regretting every inch of it. Just forget about this one
